ddx.pt: Symptoms within minutes of intense exercise, second wind, high baseline CK
Similar triggers but distinct acylcarnitine pattern (C14:1 elevation)
Triggered by volatile anaesthetics/suxamethonium with rigidity and hyperthermia; RYR1

nN: carnitine palmitoyl transferase ii cpt ii deficiency
aN: cpt ii | carnitine palmitoyl transferase ii deficiency | cpt2 deficiency | cpt ii deficiency | muscle cpt deficiency | myopathic cpt2

name: Carnitine transporter deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive SLC22A5 defect causing primary systemic carnitine deficiency with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, and myopathy, due to impaired fatty acid transport.
simple: An inherited inability to move carnitine into cells, which weakens muscles and the heart and can cause low blood sugar.
more: Plasma carnitine is very low; confirm with gene testing. Lifelong oral L-carnitine is very effective at preventing complications.

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)
formal: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist causing thumb-to-ring finger paraesthesia, nocturnal symptoms, thenar weakness; confirmed by slowed distal median conduction.
simple: Pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes numbness, tingling and weakness in the thumb and first fingers.
more: Electrodiagnostic study shows prolonged median sensory and motor latencies with preserved ulnar responses across the wrist; ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve. Treat with wrist splinting, steroid injection or surgical carpal tunnel release.
th: เส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่ข้อมือ — ชานิ้วโป้งถึงนิ้วนางครึ่งนิ้ว ปวดชาตอนกลางคืน สะบัดมือแล้วดีขึ้น
feat: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the thumb to radial ring finger; relief by shaking the hand
Sensation over the thenar eminence spared (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel)
Late thenar (APB) wasting
Associations: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis
inv: NCS: prolonged median distal latency, slowed sensory conduction across the wrist
Ultrasound: enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area

case.story: Wakes at night with numb right fingers and shakes her hand to relieve it.
case.exam: Reduced sensation on the thumb, index and middle fingers, normal palm sensation, Phalen positive, mild APB weakness.
case.tests: Median sensory latency prolonged; ulnar normal.
case.q: Why is palm sensation spared?
case.a: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

ddx.pt: Neck pain, reflex change (biceps/triceps), sensory loss extends to forearm
Little and ulnar ring finger, intrinsic hand wasting, Froment sign
Medial forearm sensory loss and thenar wasting (true neurogenic TOS)

aN: cts | carpal tunnel syndrome | median neuropathy at the wrist | carpal tunnel

det.patho: Compression of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament raises local pressure, impairs epineurial blood flow and leads to focal demyelination, then axonal loss if prolonged. Contributing factors include female sex, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, wrist fractures, dialysis and transthyretin amyloidosis (bilateral CTS often predates amyloid cardiomyopathy). It is the most common entrapment neuropathy.
det.clinical: Numbness, tingling and pain affect the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, typically waking the patient at night and relieved by shaking the hand (flick sign). Symptoms may be felt more diffusely or radiate to the forearm. Repetitive grip or wrist flexion aggravates them. Advanced cases show thenar wasting and weakness of thumb abduction. The palm over the thenar eminence is spared because its cutaneous branch bypasses the tunnel.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by provocative tests (Phalen, Tinel, carpal compression) that have moderate accuracy. Nerve conduction studies confirm focal slowing of median sensory and motor fibres across the wrist and grade severity; comparison techniques (median vs ulnar or radial) increase sensitivity. Ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area at the tunnel inlet. Consider C6–C7 radiculopathy, proximal median neuropathy, polyneuropathy and thoracic outlet syndrome, which can coexist (double crush).
det.treatment: Mild to moderate cases respond to neutral-position night splinting, activity modification and treatment of underlying conditions; local corticosteroid injection gives short- to medium-term relief. Surgical carpal tunnel release (open or endoscopic) is indicated for persistent symptoms, constant numbness, thenar weakness or wasting, or severe electrodiagnostic changes. Pregnancy-related CTS usually settles after delivery.
det.prognosis: Most improve with conservative care or surgery; advanced axonal loss may leave persistent numbness or weakness.
pearls: Spared palm sensation separates CTS from a more proximal median lesion.
Bilateral CTS in an older man: consider transthyretin amyloidosis.
Neck pain, reflex changes or forearm sensory loss suggest radiculopathy instead.
det.thd: CTS คือเส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่อุโมงค์ข้อมือ พบบ่อยที่สุดในบรรดาโรคเส้นประสาทถูกกดทับ ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือเพศหญิง อ้วน ตั้งครรภ์ เบาหวาน ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ amyloidosis อาการคือชาและปวดนิ้วโป้งถึงครึ่งนิ้วนาง ตื่นกลางดึกแล้วสะบัดมือจึงดีขึ้น ระยะท้ายมีกล้ามเนื้อโคนนิ้วโป้งลีบ ฝ่ามือส่วน thenar ไม่ชาเพราะแขนงประสาทแยกก่อนเข้าอุโมงค์ วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ NCS หรืออัลตราซาวด์ รักษาด้วยเฝือกอ่อนตอนกลางคืน ฉีดสเตียรอยด์ และผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือกล้ามเนื้อลีบ

name: Castleman disease
formal: Lymphoproliferative disorder with angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia, linked to POEMS syndrome with sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy, high VEGF, and plasma cell dyscrasia.
simple: A rare disease causing enlarged lymph nodes, which can be linked with nerve damage in some patients.
more: Lymph node biopsy diagnoses it. Treatment includes surgery for localised disease and rituximab, siltuximab, or chemotherapy for multicentric disease.

name: Cat scratch disease
formal: Bartonella henselae infection after cat scratch or bite, with regional lymphadenopathy; neurological complications include encephalopathy, neuroretinitis and myelitis.
simple: An infection from a cat scratch causing swollen glands, and rarely brain or eye problems.

name: Cataplexy
formal: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion with preserved consciousness, characteristic of narcolepsy type 1 due to hypocretin deficiency.
simple: Sudden muscle weakness or collapse triggered by strong emotions such as laughter, while staying awake.

name: Catatonia
formal: Psychomotor syndrome with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism, waxy flexibility or excitement; occurs in psychiatric and medical disorders and responds to benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A state in which a person becomes unusually still and unresponsive, or sometimes agitated, and may hold odd postures.

name: Catheter-related infections
formal: Device-associated bloodstream or local infections, including intrathecal or ventricular catheter infection causing meningitis or ventriculitis.
simple: Infections that start from a tube placed in the body, which can sometimes spread to the brain coverings.

name: Cauda equina syndrome
formal: Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter dysfunction and lower limb weakness with areflexia; a surgical emergency.
simple: Pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spine causing numbness in the groin and loss of bladder or bowel control.

name: Causalgia and dystonia
formal: Complex regional pain syndrome type 2 after nerve injury with burning pain, autonomic change, and sometimes fixed dystonic posture of the limb.
simple: Severe burning pain after nerve injury, sometimes with painful twisted muscle postures.

name: Cavernous malformation
formal: Cluster of dilated thin-walled vascular channels without intervening brain, causing seizures, haemorrhage or focal deficits; may be familial (CCM1-3).
simple: A cluster of abnormal blood vessels in the brain that can cause seizures or bleeding.

name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
formal: Lesion of the cavernous sinus involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, with ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory loss; causes include tumour, thrombosis, aneurysm and Tolosa-Hunt.
simple: Damage near the base of the brain that affects eye movement and facial feeling nerves.

name: CD8+ encephalitis
formal: Rare T-cell mediated encephalitis in HIV with CD8 lymphocytic infiltration and viral escape, causing subacute cognitive decline and seizures.
simple: A brain inflammation in people with HIV caused by overactive immune cells.

name: Celiac disease
formal: Gluten-triggered autoimmune enteropathy with neurological associations including gluten ataxia, axonal neuropathy, myopathy, and epilepsy with occipital calcifications.
simple: An immune reaction to gluten in food that damages the gut and can also affect the nerves and balance.
more: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies and duodenal biopsy diagnose it. A strict gluten-free diet may stabilise neurological features.

name: Central cord syndrome
formal: Cervical cord injury with disproportionate weakness of the arms compared with legs, variable sensory loss and bladder dysfunction; typical after hyperextension in spondylosis.
simple: A neck spinal cord injury that weakens the arms more than the legs.

name: Central core disease (CCD)
formal: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with central cores lacking oxidative enzyme activity, hypotonia and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weak, floppy muscles from birth and risk of a dangerous reaction to some anaesthetics.

name: Central core myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with hypotonia, proximal weakness, and well-defined cores lacking oxidative activity on biopsy, and association with malignant hyperthermia.
simple: An inherited muscle disease from early life with mild weakness and a risk of dangerous reactions to some anaesthetics.
more: Confirm with RYR1 sequencing and biopsy; avoid volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Treatment is supportive; usually non-progressive.

name: Central neurocytomas
formal: Rare intraventricular neuroglial tumours near the foramen of Monro in young adults, causing hydrocephalus; low-grade with good prognosis after resection.
simple: A slow-growing brain tumour in the fluid spaces of the brain that can block fluid flow.

name: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP)
formal: Neuropathic pain from thalamic or other central somatosensory lesions after stroke, often burning or allodynic and delayed by weeks to months.
simple: Long-lasting burning or painful sensations that develop after a stroke damages pain pathways in the brain.

name: Centronuclear myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with centrally placed nuclei in fibres; X-linked myotubular (MTM1) and autosomal forms (DNM2, BIN1) cause hypotonia and weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weakness and low muscle tone starting early in life.
more: Muscle biopsy shows central nuclei with radial sarcoplasmic strands; CK is usually normal, and genetics identifies MTM1 in males with severe neonatal disease. Prognosis ranges from early ventilator dependence to milder adult forms, and care is supportive.

name: Cerebellar ataxia
formal: Syndrome of incoordination with gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria from cerebellar dysfunction; causes include genetic, toxic, immune, paraneoplastic and degenerative.
simple: Poor balance and clumsy movement due to cerebellum problems.

name: Cerebellar atrophy and variants
formal: Progressive cerebellar degeneration with ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus; may be hereditary, alcoholic, paraneoplastic or idiopathic.
simple: Shrinking of the balance centre of the brain, causing unsteady walking and slurred speech.

name: Cerebellar disease
formal: General term for processes affecting the cerebellum causing ataxia, nystagmus, hypotonia, and intention tremor; ipsilateral signs for hemisphere lesions.
simple: Any illness of the cerebellum, which causes unsteadiness and clumsy movements.

name: Cerebellar disorders
formal: Group of conditions affecting cerebellar function, including degenerative, vascular, toxic, immune and genetic causes, with ataxia as the core sign.
simple: Conditions that affect the cerebellum and cause balance and coordination problems.

name: Cerebellar haemorrhage
formal: Spontaneous bleeding in the cerebellum from hypertension or vascular lesions, causing headache, vomiting, ataxia and risk of brainstem compression and hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding in the cerebellum causing sudden headache, vomiting and imbalance, which can be an emergency.

name: Cerebellar tremor
formal: Slow 3-5 Hz intention tremor from lesions of the dentato-rubro-thalamic pathway, worsening on approach to target; seen in MS, stroke and degenerative ataxias.
simple: A shaking that gets worse as you reach for something, caused by cerebellum pathway damage.

name: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome
formal: Lesions of the cerebellopontine angle affecting cranial nerves VII, VIII (and V) with hearing loss, tinnitus, facial weakness and ipsilateral ataxia; vestibular schwannoma is typical.
simple: Pressure near the hearing and balance nerve causing hearing loss, ringing in the ear and imbalance.

name: Cerebellopontine angle tumours
formal: Mass lesions in the cerebellopontine angle, most commonly vestibular schwannoma, then meningioma and epidermoid cyst.
simple: Growths near the ear nerve and brainstem, often causing one-sided hearing loss.

name: Cerebral abscess
formal: Focal pyogenic infection of brain parenchyma from contiguous spread or bacteraemia, producing headache, fever, focal deficits; ring-enhancing lesion on MRI.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain from infection, causing headache, fever and weakness.

name: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA)
formal: Deposition of amyloid-beta in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels causing lobar haemorrhages, microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis and cognitive decline in older people.
simple: Protein build-up in brain blood vessels in older adults that makes them fragile and can cause bleeding and memory loss.
th: โปรตีนอะไมลอยด์สะสมในผนังหลอดเลือดสมองผู้สูงอายุ ทำให้เลือดออกบริเวณผิวสมองซ้ำ ๆ
tempoNote: Acute lobar bleeds on a background of chronic small vessel disease; transient focal episodes
feat: Lobar haemorrhage in people over 55
Recurrent brief spreading sensory episodes ('amyloid spells')
Cognitive decline; may coexist with Alzheimer pathology
Inflammatory variant presents subacutely with headache, confusion and seizures
inv: MRI SWI: strictly lobar microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis
Apply the Boston criteria (version 2.0) for probable/possible CAA

case.story: Three episodes this month of tingling spreading from the left hand to the face over 2 minutes; now sudden left hemianopia.
case.exam: Left homonymous hemianopia, mild memory impairment.
case.tests: CT: right occipital lobar haematoma; SWI: multiple cortical microbleeds and convexity siderosis.
case.q: Why should the spreading tingling not be labelled TIA and treated with antiplatelets?
case.a: These are CAA-related transient focal episodes from cortical siderosis; antithrombotics raise the risk of further lobar haemorrhage.

TIA symptoms are negative and do not march
Amnestic decline without lobar haemorrhages; may coexist

aN: caa | cerebral amyloid angiopathy | amyloid angiopathy | congophilic angiopathy

det.patho: Beta-amyloid deposits in the walls of small cortical and leptomeningeal arteries make them brittle, causing lobar haemorrhages, cortical microbleeds, convexity SAH and cortical superficial siderosis. Prevalence rises steeply with age and APOE e4/e2 genotypes modify risk. Hereditary forms (e.g. Dutch type) start earlier, and iatrogenic CAA has been described decades after neurosurgery using cadaveric dura. An inflammatory variant (CAA-ri) reflects an immune reaction to vascular amyloid.
det.clinical: Presentations include spontaneous lobar haemorrhage in older adults, transient focal neurological episodes (spreading paraesthesia or weakness lasting minutes, from convexity siderosis), cognitive decline, and incidental microbleeds on MRI. CAA-related inflammation causes subacute headache, confusion, seizures and focal signs with asymmetric white matter oedema. Recurrent bleeds are common and cumulative disability follows.
det.diagnosis: The Boston criteria v2.0 use MRI haemorrhagic markers (strictly lobar microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis, convexity SAH) plus non-haemorrhagic white matter markers (centrum semiovale perivascular spaces, multispot subcortical white matter pattern) in people 50 or older. Pathology remains definitive. Exclude other causes of lobar bleeds: vascular malformation, tumour, venous thrombosis, coagulopathy. CAA-ri may be supported by CSF anti-amyloid antibodies or biopsy.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy; management focuses on preventing bleeding: strict BP control, avoiding anticoagulants and antiplatelets where possible, and considering left atrial appendage occlusion in patients with AF. Statins are not contraindicated when indicated. Transient focal episodes should not be treated as TIA with antithrombotics. CAA-ri responds to corticosteroids, sometimes with other immunosuppressants. People with CAA face higher ARIA risk on anti-amyloid antibody drugs.
det.prognosis: Recurrent lobar haemorrhage occurs in several percent per year, highest with siderosis; cognitive impairment is frequent.
pearls: Lobar bleed + microbleeds + siderosis in the elderly = probable CAA.
Amyloid spells mimic TIA or migraine aura; antithrombotics may cause harm.
Check SWI before starting anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer disease.
det.thd: CAA คือการสะสมของโปรตีน beta-amyloid ในผนังหลอดเลือดเล็กของผิวสมองและเยื่อหุ้มสมองในผู้สูงอายุ ทำให้หลอดเลือดเปราะ เกิดเลือดออกแบบ lobar ซ้ำ ๆ microbleeds และ cortical superficial siderosis อาการอื่นคือชาลามเป็นพัก ๆ (amyloid spells) และความจำเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI SWI ตาม Boston criteria v2.0 ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นคุมความดันและหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด/ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดถ้าทำได้ ส่วนชนิดอักเสบ (CAA-ri) ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์

name: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
formal: Hereditary NOTCH3 small-vessel disease with migraine with aura, recurrent subcortical strokes, mood disorder and dementia; MRI shows anterior temporal and external capsule hyperintensities.
simple: An inherited disease of small brain blood vessels causing migraine, strokes and dementia in mid-adult life.
ab: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
nN: cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukencephalopathy cadasil
aN: cadasil | cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukencephalopathy

name: Cerebral folate deficiency
formal: Neurological syndrome with low CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate despite normal blood folate, causing irritability, ataxia, seizures and developmental delay; due to FOLR1 mutations or folate receptor antibodies.
simple: Low folate in the brain fluid despite normal blood levels, causing developmental problems and seizures.

name: Cerebral haemorrhage and infarction
formal: Collective term for ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, the two main types of acute cerebrovascular events.
simple: Strokes caused by either a blocked or a bleeding blood vessel in the brain.

name: Cerebral infarction or haemorrhage
formal: Collective term for acute stroke of ischaemic or haemorrhagic type, distinguished by neuroimaging.
simple: A stroke caused either by a blocked or by a burst blood vessel in the brain.

name: Cerebral infarction/haemorrhage
formal: Collective term for ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, distinguished by CT or MRI.
simple: A stroke from either a blocked or a bleeding brain blood vessel.

name: Cerebral palsy
formal: Non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from early brain injury, with spastic, dyskinetic or ataxic forms; often with epilepsy and cognitive impairment.
simple: A lasting movement and posture condition caused by brain injury before or soon after birth.

name: Cerebral small-vessel disease (cSVD)
formal: Disease of perforating arterioles, capillaries and venules causing lacunes, white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds and dilated perivascular spaces; leads to stroke, gait problems and dementia.
simple: Damage to the tiny blood vessels of the brain, causing small strokes, slowed thinking and walking problems.

name: Cerebral trauma and dystonia
formal: Post-traumatic dystonia after brain injury, often delayed by months to years, typically hemidystonia contralateral to basal ganglia or thalamic damage.
simple: Painful twisting muscle postures that develop after a head injury.

name: Cerebral tumours
formal: Primary or metastatic neoplasms of the brain causing headache, seizures, focal deficits and raised intracranial pressure; gliomas and metastases are most frequent.
simple: Growths in the brain that can cause headaches, seizures or weakness.

name: Cerebral vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of CNS vessels, primary or secondary to systemic disease or infection, causing stroke-like events, headache and encephalopathy.
simple: Inflammation of brain blood vessels, which can cause strokes and confusion.

name: Cerebral vasospasm
formal: Reversible narrowing of intracranial arteries, classically 4-14 days after subarachnoid haemorrhage, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia.
simple: Narrowing of brain arteries, often after bleeding around the brain, which can cause a stroke.

name: Cerebrovascular disease
formal: Umbrella term for diseases of cerebral blood supply, including ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, aneurysm and vascular malformations.
simple: Diseases of the blood vessels that supply the brain, including stroke.

name: Cervical degenerative disease
formal: Spondylotic degeneration of cervical discs and facets that causes neck pain, radiculopathy or myelopathy with spasticity and gait disturbance.
simple: Wear and tear of the neck spine that can pinch nerves or the spinal cord.

name: Cervical disk disease
formal: Herniation or degeneration of cervical discs compressing roots or cord, producing arm pain, sensory loss, weakness and sometimes myelopathy.
simple: A slipped or worn disc in the neck pressing on nerves, causing arm pain and weakness.

name: Cervical meningioma
formal: Benign dural tumour in the cervical canal, more often in women, causing slowly progressive cord compression with weakness, sensory loss and gait trouble.
simple: A slow-growing non-cancerous tumour pressing on the neck spinal cord.

name: Cervical myelopathy
formal: Compressive or ischaemic injury to the cervical cord, often from spondylosis, with spastic gait, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign and bladder disturbance.
simple: Pressure on the spinal cord in the neck causing clumsy hands, stiff legs and walking problems.

name: Cervical myelopathy with quadriplegia
formal: Severe cervical cord compression or injury with tetraparesis or tetraplegia, spasticity, sensory level and sphincter loss.
simple: Serious neck spinal cord damage causing weakness or paralysis of all four limbs.

name: Cervical radiculopathies
formal: Disorders of cervical nerve roots, usually from disc herniation or spondylosis, giving neck and arm pain with dermatomal sensory loss and myotomal weakness, most often C6 and C7.
simple: Pinched nerves in the neck causing pain, numbness, and weakness in the arm and hand.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Most cases improve in weeks to months with conservative care; surgery for progressive or severe deficits.

name: Cervical spine disease
formal: Degenerative, inflammatory, neoplastic or traumatic conditions of the neck spine that compress roots or cord and cause pain and neurological deficit.
simple: Problems of the neck spine that can pinch nerves or the spinal cord.

name: Chagas disease
formal: Trypanosoma cruzi infection with cardiomyopathy and megaviscera; neurological features include cardioembolic stroke, meningoencephalitis in immunosuppression and autonomic neuropathy.
simple: A parasite infection from insect bites that can damage the heart and gut and sometimes the brain.

name: Channelopathies
formal: Disorders of ion channel genes causing episodic phenotypes such as periodic paralysis, myotonia, epilepsy, ataxia, migraine and pain.
simple: Diseases caused by faulty electrical channels in cells, producing attacks of weakness, seizures or pain.

name: Charcoat-Marie-Tooth disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, the commonest inherited neuropathy, with length-dependent distal weakness, pes cavus, and sensory loss, caused by mutations in genes such as PMP22 and MFN2.
simple: An inherited nerve disease that slowly weakens the feet and hands and causes high arched feet.
more: Nerve conduction studies and genetic testing define the type. Treatment is supportive with orthoses, physiotherapy, and surgery; avoid neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine.

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth (CMT) disease
formal: Most common inherited neuropathy with distal weakness, pes cavus, foot drop and sensory loss; demyelinating or axonal forms from PMP22, MPZ, GJB1, MFN2 and others.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing weakness and wasting in the feet and lower legs and high arches.
more: Diagnosed by nerve conduction (demyelinating below 38 m/s in median motor) and PMP22 duplication testing in CMT1A, the commonest form. No disease-modifying therapy exists; use ankle-foot orthoses and avoid neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม — เท้าโก่ง นิ้วเท้างอ ขาเรียวแบบขวดแชมเปญ เท้าตก
feat: Slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting from childhood/adolescence
Pes cavus, hammer toes, 'inverted champagne bottle' legs
Foot drop with steppage gait; few sensory symptoms despite signs
inv: NCS: uniform slowing (CMT1, < 38 m/s) or axonal (CMT2)
Genetic testing: PMP22 duplication first

case.story: Trips over kerbs and sprains ankles; his father has 'high-arched feet'.
case.exam: Pes cavus, bilateral foot drop, absent ankle jerks, thin calves, reduced distal vibration.
case.tests: Median motor conduction velocity 22 m/s, uniform without conduction block; PMP22 duplication.
case.q: Why does uniform slowing suggest an inherited rather than an acquired demyelinating neuropathy?
case.a: Inherited myelin defects affect all segments equally; acquired (e.g. CIDP) cause patchy slowing and conduction block.

ddx.pt: Acquired, proximal weakness, non-uniform slowing, high CSF protein
Ataxia, dysarthria, extensor plantars, cardiomyopathy
Recurrent painless pressure palsies; PMP22 deletion

aN: cmt | charcot marie tooth disease | hmsn | hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy | peroneal muscular atrophy

det.patho: A genetically diverse group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies with over 100 causative genes. CMT1A, from duplication of PMP22 on chromosome 17p, is by far the most common; other frequent causes are GJB1 (X-linked CMTX1), MPZ and MFN2 (the commonest axonal CMT2A). Demyelinating forms (CMT1) have uniformly slow conduction, axonal forms (CMT2) have preserved velocities with low amplitudes, and intermediate forms sit between. Length-dependent axonal loss underlies the clinical deficit in all types.
det.clinical: Symptoms usually begin in the first two decades with tripping, ankle sprains and difficulty running. Examination shows distal wasting and weakness of the legs (inverted champagne bottle appearance), foot drop with steppage gait, pes cavus and hammer toes, depressed reflexes and distal sensory loss, with hands affected later. Sensory symptoms are typically mild relative to signs. Severity varies widely, even within families. Additional features in some subtypes include hearing loss, optic atrophy, vocal cord paresis and scoliosis.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies classify the type: in CMT1 the upper-limb motor conduction velocity is below 38 m/s and slowing is uniform without conduction block. Family history and pedigree guide inheritance pattern. Test for PMP22 duplication first in demyelinating cases; then use multigene panels or exome sequencing. Distinguish from CIDP (patchy slowing, conduction block, proximal weakness, raised CSF protein), HNPP and acquired axonal neuropathies.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is available, although trials are ongoing. Management involves physiotherapy and stretching to prevent contractures, ankle-foot orthoses, orthopaedic foot surgery for severe deformity, occupational therapy for hand function and pain control. Avoid neurotoxic drugs, especially vincristine, which can cause severe weakness in CMT. Offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with normal life expectancy; most remain ambulant, though many need orthoses.
pearls: Uniform slowing points to inherited demyelination; patchy slowing with block suggests acquired disease.
Pes cavus in a family with clumsy feet = check PMP22 duplication.
Vincristine is dangerous in CMT.
det.thd: CMT เป็นโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม ชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ CMT1A จาก PMP22 duplication อาการเริ่มในวัยเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น สะดุดง่าย ข้อเท้าพลิก เท้าโก่ง นิ้วเท้างอ ขาเรียวแบบขวดแชมเปญคว่ำ และเท้าตก โดยอาการชามักไม่มากเทียบกับที่ตรวจพบ NCS ช่วยแยกชนิด demyelinating (CMT1 ความเร็ว <38 m/s และช้าสม่ำเสมอ) กับ axonal (CMT2) ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้กายภาพ อุปกรณ์ช่วยข้อเท้า ผ่าตัดเท้า และหลีกเลี่ยง vincristine

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease
formal: Most common inherited neuropathy with distal wasting, pes cavus, foot drop and sensory loss; many genes including PMP22 and MFN2.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing weak, thin lower legs, high foot arches and numb feet.

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1 (CMT1)
formal: Demyelinating hereditary neuropathy, commonly PMP22 duplication, with slowed conduction under 38 m/s, onion bulbs and distal weakness from childhood.
simple: An inherited nerve disease in which nerve insulation is damaged, causing weakness and wasting in feet and hands.
nN: charcot marie tooth disease type 1 cmt1
aN: cmt1 | charcot marie tooth disease type 1

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2 (CMT2)
formal: Axonal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with near-normal conduction velocities, reduced amplitudes; MFN2 is common, with later onset than CMT1.
simple: An inherited nerve disease where the nerve fibres themselves degenerate, causing foot weakness and numbness.
nN: charcot marie tooth disease type 2 cmt2
aN: cmt2 | charcot marie tooth disease type 2

name: Charles Bonnet syndrome
formal: Visual hallucinations in people with significant visual loss and preserved insight; due to deafferentation of visual cortex.
simple: Seeing vivid images that are not there in people with poor eyesight, while knowing they are not real.

name: Cherry-red spot-myoclonus syndrome (sialidosis type I)
formal: Sialidosis type I from NEU1 deficiency with macular cherry-red spot, action myoclonus, ataxia and seizures in adolescence or adulthood.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease causing jerky movements, seizures and a red spot in the eye.
nN: cherry red spot myoclonus syndrome sialidosis type i
aN: sialidosis type i | cherry red spot myoclonus syndrome

name: Chester–Erdheim disease
formal: Rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis with xanthomatous infiltration of bones, retroperitoneum and CNS; causes ataxia, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos; BRAF V600E may be present.
simple: A rare disease where abnormal immune cells build up in bones, brain and other organs.

name: Chiari I malformation
formal: Cerebellar tonsillar descent at least 5 mm below the foramen magnum, with Valsalva headache, syringomyelia, lower cranial nerve signs and downbeat nystagmus.
simple: The lower part of the cerebellum sits too low at the skull base, causing neck headaches and sometimes balance problems.

name: Chiari malformations
formal: Group of hindbrain anomalies with tonsillar or brainstem herniation through the foramen magnum, associated with hydrocephalus, syrinx and myelomeningocele.
simple: Birth differences where part of the back of the brain sits too low, which can block fluid flow and affect the spinal cord.

name: Chiasmal disease
formal: Lesions at the optic chiasm, e.g. pituitary tumours or craniopharyngioma, causing bitemporal hemianopia and reduced acuity.
simple: Damage near where the eye nerves cross, causing loss of side vision in both eyes.

name: Childhood bulbar SMA
formal: Fazio-Londe disease, a juvenile motor neuron disorder related to riboflavin transporter mutations, causing progressive bulbar palsy with facial weakness, dysphagia, and respiratory failure.
simple: A rare childhood condition in which nerves to the face, tongue, and throat degenerate, causing trouble swallowing and speaking.
more: SLC52A3 testing is useful; high-dose riboflavin can stabilise or improve the course, so early treatment matters. Respiratory support may be needed.

name: Children and young adults alternating hemiplegia of childhood
formal: Rare ATP1A3-related disorder with episodes of hemiplegia or dystonia, onset before 18 months, eye movement abnormalities and developmental delay.
simple: A rare childhood condition with repeated attacks of weakness on one side of the body.
nN: children and young adults alternating hemiplegia of childhood

name: Chin tremor
formal: Rhythmic 4-7 Hz tremor of the chin, hereditary autosomal dominant or sporadic, appearing in childhood and worsening with stress.
simple: Shaking of the chin, often running in families, that gets worse with stress.

name: Chloride channelopathies
formal: Disorders of CLCN1 channel function causing myotonia congenita, either dominant Thomsen or recessive Becker form, with muscle stiffness that eases with repeated use.
simple: Inherited conditions where faulty chloride channels leave muscles stiff, easing after repeated movement.
more: EMG shows myotonic discharges; confirmed by CLCN1 testing. Mexiletine is first-line; prognosis is good.

name: Chloroquine neuropathy
formal: Toxic neuromyopathy from chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine causing sensorimotor neuropathy with vacuolar myopathy, with curvilinear bodies on biopsy.
simple: Nerve and muscle problems caused by the malaria and arthritis drug chloroquine.
more: Stopping the drug generally leads to recovery; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles.

name: Cholesteatomas
formal: Epidermoid lesions of keratinising squamous epithelium in middle ear or petrous apex that erode bone and cause hearing loss, facial palsy and vertigo.
simple: A skin-cell growth in the ear or skull base that slowly destroys bone and affects hearing and the face nerve.

name: Choline acetyltransferase deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from CHAT mutations causing presynaptic failure of ACh synthesis, with hypotonia and episodic apnoea precipitated by fever or excitement.
simple: An inherited disorder in which nerve endings cannot make enough chemical messenger, causing weakness and sudden breathing pauses.
more: Decrement on repetitive stimulation, especially after exertion; CHAT sequencing. Pyridostigmine is helpful; families need apnoea monitoring.

name: Chondrosarcomas
formal: Malignant cartilaginous tumours of the skull base or spine causing cranial neuropathies or cord compression; slow-growing but locally invasive.
simple: Cancers of cartilage at the skull base or spine that can press on nerves.

name: Chordoma
formal: Rare locally aggressive tumour from notochordal remnants at clivus or sacrum, causing diplopia, headache and cranial nerve palsies.
simple: A rare slow-growing tumour at the skull base or tailbone that can press on nerves.

name: Chorea
formal: Hyperkinetic movement disorder with irregular, brief, flowing involuntary movements; causes include Huntington disease, drugs, Sydenham and metabolic disorders.
simple: Irregular, jerky dance-like movements that flow from one body part to another.
more: Work up by history for drugs, then check thyroid, glucose, calcium, ESR, antibodies (ASO titre, antiphospholipid), pregnancy test and MRI; genetic HTT testing if familial. Treat with dopamine-depleting agents (tetrabenazine) or antipsychotics for severe cases.

name: Chorea and dystonia
formal: Combination of choreiform movements and dystonic postures seen in Huntington disease, neuroacanthocytosis, drug-induced and paediatric disorders.
simple: A mix of dance-like jerks and twisting postures caused by basal ganglia disorders.

name: Chorea gravidarum
formal: Chorea first occurring or relapsing in pregnancy, often linked to prior rheumatic fever, antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus; usually resolves after delivery.
simple: Dance-like involuntary movements during pregnancy that usually settle after birth.

name: Chorea insaneins
formal: Historical term for severe chorea associated with psychiatric disturbance and mania, now largely obsolete.
simple: An old term for severe jerky movements combined with serious mental disturbance.

name: Chorea major
formal: Historical term for severe, violent chorea such as chorea gravidarum or severe Sydenham chorea.
simple: An old name for very severe, violent dance-like movements.

name: Chorea minor
formal: Sydenham chorea, post-streptococcal autoimmune basal ganglia disease in children with chorea, hypotonia, emotional lability; features of rheumatic fever.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements in children following strep infection, linked to rheumatic fever.

name: Chorea paralytica
formal: Historical term for chorea with such profound hypotonia that it mimics paralysis, in severe Sydenham chorea.
simple: An old term for chorea so severe that the muscles go floppy as if paralysed.

name: Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc)
formal: Autosomal recessive neuroacanthocytosis from VPS13A mutations, with progressive chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, self-biting, seizures, myopathy, neuropathy and cognitive change, plus acanthocytes and raised CK.
simple: A rare inherited disease with uncontrolled movements, biting of the tongue and lips, and mood and memory changes.
more: Blood film may show acanthocytes; MRI shows caudate atrophy and genetics confirm. There is no cure and treatment is symptomatic; deep brain stimulation has helped some.

name: Choreoacanthocytosis
formal: Autosomal recessive VPS13A disease with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, tongue and lip biting, acanthocytes, seizures, myopathy and raised creatine kinase.
simple: An inherited disease causing jerky movements, mouth injuries, seizures and unusually shaped red blood cells.

name: Choreoacantocytosis
formal: Autosomal recessive VPS13A disease with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, lip biting, acanthocytes and myopathy.
simple: An inherited condition causing involuntary movements and unusually shaped red blood cells.

name: Choroid plexus tumours
formal: Neoplasms of choroid plexus epithelium, papilloma to carcinoma, mainly in children, causing hydrocephalus from CSF overproduction or obstruction.
simple: Tumours in the fluid-making tissue of the brain, mostly in young children, that can cause head swelling.

name: Chronic acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
formal: Hepatic encephalopathy complication from portosystemic shunting with parkinsonism, ataxia, cognitive decline and manganese deposition in basal ganglia.
simple: Long-term brain damage in severe liver disease causing slowness, tremor and thinking problems.

name: Chronic ataxic neuropathy and vestibular areflexia
formal: CANVAS: late-onset cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuropathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia, due to biallelic RFC1 expansions.
simple: A slowly progressive condition of poor balance, numb feet and inner ear failure.
nN: chronic ataxic neuropathy and vestibular areflexia

name: Chronic daily headache
formal: Headache occurring 15 or more days per month for over 3 months, including chronic migraine, tension-type and medication overuse headache.
simple: A headache that occurs on most days for months.

name: Chronic epilepsy
formal: Long-standing recurrent seizure disorder with ongoing seizures despite treatment, with cognitive and psychosocial burden; may be refractory.
simple: Epilepsy that has lasted a long time with continuing seizures.

name: Chronic idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy
formal: Slowly progressive, length-dependent sensory axonal polyneuropathy in older adults with no identifiable cause after thorough work-up.
simple: Slowly worsening numbness and tingling in the feet and hands in older people, with no known cause found.
more: Diagnosis requires excluding diabetes, B12 deficiency, toxins, paraproteins, and other causes. Treat symptoms and prevent falls; prognosis is benign.

name: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
formal: Immune-mediated neuropathy with progressive or relapsing proximal and distal weakness and sensory loss for 8 weeks or more; demyelination on nerve conduction; responds to IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange.
simple: A long-term immune attack on nerves causing weakness and numbness that responds to immune treatments.
more: Diagnose with nerve conduction showing demyelination (conduction block, prolonged distal latencies) and raised CSF protein; nerve MRI or ultrasound shows enlargement. Maintenance IVIG or subcutaneous immunoglobulin is common; rituximab in refractory cases.

case.q: Why does weakness of hip flexors argue against diabetic neuropathy?
case.a: Length-dependent axonal neuropathies affect distal muscles first; proximal weakness implies root/demyelinating involvement such as CIDP.

aN: cidp | chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy | chronic gbs

det.patho: An immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of nerves and roots involving both cellular and humoral mechanisms; inflammation at the roots and plexuses explains proximal weakness and the high CSF protein. A subgroup has IgG4 antibodies against nodal or paranodal proteins (neurofascin-155, contactin-1, Caspr1, neurofascin-186), now classified separately as autoimmune nodopathies because they behave differently. Prevalence rises with age and men are affected more often.
det.clinical: Typical CIDP produces symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss and generalised hypo- or areflexia, progressing over more than 8 weeks with a progressive or relapsing course. Variants include distal (DADS), multifocal (Lewis–Sumner), focal, motor and sensory forms. Tremor, sensory ataxia and cranial nerve involvement can occur. Around one in six starts acutely, mimicking GBS. Pain, prominent autonomic failure or weight loss suggests POEMS, amyloidosis or another mimic.
det.diagnosis: The 2021 EAN/PNS guideline relies on clinical criteria plus electrodiagnostic evidence of demyelination (prolonged distal latency, slowed conduction velocity, conduction block, temporal dispersion, prolonged or absent F waves) affecting two or more nerves. Supportive features are raised CSF protein, nerve root or plexus enlargement on MRI or ultrasound, objective response to treatment and nerve biopsy. Screen for paraprotein (IgM with anti-MAG, POEMS with VEGF), diabetes, HIV, hepatitis and hereditary neuropathy. Over-diagnosis based on mild slowing is a frequent pitfall.
det.treatment: First-line options are IVIG (2 g/kg loading, then maintenance about 1 g/kg every 3 weeks titrated to response), corticosteroids (daily prednisolone or pulsed dexamethasone/methylprednisolone) and plasma exchange. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin and efgartigimod are maintenance options. Pure motor CIDP may worsen with steroids, so IVIG is preferred. Refractory cases may need rituximab (especially nodopathies) or other immunosuppressants. Use objective measures (grip strength, INCAT, I-RODS) to guide dose tapering.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to treatment and many reach remission, but a substantial fraction need long-term therapy and some accumulate axonal damage.
pearls: Proximal plus distal weakness with global areflexia = think CIDP, not length-dependent neuropathy.
Poor IVIG response with tremor or sensory ataxia: test nodal/paranodal antibodies.
IgM paraprotein with distal sensory ataxia: check anti-MAG.

name: Chronic inflammatory neuropathies
formal: Immune-mediated neuropathies lasting beyond 8 weeks including CIDP, MMN, anti-MAG and nodopathies, with demyelinating or axonal changes.
simple: Long-lasting nerve problems caused by the immune system attacking nerves.

name: Chronic liver disease
formal: Hepatic disease with neuromuscular consequences including hepatic encephalopathy, myopathy and sarcopenia, axonal polyneuropathy, and movement disorders such as asterixis.
simple: Long-term liver damage that can affect the brain, nerves, and muscles.
more: Management centres on treating liver disease, using lactulose or rifaximin for encephalopathy, and nutrition; transplantation may reverse neurological features.

name: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
formal: B-cell malignancy that may cause neurological complications such as meningeal infiltration, paraneoplastic syndromes, and opportunistic infections.
simple: A slow-growing blood cancer that can affect the nervous system through spread or infection.

name: Chronic meningitis
formal: Meningeal inflammation persisting at least 4 weeks from tuberculosis, fungal, syphilis, sarcoid or malignancy, with headache, cranial neuropathies and hydrocephalus.
simple: Long-lasting inflammation of the brain coverings from infection or other causes.

name: Chronic ocular ischaemic syndromes
formal: Visual loss from chronic hypoperfusion due to carotid stenosis or occlusion, with venous stasis retinopathy, neovascular glaucoma and ocular pain.
simple: Eye damage from poor blood flow, usually from a narrowed neck artery.

name: Chronic peripheral vertigo
formal: Persistent peripheral vestibular imbalance for months, with dizziness, oscillopsia and imbalance from incomplete compensation or bilateral vestibular loss.
simple: Ongoing dizziness caused by an inner ear problem.

name: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)
formal: Mitochondrial disorder with progressive ptosis and bilateral ophthalmoparesis with minimal diplopia, from mtDNA deletions or POLG mutations; part of Kearns-Sayre spectrum.
simple: A slowly worsening drooping of the eyelids and loss of eye movement due to energy problems in cells.
more: Muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibres and COX-negative fibres with large-scale deletions; check ECG for conduction block and screen for endocrinopathy. Mostly sporadic; no cure, so use ptosis crutches or surgery, and monitor cardiac status.

tempoNote: Very slow progression over years to decades; onset any age, often adulthood
feat: Bilateral, fairly symmetric ptosis, often the first sign; patients tilt the head back or use the frontalis
Gradual limitation of eye movements in all directions, with little or no double vision
Weak eye closure and mild facial weakness; pupils spared
No day-to-day fatigability
May add proximal weakness, dysphagia, neuropathy, ataxia or hearing loss (PEO-plus)
inv: CK normal or mildly raised; lactate may be normal
Muscle biopsy: ragged-red fibres and COX-deficient fibres
Genetics: single large mtDNA deletion (muscle), or nuclear genes such as POLG, TWNK, RRM2B with multiple deletions
ECG for conduction defects; AChR antibodies and repetitive stimulation to exclude myasthenia

case.who: 48-year-old woman, office clerk in Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Eyelids have drooped for 10 years; colleagues say she looks sleepy. She never sees double.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis covering upper pupil, eyes move only a few millimetres in every direction, weak orbicularis oculi, normal pupils; no worsening with sustained upgaze.
case.tests: AChR antibody negative; RNS normal; deltoid biopsy shows ragged-red and COX-negative fibres; long-range PCR finds a single mtDNA deletion.
case.q: Why does she not complain of diplopia despite marked ophthalmoplegia?
case.a: The paresis is symmetric and very slowly progressive, so the eyes stay roughly aligned and the brain adapts; this contrasts with fluctuating, asymmetric ocular myasthenia.

det.patho: CPEO results from defective mitochondrial respiration in extraocular muscle, which has very high energy demand and many mitochondria. Sporadic cases usually carry a single large mtDNA deletion arising early in development; familial cases (dominant or recessive) usually come from nuclear genes that maintain mtDNA, such as POLG, TWNK or RRM2B, which lead to multiple deletions.
det.clinical: Ptosis comes first, followed over years by symmetric limitation of gaze; Bell's phenomenon may be lost. Patients rarely notice diplopia but may have trouble reading in downgaze. In 'PEO-plus' there is also limb myopathy, dysphagia, sensory ataxic neuropathy, parkinsonism, hearing loss or premature ovarian failure, especially with POLG. Examiners look for absence of fatigability and preserved pupils.
det.diagnosis: Myasthenia must be excluded first with antibodies, repetitive stimulation or single-fibre EMG and, if needed, an ice-pack test. Muscle biopsy showing ragged-red and COX-negative fibres plus mtDNA analysis of muscle confirms the diagnosis; blood is often uninformative for single deletions. Check ECG because conduction block can occur even without full Kearns–Sayre features.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying drug. Ptosis can be helped by lid crutches or conservative frontalis-sling surgery, avoiding overcorrection because corneal exposure is a risk with weak eye closure. Prisms help rare diplopia. Monitor swallowing, heart conduction and, in POLG cases, avoid valproate. Exercise training is safe and helpful.
det.prognosis: Usually a slowly progressive disorder with normal lifespan in isolated CPEO; outlook depends on extra-ocular involvement, especially cardiac.
pearls: Severe ophthalmoplegia without diplopia points to a myopathic, symmetric cause rather than MG.
Single deletion: sporadic, low recurrence risk; multiple deletions: think nuclear gene and family risk.
Lift ptosis cautiously: weak orbicularis plus lost Bell's phenomenon invites exposure keratitis.
det.thd: CPEO เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่ทำให้หนังตาตกและกลอกตาได้น้อยลงทั้งสองข้างอย่างช้า ๆ เป็นปี ผู้ป่วยมักไม่เห็นภาพซ้อนเพราะอ่อนแรงเท่ากันสองข้าง ต้องแยกจาก ocular MG ด้วยการตรวจแอนติบอดีและ RNS ยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อพบ ragged-red fibres และตรวจ mtDNA deletion การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เช่น ผ่าตัดยกหนังตาอย่างระวัง และตรวจหัวใจเป็นระยะ

ddx.pt: Fatigable, fluctuating asymmetric ptosis with diplopia; positive antibodies or decrement
Later onset with prominent dysphagia; PABPN1 repeat expansion, rimmed vacuoles
Onset before 20 with pigmentary retinopathy plus heart block, ataxia or high CSF protein

aN: cpeo | chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia | peo | progressive external ophthalmoplegia | ophthalmoplegia plus

name: Chronic relapsing axonal neuropathy
formal: Relapsing axonal neuropathy with episodes of weakness and sensory loss, a variant of chronic polyneuropathy such as vasculitic or inflammatory.
simple: A nerve disease that keeps coming back with weakness and numbness.

name: Chronic relapsing inflammatory optic neuropathy (CRION)
formal: Steroid-dependent recurrent optic neuritis with pain and visual loss, often MOG or GFAP antibody related, lacking systemic disease.
simple: Repeated painful eye nerve inflammation that needs long steroid treatment.
nN: chronic relapsing inflammatory optic neuropathy crion
aN: crion | chronic relapsing inflammatory optic neuropathy

name: Chronic vestibular disorders
formal: Persistent inner ear or central vestibular disorders, such as Meniere disease, vestibular migraine and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, with chronic vertigo and imbalance.
simple: Long-lasting balance system conditions causing dizziness.

name: Circadian rhythm disorders
formal: Disorders of timing of the sleep-wake cycle such as delayed phase, advanced phase, non-24-hour and shift work disorder.
simple: Problems where the body clock is out of step with normal day and night, causing trouble sleeping.

name: Classical essential tremor
formal: Slowly progressive bilateral postural and action tremor of hands, 4-12 Hz, often familial, improving with alcohol, treated with propranolol or primidone.
simple: A common shaking of the hands when using them, often running in families.

name: Clival chordoma
formal: Chordoma at the clivus with headache, diplopia from sixth nerve palsy and brainstem compression; locally recurrent.
simple: A slow-growing tumour at the base of the skull that can cause double vision.

name: Clivus/skull base syndromes
formal: Lesions at the clivus and skull base, such as chordoma, chondrosarcoma and metastases, causing multiple cranial neuropathies and headache.
simple: Problems at the base of the skull that press on several nerves.

name: Clonazepam akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to clonazepam, usually from withdrawal or paradoxical reaction, with inner restlessness and inability to sit still.
simple: A feeling of inner restlessness related to taking or stopping clonazepam.

name: Clonic seizures
formal: Brief, repeated rhythmic jerking seizures, focal or generalised, with loss of awareness when generalised.
simple: Seizures in which the limbs jerk rhythmically.

name: Clonidine akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to clonidine, often on withdrawal, with sympathetic overactivity.
simple: Restlessness and inability to stay still related to clonidine.

name: Cluster headache
formal: Primary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with severe unilateral orbital pain, 15-180 min, with ipsilateral lacrimation, ptosis and agitation; treated with oxygen, sumatriptan and verapamil.
simple: Very severe one-sided eye pain in short attacks, often at night, with tearing and a runny nose.
th: ปวดศีรษะเป็นชุด — ปวดรอบตาข้างเดียวรุนแรงมาก 15 นาที–3 ชั่วโมง น้ำตาน้ำมูกไหลข้างเดียวกัน กระสับกระส่าย
tempoNote: Attacks 15–180 min, up to 8/day, in bouts of weeks
feat: Excruciating strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain
Ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, ptosis/miosis
Restlessness and pacing (opposite of migraine)
Circadian timing, often waking from sleep; alcohol triggers within a bout
inv: MRI with pituitary views in first presentation

case.story: For 3 weeks, every night at 2 a.m. a stabbing pain behind the left eye for 45 minutes; he paces and bangs his head.
case.exam: During an attack: left tearing, red eye, partial ptosis and miosis.
case.tests: MRI brain normal.
case.q: What acute treatments work best?
case.a: High-flow 100% oxygen and subcutaneous/nasal triptan; verapamil for prevention.

ddx.pt: Longer attacks, patient lies still, nausea
Seconds-long electric shocks with triggers, no autonomic signs
Shorter, more frequent attacks; absolute indomethacin response

aN: cluster headache | trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia | tac | horton headache | suicide headache

det.patho: Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia: activation of the trigeminal–autonomic reflex produces severe orbital pain alongside parasympathetic outflow (tearing, nasal symptoms) and sympathetic dysfunction (partial Horner syndrome). The striking circadian and seasonal rhythm implicates the posterior hypothalamus. It is uncommon (about 1 in 1,000), more frequent in men and strongly associated with smoking.
det.clinical: Attacks are side-locked, reach peak intensity quickly and last 15–180 minutes, recurring from every other day to eight times a day, often at the same hour and frequently from sleep. During attacks patients pace, rock or press on the eye, unlike the stillness of migraine. Episodic cluster occurs in bouts of weeks to months separated by remissions of three months or more; the chronic form lacks meaningful remission. Alcohol, nitrates and strong smells can trigger attacks during a bout. Suicidal thoughts during severe bouts are well recognised.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical by ICHD-3. MRI brain with pituitary views is recommended at first presentation because pituitary tumours and other structural lesions can mimic TACs. Distinguish from paroxysmal hemicrania (shorter, more frequent, indomethacin-responsive), SUNCT/SUNA (seconds-long attacks), migraine and trigeminal neuralgia. Carotid dissection can cause painful Horner syndrome and must be considered if the history is atypical.
det.treatment: Acute: 100% oxygen at 12–15 L/min via a non-rebreathing mask for about 15 minutes, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg, or nasal zolmitriptan/sumatriptan. Transitional treatment while prevention takes effect: short oral prednisolone course or greater occipital nerve block. Preventive: verapamil is first-line, titrated with ECG monitoring for heart block; lithium, topiramate and galcanezumab (for episodic) are alternatives. Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation and, for refractory chronic cases, specialist neuromodulation are options; encourage stopping smoking.
det.prognosis: The disorder may persist for decades, though bouts often become less frequent with age; some episodic cases convert to chronic and vice versa.
pearls: Restless pacing during attacks separates cluster from migraine at a glance.
Order an ECG before each verapamil dose increase.
Oral triptans are too slow for cluster attacks — use injected or nasal routes.
det.thd: Cluster headache เป็นปวดศีรษะชนิด trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia ปวดรอบตาข้างเดียวรุนแรงมาก นาน 15–180 นาที เป็นวันละหลายครั้งในช่วงเวลาเดียวกัน มักตื่นมาปวดตอนกลางคืน ร่วมกับน้ำตาไหล ตาแดง น้ำมูก หนังตาตกข้างเดียวกัน และกระสับกระส่ายเดินไปมา พบบ่อยในชายสูบบุหรี่ ควรทำ MRI ครั้งแรก รักษาเฉียบพลันด้วยออกซิเจน 100% อัตราสูงหรือ sumatriptan ฉีด ป้องกันด้วย verapamil โดยติดตาม ECG

name: CMT disease type 1
formal: Demyelinating CMT with uniform slow conduction velocities below 38 m/s, most commonly CMT1A from PMP22 duplication, giving distal weakness, areflexia, and palpable nerves.
simple: The common inherited nerve condition affecting the insulation of nerves, causing slowly worsening leg and hand weakness.
more: PMP22 duplication testing is first-line. Care is supportive with orthotics and physiotherapy; progression is slow.

name: CMT disease type 2
formal: Axonal CMT with near-normal conduction velocities but reduced amplitudes, caused by MFN2, GDAP1 and others, with distal weakness and sensory loss.
simple: An inherited nerve condition affecting the nerve fibres themselves, causing foot and hand weakness with numbness.
more: Genetic panels identify the mutation; treatment is supportive; onset and severity vary, MFN2 forms can be severe.

name: CMT disease type 3
formal: Dejerine-Sottas disease, severe early-onset demyelinating neuropathy with very slow conduction velocities, hypotonia, delayed motor milestones, and often de novo PMP22, MPZ, or EGR2 mutations.
simple: A severe inherited nerve disease starting in infancy, causing delayed walking and marked weakness.
more: Nerve biopsy shows hypomyelination and onion bulbs; genetic testing confirms. Treatment is supportive with rehabilitation; disability is significant.

name: CMT disease type 4
formal: Autosomal recessive demyelinating CMT with early onset and severe disability, caused by mutations in genes such as GDAP1, MTMR2, SH3TC2, and PRX.
simple: A group of inherited nerve diseases passed on by both parents, with early-onset weakness and foot deformities.
more: Genetic testing identifies the subtype; scoliosis is common; supportive care and surgery for deformities; progression is often significant.

name: Cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration with posterior column loss, spastic paraparesis, neuropathy, cognitive change and macrocytosis.
simple: Low vitamin B12, which can cause numbness, weakness, balance trouble and memory problems.
more: Check serum B12, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, with anti-intrinsic factor antibodies for pernicious anaemia; MRI spine may show dorsal column T2 hyperintensity. Treat promptly with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, since delay risks permanent deficits.

name: Cobblestone malformation
formal: Cortical malformation from over-migration of neurons through pial defects, seen in dystroglycanopathies such as Walker-Warburg, causing congenital muscular dystrophy and ocular anomalies.
simple: A brain development defect with a bumpy brain surface, seen with some inherited muscle diseases.

name: Cocaine vasculopathy
formal: Cocaine-related stroke from vasospasm, vasculitis, thrombosis or hypertension with intracranial haemorrhage or infarction.
simple: Blood vessel damage and strokes caused by cocaine use.

name: Cockayne’s syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder with growth failure, photosensitivity, microcephaly, deafness, retinopathy, neuropathy and leukodystrophy.
simple: An inherited condition with slow growth, sun sensitivity, hearing loss and brain and nerve problems.
more: Caused by ERCC6 (CSB) or ERCC8 (CSA) mutations; MRI shows basal ganglia calcification and white matter hypomyelination. Skin cells show impaired transcription-coupled repair; treatment is supportive, with early childhood death in severe types.

name: Coeliac disease
formal: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy with neurological associations including gluten ataxia, neuropathy, epilepsy with occipital calcifications and myopathy.
simple: A gut disease triggered by gluten that can also cause balance problems and nerve damage.

name: Cogan syndrome
formal: Rare autoimmune disorder with interstitial keratitis and vestibuloauditory dysfunction causing vertigo and hearing loss, sometimes with vasculitis.
simple: A rare immune disease causing eye inflammation along with hearing loss and dizziness.

name: Cognitive disorders
formal: Conditions with impaired memory, attention, language, executive or visuospatial function, including mild cognitive impairment, delirium and dementias.
simple: Conditions that affect thinking, memory and reasoning.

name: Collagen vascular diseases
formal: Autoimmune diseases like SLE and vasculitis with neurological features such as stroke, myelitis, neuropathy and seizures.
simple: Immune diseases such as lupus that inflame blood vessels and can affect the nerves and brain.

name: Colour vision disorders
formal: Congenital (X-linked red-green) or acquired (optic nerve, occipital lesions, drugs) impairment of colour perception; central achromatopsia arises from ventral occipital lesions.
simple: Difficulty telling colours apart, either from birth or after eye or brain damage.

name: Coma
formal: State of unarousable unresponsiveness with eyes closed from bilateral hemispheric or brainstem reticular activating dysfunction; many causes.
simple: A deep unconsciousness in which a person cannot be woken.

name: Compartment syndromes
formal: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromising perfusion, causing severe pain, tense swelling, and nerve and muscle ischaemia.
simple: Pressure builds in a muscle space, cutting off blood supply and risking nerve and muscle damage.
more: Diagnosed clinically with pressure measurement; urgent fasciotomy is required to avoid permanent damage.

name: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
formal: Chronic limb pain with allodynia, oedema, vasomotor and sudomotor change, trophic change and motor dysfunction after injury, type 1 without and type 2 with nerve lesion.
simple: Long-lasting severe limb pain with swelling and skin changes, usually after an injury.

name: Complex regional pain syndrome type
formal: Chronic limb pain disproportionate to an inciting injury, with allodynia, oedema, vasomotor and sudomotor change, and motor features such as dystonia; type I has no nerve lesion, type II follows nerve injury.
simple: A long-lasting severe pain condition in a limb after injury, with swelling, skin colour change and sensitivity to touch.
more: Diagnosed clinically by the Budapest criteria. Early physiotherapy, neuropathic pain drugs, bisphosphonates, steroids and sympathetic blocks are used; many improve within a year but some are left with chronic disability.

name: Compressive neuropathies
formal: Entrapment neuropathies from mechanical nerve compression, such as carpal tunnel, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and peroneal palsy, with focal slowing or block on nerve conduction.
simple: Nerve damage from pressure at places where nerves are squeezed.

name: Compressive neuropathy and radiculopathy
formal: Combined focal nerve root compression and entrapment neuropathy causing pain, sensory loss and weakness; double crush phenomenon may exist.
simple: Nerves pinched at the spine or along the limb causing pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Compressive optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve compression from tumour, aneurysm, thyroid eye disease or hyperostosis causing progressive painless visual loss with colour desaturation and disc pallor.
simple: Pressure on the eye nerve, causing slow vision loss.

name: Compulsive behavioral disorders
formal: Impulse control and compulsive behaviours such as gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating and punding, most often triggered by dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease or restless legs syndrome.
simple: Out-of-control urges such as gambling, shopping or repetitive tasks, often caused by Parkinson medicines.
more: Treat by reducing or stopping the dopamine agonist, with counselling and sometimes naltrexone or amantadine; withdrawing the drug too fast can cause an agonist withdrawal syndrome.

name: Conceptual/ideational apraxia
formal: Failure to conceive or sequence the actions of an object use despite intact motor function, with lesion of the left parietal or temporal region; seen in Alzheimer disease.
simple: Not knowing how or in what order to use an object, though the muscles work fine.

name: Conduct disorder
formal: Persistent pattern of violating rules or others' rights in childhood and adolescence, with aggression, deceit and truancy; psychiatric diagnosis often comorbid with ADHD.
simple: A pattern in children of serious rule-breaking and aggression toward others.

name: Congenital ataxia
formal: Early-onset non-progressive or slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia due to cerebellar malformation or genetic causes, with hypotonia and delayed motor milestones.
simple: Poor balance and coordination present from early childhood.

name: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN)
formal: Early-onset neuropathy with severely slowed conduction, hypotonia and arthrogryposis, from myelin gene mutations (EGR2, PMP22, MPZ).
simple: A rare inherited nerve disease in newborns with floppy muscles and poor movement.

name: Congenital inherited ataxic disorders
formal: Group of genetic cerebellar ataxias present from birth including Joubert syndrome, Gillespie syndrome and cerebellar hypoplasias.
simple: Inherited conditions in which poor coordination is present from infancy.

name: Congenital muscular dystrophies (CMD)
formal: Inherited muscle diseases onset at birth or infancy with hypotonia and weakness; subtypes include merosin deficiency and dystroglycanopathies, sometimes with brain involvement.
simple: Inherited muscle diseases causing floppy, weak muscles from birth.

name: Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS)
formal: Inherited neuromuscular junction disorders with fatigable weakness since early life, ptosis and feeding problems; mutations in CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7 and others.
simple: Inherited conditions where nerves cannot signal properly to muscles, causing tiring weakness.
more: Diagnose by decrement on low-rate repetitive nerve stimulation and a genetic panel; response to treatment varies by subtype. Pyridostigmine, 3,4-diaminopyridine, salbutamol or ephedrine are used, but pyridostigmine can worsen DOK7 and slow-channel forms.
