feat: Fatigable weakness from birth or childhood; ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, feeding and breathing crises
Family history or consanguinity; antibodies negative
Clues to subtype: limb-girdle pattern without eye involvement (DOK7, GFPT1), episodic apnoea (CHAT), repetitive CMAP (slow-channel, COLQ)
inv: RNS decrement; single-fibre EMG jitter; look for a repetitive CMAP after one stimulus
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic panel (CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7, COLQ, GFPT1 …)

case.story: Weak hips and frequent falls since early childhood, worse by evening; diagnosed with 'seronegative MG' but pyridostigmine made her weaker.
case.exam: Limb-girdle fatigable weakness, mild ptosis, normal eye movements.
case.tests: RNS decrement 30%; AChR/MuSK negative; DOK7 compound heterozygous variants.
case.q: Which drug is usually helpful in DOK7 CMS?
case.a: Salbutamol (or ephedrine); acetylcholinesterase inhibitors often worsen DOK7 and COLQ forms — hence the genetic diagnosis matters.

ddx.pt: Acquired, antibody positive, responds to immunotherapy
Non-fatigable weakness, normal RNS, myopathic biopsy
Progressive, raised CK, no decrement

aN: cms | congenital myasthenic syndrome | congenital myasthenia | dok7 myasthenia | slow channel syndrome

det.patho: CMS are inherited defects of neuromuscular transmission caused by mutations in presynaptic, synaptic basal lamina, postsynaptic or glycosylation genes. The most frequent are AChR subunit mutations (especially CHRNE) causing receptor deficiency, followed by RAPSN, DOK7, COLQ and GFPT1. Kinetic defects either prolong channel opening (slow-channel, usually dominant) or shorten it (fast-channel). Most forms are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, axial or limb muscles begins at birth or in childhood, though some forms present in adolescence or adulthood. Neonates may have hypotonia, poor feeding, arthrogryposis or episodic apnoea (CHAT, RAPSN). DOK7 and GFPT1 forms often show limb-girdle weakness with little eye involvement. Slow-channel and COLQ forms may show selective neck, wrist and finger extensor weakness and pupils that react slowly.
det.diagnosis: RNS decrement and increased jitter on single-fibre EMG establish a transmission defect; a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus suggests slow-channel syndrome or COLQ deficiency. AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies should be negative. Next-generation sequencing panels or exome sequencing identify the gene. Consider CMS in any 'seronegative MG' with early onset, family history or poor response to immunotherapy.
det.treatment: Therapy is genotype-specific. AChR deficiency and fast-channel forms respond to pyridostigmine, often with 3,4-diaminopyridine. Slow-channel syndrome is treated with open-channel blockers such as fluoxetine or quinidine, and cholinesterase inhibitors should be avoided. DOK7 and COLQ forms respond to beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, ephedrine) and may worsen with pyridostigmine. Immunotherapy has no role.
det.prognosis: Many forms are static or slowly progressive and compatible with normal life expectancy if crises are managed; some have life-threatening apnoeic episodes in childhood.
pearls: Antibody-negative 'MG' that worsens with pyridostigmine suggests DOK7, COLQ or slow-channel CMS.
A repetitive CMAP after one stimulus is a key electrophysiological clue.
det.thd: CMS เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้การส่งสัญญาณที่รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ มีอาการอ่อนแรงแบบล้าง่ายตั้งแต่เด็ก เช่น หนังตาตก กลืนลำบาก หรืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา โดยไม่มีแอนติบอดี AChR หรือ MuSK การวินิจฉัยใช้ RNS, single-fibre EMG และตรวจยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดของยีน บางชนิดตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine แต่ชนิด DOK7, COLQ และ slow-channel อาจแย่ลงจากยานี้ และควรใช้ salbutamol หรือ fluoxetine แทน

name: Congenital myopathies
formal: Inherited muscle diseases with hypotonia and weakness from birth, with distinct structural features: nemaline, core and centronuclear myopathies.
simple: A group of inherited muscle diseases causing weak, floppy muscles from early life.
more: Diagnosis uses CK, EMG, muscle MRI pattern and biopsy with enzyme histochemistry, but a next-generation sequencing panel is now first line. Management is mainly supportive with respiratory, orthopaedic and cardiac follow-up, and prognosis depends on the gene.
th: กล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติแต่กำเนิด — ทารกตัวอ่อน อ่อนแรงไม่ค่อยลุกลาม แยกชนิดด้วยลักษณะชิ้นเนื้อและยีน
feat: Floppy infant or delayed milestones; static or slowly progressive weakness
Facial weakness, high-arched palate, long face; ptosis/ophthalmoparesis in centronuclear forms
RYR1 core myopathy: malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
inv: CK normal or mildly raised; EMG myopathic
Muscle biopsy: rods (nemaline), cores (central core), central nuclei (centronuclear)
Gene panel (RYR1, ACTA1, NEB, MTM1, DNM2 …)

case.story: Floppy at birth, walked at 2 years, always last in sports; no worsening.
case.exam: Mild proximal and neck flexor weakness, long thin face, high palate, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 180 U/L; biopsy: central cores; RYR1 variant.
case.q: Why should the anaesthetist be told?
case.a: RYR1-related core myopathy carries a risk of malignant hyperthermia with volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium.

ddx.pt: Tongue fasciculation, areflexia, neurogenic EMG, SMN1 deletion
Fatigability and decrement on RNS
Congenital form has an affected mother with myotonia

aN: congenital myopathy | nemaline myopathy | central core disease | centronuclear myopathy | myotubular myopathy | ryr1

det.patho: Congenital myopathies are genetic disorders of muscle structure and excitation–contraction coupling, defined historically by biopsy features: cores (RYR1, SELENON), rods (NEB, ACTA1 and others), central nuclei (MTM1, DNM2, BIN1, RYR1) and fibre-type disproportion. RYR1 is the most common gene overall. One gene can cause several pathological pictures, and one picture can come from several genes, so genetic diagnosis now takes priority.
det.clinical: Most present at birth or in infancy with hypotonia, weakness, feeding problems and delayed motor milestones, followed by a static or slowly progressive course. Facial weakness, a long narrow face, high-arched palate, scoliosis and joint contractures are common. Respiratory weakness may be disproportionate to limb weakness, especially in nemaline, SELENON and centronuclear forms. X-linked myotubular myopathy causes severe neonatal weakness in boys, often with ventilator dependence; ptosis and ophthalmoparesis suggest centronuclear myopathy or some RYR1 forms.
det.diagnosis: CK is normal or mildly raised and EMG shows myopathic or non-specific changes. Muscle MRI patterns can point to particular genes. Biopsy with histochemistry and electron microscopy remains useful, but next-generation sequencing panels or exome sequencing usually establish the diagnosis. Exclude SMA, congenital myasthenic syndromes, congenital myotonic dystrophy and Pompe disease.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy. Management focuses on respiratory monitoring with nocturnal ventilation when needed, nutrition, scoliosis care, physiotherapy and orthopaedic support. Patients with RYR1 variants should avoid triggering anaesthetic agents. Some CMS-like transmission defects in centronuclear myopathy may respond to pyridostigmine.
det.prognosis: Ranges from near-normal life with mild weakness to early death from respiratory failure in severe neonatal forms.
pearls: Check FVC lying down — diaphragm weakness can be hidden.
RYR1 myopathy: alert the anaesthetist about malignant hyperthermia.
A floppy infant with normal CK and a myopathic face suggests congenital myopathy.
det.thd: Congenital myopathies เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่เป็นตั้งแต่เกิด ทารกตัวอ่อน กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ดูดนมลำบาก พัฒนาการช้า แต่โรคมักไม่ค่อยลุกลาม เดิมแบ่งชนิดตามลักษณะชิ้นเนื้อ เช่น core, rod และ central nuclei ยีนที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ RYR1 การวินิจฉัยปัจจุบันใช้การตรวจยีนเป็นหลัก การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง โดยเฉพาะการเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ และผู้ป่วยที่มี RYR1 ต้องแจ้งวิสัญญีแพทย์เพราะเสี่ยงต่อ malignant hyperthermia

name: Congenital myotonic dystrophy
formal: Severe neonatal form of DM1 with large maternal CTG expansions causing hypotonia, respiratory failure, facial weakness, and intellectual disability.
simple: A serious form of myotonic dystrophy present at birth, causing floppiness and breathing problems.
more: Genetic testing in baby and mother; ventilatory support and feeding care; survivors improve in motor strength but have cognitive impairment.

name: Connective tissue diseases
formal: Heterogeneous group including Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan and SLE; neurological complications include dissection, stroke, aneurysm and myelopathy.
simple: Diseases of the supporting tissue of the body that can sometimes affect blood vessels, nerves and the spine.

name: Constructional apraxia
formal: Inability to copy or assemble spatial figures, a disorder of visuospatial organisation, usually from right parietal lesions.
simple: Trouble drawing or building shapes, caused by damage to a part of the brain involved with space.

name: Conversion disorder
formal: Functional neurological disorder with motor or sensory symptoms incompatible with recognised disease, with positive signs such as Hoover sign.
simple: Real neurological symptoms like weakness or blackouts caused by a problem with brain function rather than by damage to nerves.

name: Copper deficiency
formal: Acquired deficiency from malabsorption or zinc excess causing myeloneuropathy resembling B12 deficiency, with anaemia and neutropenia.
simple: Too little copper in the body, causing numbness, balance problems and low blood counts.
more: Diagnosed by low serum copper and caeruloplasmin, with MRI spinal cord dorsal column signal change as in B12 deficiency; marrow shows vacuolated precursors. Replace copper and remove zinc excess; haematology recovers but neurological improvement is partial.

name: Copper dystonia
formal: Dystonia in Wilson disease from copper accumulation in basal ganglia, with Kayser-Fleischer rings and hepatic disease.
simple: Twisting muscle postures caused by copper build-up in the brain.

name: Copper metabolism disorders
formal: Disorders including Wilson disease, Menkes disease and acquired copper deficiency, causing neurological, hepatic and haematological disease.
simple: Conditions where the body has too much or too little copper.

name: Cortical agnosia
formal: Failure to recognise objects despite intact primary sensation from cortical lesion, such as visual, tactile or auditory agnosia.
simple: Not being able to recognise things like objects or sounds despite seeing or hearing them normally, due to brain damage.

name: Cortical dementia
formal: Dementia with predominant cortical features such as aphasia, apraxia, agnosia and amnesia, as in Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Memory loss and language and thinking problems from damage to the brain's outer layer.

name: Cortical disease
formal: Disorders involving cerebral cortex, with focal deficits, seizures or cognitive dysfunction such as aphasia, agnosia and neglect.
simple: Problems in the outer layer of the brain that affect thinking, language, senses or cause seizures.

name: Cortical myoclonic tremor
formal: Rhythmic or irregular tremor-like action jerks of hands from cortical hyperexcitability, as in familial adult myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: A fine shaking of the hands that is actually very small muscle jerks from brain overactivity.

name: Cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from sensorimotor cortex hyperexcitability, focal, action- or stimulus-sensitive, with giant SEPs; in post-hypoxic, metabolic and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Quick shock-like jerks of muscles caused by overactive brain surface cells.

name: Cortical tremor
formal: Rhythmic tremor-like movement from cortical hyperexcitability, a form of cortical myoclonus, with enlarged SEPs and EEG correlate.
simple: A tremor-like shaking caused by overactive nerve cells in the brain surface.

name: Cortical–subcortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus with both cortical and subcortical generators, seen in some progressive myoclonic epilepsies and post-hypoxic states.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks arising from both the brain surface and deeper brain areas.

name: Corticobasal degeneration (CBD)
formal: Tauopathy with asymmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome, limb apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss, dystonia and myoclonus; poor levodopa response.
simple: A rare brain disease causing stiffness, clumsiness and an unusual loss of control of one limb, which worsens over time.
more: MRI shows asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy and FDG-PET reveals asymmetric hypometabolism; diagnosis is clinical with pathology confirmation. No disease-modifying treatment; manage with botulinum toxin for dystonia, clonazepam for myoclonus.

name: Corticobasal syndrome (CBS)
formal: Asymmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome with apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb phenomenon, dystonia and myoclonus; pathology most often corticobasal degeneration, but also PSP, Alzheimer or FTD.
simple: A progressive brain condition that makes one arm or leg stiff, clumsy and sometimes act on its own, with trouble using the hand.
more: MRI shows asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy; levodopa response is poor. Treatment is symptomatic with physiotherapy, botulinum toxin and support; survival is around 6 to 8 years.

name: Corticodentatonigral degeneration
formal: Rare progressive disorder with neuronal achromasia in cortex, dentate and substantia nigra producing parkinsonism, dystonia and ataxia; historically described as a corticobasal-like entity.
simple: A rare brain degeneration causing stiffness, slowness and loss of coordination.
more: Diagnosis is made at autopsy; it overlaps with corticobasal degeneration. No specific treatment exists, and care is symptomatic.

name: Corticostriato-spinal degeneration
formal: Old term for combined degeneration of cortex, striatum and spinal cord, referring to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
simple: An old name for a rare brain disease now called Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

name: Cough headache
formal: Headache triggered by coughing or Valsalva, primary and benign or secondary to posterior fossa lesions such as Chiari malformation.
simple: A short severe headache set off by coughing, straining or sneezing.

name: CPT2 deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder of mitochondrial long-chain fatty acid oxidation causing recurrent exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria triggered by prolonged exercise, fasting, or fever.
simple: An inherited problem burning fat for energy, causing muscle pain and dark urine after long exercise or fasting.
more: Acylcarnitine profile and CPT2 testing; avoid fasting, use carbohydrate before exercise and a low-fat diet; medium-chain triglycerides may help.

name: Craft cramp
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia such as writer's cramp, in occupations needing repetitive fine movement; symptoms occur only with the specific task.
simple: Muscle cramping in the hand that occurs only during one specific skilled task such as writing or playing an instrument.

name: Cramp-fasciculation syndrome
formal: Benign peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder with muscle cramps, fasciculations, and myokymia, sometimes associated with CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies.
simple: A condition of frequent muscle cramps and twitching with no weakness.
more: EMG shows fasciculations; check CASPR2 antibodies; carbamazepine or sodium channel blockers help.

name: Cramps
formal: Painful involuntary muscle contractions, often nocturnal in calves, arising from hyperexcitable motor axons and associated with age, drugs, electrolyte disorders, cirrhosis, and neuropathy.
simple: Sudden painful tightening of a muscle, often in the calf at night.
more: Look for reversible causes such as medications and electrolyte disturbance. Stretching helps; evidence for quinine is limited by safety concerns, and mexiletine may be used in severe cases.

name: Cranial dystonias
formal: Focal dystonias affecting face, jaw, tongue, eyelids or neck, including blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and Meige syndrome.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the face, mouth, jaw or eyelids.

name: Cranial neuropathy
formal: Disease of one or more cranial nerves with sensory, motor or autonomic dysfunction; causes include compression, infection, ischaemia and inflammation.
simple: Damage to one of the nerves running from the brain to the face, eyes, ears or throat.

name: Craniopharyngioma
formal: Suprasellar epithelial tumour from Rathke pouch remnants causing bitemporal hemianopia, endocrine deficits and hydrocephalus.
simple: A non-cancerous tumour near the pituitary gland that can affect vision and hormones.

name: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)
formal: Prion disease with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia and akinetic mutism; MRI cortical ribboning, periodic EEG complexes and positive RT-QuIC.
simple: A rare, rapidly worsening brain disease from abnormal prion proteins, causing dementia and jerking.
more: Diagnostic EEG, DWI MRI and CSF 14-3-3 or total tau support; RT-QuIC on CSF has high sensitivity and specificity. Sporadic form predominates, with PRNP mutation in genetic types and variant CJD linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy.
th: โรคพรีออน — สมองเสื่อมเร็วมากภายในเดือน กระตุก (myoclonus) เดินเซ
tempoNote: Rapidly progressive over weeks to months
feat: Rapidly progressive dementia
Startle-sensitive myoclonus
Ataxia, visual disturbance, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, akinetic mutism
inv: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning and/or caudate–putamen restriction
CSF RT-QuIC (high specificity), 14-3-3
EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes

case.story: Within 3 months went from working to needing help dressing; jerks when startled.
case.exam: Disoriented, startle myoclonus, gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning and bilateral caudate restriction; RT-QuIC positive.
case.q: What must be excluded before accepting this diagnosis?
case.a: Treatable rapidly progressive dementias — autoimmune encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, lymphoma, metabolic causes.

ddx.pt: Antibody-mediated, CSF inflammation, responds to immunotherapy
Years not months
Slower, fluctuations, hallucinations

aN: cjd | creutzfeldt jakob disease | scjd | prion disease | spongiform encephalopathy

det.patho: Prion disease results from conversion of normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into a misfolded, protease-resistant form (PrPSc) that templates further misfolding, causing spongiform change, neuronal loss and gliosis. Sporadic CJD (about 85%) arises spontaneously, with codon 129 polymorphism of PRNP shaping the phenotype; genetic forms (PRNP mutations) and acquired forms (iatrogenic, variant CJD from BSE) make up the rest. Incidence is roughly 1–2 per million per year.
det.clinical: Sporadic CJD usually starts in the 60s with rapidly progressive cognitive decline, often with behavioural change, visual disturbance (Heidenhain variant) or ataxia (Brownell–Oppenheimer variant) as early features. Myoclonus, frequently startle-provoked, appears in most patients, together with pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. Within months the patient becomes mute and immobile (akinetic mutism). Variant CJD affects younger people, begins with psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory symptoms, and has a longer course.
det.diagnosis: Updated international criteria combine the clinical syndrome with supportive tests. MRI DWI/FLAIR showing cortical ribboning and/or caudate and putamen hyperintensity is highly sensitive. CSF RT-QuIC is the most specific test; 14-3-3 and total tau are sensitive but non-specific. EEG may show periodic sharp-wave complexes, mostly in later stages. Definite diagnosis requires neuropathology. Always look for treatable mimics: autoimmune encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, CNS lymphoma, vasculitis, metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: There is no effective treatment; care is supportive and palliative, with clonazepam or levetiracetam for myoclonus and attention to nutrition, comfort and family support. Notify public health authorities as required, and follow infection-control guidance for neurosurgical and ophthalmic instruments. Routine nursing contact poses no transmission risk. Genetic counselling is offered for familial forms.
det.prognosis: Median survival in sporadic CJD is about 4–6 months, with most patients dying within a year.
pearls: Rapid dementia over weeks to months plus myoclonus: get DWI MRI and CSF RT-QuIC.
Cortical ribboning is best seen on DWI and can be missed on routine T2.
Exclude autoimmune encephalitis before labelling a patient with CJD.
det.thd: CJD เป็นโรคพรีออนที่โปรตีน prion พับผิดรูปแล้วชักนำโปรตีนปกติให้ผิดตาม ทำให้สมองเป็นรูพรุนแบบฟองน้ำ ผู้ป่วยสมองเสื่อมเร็วมากภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน มีกระตุกเมื่อตกใจ เดินเซ ตามัว จนพูดและขยับไม่ได้ การตรวจที่ช่วยมาก ได้แก่ MRI DWI เห็น cortical ribboning และ basal ganglia และ CSF RT-QuIC ซึ่งจำเพาะสูง ก่อนวินิจฉัยต้องตัดสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น autoimmune encephalitis ยังไม่มียารักษา เน้นดูแลแบบประคับประคองและแจ้งหน่วยงานสาธารณสุข

name: Crigler–Najjar syndrome
formal: Inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation (UGT1A1) causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; type I may lead to kernicterus.
simple: An inherited liver enzyme problem that causes high bilirubin and can damage the baby's brain if untreated.

name: Critical illness myopathy (CIM)
formal: Acute myopathy with flaccid weakness in ICU patients, associated with steroids, neuromuscular blockers and sepsis; with thick filament loss.
simple: Muscle weakness that develops in very sick patients in intensive care.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงที่เกิดระหว่างป่วยหนักใน ICU — สูญเสีย myosin โดยเฉพาะหลังได้ steroid และยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ
tempoNote: Develops during the first 1–2 weeks of critical illness; often noticed at ventilator weaning
feat: Flaccid, often proximal-predominant quadriparesis with failure to wean from the ventilator
Facial weakness possible; eye movements usually spared
Reflexes reduced; sensation preserved (if testable)
Risk factors: sepsis, multiorgan failure, high-dose corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockers, hyperglycaemia
inv: CK normal or modestly raised
NCS: low CMAP amplitudes with long CMAP duration, normal sensory potentials; direct muscle stimulation shows reduced excitability
Muscle biopsy (if needed): selective loss of thick myosin filaments, scattered necrosis

case.story: Ventilated 10 days for status asthmaticus with IV methylprednisolone and a cisatracurium infusion; now awake but cannot lift arms or breathe unaided.
case.exam: Flaccid quadriparesis, worse proximally, mild bilateral facial weakness, reduced reflexes; withdraws to pain normally and reports touch.
case.tests: CK 900 U/L; NCS: low broad CMAPs, normal sural SNAPs; needle EMG: short, small units with early recruitment.
case.q: What distinguishes CIM from CIP electrophysiologically?
case.a: CIM preserves sensory potentials, shows broad low CMAPs and myopathic units, and muscle is inexcitable on direct stimulation; CIP reduces both sensory and motor amplitudes with neurogenic EMG.

det.patho: Sepsis-related inflammation, immobility and high-dose glucocorticoids trigger rapid proteolysis that preferentially removes myosin heavy chains, together with sodium-channel dysfunction that makes the muscle membrane electrically inexcitable. Neuromuscular blocking agents add to the risk, probably through functional denervation. CIM frequently coexists with critical illness polyneuropathy.
det.clinical: Weakness is usually discovered when sedation is lightened or weaning fails. It is generalised and flaccid, often proximal more than distal, and may involve facial and neck muscles while sparing the eyes. Sensory examination, when possible, is intact. Prolonged ventilation, longer ICU and hospital stay, and post-ICU functional impairment are typical consequences.
det.diagnosis: ICU-acquired weakness is defined clinically (for example MRC sum score below 48 in a cooperative patient) after excluding other causes. Electrophysiology distinguishes myopathy from neuropathy: preserved SNAPs, low-amplitude prolonged CMAPs, and myopathic or inexcitable muscle on needle and direct stimulation favour CIM. CK can be normal. Biopsy showing myosin loss confirms but is rarely necessary.
det.treatment: There is no specific treatment. Prevention and mitigation include treating sepsis, avoiding hyperglycaemia, minimising steroid doses and paralytic agents, daily sedation interruption and early mobilisation. Rehabilitation, nutritional support and staged ventilator weaning are central.
det.prognosis: Recovery is often good over weeks to months, generally faster and more complete than in CIP, though some patients have lasting weakness and fatigue.
pearls: Normal sural SNAP with tiny motor responses in an ICU patient favours myopathy over neuropathy.
Steroids plus neuromuscular blockade in asthma is the textbook setting.
Eye movements are spared — ptosis and ophthalmoplegia suggest another diagnosis such as MG or botulism.
det.thd: CIM คือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงที่เกิดในผู้ป่วยวิกฤต โดยเฉพาะผู้ที่ติดเชื้อรุนแรง ได้ steroid ขนาดสูงหรือยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ เกิดจากการสูญเสีย myosin และเยื่อหุ้มกล้ามเนื้อไม่ตอบสนองต่อไฟฟ้า ผู้ป่วยแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียกและถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจไม่ได้ แต่ความรู้สึกปกติ NCS พบ SNAP ปกติ CMAP เล็กและกว้าง การรักษาคือคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงและฟื้นฟู ส่วนใหญ่หายดีภายในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

Weakness preceding ICU stay, demyelinating NCS, CSF protein raised

name: Critical illness neuropathy
formal: Axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in ICU patients with sepsis, causing limb weakness and difficulty weaning from ventilation.
simple: Nerve damage in critically ill patients causing weakness and trouble breathing independently.

name: Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP)
formal: Axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy in ICU patients with sepsis or multi-organ failure, causing flaccid limb weakness and ventilator weaning difficulty.
simple: Widespread nerve damage in very ill patients, causing weakness and slow recovery.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced compound muscle and sensory amplitudes with spontaneous denervation on EMG; CK is normal and the facial muscles are spared. Treat sepsis and optimise glycaemic control; recovery takes weeks to months and can be incomplete.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมแบบ axonal ระหว่างป่วยหนัก/ติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด — อ่อนแรงส่วนปลายและถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจยาก
tempoNote: Begins within days of sepsis or multiorgan failure; recognised at weaning
feat: Symmetric distal-predominant flaccid weakness and wasting with reduced or absent reflexes
Distal loss of pain, temperature and vibration sense
Difficulty weaning due to phrenic nerve and diaphragm involvement
Facial muscles relatively spared; often combined with CIM
inv: NCS: reduced motor and sensory amplitudes with normal conduction velocity (axonal)
Needle EMG: fibrillations and positive sharp waves, later neurogenic units
CSF normal protein (helps exclude GBS) when the diagnosis is uncertain

case.story: Three weeks in ICU with leptospirosis, septic shock and renal failure; now alert but legs are floppy and she fails spontaneous breathing trials.
case.exam: Distal > proximal weakness, foot drop, absent ankle jerks, stocking sensory loss, grimaces normally.
case.tests: NCS: low CMAPs and absent sural SNAPs with preserved velocities; needle EMG: fibrillations in leg and diaphragm.
case.q: Why is GBS unlikely, and what is the prognosis?
case.a: Weakness began during critical illness, NCS show pure axonal loss without demyelination and CSF protein is normal. Recovery is slow over months and may be incomplete.

det.patho: Systemic inflammation in sepsis impairs nerve microcirculation, increases vascular permeability and causes bioenergetic failure of axons; sodium-channel inactivation produces early functional block before structural degeneration. The result is a length-dependent sensorimotor axonal neuropathy. Hyperglycaemia and multiorgan failure increase risk, and severity tracks with the duration of sepsis.
det.clinical: Most cases present as failure to wean or limp limbs once sedation is reduced. Weakness is distal-predominant with reduced reflexes and distal sensory loss, though examination is limited by encephalopathy. Phrenic neuropathy prolongs ventilation. CIP and CIM overlap in many patients and together form ICU-acquired weakness, a major cause of long-term disability after intensive care.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible setting with NCS showing reduced CMAP and SNAP amplitudes and normal velocities, and EMG showing denervation. Phrenic NCS and diaphragm EMG help explain ventilator dependence. Preserved SNAPs, inexcitable muscle on direct stimulation or a pure motor pattern suggest CIM instead. Exclude GBS, myasthenia, botulism, high cervical cord lesions and drug effects.
det.treatment: There is no proven specific therapy. Intensive insulin therapy reduces incidence but must be balanced against hypoglycaemia; current practice targets moderate glucose control. Treat sepsis aggressively, minimise sedation, mobilise early and provide physiotherapy, splints and long-term rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Recovery takes months; many patients regain walking, but residual distal weakness, sensory loss and fatigue are common, more so than with CIM.
pearls: Absent sural SNAP plus low CMAP with normal velocities in a septic patient = CIP pattern.
Check phrenic nerve function in unexplained weaning failure.
CIP and CIM often coexist; electrophysiology defines the mix.
det.thd: CIP คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal ที่เกิดระหว่างติดเชื้อรุนแรงหรืออวัยวะล้มเหลวหลายระบบ ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงส่วนปลาย reflex หาย ชาแบบถุงเท้า และถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจยากเพราะเส้นประสาท phrenic เสีย NCS พบ amplitude ลดลงทั้ง motor และ sensory แต่ความเร็วปกติ ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นรักษาการติดเชื้อ คุมน้ำตาล เคลื่อนไหวเร็ว และฟื้นฟูยาวนานหลายเดือน

name: CRMP-5 neuronal antibody-associated limbic encephalitis
formal: Paraneoplastic limbic or multifocal encephalitis with anti-CV2/CRMP5 antibodies, associated with small cell lung cancer and thymoma, often with neuropathy and chorea.
simple: Brain inflammation triggered by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer, causing memory and mood changes.
nN: crmp 5 neuronal antibody associated limbic encephalitis

name: Crohn’s disease
formal: Inflammatory bowel disease with neurological complications including peripheral neuropathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, myelopathy and treatment-related effects.
simple: A bowel inflammatory disease that can also affect nerves and brain blood vessels.
more: Check for ulcerative thrombotic complications, B12 and folate deficiency, vitamin deficiency and anti-TNF-related demyelination; neuropathy and CNS involvement should be sought on imaging. Treat the bowel disease, anticoagulate venous thrombosis.

name: Cruciate paralysis
formal: Weakness of both arms with relative sparing of legs, caused by a lesion at the cervicomedullary junction affecting decussating pyramidal fibres.
simple: A weakness mostly in the arms, due to damage at the junction of brain and spinal cord.

name: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome
formal: Autoinflammatory NLRP3 disease including CINCA/NOMID with chronic aseptic meningitis, hearing loss, papilloedema and rashes.
simple: An inherited inflammatory condition causing fever, rash, joint pain and brain-lining inflammation.

name: Cryptococcal meningitis
formal: Cryptococcus infection of meninges, mostly in immunosuppression with HIV, causing headache and raised intracranial pressure; India ink or antigen positive, treated with amphotericin and flucytosine.
simple: A fungal infection of the brain coverings in people with weak immunity, causing headache and confusion.

name: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis
formal: Cryptococcal infection of meninges and brain parenchyma with encephalopathy, cryptococcomas and raised pressure, mainly in immunocompromised patients.
simple: A fungal infection of the brain and its coverings that mainly affects people with weak immunity.

name: Cryptogenic myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Myoclonic epilepsy without an identifiable cause, with seizures featuring brief myoclonic jerks.
simple: Epilepsy with sudden muscle jerks for which no cause is found.

name: Cuban epidemic neuropathy
formal: Epidemic optic and peripheral neuropathy and myeloneuropathy during 1990s in Cuba, linked to nutritional deficiency including B vitamins.
simple: A nutritional illness in Cuba that caused vision loss and numb, weak limbs.

name: Cushing syndrome
formal: Endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoid excess causing proximal myopathy, psychiatric symptoms, hypertension and stroke risk.
simple: A condition of too much cortisol hormone, which can cause muscle weakness and mood changes.
more: Confirm with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression test; CK is normal in steroid myopathy and EMG is often normal. Treat the underlying cause and reduce steroids.

name: Cutaneous neurofibromas
formal: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours in the skin, characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1 and appearing from adolescence.
simple: Soft skin bumps made of nerve tissue, typical of neurofibromatosis.

name: Cyanide poisoning
formal: Cytochrome oxidase inhibition causing histotoxic hypoxia with headache, seizures, coma and lactic acidosis; delayed parkinsonism possible.
simple: Poisoning by cyanide that stops cells using oxygen, causing collapse, seizures and coma.

name: Cyanide toxicity
formal: Mitochondrial toxicity from cyanide exposure with histotoxic hypoxia and basal ganglia injury, including konzo from cassava.
simple: Harm to the body from cyanide, which stops cells using oxygen.

name: Cycad toxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from cycad seed consumption (BMAA), linked to Guam ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex.
simple: Brain harm from eating cycad seeds that has been linked to a disease similar to motor neuron disease and dementia.

name: Cyclothymic disorder
formal: Chronic mood instability with numerous hypomanic and depressive episodes insufficient for bipolar disorder.
simple: Ongoing mood swings between mild highs and lows.

name: Cystic fibrosis
formal: CFTR genetic disease with chronic lung and pancreatic disease; neurological aspects include vitamin E deficiency, stroke and ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease causing sticky mucus in lungs and gut, which can sometimes affect nerves.

name: Cytokine release encephalopathy syndrome (CRES)
formal: Reversible severe encephalopathy after CAR T therapy or T-cell engagers with cytokine release, aphasia, seizures and cerebral oedema.
simple: Confusion and brain swelling from an overactive immune response after some cancer immunotherapies.

name: Cytokine-driven neurological disease
formal: Neurological disease from excessive cytokine activity, such as in CRES, neuroinflammation and autoinflammatory conditions.
simple: Brain and nerve problems caused by too much immune signalling.

name: D-glyceric acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from GLYCTK deficiency or related defect, with hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic condition causing developmental delay and seizures.

name: DADS neuropathy
formal: Distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy, a sensory-predominant chronic demyelinating neuropathy often with IgM anti-MAG antibodies, causing distal numbness and ataxia.
simple: A chronic nerve disease with damage to the nerve insulation of the feet and hands, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Search for anti-MAG IgM; rituximab for anti-MAG cases; IVIG for others.

name: Dancing eyes syndrome
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: chaotic saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, in children with neuroblastoma or post-infectious, and in adults paraneoplastic.
simple: A condition of rapid, uncontrolled eye movements with jerky muscles and unsteadiness, often immune-related.

name: Dancing eyes–dancing feet syndrome (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infancy with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus and ataxia, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma.
simple: Rapid uncontrolled eye movements and jerking in babies, often linked with a hidden tumour.
nN: dancing eyes dancing feet syndrome myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
aN: myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy | dancing eyes dancing feet syndrome

name: Danon disease
formal: X-linked LAMP2 deficiency with vacuolar cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy, usually with intellectual disability, retinopathy, and Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern.
simple: An inherited disease causing thickened weak heart muscle, muscle weakness, and sometimes learning difficulties.
more: Biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles lacking LAMP2; confirm genetically. Heart transplant is often required; gene therapy is under study.

name: Davidenkow disease
formal: Scapuloperoneal syndrome with weakness of shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles, due to neurogenic or myopathic causes such as SPSMA or TRPV4.
simple: A rare condition in which weakness affects the shoulder and front leg muscles.
more: EMG and gene testing; supportive therapy with orthoses.

name: Deafness dystonia syndrome
formal: X-linked Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with progressive sensorineural deafness, dystonia, visual impairment and cognitive decline, with a mitochondrial import defect.
simple: An inherited condition in boys causing hearing loss in childhood followed by dystonia, vision loss and dementia.
more: Genetic testing of TIMM8A confirms it. Treatment is supportive with hearing aids or cochlear implants; dystonia and cognitive decline progress over years.

name: Degenerative spinal disease
formal: Age-related disc and facet degeneration with canal stenosis causing back pain, radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication or myelopathy.
simple: Wear and tear of the spine that can press on the spinal cord or nerves.

name: Degenerative vascular disease
formal: Atherosclerotic or small vessel degeneration causing cerebral ischaemia, white matter disease and vascular cognitive impairment.
simple: Age-related damage to blood vessels that supply the brain.

name: Degos’ disease
formal: Malignant atrophic papulosis, a thrombo-occlusive vasculopathy with porcelain-white skin papules, bowel infarction and cerebral infarcts and haemorrhage.
simple: A rare blood vessel disease with white skin spots that can cause strokes and bowel problems.

name: Dejerine–Roussy syndrome
formal: Thalamic pain syndrome after thalamic stroke with contralateral sensory loss, hemiataxia, burning pain and allodynia, later with choreoathetoid movements.
simple: One-sided burning pain and numbness that follow a stroke in the thalamus.

name: Dejerine–Sottas disease (DSD)
formal: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathy (CMT3) with severe early-onset weakness, hypertrophic nerves, marked conduction slowing and high CSF protein.
simple: An inherited nerve disease starting in childhood with severe weakness and thickened nerves.

name: Dejerine–Thomas type of olivoponto-cerebellar atrophy
formal: Old term for late-onset cerebellar atrophy with olivopontocerebellar involvement, now part of multiple system atrophy-cerebellar type.
simple: An old name for a progressive balance disease that overlaps with multiple system atrophy.
nN: dejerine thomas type of olivoponto cerebellar atrophy

name: Delayed post-hypoxic encephalopathy
formal: Neurological deterioration days to weeks after apparent recovery from hypoxic injury such as carbon monoxide, with leukoencephalopathy and cognitive change.
simple: Brain problems appearing weeks after recovery from oxygen shortage such as carbon monoxide poisoning.

name: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder
formal: Circadian disorder with persistent late sleep and wake times, causing difficulty falling asleep and waking for conventional hours.
simple: Being unable to fall asleep until very late and waking late, because the body clock runs behind.

name: Delayed-onset dystonia
formal: Dystonia appearing months or years after perinatal or acquired brain injury, such as hypoxic-ischaemic injury or kernicterus.
simple: Twisting muscle postures that develop long after a brain injury.

name: Delirium
formal: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition from medical illness, drug or withdrawal; may be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed.
simple: A sudden state of confusion and reduced awareness that fluctuates, often during illness.

name: Dementia
formal: Acquired decline in multiple cognitive domains interfering with independence, from Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal or other causes.
simple: A decline in memory and thinking that gets in the way of everyday life.

name: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
formal: Alpha-synucleinopathy with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and neuroleptic sensitivity; dementia precedes parkinsonism by one year or less.
simple: A dementia with fluctuating thinking, vivid hallucinations and stiff slow movements.
more: Amyloid and tau biomarkers are usually negative; DAT-SPECT shows reduced striatal uptake and polysomnography confirms RBD. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations; avoid typical antipsychotics.

Well-formed visual hallucinations (people, animals)
REM sleep behaviour disorder
Parkinsonism; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
inv: DAT SPECT reduced uptake; MIBG cardiac scintigraphy reduced
Polysomnography for REM sleep without atonia

case.story: Some days he is sharp, other days confused; he sees small children sitting in the living room. Gets worse rigid after haloperidol given in hospital.
case.exam: Poor attention and visuospatial copying, mild symmetric bradykinesia.
case.tests: DAT SPECT: reduced striatal uptake.
case.q: Why was haloperidol dangerous?
case.a: Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB can cause severe rigidity, confusion and even death.

Memory-led, no prominent fluctuations or hallucinations early

aN: dlb | dementia with lewy bodies | lewy body dementia | lbd | diffuse lewy body disease

det.patho: Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies are widespread in limbic and neocortical regions as well as the brainstem, often with coexisting Alzheimer pathology. Profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain loss contributes to fluctuations and hallucinations and explains the good response to cholinesterase inhibitors. It is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia in older adults.
det.clinical: Cognitive decline affects attention, executive function and visuospatial skills earlier than memory. Core features are fluctuating cognition and alertness (staring spells, daytime drowsiness), recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism. Supportive features include severe antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, syncope, autonomic dysfunction, hypersomnia, anosmia, delusions and depression. By convention, if dementia appears before or within a year of parkinsonism the label is DLB; if parkinsonism precedes dementia by more than a year it is PD dementia. Episodes of delirium-like confusion are common and may be the first presentation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 consortium criteria classify probable DLB as dementia with two or more core features, or one core feature plus an indicative biomarker. Indicative biomarkers are reduced striatal DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, low cardiac MIBG uptake, and polysomnographic REM sleep without atonia. MRI shows relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes compared with AD; FDG-PET may show occipital hypometabolism with a cingulate island sign. CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification is a promising test. Delirium, AD and vascular dementia are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) often help cognition, fluctuations and hallucinations. Levodopa can be tried cautiously for disabling parkinsonism but may worsen psychosis. For distressing psychosis use the lowest dose of quetiapine or clozapine; avoid haloperidol and other potent D2 blockers. Melatonin or clonazepam help RBD; manage orthostasis, constipation and falls. Educate carers and hospital staff about neuroleptic sensitivity.
det.prognosis: Decline is often faster than in AD, with survival of around 5–8 years from diagnosis.
pearls: Hallucinations of small people or animals in the room, often without distress, are typical.
Haloperidol in an agitated patient with DLB can trigger catastrophic rigidity — flag the notes.
Visuospatial failure (poor pentagon copy) with relatively better recall points to DLB over AD.
det.thd: DLB เป็นสมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน alpha-synuclein กระจายในเปลือกสมอง อาการหลักคือ ความตื่นตัวและความคิดขึ้นลงเป็นวัน เห็นภาพหลอนชัดเจน ละเมอตามความฝัน และมีอาการพาร์กินสัน ผู้ป่วยไวต่อยาต้านโรคจิตมากจนอาจเกร็งรุนแรงหรือเสียชีวิต วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ 2017 ร่วมกับ DAT scan, MIBG หรือ polysomnography รักษาด้วย rivastigmine หรือ donepezil ถ้าจำเป็นใช้ quetiapine ขนาดต่ำ หลีกเลี่ยง haloperidol

name: Dementia with Lewy Body
formal: Alpha-synuclein disease with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder; dementia precedes or occurs within a year of motor signs.
simple: A type of dementia with changing alertness, vivid hallucinations, stiffness and acting out dreams.
more: DaT scan, polysomnography and cognitive testing help; avoid neuroleptic drugs. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations, and survival averages about 8 years.

name: Demyelination, osmotic
formal: Central pontine or extrapontine myelinolysis from rapid sodium correction, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia and locked-in state.
simple: Brain damage caused by changing blood salt levels too fast, causing weakness and difficulty speaking and swallowing.

name: Dental disease
formal: Dental conditions such as infection or abscess that may cause trigeminal pain or neurological complications including brain abscess.
simple: Tooth or gum problems that can cause facial pain or spread infection to the brain.

name: Dentatorubral pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA)
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease (ATN1) with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia; anticipation, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by genetic testing for ATN1 CAG expansion; MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy with white matter changes. Epilepsy is more frequent in juvenile onset, and chorea in adults; therapy is symptomatic and prevalence is higher in Japan.

name: Dentatorubro-pallidoloysian atrophy
formal: Misspelled form of DRPLA, CAG-repeat ATN1 disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing poor coordination, jerky movements, seizures and dementia.

name: Dentatorubro-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA)
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia, more common in Japan.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing clumsiness, jerky movements, seizures and memory loss.

name: Dermatomyositis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; perifascicular atrophy on biopsy; associated with malignancy and anti-MDA5, Mi-2 or TIF1 antibodies.
simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and a typical skin rash.
more: Check CK and myositis-specific antibodies, and screen for malignancy with age-appropriate imaging; MRI shows muscle oedema and EMG shows irritability. First-line is corticosteroids with methotrexate, azathioprine or IVIG; skin disease needs sun protection.

Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign, nailfold changes

Biopsy: perifascicular atrophy

case.q: What must be searched for next?
case.a: An underlying malignancy (anti-TIF1γ carries a high cancer association).

Older, asymmetric finger flexor/quadriceps weakness, steroid unresponsive

det.patho: An immune-mediated myopathy driven largely by type I interferon, with complement-mediated injury to small vessels causing capillary loss and perifascicular fibre damage. Myositis-specific antibodies define clinical subsets: anti-Mi-2 (classic skin and muscle, good response), anti-TIF1γ and anti-NXP2 (cancer association in adults), anti-MDA5 (minimal myositis, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, notable in East Asia) and anti-SAE. Adult disease carries an increased risk of malignancy, especially within three years of diagnosis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness evolves over weeks to months, often with myalgia, dysphagia and neck flexor weakness. Skin signs may precede weakness: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over the knuckles, V-sign and shawl sign, nailfold capillary changes and mechanic's hands. Some patients have skin disease without weakness (amyopathic). Interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis (especially in juvenile disease) and cardiac involvement occur. Ovarian, lung, gastric, nasopharyngeal and haematological cancers are typical associations.
det.diagnosis: The EULAR/ACR 2017 classification criteria combine age, weakness pattern, skin features, CK, anti-Jo-1 and biopsy findings. CK is often raised but may be normal. EMG shows an irritable myopathy and MRI STIR shows muscle and fascial oedema guiding biopsy. Biopsy features perifascicular atrophy, MxA expression and capillary loss. Screen all adults for cancer (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, gynaecological and age-appropriate tests, PET in high-risk subsets) and for lung involvement with HRCT and lung function.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day, with IV pulses in severe cases) combined early with methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to limit steroid exposure. IVIG is effective for refractory disease and dysphagia, and rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors and JAK inhibitors are further options. Anti-MDA5 ILD needs aggressive combined immunosuppression. Treat associated cancer, protect skin from sun, use hydroxychloroquine for skin disease, and give rehabilitation plus bone and infection prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with treatment, though relapses are common; survival is reduced mainly by malignancy and rapidly progressive lung disease.
pearls: Rash plus proximal weakness in an adult = search for cancer.
Anti-MDA5: little weakness, ulcerating skin lesions, rapidly progressive lung disease.
Perifascicular atrophy on biopsy is the classic pathological clue.
det.thd: Dermatomyositis เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อและผิวหนังอักเสบ เกี่ยวข้องกับ interferon และการทำลายหลอดเลือดเล็กในกล้ามเนื้อ อาการคืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสองข้างเท่ากันภายในหลายสัปดาห์ ผื่นม่วงรอบตา (heliotrope) ผื่นที่ข้อนิ้ว (Gottron) และอาจมีปอดอักเสบ ในผู้ใหญ่ต้องค้นหามะเร็งแฝงโดยเฉพาะเมื่อพบ anti-TIF1γ วินิจฉัยด้วย CK, myositis antibodies, MRI และตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ perifascicular atrophy รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ เช่น methotrexate และให้ IVIG ในรายที่ดื้อยา

name: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs)
formal: Severe early-onset epilepsies in which epileptic activity and the underlying cause contribute to developmental slowing, e.g. West, Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes.
simple: Severe childhood epilepsies in which frequent seizures also hold back development.

name: Devic’s disease
formal: Neuromyelitis optica, an antibody-mediated (AQP4-IgG) disease with optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, plus area postrema syndrome.
simple: An immune disease that attacks the eye nerves and spinal cord, causing vision loss and weakness.

name: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Small-fibre autonomic neuropathy in diabetes causing orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, resting tachycardia, and hypoglycaemia unawareness.
simple: Damage to the nerves that run automatic body functions in people with diabetes, causing dizziness, stomach and bladder problems.
more: Autonomic reflex testing and tilt table assess it. Tight glucose control, fludrocortisone or midodrine, prokinetics, and symptomatic care are used.

name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
formal: Metabolic complication of insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia and acidosis; may cause cerebral oedema, particularly in children, and altered consciousness.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and acid build-up, causing drowsiness and sometimes brain swelling.

name: Diabetic mononeuropathies
formal: Focal nerve lesions in diabetes, including cranial nerve III and VI palsies, and median, ulnar, and peroneal neuropathies, mediated by ischaemia and entrapment.
simple: Damage to a single nerve in people with diabetes, such as a sudden eye-movement palsy.
more: Control glucose, treat entrapment; cranial palsies usually recover in 2 to 3 months.

name: Diabetic neuropathic cachexia
formal: Acute painful diabetic neuropathy with severe weight loss, burning pain, allodynia, and depression, often after starting insulin or glycaemic improvement.
simple: A rare form of painful diabetic nerve damage with marked weight loss, often after blood sugar is brought under control.
more: Pain control with neuropathic agents and good nutrition; it generally improves spontaneously within about a year.

name: Diabetic neuropathies
formal: Neuropathies due to diabetes: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, radiculoplexopathy, mononeuropathies and cranial neuropathies.
simple: Nerve damage caused by diabetes, causing numbness, pain, weakness or dizziness.

name: Diabetic neuropathy
formal: Most common form is length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy with painful feet, numbness and loss of ankle reflexes, from chronic hyperglycaemia and small-vessel disease.
simple: Nerve damage from diabetes, usually causing numb, tingling or painful feet.

name: Diabetic polyradiculopathy
formal: Diabetic lumbosacral or thoracic radiculoplexus syndrome with asymmetric severe pain, weight loss, and proximal leg weakness, thought to be microvasculitic and immune-mediated.
simple: Sudden severe pain and weakness in the thigh or trunk in people with diabetes, usually on one side.
more: MRI excludes compressive lesions; nerve biopsy may show microvasculitis. Treatment is pain control and rehabilitation, sometimes with immunotherapy; recovery is slow.

name: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy
formal: Painful asymmetric lumbosacral or cervical radiculoplexus syndrome in diabetes, with proximal weakness and weight loss, linked to microvasculitis.
simple: A painful nerve disease in diabetes affecting the thigh or hip, with wasting and weight loss.
more: Pain control, glycaemic control, and sometimes immunotherapy such as IVIG or steroids; recovery over months to years.

tempoNote: Pain and weakness evolve over weeks to months; slow partial recovery

Severe thigh/hip pain, then asymmetric proximal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, hip flexors)
Absent knee jerk; often spreads to the other side; caused by microvasculitis

case.a: Gradual improvement over months to years, often incomplete; pain control and rehabilitation are central (immunotherapy is debated).

Symmetric, demyelinating NCS, no weight loss
Systemic vasculitis markers, upper limb mononeuropathies

det.patho: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy is caused by an immune-mediated microvasculitis of small epineurial and perineurial vessels, leading to ischaemic axonal injury across roots, plexus and peripheral nerves. It typically occurs in older people with type 2 diabetes, often with relatively mild or recently improved glycaemic control, so it is not simply a consequence of hyperglycaemia. Similar non-diabetic and cervical/thoracic forms exist.
det.clinical: Onset is usually with intense unilateral thigh, hip or buttock pain, followed within days to weeks by weakness of proximal leg muscles (quadriceps, iliopsoas, adductors) and sometimes distal muscles. Substantial unintentional weight loss is very common. The opposite leg is often involved weeks to months later. The knee jerk is lost on the affected side, and patients may need walking aids or a wheelchair at the nadir. Thoracic radiculopathy can coexist, causing abdominal pain or bulging.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture plus EMG showing active denervation in multiple lumbosacral root and nerve territories, including paraspinals. MRI of the lumbar spine and plexus excludes compressive or neoplastic lesions and may show plexus enhancement. CSF protein is often raised. Consider malignancy, lymphoma infiltration, retroperitoneal haematoma, CIDP and vasculitis in the differential.
det.treatment: Management is largely supportive: aggressive neuropathic pain control, physiotherapy, falls prevention and maintaining diabetes control. Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone or IVIG) has been used, particularly for severe pain, but randomised evidence shows benefit mainly for pain and sensory symptoms rather than motor recovery, so use is individualised. Steroids worsen glycaemic control and require close monitoring.
det.prognosis: The illness is monophasic in most; pain improves first and strength recovers gradually over months to years, often incompletely. Recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Painful thigh wasting with weight loss in a diabetic: DLRPN — exclude cancer and compression.
Often follows a period of improved or tight glucose control.
Contralateral spread is common; warn the patient.
det.thd: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) เกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กที่เลี้ยงรากประสาทและ plexus อักเสบ มักในผู้สูงอายุเบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 ซึ่งคุมน้ำตาลได้ไม่แย่ เริ่มด้วยปวดต้นขาหรือสะโพกรุนแรงข้างเดียว น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง knee jerk หาย และมักลามไปอีกข้าง วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และ MRI เพื่อแยกการกดทับหรือมะเร็ง รักษาหลักคือคุมปวด กายภาพ ส่วน steroid/IVIG พิจารณาเป็นราย ๆ และค่อย ๆ ฟื้นตัวเป็นเดือนถึงปี

name: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
formal: Cerebral oedema from rapid osmotic shifts during haemodialysis, causing headache, nausea, confusion and seizures.
simple: Headache, confusion or seizures during or after dialysis because of fast changes in body fluids.

name: Dialysis encephalopathy
formal: Progressive encephalopathy in long-term dialysis from aluminium toxicity, with speech arrest, myoclonus, seizures and dementia.
simple: A brain disorder in long-term dialysis patients, once from aluminium, with speech problems and seizures.

name: Diaphragmatic myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic or irregular involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, causing hiccup-like belly jerks, often from phrenic nerve irritation or drugs.
simple: Repeated jerks of the breathing muscle that cause belly movements like hiccups.

name: Diaphragmatic myoclonus/flutter
formal: Rhythmic involuntary diaphragm contractions, with 'belly dancer' movements, seen with phrenic nerve irritation or brainstem lesions.
simple: Repeated jerks or flutters of the breathing muscle.

name: Diazepam akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to diazepam, usually on withdrawal, with inability to sit still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness related to using or stopping diazepam.

name: Diffuse astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 2 infiltrating glioma, often IDH mutated, in young adults presenting with seizures; slow growth with eventual malignant transformation.
simple: A slow-growing but spreading brain tumour, often first noticed through seizures.

name: Diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia
formal: Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome) with sudden skin thickening and induration of limbs sparing hands, peripheral eosinophilia, and inflammation of fascia on MRI or biopsy.
simple: A rare condition where the tissue layer under the skin thickens and tightens the limbs, often after strenuous exercise.
more: Full-thickness biopsy including fascia is diagnostic; corticosteroids work well, with methotrexate as an adjunct.

name: Diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia/Shulman syndrome
formal: Eosinophilic fasciitis with rapid skin and fascial induration, peripheral eosinophilia, groove sign, and responsiveness to corticosteroids.
simple: A rare disease where tissue under the skin thickens, tightening the limbs.
more: Deep biopsy and MRI; prednisolone with methotrexate for steroid sparing.
nN: diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia shulman syndrome

name: Diffuse inflammatory lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)
formal: HIV-related CD8 lymphocytosis with salivary gland swelling, sicca and extraglandular disease including peripheral neuropathy, meningitis and cranial neuropathies.
simple: A condition in HIV with dry mouth, swollen glands and sometimes nerve damage.

name: Diffuse Lewy body disease (DLBD)
formal: Alpha-synucleinopathy with widespread cortical and subcortical Lewy bodies, causing dementia, parkinsonism and psychosis; synonym for dementia with Lewy bodies.
simple: A brain disease with protein deposits that causes dementia, hallucinations and stiffness.
more: Pathologically widespread Lewy bodies on alpha-synuclein staining, often with Alzheimer-type changes; DAT-SPECT is abnormal. Management follows DLB with cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid dopamine antagonists, since neuroleptic sensitivity is severe.

name: Diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification (DNTC)
formal: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and basal ganglia calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism, mainly in Japan.
simple: A rare dementia with tangles and calcium deposits in the brain.
nN: diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification dntc
aN: dntc | diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification

name: Diffuse NFTs with calcification
formal: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism.
simple: A rare dementia with brain tangles and calcium deposits.

name: Diffuse non-necrotising cachectic myopathy
formal: Muscle wasting in cachexia from cancer or chronic disease with atrophic non-necrotic fibres, without inflammation.
simple: Muscle wasting and weakness in people who are severely underweight from long-term illness.

name: Diphasic dyskinesias
formal: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias occurring at onset and end of dose, with improvement during peak dose, mainly involving the legs.
simple: Involuntary movements in Parkinson disease that appear when levodopa starts and wears off.

name: Diphasic dystonia
formal: Levodopa-induced dystonia occurring when drug levels rise and fall, mostly in legs.
simple: Painful muscle twisting in Parkinson disease when levodopa starts to work or wear off.

name: Diphtheritic neuropathy
formal: Demyelinating neuropathy following diphtheria toxin, starting with palatal and accommodation paralysis, then generalised sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: Nerve damage that follows infection with diphtheria bacteria, with throat and eye muscle weakness first.
more: Antitoxin and antibiotics for infection; prevention by vaccination; most patients recover fully.
