Calf pseudohypertrophy, lumbar lordosis, waddling gait
Loss of ambulation in early teens without treatment; scoliosis, respiratory failure
Cardiomyopathy and learning difficulties are common
inv: CK very high (often >10,000 U/L)
DMD gene deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing
Echocardiography/cardiac MRI and lung function surveillance

case.story: Walked late at 18 months; falls often and cannot keep up with friends; climbs stairs one step at a time.
case.exam: Gowers manoeuvre, big firm calves, waddling gait, reflexes reduced at the knees.
case.tests: CK 18,500 U/L; deletion of DMD exons 45–50 (out of frame).
case.q: Why does it matter whether the deletion is in frame or out of frame?
case.a: Out-of-frame deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame deletions leave a shortened protein (milder Becker). It also guides exon-skipping eligibility.

ddx.pt: Later onset, walks beyond 16, in-frame deletion, partial dystrophin
Fasciculation, normal or mildly raised CK, neurogenic EMG
Either sex, autosomal inheritance, normal dystrophin

aN: dmd | duchenne muscular dystrophy | duchenne | dystrophinopathy | pseudohypertrophic muscular dystrophy

det.patho: DMD is X-linked and caused by mutations (mostly deletions) in the dystrophin gene that disrupt the reading frame and abolish dystrophin expression. Without dystrophin the sarcolemma is fragile during contraction, leading to repeated fibre necrosis, inflammation, failed regeneration and replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. It affects about 1 in 3,500–5,000 male births, and about a third of cases arise from new mutations.
det.clinical: Boys show delayed walking and speech, frequent falls, toe walking, Gowers manoeuvre and calf pseudohypertrophy between 2 and 5 years. Without treatment, walking is lost around age 10–12, followed by scoliosis, respiratory failure and dilated cardiomyopathy. Learning difficulties, ADHD and autism spectrum features are more common. Female carriers can have cardiomyopathy or mild weakness.
det.diagnosis: A very high CK (often 50–100 times normal) is the first clue. Genetic testing with MLPA for deletions and duplications, followed by sequencing if negative, confirms the diagnosis and identifies eligibility for mutation-specific therapies. Muscle biopsy is now only needed if genetics is inconclusive. Baseline cardiac, respiratory and bone health assessments are required.
det.treatment: Daily corticosteroids (prednisone or deflazacort; vamorolone as an alternative with fewer growth and bone effects) are standard from early childhood and prolong walking. Exon-skipping antisense drugs are approved in some countries for eligible deletions, and givinostat is approved in some regions. An AAV micro-dystrophin gene therapy is licensed in some countries with restrictions after serious liver-related safety events. Multidisciplinary care includes cardioprotection with ACE inhibitors, non-invasive ventilation, scoliosis surgery, bone health and stress-dose steroid awareness.
det.prognosis: With modern multidisciplinary care, survival commonly extends into the 30s and beyond; cardiac and respiratory failure are the main causes of death.
pearls: A very high ALT/AST in a young boy may come from muscle — check CK before investigating the liver.
Avoid suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics because of rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalaemia risk.
Reading frame, not deletion size, predicts Duchenne versus Becker.
det.thd: DMD เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน dystrophin ทำให้ไม่มีโปรตีน dystrophin เยื่อหุ้มเซลล์กล้ามเนื้อจึงฉีกขาดง่ายและถูกแทนที่ด้วยไขมันและพังผืด เด็กชายอายุ 2–5 ปี มีอาการเดินช้า ล้มบ่อย ลุกจากพื้นลำบาก น่องโต และ CK สูงมาก การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน การรักษาหลักคือสเตียรอยด์ทุกวัน ร่วมกับการดูแลหัวใจ การหายใจ และกระดูกสันหลัง และบางรายอาจได้ยาเฉพาะตามชนิดการกลายพันธุ์

name: Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy
formal: X-linked dystrophin-deficiency myopathy with proximal weakness from early childhood, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, very high CK, loss of ambulation by teens and cardiorespiratory failure.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in boys where muscles gradually weaken from early childhood, eventually affecting walking, breathing and the heart.

name: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours (DNET)
formal: Benign, cortically based glioneuronal tumours, typically temporal, presenting with drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children or young adults and cured by resection.
simple: Slow-growing harmless brain tumours near the surface that cause hard-to-treat seizures in young people and can be cured by surgery.

name: Dysexecutive syndrome
formal: Frontal-subcortical cognitive syndrome with impaired planning, set shifting, inhibition and working memory, causing poor judgement and behavioural change; seen after frontal lesions, trauma or in neurodegeneration.
simple: Difficulty planning, organising, solving problems and controlling behaviour because of frontal lobe problems.
more: Assessed with the frontal assessment battery and trail making. Treat the cause and use cognitive rehabilitation; response to drugs is limited.

name: Dysferlinopathy (LGMD R2/2B)
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle or distal (Miyoshi) myopathy from dysferlin mutations, with young-adult onset, very high CK, calf atrophy and inflammatory-looking biopsies.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in young adults that weakens the hip, shoulder or calf muscles slowly over time.

name: Dyskinesia
formal: Involuntary, excessive, purposeless movements, including chorea, athetosis and stereotypies, seen as levodopa-induced or tardive syndromes and reflecting basal ganglia dysfunction.
simple: Unwanted, uncontrolled twisting or jerking movements, often caused by long-term medicines for Parkinson disease or psychiatric illness.
more: Treatment depends on cause; levodopa-induced dyskinesia is managed by amantadine, dose fractionation or DBS, while tardive dyskinesia is managed with VMAT2 inhibitors. Examine for peak-dose pattern versus biphasic pattern in Parkinson disease.

name: Dysmyelinating diseases
formal: Inherited disorders of myelin formation or maintenance, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy and Pelizaeus-Merzbacher, producing progressive motor and cognitive decline with white matter change.
simple: Genetic diseases in which the protective coating of nerve fibres forms badly or breaks down, causing progressive weakness and developmental loss.
more: MRI shows symmetrical white matter signal change; enzyme assays and gene tests identify the type. Stem cell transplant or gene therapy helps some; most care is supportive.

name: Dystonia
formal: Movement disorder of sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting, repetitive movements or abnormal postures, arising from basal ganglia and cerebello-thalamic network dysfunction.
simple: A condition where muscles tighten on their own and twist the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, positions.
more: Classified as isolated, combined or acquired with focal, segmental or generalised distribution; MRI is normal in isolated forms. Treat with anticholinergics, botulinum toxin for focal forms, and DBS of globus pallidus internus for generalised dystonia.

name: Dystonia and retinitis pigmentosa
formal: Combination of dystonia with pigmentary retinal degeneration, seen in neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation phenotypes such as PKAN (HARP) and some mitochondrial disorders.
simple: A rare inherited combination of twisting muscle spasms and slowly worsening vision from damage to the retina.

name: Dystonia parkinsonism
formal: Syndrome combining dystonia with bradykinesia and rigidity, seen in X-linked Lubag, rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism, dopa-responsive dystonia and young-onset Parkinson disease.
simple: A condition with both twisting muscle spasms and Parkinson-like slowness and stiffness, often starting at a younger age.

name: Dystonia with neural deafness
formal: Rare X-linked disorder (Mohr–Tranebjaerg, DDON) with progressive sensorineural deafness, dystonia, visual loss and cognitive decline from TIMM8A mutations.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing hearing loss, twisting muscle spasms, sight problems and memory decline.

name: Dystonia-parkinsonism
formal: Syndrome combining dystonia with bradykinesia and rigidity, seen in X-linked Lubag, rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism, dopa-responsive dystonia and young-onset Parkinson disease.
simple: A condition with both twisting muscle spasms and Parkinson-like slowness and stiffness, often starting at a younger age.

name: Dystonia-plus syndromes
formal: Group of genetic disorders where dystonia coexists with another movement disorder, such as dopa-responsive dystonia, myoclonus-dystonia and rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism, without neurodegeneration.
simple: A group of inherited conditions where muscle spasms come together with another movement problem, such as jerks or Parkinson-like symptoms.

name: Dystonic lipidosis (Niemann–Pick type C disease)
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal cholesterol transport disorder (NPC1 or NPC2) with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, cognitive decline, gelastic cataplexy and hepatosplenomegaly.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease causing clumsiness, twisting spasms, trouble looking up and down, and declining thinking.
nN: dystonic lipidosis niemann pick type c disease
aN: niemann pick type c disease | dystonic lipidosis

name: Dystonic storms
formal: Life-threatening episodes of severe generalised dystonia (status dystonicus) with fever, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory compromise, often triggered by infection or drug changes in people with dystonia.
simple: A dangerous flare of severe, constant muscle spasms that can cause exhaustion, muscle breakdown and breathing problems.

name: Dystonic tremor
formal: Irregular, jerky, position-dependent tremor in a body part affected by dystonia, which often improves with a sensory trick or by relaxing into the null position.
simple: A shaking that occurs in a part of the body affected by dystonia and usually changes with position or touch.

name: Dystonic writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia triggered by writing, causing abnormal finger and wrist postures, often with tremor, and reflecting abnormal sensorimotor cortical plasticity.
simple: Muscle spasms in the hand and fingers that appear only when writing, making the handwriting difficult or painful.

name: Dystrophinopathies
formal: Spectrum of X-linked disorders caused by dystrophin gene mutations, from Duchenne and Becker dystrophy to isolated cardiomyopathy and asymptomatic hyperCKaemia in carriers.
simple: A family of inherited muscle diseases caused by faults in one gene, ranging from severe childhood weakness to mild adult disease.
more: Diagnosed with DMD gene testing by MLPA or sequencing and muscle dystrophin immunostaining. Treatment includes glucocorticoids, exon-skipping or gene therapy in selected mutations, plus cardiac and respiratory care; female carriers need cardiac screening.

name: Edentulous oral dyskinesia
formal: Orofacial dyskinesia of chewing, lip and tongue movements in elderly people who lack teeth, thought to be related to loss of sensory feedback and sometimes to neuroleptic exposure.
simple: Repeated chewing, lip or tongue movements that happen without control, mostly in older people who have lost their teeth.

name: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
formal: Heritable connective tissue disorders with joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility and tissue fragility; neurological complications include vascular dissection, aneurysm, neuropathic pain and Chiari symptoms.
simple: An inherited weakness of the body's connective tissue causing very flexible joints and fragile skin and blood vessels.

name: Electrical status epilepticus in sleep
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy with near-continuous spike-wave discharges during non-REM sleep and regression in cognition and behaviour, as in Landau–Kleffner and CSWS syndromes.
simple: A childhood epilepsy disorder where abnormal brain electrical activity during sleep leads to loss of language, learning or behaviour skills.

name: Electron microscopy multi/minicore myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with multifocal cores lacking oxidative activity on biopsy, mostly from RYR1 or SEPN1 variants; hypotonia, proximal weakness, scoliosis and respiratory involvement.
simple: A muscle disease present from early life where muscle samples show small patches lacking energy enzymes, causing weak, floppy muscles.
more: Diagnosis by muscle biopsy with oxidative stains and genetic testing (RYR1, SEPN1). Inheritance varies; care is supportive with respiratory and orthopaedic monitoring; RYR1 cases carry malignant hyperthermia risk.

name: Electrontransferring flavoprotein (ETF) deficiency
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency from ETF or ETF-dehydrogenase defects, impairing fatty-acid and amino-acid oxidation; causes lipid storage myopathy with episodic metabolic decompensation.
simple: An inherited fault in energy processing of fats and proteins that causes muscle weakness and episodes of illness when the body is stressed.
more: Elevated acylcarnitines and organic aciduria; autosomal recessive (ETFA, ETFB, ETFDH). The late-onset form often responds dramatically to riboflavin, plus diet modification and avoidance of fasting.

name: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy
formal: Muscular dystrophy with early joint contractures, humeroperoneal weakness and cardiac conduction disease, due to EMD, LMNA or related nuclear envelope gene variants.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with stiff joints, weakness in upper arms and lower legs, and heart rhythm problems.
more: X-linked (EMD) or autosomal dominant (LMNA) forms; CK mildly raised. Cardiac monitoring with pacemaker or defibrillator is life-saving; sudden cardiac death is the main prognostic concern.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมเอเมอรี-ไดรฟัส — ข้อติดยึดตั้งแต่ต้น ต้นแขน-ปลายขาอ่อนแรง และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ
feat: Triad: early contractures (elbows, Achilles, posterior neck), humero-peroneal weakness, cardiac conduction disease
Contractures appear before significant weakness
Heart block and atrial arrhythmias can cause sudden death
inv: ECG/Holter, echocardiography
EMD (X-linked) or LMNA (autosomal) gene testing

case.story: Cannot fully straighten his elbows or bend his neck forward since childhood; recently fainted while playing.
case.exam: Elbow and ankle contractures, rigid spine, weak biceps and ankle dorsiflexors.
case.tests: ECG: slow atrial rhythm with first-degree block; EMD variant.
case.q: What intervention may be life-saving?
case.a: A pacemaker or ICD — cardiac conduction disease is the main cause of death in EDMD.

ddx.pt: Calf hypertrophy, no early contractures, DMD in-frame deletion
Facial weakness, asymmetric winging, no early contractures

det.patho: EDMD is caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins of the nuclear envelope: emerin (EMD, X-linked), lamin A/C (LMNA, usually autosomal dominant), and less often FHL1 and others. Defective nuclear lamina mechanics and gene regulation damage skeletal and cardiac muscle. The cardiac conduction system is particularly vulnerable.
det.clinical: Elbow, heel-cord and posterior neck contractures (rigid spine) develop early in childhood, often before notable weakness. Weakness and wasting follow a humero-peroneal distribution and later become more widespread. Cardiac disease includes atrial standstill, conduction block, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and dilated cardiomyopathy, typically from the late teens or 20s. LMNA disease may also include lipodystrophy and has a high risk of sudden death.
det.diagnosis: The clinical triad suggests the diagnosis, and genetic testing for EMD, LMNA and related genes confirms it. CK is normal or moderately raised. ECG, Holter monitoring, echocardiography and cardiac MRI are essential at diagnosis and regularly thereafter. Muscle MRI may show characteristic involvement patterns, and emerin immunostaining is absent in X-linked cases.
det.treatment: Cardiac management is the priority: pacemaker for conduction disease, and an ICD for LMNA patients at high arrhythmic risk even without severe heart failure. Anticoagulation is often needed for atrial standstill or fibrillation because of stroke risk. Physiotherapy and surgical release may help contractures, and respiratory function needs monitoring. Female EMD carriers need cardiac screening.
det.prognosis: Survival depends largely on cardiac management; sudden cardiac death is the main threat, whereas muscle weakness progresses slowly.
pearls: Contractures before weakness plus a slow pulse in a young man: think EDMD.
A pacemaker alone may not prevent sudden death in LMNA disease — ICD is often needed.
det.thd: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy เกิดจากความผิดปกติของโปรตีนเยื่อหุ้มนิวเคลียส เช่น emerin และ lamin A/C ลักษณะเด่นคือข้อติดตั้งแต่เด็ก เช่น ข้อศอก เอ็นร้อยหวาย และคอ ร่วมกับต้นแขนและหน้าแข้งอ่อนแรง และที่สำคัญที่สุดคือหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะหรือนำไฟฟ้าผิดปกติจนอาจเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีนร่วมกับ ECG และ Holter การรักษาเน้นป้องกันการเสียชีวิตจากหัวใจด้วย pacemaker หรือ ICD และให้ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophies (EDMDs)
formal: Nuclear envelope disorders (EMD, LMNA and others) with early joint contractures of elbows, Achilles and spine, humeroperoneal weakness and cardiac conduction defects with arrhythmia risk.
simple: Inherited muscle diseases with tight joints, weakness in upper arms and lower legs, and heart rhythm problems.

name: Emotional stress ballism
formal: Hemiballism-like violent flinging movements triggered by emotional stress, usually functional in nature or rarely a paroxysmal hyperkinetic disorder.
simple: Sudden wild flinging movements of a limb brought on by emotional stress.

name: Encephalitis
formal: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma, usually viral or autoimmune, presenting with fever, headache, altered consciousness, seizures and focal deficits; herpes simplex is the commonest treatable cause.
simple: Swelling of the brain, usually from a virus or the immune system, causing fever, confusion, seizures and sometimes lasting damage.

name: Encephalitis lethargica
formal: Post-epidemic (1916 to 1930s) encephalitic illness with sleep inversion, oculogyric crises and later postencephalitic parkinsonism, likely due to basal ganglia and midbrain involvement; cause remains unclear.
simple: A rare illness that spread widely a century ago, causing extreme sleepiness, eye movement spasms and later Parkinson-like symptoms.

name: Encephalitis lethargica (Von Economo’s disease)
formal: Post-epidemic (1916 to 1930s) encephalitic illness with sleep inversion, oculogyric crises and later postencephalitic parkinsonism, likely due to basal ganglia and midbrain involvement; cause remains unclear.
simple: A rare illness that spread widely a century ago, causing extreme sleepiness, eye movement spasms and later Parkinson-like symptoms.

name: Encephalo-myelo-radiculopathy
formal: Combined inflammatory or infectious involvement of brain, spinal cord and nerve roots, as in Lyme disease, neurosyphilis, and some viral and parainfectious syndromes.
simple: Damage to the brain, spinal cord and nerve roots at the same time, usually from infection or inflammation.

name: Encephalomyelitis
formal: Inflammation affecting both brain and spinal cord, either post-infectious (ADEM), autoimmune or viral, causing multifocal deficits, encephalopathy and often demyelinating lesions on MRI.
simple: Swelling in both the brain and spinal cord, often after an infection, causing weakness, numbness and confusion.

name: Encephalomyelitis with rigidity
formal: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), a stiff-person-spectrum disorder often linked to glycine receptor or GAD antibodies, causing spasms, brainstem signs and autonomic instability.
simple: A rare immune illness causing severe muscle stiffness, painful spasms, jerks and brainstem problems.

name: Encephalomyopathy
formal: Combined brain and muscle involvement, classically in mitochondrial disease such as MELAS, MERRF or Leigh syndrome, with seizures, stroke-like episodes, myopathy and lactic acidosis.
simple: A condition affecting both the brain and the muscles, often from faulty cell energy production.
more: Lactate, MRI, muscle biopsy and mitochondrial DNA or nuclear gene testing. Treatment is supportive with cofactors such as CoQ10 and avoiding valproate.

name: Encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction causing altered consciousness or cognition from metabolic, toxic, infective, inflammatory or hypoxic causes, often with fluctuating attention and slowed EEG.
simple: A general state of brain malfunction causing confusion or drowsiness that can result from many illnesses, toxins or medicines.

name: End-plate acetylcholinesterase (AChE) deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from COLQ mutations that remove acetylcholinesterase from the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged endplate currents, repetitive compound muscle action potentials and fatigable weakness.
simple: An inherited problem where the enzyme that clears the nerve signal chemical at the muscle junction is missing, causing weakness that tires easily.
more: Autosomal recessive COLQ; repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus on EMG. Cholinesterase inhibitors worsen it; ephedrine or salbutamol often helps.

name: End-plate AChE deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from COLQ mutations that remove acetylcholinesterase from the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged endplate currents, repetitive compound muscle action potentials and fatigable weakness.
simple: An inherited problem where the enzyme that clears the nerve signal chemical at the muscle junction is missing, causing weakness that tires easily.
more: Autosomal recessive COLQ; repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus on EMG. Cholinesterase inhibitors worsen it; ephedrine or salbutamol often helps.

name: Endocarditis
formal: Infection of the heart valves that causes neurological complications through septic emboli, mycotic aneurysms, cerebral abscess, haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke.
simple: An infection of the heart's inner lining or valves that can send clots or germs to the brain and cause strokes.

name: Endocrine myopathies
formal: Muscle weakness, usually proximal, caused by hormone imbalance such as thyroid disease, Cushing syndrome, steroid excess, hyperparathyroidism or acromegaly, typically with normal or mildly raised CK.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by hormone problems such as an overactive or underactive thyroid or too much steroid.
more: Diagnosed by hormone assay such as TSH, cortisol or calcium with EMG and CK, which are often normal or mildly raised. Weakness improves on correcting the hormone abnormality, usually over months, and myopathy may present before other signs.

name: Endolymphatic hydrops
formal: Distension of the endolymphatic space of the inner ear, underlying Meniere disease, causing episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
simple: Too much fluid pressure in the inner ear, causing spinning attacks, hearing loss, ringing and a feeling of fullness in the ear.

name: Enhanced physiological tremor (EPT)
formal: Fine, rapid postural tremor of 8 to 12 Hz that is an exaggeration of normal tremor due to anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, drugs or fatigue and resolves when the cause is removed.
simple: A fine, fast hand shake that is stronger than usual because of things like caffeine, stress, an overactive thyroid or some medicines.

name: Entrapment neuropathies
formal: Focal nerve injuries from compression at anatomical tunnels, such as carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel and fibular head, causing local sensory loss, weakness and slowed conduction across the site.
simple: Nerves pinched at narrow spots in the body, such as the wrist or elbow, causing tingling, numbness or weakness.

name: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome
formal: Epidemic multisystem illness linked to contaminated L-tryptophan, characterised by severe myalgia, marked eosinophilia, fasciitis, and later sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
simple: A serious illness tied to contaminated tryptophan supplements, causing severe muscle pain and nerve damage.
more: Stop tryptophan; corticosteroids are used. Neuropathy and myalgia may persist for years in many patients.

name: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)
formal: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis in people with asthma and eosinophilia, frequently causing mononeuritis multiplex and occasionally stroke or cranial neuropathy.
simple: An immune disease causing inflamed blood vessels in people with asthma, which can damage nerves and lead to weakness or numbness.

name: Eosinophilic myopathic syndromes
formal: Muscle disorders with eosinophilic infiltration, including eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome and focal eosinophilic myositis, causing myalgia, weakness and peripheral eosinophilia.
simple: Muscle conditions in which a type of white blood cell builds up in the muscles, causing pain and weakness.

name: Eosinophilic myopathy
formal: Myopathy with prominent eosinophilic infiltration in muscle, in hypereosinophilic syndromes, EGPA, parasitic infection, or drug reactions, causing myalgia and weakness.
simple: Muscle inflammation with large numbers of eosinophil white cells, causing pain and weakness.
more: Biopsy shows eosinophils and CK is raised. Treat the cause and use corticosteroids.

name: Ependymomas
formal: Glial tumours arising from ependymal cells lining the ventricles or central canal, typically in the posterior fossa in children or the spinal cord in adults, causing hydrocephalus or myelopathy.
simple: Brain or spinal cord tumours growing from cells lining the fluid spaces, which can block fluid flow or press on the spinal cord.

name: Epilepsia partialis continua
formal: Continuous focal motor seizures, usually of a limb or face, lasting hours to years, caused by cortical lesions, stroke, Rasmussen encephalitis or metabolic derangement and often refractory to treatment.
simple: Constant small jerking of one part of the body, such as a hand, that lasts for hours or longer because of an irritated area of the brain.
more: EEG may show correlated spikes; MRI may reveal cortical lesion or be normal. Often resistant to antiepileptics; consider immunotherapy or hemispherectomy in Rasmussen, correct hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia, and note Kozhevnikov syndrome in Russia.

name: Epilepsy
formal: Chronic brain disorder with a predisposition to unprovoked recurrent seizures from abnormal synchronised neuronal discharge, with structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune or unknown causes.
simple: A condition in which the brain repeatedly sends abnormal electrical signals, causing seizures that happen without an obvious trigger.

name: Epileptic myoclonus
formal: Brief, shock-like muscle jerks of cortical origin in epilepsy, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and progressive myoclonic epilepsies, with time-locked EEG spike or polyspike discharges.
simple: Quick, lightning-like jerks of the muscles caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

name: Epileptic syndromes
formal: Electroclinical entities defined by age of onset, seizure types, EEG findings and aetiology, such as childhood absence epilepsy, West syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, guiding treatment and prognosis.
simple: Recognised patterns of epilepsy that share the same age of onset, kind of seizures and brain-wave pattern.

name: Episodic ataxia
formal: Group of autosomal dominant channelopathies with recurrent attacks of cerebellar ataxia, often triggered by stress or exertion, with interictal myokymia or nystagmus in some types.
simple: Inherited conditions in which attacks of clumsiness and unsteadiness come and go, often brought on by stress or exercise.

name: Episodic ataxia type 1
formal: KCNA1 potassium channel disorder with brief attacks of ataxia lasting seconds to minutes, startle or exercise provoked, with interictal myokymia and neuromyotonia.
simple: An inherited condition with short attacks of unsteadiness lasting minutes, with muscle twitching between attacks.

name: Episodic ataxia type 2
formal: CACNA1A calcium channel disorder with hours-long attacks of ataxia, vertigo and nausea, interictal downbeat nystagmus, and a response to acetazolamide; allelic with familial hemiplegic migraine type 1.
simple: An inherited condition with attacks of dizziness and unsteadiness lasting hours, which often improve with the drug acetazolamide.

name: Episodic vertigo
formal: Recurrent spells of vertigo from vestibular migraine, Meniere disease, BPPV, vertebrobasilar ischaemia or episodic ataxia, distinguished by duration, triggers and associated auditory or neurological features.
simple: Repeated attacks of a spinning sensation that come and go, with causes ranging from inner ear problems to migraine.

name: Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD)
formal: Non-Langerhans histiocytosis, often BRAF V600E-mutated, with bone sclerosis, retroperitoneal fibrosis and CNS involvement causing cerebellar ataxia, diabetes insipidus, orbital masses and pyramidal signs.
simple: A rare disease where abnormal immune cells build up in bones and other organs, sometimes the brain, causing unsteadiness and other problems.

name: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D) deficiency
formal: Vitamin D deficiency leading to rickets or osteomalacia, with proximal myopathy, bone pain, hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany and, in some reports, other neurological symptoms.
simple: Too little vitamin D, which can weaken bones and muscles and lower calcium in the blood.

name: Ergot poisoning
formal: Ergotism from ergot alkaloids or overuse of ergotamine, causing severe vasoconstriction, limb ischaemia, headache, seizures and cerebral vasospasm or stroke.
simple: Poisoning from a fungus on grain or too much of an ergot migraine drug, narrowing blood vessels and causing pain, cramps or stroke.

name: Essential myoclonus
formal: Idiopathic or familial disorder of non-epileptic myoclonic jerks without other neurological signs, often alcohol-responsive, and frequently overlapping with myoclonus-dystonia due to SGCE mutations.
simple: A condition of sudden muscle jerks with no other illness, which sometimes runs in families and may improve with alcohol.

name: Essential palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic, often audible clicking of the soft palate from tensor veli palatini contraction, without structural brainstem lesion, usually in younger people and often with ear clicking.
simple: A rhythmic movement of the soft palate at the back of the mouth with no clear cause, sometimes causing a clicking sound in the ear.

name: Essential tremor
formal: Common bilateral postural and kinetic tremor of the arms, sometimes head and voice, familial in many cases, slowly progressive, improved by alcohol, propranolol and primidone.
simple: A common condition causing shaking of the hands, especially when doing tasks, which often runs in families and can be treated.
th: มือสั่นขณะใช้งานหรือยกมือค้าง ทั้งสองข้าง มักมีคนในครอบครัวเป็น ดื่มแอลกอฮอล์แล้วดีขึ้น
feat: Bilateral postural and kinetic tremor of the hands (often with head or voice tremor)
No bradykinesia or rigidity
Family history and alcohol responsiveness common
inv: Clinical; thyroid function and drug review
DAT scan normal if parkinsonism is a question

case.story: Shaky hands for 10 years; worse when writing on the board or drinking from a cup. A glass of wine helps.
case.exam: Bilateral postural tremor and tremor on finger-nose testing, mild 'no-no' head tremor, normal tone and finger taps.
case.tests: TSH normal.
case.q: Which examination finding most clearly separates this from Parkinson’s disease?
case.a: Absence of bradykinesia (no decrement) — plus the tremor is postural/kinetic rather than at rest.

ddx.pt: Rest tremor, bradykinesia, asymmetric
Irregular, position-specific, with dystonic posturing and a sensory trick
Fine, fast, caused by thyrotoxicosis, caffeine or drugs

aN: et | benign essential tremor | familial tremor

det.patho: Essential tremor is thought to arise from abnormal oscillation in cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits; pathology studies describe Purkinje cell changes in some brains. It is among the most frequent movement disorders, rising steeply with age, and about half of patients report an affected relative, consistent with autosomal dominant transmission of uncertain genes.
det.clinical: The tremor is bilateral (mildly asymmetric is allowed), affects the hands and forearms during posture and action, and is present for at least three years by definition. It may also involve the head, voice or legs and typically worsens with stress, caffeine and fatigue; many patients notice temporary improvement with alcohol. The 2018 consensus introduced 'ET plus' for patients with soft additional signs such as impaired tandem gait, questionable dystonic posturing or mild memory change. Isolated head or voice tremor, sudden onset, task-specific tremor or rest tremor should prompt reconsideration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: isolated bilateral upper-limb action tremor of three years or more, without other neurological signs. Watch the patient pour water or draw an Archimedes spiral to judge severity and axis. Check thyroid function and review drugs (valproate, lithium, beta-agonists, amiodarone, SSRIs). Copper studies are needed in young patients. DAT SPECT is normal and is useful only when distinguishing from tremor-dominant parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Treat when tremor interferes with daily life. Propranolol (avoid in asthma) and primidone are first-line, either alone or combined; topiramate and gabapentin are second-line options. Weighted cutlery, wrist weights and occupational therapy help. For disabling, drug-resistant tremor, options are thalamic (VIM) deep brain stimulation or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy, which is usually done on one side.
det.prognosis: It progresses slowly over decades and does not shorten life, though severe tremor can cause real disability and social embarrassment.
pearls: Tremor that is worse at the end of a finger-nose movement is kinetic/intention and fits ET; true rest tremor does not.
Spiral drawing shows a fixed tremor axis in ET; a variable, irregular pattern hints at dystonic tremor.
Primidone can make some patients feel sick and drowsy after the first dose — start very low.
det.thd: Essential tremor เป็นภาวะมือสั่นทั้งสองข้างขณะยกมือค้างหรือขณะใช้งาน เกิดจากวงจร cerebellum-thalamus-cortex ทำงานผิดจังหวะ มักมีคนในครอบครัวเป็นและดีขึ้นชั่วคราวเมื่อดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกโดยไม่มีอาการเคลื่อนไหวช้าหรือเกร็ง ควรตรวจไทรอยด์และทบทวนยาที่ทำให้สั่น ยาหลักคือ propranolol หรือ primidone ถ้าไม่ได้ผลพิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound

name: ETF deficiency
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency from ETFA or ETFB mutations, impairing fatty acid and amino acid oxidation, with metabolic crises and sometimes lipid-storage myopathy.
simple: An inherited disorder in which the body cannot properly use fats and proteins for energy, causing weakness and metabolic crises.
more: Organic acids and acylcarnitines are abnormal; the late-onset form often responds to riboflavin, carnitine, and a low-fat diet.

name: ETF-QO deficiency
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency caused by ETFDH mutations, the commonest cause of riboflavin-responsive lipid storage myopathy with proximal weakness and episodic vomiting.
simple: An inherited energy-metabolism defect causing muscle weakness and episodes of illness, which often improves with vitamin B2.
more: Biopsy shows lipid vacuoles; high-dose riboflavin and CoQ10 give dramatic improvement.

name: Exaggerated physiological tremor
formal: Fine, rapid postural tremor of 8 to 12 Hz that is an exaggeration of normal tremor due to anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, drugs or fatigue and resolves when the cause is removed.
simple: A fine, fast hand shake that is stronger than usual because of things like caffeine, stress, an overactive thyroid or some medicines.

name: Exaggerated startle syndromes
formal: Disorders with excessive startle responses to unexpected stimuli, including hyperekplexia (GLRA1 mutations), startle epilepsy and functional startle, sometimes with stiffness and falls.
simple: Conditions where a surprise sound or touch triggers a very strong jump or stiffening, sometimes causing falls.
more: Diagnosis by clinical triad of startle, stiffness and falls with a positive nose-tap sign; genetic testing for GLRA1, SLC6A5 and GLRB. Clonazepam is first-line treatment and Vigevano manoeuvre can abort infant attacks; refractory cases may need valproate.

name: Excessive fragmentary sleep myoclonus
formal: Benign electrophysiological finding of brief muscle twitches during non-REM sleep, with small amplitude and asynchronous EMG bursts, mostly incidental and not requiring treatment.
simple: Tiny muscle twitches during sleep that are usually harmless and found by chance.

name: Exertional headache
formal: Primary headache provoked by sustained physical exercise, throbbing and bilateral, lasting minutes to hours, but secondary causes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage or cardiac cephalalgia must be excluded.
simple: A headache that starts during or after hard exercise, usually harmless but sometimes a sign of a more serious problem.

name: Exploding head syndrome
formal: Benign parasomnia with perception of a loud bang or explosion at sleep-wake transitions, without pain, thought to arise from brainstem dysregulation of auditory sleep-wake transition.
simple: Hearing a sudden loud bang or explosion in the head while falling asleep or waking up, without pain and without danger.

name: Extradural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood between skull and dura, typically from middle meningeal artery tear after temporal bone fracture, with lucid interval, rapid deterioration and a biconvex lentiform CT appearance.
simple: Bleeding between the skull and the brain's outer covering after a head injury, which can quickly press on the brain and needs urgent surgery.

name: Extrapyramidal diseases
formal: Disorders of the basal ganglia and associated pathways, including parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, tics and tremor, with disturbed tone, posture and involuntary movement without paralysis.
simple: Illnesses of deep brain areas that control movement, causing slowness, stiffness or unwanted movements rather than weakness.

name: Extrapyramidal rigidity
formal: Increased resistance throughout the range of passive movement (lead-pipe or cogwheel) from basal ganglia dysfunction, as in Parkinson disease, independent of movement speed.
simple: A steady stiffness in the muscles when someone moves your limb, typical of Parkinson disease.

name: Fabry disease
formal: X-linked lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A deficiency with acral neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal opacities, renal and cardiac disease and early-onset stroke.
simple: An inherited condition where a fatty substance builds up in cells, causing burning hand and foot pain, and kidney, heart and stroke problems.
more: Diagnose with leucocyte alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity in men and GLA sequencing in women; plasma lyso-Gb3 and MRI showing pulvinar T1 hyperintensity help. Treat with agalsidase enzyme replacement or migalastat; control pain with carbamazepine.
th: โรค lysosomal storage X-linked — ปวดแสบร้อนมือเท้าตั้งแต่เด็ก, angiokeratoma, ไตเสื่อม, หัวใจหนา, stroke อายุน้อย รักษาด้วย ERT ได้
tempoNote: Painful crises from childhood; organ damage accumulates through adult life
feat: Burning hand and foot pain and episodic pain crises with fever, heat or exercise (small-fibre neuropathy)
Reduced sweating, heat intolerance, gastrointestinal cramps
Angiokeratomas (bathing-trunk area), whorled corneal opacities (cornea verticillata)
Proteinuria and renal failure, left ventricular hypertrophy, young stroke (posterior circulation, dolichoectasia)
Women heterozygotes can be significantly affected
inv: Males: α-galactosidase A enzyme activity (dried blood spot or leukocytes)
Females: GLA gene sequencing (enzyme often normal); plasma lyso-Gb3
Urine protein, eGFR, echo/cardiac MRI, ECG, brain MRI, slit-lamp exam

case.story: Burning hands and feet since childhood, worse with fever and hot weather; barely sweats; now admitted with sudden vertigo and ataxia.
case.exam: Clusters of dark red papules around the umbilicus and thighs; right limb ataxia; corneal whorls on slit lamp.
case.tests: MRI: acute right cerebellar infarct, white-matter lesions and dilated basilar artery; proteinuria 1.2 g/day; low α-Gal A activity; GLA variant.
case.q: Which other organs need staging, and what disease-specific therapy exists?
case.a: Kidney, heart (LVH, arrhythmia) and eyes. Enzyme replacement (agalsidase alfa/beta, pegunigalsidase) or oral migalastat for amenable variants; plus standard stroke prevention.

det.patho: Pathogenic GLA variants reduce α-galactosidase A, so globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and lyso-Gb3 accumulate in vascular endothelium, smooth muscle, dorsal root ganglia, kidney podocytes and cardiomyocytes. Inheritance is X-linked; hemizygous males with classic variants are most severe, but heterozygous females show variable disease due to X-inactivation. Late-onset variants may affect mainly the heart or kidney.
det.clinical: Classic males present in childhood with acroparaesthesia, pain crises triggered by fever, heat or exertion, hypohidrosis and gastrointestinal symptoms. Angiokeratomas and corneal whorls appear early. In adulthood proteinuria progresses to renal failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia develops, and strokes or TIAs occur at young age, often posterior circulation with vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia. Hearing loss and depression are common.
det.diagnosis: In males, low α-Gal A enzyme activity is diagnostic and gene testing confirms the variant. In females enzyme activity can be normal, so GLA sequencing is required; lyso-Gb3 helps assess pathogenicity of uncertain variants. Brain MRI may show white-matter lesions and pulvinar T1 hyperintensity. Fabry should be screened in young cryptogenic stroke, unexplained LVH and unexplained proteinuria. Cascade testing of relatives is essential.
det.treatment: Disease-specific options are enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase alfa, agalsidase beta, pegunigalsidase alfa) and the oral chaperone migalastat for amenable variants; earlier treatment gives better outcomes. Adjunctive care includes ACE inhibitors/ARBs for proteinuria, antiplatelets and risk-factor control for stroke prevention, cardiac rhythm monitoring, and neuropathic pain treatment (carbamazepine, gabapentinoids). Avoid triggers such as overheating.
det.prognosis: Untreated classic males have reduced life expectancy due to renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease; treatment slows organ decline, particularly if started before irreversible damage.
pearls: Childhood burning hands and feet with heat intolerance and poor sweating: look for angiokeratomas.
Women are not just carriers — test the gene, not the enzyme.
Consider Fabry in young stroke with a dilated basilar artery or proteinuria.
det.thd: Fabry disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked ที่ขาดเอนไซม์ α-galactosidase A ทำให้ Gb3 สะสมในหลอดเลือด เส้นประสาท ไต และหัวใจ ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนมือเท้าตั้งแต่เด็ก เหงื่อออกน้อย มี angiokeratoma และ cornea verticillata ต่อมามีโปรตีนรั่วในปัสสาวะ หัวใจหนา และ stroke อายุน้อย ผู้ชายวินิจฉัยด้วยระดับเอนไซม์ ผู้หญิงต้องตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย enzyme replacement หรือ migalastat ร่วมกับดูแลไต หัวใจ และป้องกัน stroke

ddx.pt: Idiopathic or diabetic/immune causes; no angiokeratoma, renal or cardiac involvement
Migraine with aura, anterior temporal white-matter lesions, NOTCH3; no painful neuropathy
Relapsing deficits, periventricular ovoid lesions and CSF oligoclonal bands

aN: anderson fabry disease | alpha galactosidase a deficiency | gla deficiency | angiokeratoma corporis diffusum

name: Facial palsy
formal: Weakness of facial muscles from lesion of the facial nerve or its pathway; lower motor neuron types affect the whole face (Bell palsy, Ramsay Hunt), upper motor neuron types spare the forehead.
simple: Weakness or drooping of one side of the face because the nerve or brain pathways controlling it are damaged.

name: Facial palsy/weakness
formal: Weakness of facial muscles from lesion of the facial nerve or its pathway; lower motor neuron types affect the whole face (Bell palsy, Ramsay Hunt), upper motor neuron types spare the forehead.
simple: Weakness or drooping of one side of the face because the nerve or brain pathways controlling it are damaged.

name: Facial-onset sensory motor neuronopathy (FOSMN)
formal: Rare slowly progressive disorder starting with perioral and facial numbness, then bulbar and limb weakness, with abnormal blink reflexes, resembling a motor neuron disease with trigeminal sensory involvement.
simple: A rare disease that starts with numbness around the face, followed by weakness of the face, throat and limbs.
nN: facial onset sensory motor neuronopathy fosmn
aN: fosmn | facial onset sensory motor neuronopathy

name: Faciomandibular myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic or irregular jerks of the facial and jaw muscles, as in propriospinal or brainstem myoclonus, or symptomatic of anti-IgLON5 disease, brainstem lesions and the like.
simple: Quick jerks of the face and jaw muscles that the person cannot control.

name: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD)
formal: Autosomal dominant dystrophy from D4Z4 repeat contraction with DUX4 derepression, causing facial, scapular and humeral weakness, scapular winging and asymmetric progression, often with retinal vasculopathy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that weakens the face, shoulders and upper arms, usually starting in teens or adulthood.
more: Diagnosis rests on 4q35 D4Z4 repeat contraction testing; CK is normal or mildly raised, and MRI shows asymmetric fatty replacement with STIR signal. Care is supportive with scapular fixation in selected patients; hearing and retinal screening is advised.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม — หน้า สะบัก ต้นแขนอ่อนแรงแบบไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง สะบักยกเวลายกแขน
feat: Facial weakness: cannot whistle or bury eyelashes
Asymmetric scapular winging that rides up when the arms are raised
Biceps/triceps wasting with relatively preserved forearm ('Popeye arm')
Abdominal weakness (Beevor sign) and later foot drop
inv: Genetic testing: D4Z4 repeat contraction on 4q35 (FSHD1) or SMCHD1-related hypomethylation (FSHD2)
CK normal to modestly raised
Audiology and retinal screening in early-onset cases

case.story: Cannot lift his right arm above shoulder level to put things on a shelf; friends say his smile looks flat.
case.exam: Weak eye closure, asymmetric winging worse on the right, umbilicus moves up on sitting up.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L; genetic test: shortened D4Z4 array on a permissive 4qA allele.
case.q: Name the abdominal sign and what it implies.
case.a: Beevor sign — lower abdominal muscles weaker than upper; common in FSHD.

read.where: Slides: clinical pattern, scapular winging patterns, genetics (FSHD1/2), 2025 diagnostic algorithm, board pearls

ddx.pt: Symmetric, face spared, often higher CK
Early respiratory weakness, paraspinal involvement
Older onset, finger flexors and quadriceps

aN: fshd | facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy | landouzy dejerine | facioscapulohumeral dystrophy

det.patho: FSHD results from inappropriate expression of the DUX4 gene in skeletal muscle, which is toxic to muscle cells. In FSHD1 (about 95%) the D4Z4 macrosatellite array on chromosome 4q35 is contracted to 1–10 units on a permissive 4qA haplotype that supplies a polyadenylation signal; in FSHD2, variants in SMCHD1 (or DNMT3B, LRIF1) cause D4Z4 hypomethylation. Inheritance in FSHD1 is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, and de novo cases occur. It is among the most common muscular dystrophies.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the teens or twenties with facial weakness (difficulty whistling, drinking through a straw, incomplete eye closure) and scapular fixator weakness that causes winging, a high-riding scapula on arm abduction and difficulty lifting arms overhead. Asymmetry is a hallmark. Later involvement includes biceps and triceps with sparing of deltoid and forearm, abdominal weakness with Beevor sign and lumbar lordosis, and foot drop. Early-onset severe forms have hearing loss and retinal vasculopathy (Coats-like). Cardiac and respiratory involvement are uncommon but can occur in severe cases.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis: measurement of D4Z4 repeat size and 4qA haplotype for FSHD1, and methylation analysis plus SMCHD1 sequencing for FSHD2. CK is normal or mildly raised, and EMG is myopathic. Muscle MRI shows asymmetric, selective involvement and can direct testing. Biopsy is seldom required and may show inflammation, causing confusion with myositis. Consider Pompe disease, LGMDs, scapuloperoneal syndromes, myasthenia and IBM in the differential.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment yet; DUX4-targeted therapies are in trials. Care includes physiotherapy and aerobic exercise, ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, scapular fixation surgery in selected patients with good deltoid strength, eye protection for incomplete closure, and pain management. Screen hearing and retina in early-onset cases, check respiratory function in severe or early-onset disease, and offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow and variable; most remain ambulant, though about one in five eventually need a wheelchair. Life expectancy is usually normal.
pearls: Asymmetric scapular winging plus facial weakness = FSHD.
Beevor sign (umbilicus moves upward on sitting up) is common in FSHD.
Deltoid and forearm are relatively spared, giving the 'Popeye arm' appearance.
det.thd: FSHD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน DUX4 ที่ถูกแสดงออกผิดปกติในกล้ามเนื้อ ชนิด FSHD1 เกิดจาก D4Z4 บนโครโมโซม 4q35 สั้นลง ส่วน FSHD2 เกิดจากยีน SMCHD1 อาการเริ่มวัยรุ่นหรือวัยหนุ่มสาว ใบหน้าอ่อนแรง ผิวปากไม่ได้ หลับตาไม่สนิท สะบักยกและกางเวลายกแขน มักไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง และต่อมามีกล้ามเนื้อท้องอ่อนแรง (Beevor sign) และเท้าตก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจพันธุกรรม ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเน้นกายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์ช่วยเท้าตก และคำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Fahr’s disease
formal: Primary familial brain calcification with symmetrical calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms; SLC20A2 and others implicated.
simple: A condition where calcium builds up in deep parts of the brain, leading to movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.

name: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME)
formal: Autosomal dominant epilepsy from intronic TTTCA repeat expansions with adult-onset cortical tremor, myoclonus and infrequent generalised seizures, a form of cortical tremor with epilepsy.
simple: An inherited condition of fine shaking, jerks and occasional seizures that begins in adulthood.

name: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy (FAP)
formal: Autosomal dominant transthyretin amyloidosis with length-dependent sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and cardiac involvement; treatable with silencers or stabilisers.
simple: An inherited disease where an abnormal protein builds up in nerves, causing numbness, weakness and problems with blood pressure and digestion.
more: Confirm with TTR gene sequencing and tissue biopsy with Congo red apple-green birefringence; scintigraphy detects cardiac involvement. Liver transplantation, tafamidis, patisiran, vutrisiran or inotersen treat the disease.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจาก amyloid ของ transthyretin ที่กลายพันธุ์ — ชาปวดปลายเท้า ระบบอัตโนมัติเสีย หัวใจหนา รักษาได้ด้วย TTR silencer/stabiliser
tempoNote: Adult onset (20s–70s depending on variant); progresses over years
feat: Length-dependent painful sensory neuropathy beginning with small fibres, later motor weakness
Autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea/constipation, erectile dysfunction, weight loss
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, often years before
Cardiomyopathy (thick ventricular walls, conduction disease); vitreous opacities, nephropathy
inv: NCS/EMG: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; small-fibre and autonomic testing
TTR gene sequencing (e.g. Val30Met, Ala97Ser — the latter frequent in Taiwan/Asia)
Tissue for amyloid (fat pad, salivary gland, nerve) with typing; echocardiogram, NT-proBNP, cardiac MRI or scintigraphy

case.story: Two years of burning feet, then lightheadedness on standing, alternating diarrhoea and 10 kg weight loss; carpal tunnel surgery on both hands 5 years ago.
case.exam: Distal pin and temperature loss to knees, mild toe weakness, absent ankle jerks, postural BP fall 35 mmHg.
case.tests: NCS: axonal neuropathy; echo: LV wall 15 mm; fat pad Congo red positive; TTR variant confirmed; free light chains normal.
case.q: Why exclude AL amyloidosis, and what treatments are available?
case.a: AL is treated by chemotherapy against the plasma cell clone, so light chains must be checked. For ATTRv neuropathy, TTR gene silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) or the stabiliser tafamidis slow progression.

det.patho: Point mutations in TTR destabilise the transthyretin tetramer, which dissociates into monomers that misfold and deposit as amyloid in nerve, dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, heart, kidney and eye. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; the liver produces almost all circulating TTR. Endemic early-onset Val30Met clusters exist in Portugal, Sweden and Japan, while Asian populations show other variants and later onset.
det.clinical: Typical disease starts with painful small-fibre symptoms in the feet, progressing upward and later to motor weakness and gait failure. Autonomic dysfunction is early and prominent. Carpal tunnel syndrome, unexplained weight loss, heart failure with thick ventricles, and vitreous opacities are important clues. Late-onset forms in men over 50 may lack family history and mimic CIDP or idiopathic axonal neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ATTRv in progressive axonal neuropathy with autonomic failure, carpal tunnel or cardiac thickening. TTR genetic testing is the key test; tissue biopsy with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing confirms amyloid. Always exclude AL amyloid with serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains. Staging includes NCS, autonomic tests, echocardiography, cardiac MRI or bone scintigraphy, renal and eye assessment.
det.treatment: Disease-modifying options include TTR silencers—siRNA (patisiran, vutrisiran) and antisense oligonucleotides (inotersen, eplontersen)—and the tetramer stabiliser tafamidis (diflunisal off-label); liver transplantation is now rarely used. Supportive care covers neuropathic pain, orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms, nutrition, pacing for conduction disease and heart failure. Inotersen requires platelet and renal monitoring; silencers require vitamin A supplementation. Offer genetic counselling and screen carriers.
det.prognosis: Untreated, death occurs about 7–12 years after onset from cachexia, cardiac disease or infection; early treatment considerably slows progression.
pearls: Neuropathy plus autonomic failure plus bilateral carpal tunnel = test TTR.
Exclude AL amyloid with free light chains before labelling ATTR.
Late-onset sporadic-looking cases are common; family history is often absent.
det.thd: FAP หรือ ATTRv amyloidosis เกิดจาก mutation ของยีน TTR ทำให้ transthyretin พับผิดรูปและสะสมเป็น amyloid ที่เส้นประสาท หัวใจ ไต และตา ผู้ป่วยชาแสบร้อนปลายเท้า ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ท้องเสียสลับท้องผูก น้ำหนักลด มี carpal tunnel ทั้งสองข้าง และหัวใจห้องล่างหนา วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน TTR และชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red ต้องแยก AL amyloid เสมอ รักษาด้วย TTR silencer หรือ tafamidis

ddx.pt: Monoclonal light chain present; no TTR variant; treated with plasma-cell therapy
Demyelinating NCS, high CSF protein, responds to IVIG/steroids; no autonomic failure
Diabetes present; slower course, less weight loss and cardiac involvement

name: Familial ataxia with coenzyme Q10
formal: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia with coenzyme Q10 deficiency (ADCK3/COQ8A and others), with cerebellar atrophy, seizures, cognitive impairment and exercise intolerance.
simple: An inherited balance disorder caused by low levels of a cell energy molecule called coenzyme Q10.
more: Muscle biopsy CoQ10 level and genetic testing confirm it. High-dose oral CoQ10 may improve symptoms, especially if started early.

name: Familial basal ganglia calcification
formal: Primary familial brain calcification with symmetrical calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms; SLC20A2 and others implicated.
simple: A condition where calcium builds up in deep parts of the brain, leading to movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.

name: Familial calcification of basal ganglia and dystonia
formal: Primary familial brain calcification with symmetrical calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms; SLC20A2 and others implicated.
simple: A condition where calcium builds up in deep parts of the brain, leading to movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.
nN: familial calcification of basal ganglia and dystonia

name: Familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy
formal: Autosomal dominant syndrome of fine postural tremor-like cortical myoclonus, infrequent seizures and photosensitivity, with giant SEPs, now largely overlapping with FAME.
simple: An inherited condition of fine shaking and jerks, with occasional seizures, caused by overactive brain cells.
nN: familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy

name: Familial cramps
formal: Inherited tendency to frequent painful muscle cramps, often benign and of autosomal dominant pattern, sometimes with fasciculations, after exclusion of metabolic and neuropathic causes.
simple: An inherited tendency to get frequent painful muscle cramps.

name: Familial dyskinesia and facial myokimia
formal: Autosomal dominant ADCY5-related disorder with early-onset chorea, dystonia and myoclonus, especially orofacial, with facial myokimia and nocturnal exacerbations.
simple: An inherited condition with writhing and jerking movements from early life, and fine rippling of the facial muscles.

name: Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 2
formal: Autosomal dominant periodic paralysis due to SCN4A mutations, with attacks of flaccid weakness with low potassium, triggered by carbohydrate meals or rest after exercise.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium falls, usually after rest or a carbohydrate-rich meal.
more: Genetic testing; attacks respond to potassium; prevent with acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide and trigger avoidance.

name: Familial periodic ataxia
formal: Autosomal dominant episodic ataxia caused by ion channel mutations, such as KCNA1 and CACNA1A, with recurrent attacks of unsteadiness lasting seconds to days.
simple: An inherited condition in which attacks of clumsiness and unsteadiness come and go.

name: Familial spastic paraplegia
formal: Heritable upper motor neuron disorders with progressive lower limb spasticity and weakness from corticospinal tract axonopathy, pure or complicated, with many genes (SPG4 commonest).
simple: Inherited conditions that gradually make the legs stiff and weak because of damage to nerve fibres from the brain.

name: Fanconi syndrome
formal: Generalised proximal renal tubular dysfunction causing phosphate, glucose and amino acid wasting; hypophosphataemic osteomalacia and proximal myopathy, and may accompany mitochondrial and metabolic diseases.
simple: A kidney problem that loses salts, sugar and minerals in the urine, weakening bones and muscles.

name: Fast channel syndrome
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from CHRNE mutations causing rapid acetylcholine receptor channel closure, with reduced endplate response and fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: An inherited form of muscle weakness from birth where signals from nerve to muscle do not work properly.

name: Fatal familial insomnia
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (D178N with M129 on PRNP) with progressive insomnia, dysautonomia, myoclonus, ataxia and dementia, and thalamic degeneration, death in 12 to 18 months.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease that causes worsening inability to sleep, then confusion and loss of body control, leading to death.

name: Fazio–Londe disease
formal: Rare progressive bulbar palsy of childhood from SLC52A3 or SLC52A2 mutations, a riboflavin transporter deficiency presenting with facial weakness, dysphagia and respiratory failure, treatable with riboflavin.
simple: A rare inherited childhood illness causing weakness of the face and throat muscles, helped by vitamin B2.
more: Typically begins in childhood or adolescence; diagnose by SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 testing with an acylcarnitine profile and blood flavin studies. High-dose oral riboflavin improves outcome, and early treatment is critical for ventilation and swallowing.

name: Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES)
formal: Catastrophic epileptic encephalopathy with refractory status epilepticus after a febrile illness in a previously healthy child or adult, with poor outcome and probable inflammatory pathogenesis.
simple: A severe condition in which previously healthy children develop non-stop seizures after a fever, often with lasting brain damage.
nN: febrile infection related epilepsy syndrome fires
aN: fires | febrile infection related epilepsy syndrome

name: Femoral neuropathy
formal: Injury of the femoral nerve from diabetic infarct, retroperitoneal haematoma, hip surgery or pelvic compression, causing quadriceps weakness, absent knee jerk and anteromedial thigh sensory loss.
simple: Damage to the nerve in the front of the thigh, causing a weak knee that gives way and numbness in the front of the thigh.

name: Fingerprint body myopathy
formal: Rare myopathy with distinctive fingerprint-like inclusions on electron microscopy, with variable proximal weakness, sometimes with cardiomyopathy, and unclear genetic basis.
simple: A very rare muscle disease named for the fingerprint-like patterns seen in muscle under an electron microscope.
more: Electron microscopy of biopsy is diagnostic; management is supportive.

name: Fixed dystonia
formal: Dystonic posture of limbs with rapid onset and no relaxation, usually of functional origin, often after minor injury and painful, with an associated complex regional pain syndrome.
simple: A twisted posture of a limb that does not relax, often appearing after a minor injury and usually functional in origin.

name: Flail arm/leg syndrome
formal: Regional variants of motor neuron disease with progressive proximal arm (Vulpian–Bernhardt) or leg weakness and atrophy and slower progression than classic ALS.
simple: A slowly progressing form of motor neuron disease where weakness mainly affects one arm or one leg.

name: Focal aware seizures (auras)
formal: Focal seizures with preserved awareness giving sensory, autonomic, psychic or motor symptoms, such as rising epigastric sensation or deja vu, often from mesial temporal onset.
simple: Short seizures where the person stays awake but has odd feelings, smells, sights or movements, often a warning of a bigger seizure.

name: Focal cortical myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks confined to one body part from a discrete sensorimotor cortical focus, with giant SEPs and EEG correlates, as in epilepsia partialis continua.
simple: Quick jerks of one body part caused by a small overactive area on the brain surface.

name: Focal epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy with seizures originating in one hemisphere, causing semiology based on the network involved and often due to structural lesions such as hippocampal sclerosis or cortical dysplasia.
simple: Epilepsy where seizures start in one area of the brain, causing symptoms that depend on where it begins.

name: Focal impaired awareness seizures
formal: Focal seizures with impaired consciousness, typically temporal, with staring, automatisms, post-ictal confusion and often a preceding aura.
simple: Seizures starting in one part of the brain in which the person is not fully aware, may stare or make repeated movements, and then feels confused.

name: Focal mononeuropathy
formal: Damage to a single peripheral nerve by compression, trauma, ischaemia or entrapment, causing weakness and sensory loss in that nerve's territory.
simple: Damage to one single nerve, causing weakness or numbness in the area that nerve supplies.

name: Focal motor seizures
formal: Seizures with localised clonic or tonic motor activity from the contralateral primary motor cortex, which may march (Jacksonian) and may be followed by transient Todd paralysis.
simple: Seizures causing jerking or stiffening of one part of the body, which may spread to nearby areas.

name: Focal myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks restricted to a body part from cortical, brainstem, spinal or peripheral causes such as stroke, tumour, spinal cord lesion or nerve injury.
simple: Quick jerks in just one part of the body, caused by a lesion in the nervous system.

name: Focal myositis
formal: Localised benign inflammatory pseudotumour of one muscle, often the calf, presenting with a painful swelling and raised CK, with biopsy showing inflammatory changes.
simple: Inflammation in one muscle, which causes a lump and pain, usually in the calf.
more: MRI and biopsy exclude tumour; it often resolves spontaneously or with steroids.

name: Focal neuropathies
formal: Isolated peripheral nerve disorders, such as median, ulnar, radial, fibular nerve lesions, mainly from compression or trauma, and diagnosed with nerve conduction studies.
simple: Problems affecting single nerves, such as pinched nerves, causing numbness or weakness in a specific area.

name: Focal segmental myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus affecting adjacent muscles from a spinal cord lesion, giving rhythmic segmental jerks, often continuous, as in spinal myoclonus due to myelopathy.
simple: Rhythmic jerks of a few muscles of the trunk or limb caused by damage in the spinal cord.

name: Focal seizure
formal: Seizure arising from a network within one hemisphere, with motor, sensory, autonomic or cognitive features, with or without impaired awareness and with possible evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic.
simple: A seizure that begins in one area of the brain and causes symptoms depending on where it starts.

name: Foeral alcohol syndrome
formal: Prenatal alcohol exposure syndrome with growth restriction, facial dysmorphism (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), microcephaly and neurodevelopmental disability.
simple: A lifelong condition from alcohol drunk during pregnancy, causing small size, facial changes, and learning and behaviour problems.

name: Folate (vitamin B9) deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy, myelopathy, cognitive impairment and neural tube defects in pregnancy; frequently induced by antiepileptic drugs and malabsorption.
simple: Too little folate (vitamin B9), which can cause anaemia, nerve problems and, in pregnancy, spinal defects in the baby.
more: Check serum and red cell folate with homocysteine and MMA to separate from B12 deficiency; folic acid alone can worsen subacute combined degeneration if B12 deficiency is missed. Periconceptual supplementation prevents neural tube defects.

name: Folic acid deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy, myelopathy, cognitive impairment and neural tube defects in pregnancy; frequently induced by antiepileptic drugs and malabsorption.
simple: Too little folate (vitamin B9), which can cause anaemia, nerve problems and, in pregnancy, spinal defects in the baby.

name: Fowler syndrome
formal: Urinary retention in young women from failed urethral sphincter relaxation, associated with polycystic ovaries and abnormal sphincter EMG with complex repetitive discharges.
simple: A condition in which young women cannot empty their bladder because the outlet muscle does not relax.

name: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS)
formal: Late-onset neurodegeneration in FMR1 premutation carriers with intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline and MRI middle cerebellar peduncle T2 hyperintensity.
simple: An inherited disease in older carriers of a gene change on the X chromosome, causing shaking, unsteadiness and memory decline.
more: Diagnosis by FMR1 CGG repeat of 55 to 200; MRI middle cerebellar peduncle sign, with male predominance and variable penetrance in women. Treatment is symptomatic, with genetic counselling for risk of fragile X syndrome in descendants, especially grandchildren.
nN: fragile x associated tremor ataxia syndrome fxtas
aN: fxtas | fragile x associated tremor ataxia syndrome

name: Fragile-X syndrome
formal: X-linked FMR1 full-mutation disorder (CGG greater than 200) with intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, macro-orchidism, long face and large ears; commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability.
simple: A common inherited condition causing learning difficulties and behaviour differences, with typical facial features.

name: Freezing
formal: Brief episodic inability to initiate or continue stepping, with feet feeling glued to the floor, in parkinsonism and related disorders; triggers include turning, doorways and cueing helps.
simple: Sudden moments when the feet seem stuck to the floor and walking cannot start or continue, common in Parkinson disease.

name: Friedreich’s ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN with frataxin deficiency causing early-onset progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, dorsal column loss, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease starting in childhood or teens causing worsening clumsiness, loss of balance and often heart disease.
more: Diagnose by FXN GAA repeat expansion testing; nerve conduction shows absent sensory responses and MRI shows cervical cord atrophy. Idebenone has uncertain benefit and omaveloxolone is approved; monitor for cardiomyopathy, diabetes and scoliosis.
th: โรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่พบบ่อยที่สุด — เซ + reflex หาย + Babinski + cardiomyopathy เริ่มในวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Usually starts before 25; steady progression over years; late-onset forms exist
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia beginning in childhood or adolescence
Absent ankle and knee jerks with extensor plantars; loss of vibration and position sense
Dysarthria, scoliosis, pes cavus, square-wave jerks
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes are common non-neurological features
inv: FXN gene test: biallelic GAA repeat expansion (rarely one expansion plus a point variant)
NCS: absent or reduced sensory potentials (sensory neuronopathy)
ECG and echocardiogram; HbA1c; spine X-ray for scoliosis

case.story: Clumsy in sport since age 11, now falls frequently and his handwriting has deteriorated; parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Broad-based ataxic gait, positive Romberg, absent reflexes in legs, bilateral Babinski, pes cavus, mild thoracic scoliosis.
case.tests: Sural SNAPs absent; ECG shows widespread T inversion and echo shows concentric LV hypertrophy.
case.q: Which genetic test confirms the diagnosis, and what drug is now approved?
case.a: GAA repeat expansion in FXN on both alleles. Omaveloxolone is approved for patients aged 16 and over; cardiac follow-up is lifelong.

det.patho: Most patients carry an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat in intron 1 of FXN on both alleles, which silences the gene and reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron–sulfur cluster assembly. Mitochondrial iron overload and oxidative stress damage dorsal root ganglia, spinocerebellar tracts, corticospinal tracts, dentate nucleus and heart. Shorter repeats on the smaller allele generally predict later onset and milder course.
det.clinical: Gait ataxia is the usual first sign, followed by limb ataxia, dysarthria and loss of proprioception, so Romberg is positive. Reflexes vanish early yet plantars become extensor, a classic combination. Scoliosis, pes cavus, optic atrophy, hearing loss and diabetes accumulate; many patients need a wheelchair 10–20 years after onset. Late-onset and retained-reflex variants occur and are easily missed.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the FXN GAA expansion is diagnostic and should be requested in any young patient with progressive ataxia and areflexia. NCS show a sensory neuronopathy with preserved motor conduction. MRI often shows cervical cord thinning with relatively little cerebellar atrophy early on. Always measure vitamin E, and consider other recessive ataxias if testing is negative.
det.treatment: Omaveloxolone, an Nrf2 activator, has regulatory approval for patients 16 years and older and modestly slows decline; liver enzymes and lipids need monitoring. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, orthoses, scoliosis surgery when indicated, speech therapy and diabetes management. Regular cardiac review with ECG and echo is essential, treating heart failure and arrhythmia promptly.
det.prognosis: Disability progresses over decades; cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of death, often in middle age. Later onset generally means slower course.
pearls: Areflexia with upgoing toes in a teenager with ataxia = Friedreich until proven otherwise.
Cerebellar atrophy is usually mild early; the spinal cord is the thin structure on MRI.
Screen the heart at diagnosis even if the patient has no cardiac symptoms.

Dominant inheritance, reflexes often preserved or brisk, cerebellar atrophy on MRI
Distal wasting and pes cavus but no cerebellar signs, cardiomyopathy or Babinski

aN: fa | frda | friedreich ataxia | frataxin deficiency

name: Friedrich’s ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar and sensory ataxia from GAA expansions in FXN, causing frataxin deficiency, areflexia, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive loss of balance and coordination, with heart and spine problems, starting in childhood or teenage years.
more: Diagnosed by FXN repeat expansion testing; ECG and echo monitor the heart. Omaveloxolone is approved for treatment; otherwise supportive; typically wheelchair use within 10-15 years and cardiac cause of death.

name: Friedriech ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN causing frataxin deficiency, with progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, sensory neuronopathy, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive loss of balance and coordination from teenage years, with heart problems.
more: Diagnosed by FXN repeat testing; omaveloxolone is approved; treat cardiac disease and diabetes; wheelchair dependence is common within about 15 years.

name: Frontal lobe syndrome
formal: Constellation of executive dysfunction, apathy or disinhibition, personality change, perseveration and primitive reflexes with gait apraxia from frontal damage by tumour, trauma, stroke or degeneration.
simple: Changes in personality, motivation, judgement and behaviour after damage to the front of the brain.
more: MRI or functional imaging localises the lesion. Treatment targets the cause with behavioural management; recovery depends on the underlying disease.

name: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD)
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A brain disease that mainly harms the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.

name: Frontotemporal dementias
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A group of brain diseases that mainly harm the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.

name: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD)
formal: Pathological umbrella for frontotemporal dementia syndromes with selective frontal and temporal atrophy and tau, TDP-43 or FET protein inclusions, linked to behavioural, language and motor presentations.
simple: The brain-tissue changes underlying frontotemporal dementia, with shrinking of the front and side parts of the brain.
more: Subtypes include behavioural variant, semantic and nonfluent aphasia, and overlap with ALS or atypical parkinsonism; genes include MAPT, GRN and C9orf72. MRI or FDG-PET shows focal atrophy or hypometabolism; no disease-modifying therapy exists.

name: Frontotemporal lobe dementia (FTD)
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A brain disease that mainly harms the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.

name: FTD with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
formal: Overlap syndrome of behavioural or language-variant FTD with upper and lower motor neuron disease, commonly from C9orf72 repeat expansion and TDP-43 proteinopathy.
simple: A combination of frontotemporal dementia and motor neuron disease, causing both behaviour or language changes and muscle weakness.

name: Functional dystonia
formal: Dystonic postures that are inconsistent with organic dystonia, often fixed, of sudden onset and with distractibility, painful and associated with other functional signs.
simple: Abnormal muscle spasms and twisted postures without a structural cause in the nervous system, real and treatable with rehabilitation.

name: Functional movement disorder (FMD)
formal: Abnormal movements such as tremor, dystonia, jerks or gait disturbance that are variable and distractible, with positive features such as entrainment, and arising from altered network function not structural disease.
simple: Real, involuntary movements such as shaking or odd walking that come from a problem in how the brain functions, not from damage.

name: Functional myoclonus
formal: Jerks with a variable pattern, often with a long latency Bereitschaftspotential, distractibility and suggestibility, which are non-epileptic, and diagnosed from clinical and neurophysiology.
simple: Sudden jerks of the body that come from a change in how the brain functions rather than from structural damage.

name: Functional neurological disorder (FND)
formal: Neurological symptoms such as weakness, seizures or movement disorders, genuinely experienced and diagnosed by positive signs like Hoover sign, due to altered nervous system function rather than structural disease.
simple: Real nerve-related symptoms, such as weakness or shaking, caused by a problem with how the brain works rather than damage to it.
