name: Histone mutant gliomas
formal: Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant, aggressive tumours of children and young adults, such as diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma.
simple: Aggressive brain tumours in children and young adults caused by a specific gene change, often in the brainstem.

name: HIV dementia
formal: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, ranging from asymptomatic to dementia, with subcortical features of slowed thinking, motor slowing, apathy and white-matter change, improved by antiretrovirals.
simple: Memory and thinking problems, with slowed movement, caused by HIV infection of the brain.

name: HIV infection
formal: Chronic retroviral infection of CD4 cells that causes progressive immunodeficiency and can directly injure brain, cord and nerve, or permit opportunistic CNS infections and lymphoma.
simple: A virus that weakens the immune system over time and can also affect the brain, spinal cord and nerves, directly or by allowing other infections.

name: HIV-1 (retrovirus)
formal: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 retrovirus, the commonest cause of HIV disease, which infects CD4 T cells and microglia and enters the CNS early in infection.
simple: The main virus that causes HIV, which attacks the body's immune cells and can get into the brain early on.

name: HIV-associated dementia (HAD)
formal: Severe subcortical dementia from advanced HIV, with psychomotor slowing, impaired attention and memory, and motor signs; reflects HIV-driven microglial and macrophage injury, now uncommon with antiretrovirals.
simple: A serious loss of thinking, memory and movement speed in advanced HIV infection, now rare because modern treatment protects the brain.

name: HIV-associated myopathy
formal: Muscle disease in HIV from the virus itself, an inflammatory polymyositis-like picture, or zidovudine toxicity, causing proximal weakness with raised creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle weakness in a person with HIV, caused by the virus, by inflammation, or by certain HIV drugs.

name: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)
formal: Spectrum of cognitive impairment in HIV, graded as asymptomatic, mild neurocognitive disorder or dementia, with attention, executive and motor slowing that persists despite viral suppression.
simple: Problems with thinking, concentration and memory that can occur in people with HIV, ranging from very mild to severe.

name: HIV-related autonomic neuropathy
formal: Autonomic neuropathy in HIV infection, causing orthostatic hypotension, sweating abnormalities and gastrointestinal or bladder dysfunction, often with advanced disease.
simple: Nerve damage from HIV that disturbs automatic body functions such as blood pressure and digestion.
more: Assessed with autonomic function tests; antiretroviral therapy and symptomatic measures such as fluids and midodrine are used.

name: HIV-related inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
formal: HIV-associated acute or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, often at seroconversion or with CD4 recovery, with CSF pleocytosis in contrast to typical GBS.
simple: An immune-driven nerve condition in people with HIV that causes weakness and loss of reflexes.
more: Nerve studies show demyelination; CSF has raised cells. Treated with IVIG or plasma exchange, with steroids in chronic forms, along with antiretroviral therapy.

name: HIV-related multiple mononeuropathies
formal: Vasculitic multiple mononeuropathy in HIV, either from immune reconstitution or CMV or other infection, producing stepwise multifocal nerve deficits.
simple: Several separate nerves become damaged in people with HIV, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve biopsy and CMV testing guide therapy; treatments include ganciclovir for CMV, immunotherapy for vasculitis and antiretroviral therapy.

name: HIV-related progressive polyradiculopathy
formal: CMV-related cauda equina syndrome in advanced HIV, with rapidly progressive flaccid paraparesis, sphincter dysfunction and neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis.
simple: A fast-worsening leg weakness and bladder problem from infection of lower spinal nerve roots in advanced HIV.
more: MRI shows root enhancement; CSF PCR confirms CMV. Prompt ganciclovir or foscarnet with antiretroviral therapy is needed to prevent permanent damage.

name: HIV-related sensory neuropathy
formal: Distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy, the commonest HIV neurological complication, with painful burning feet from HIV itself or from antiretroviral toxicity.
simple: Burning, painful or numb feet and hands in people with HIV.
more: Diagnosed clinically with nerve studies or skin biopsy. Stopping neurotoxic drugs, antiretroviral therapy, and neuropathic pain agents such as gabapentin help.

name: HIV-related vacuolar myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord degeneration in advanced AIDS with vacuolation of the posterior and lateral columns, giving spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and bladder dysfunction, resembling B12 deficiency.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord in advanced HIV that causes stiff, weak legs, poor balance and bladder trouble.

name: HIV/AIDS
formal: Acquired immunodeficiency from HIV, with neurological disease from direct viral effects, opportunistic infections such as toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus and PML, lymphoma, and neuropathy.
simple: Late-stage HIV infection, when the weakened immune system lets many illnesses, including brain and nerve problems, develop.

name: HIV/AIDS basal ganglia calcification
formal: Bilateral basal ganglia calcification in children with HIV, often with encephalopathy, probably from vascular injury and mineral deposition, seen on CT as symmetric dense deposits.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas, seen on scans of some children with HIV, often linked to developmental problems.

name: Hodgkin’s disease
formal: Lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells; neurological involvement includes spinal cord compression, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis and neuropathy.
simple: A cancer of the lymph glands that can press on the spinal cord or trigger immune attacks on the brain and nerves.

name: Holmes tremor
formal: Rest, postural and kinetic tremor of low frequency (under 4.5 Hz) from midbrain lesions affecting the cerebello-thalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
simple: A slow, large, shaking tremor of the arm, present at rest and with movement, usually after damage to the midbrain.

name: Holmes–Adie syndrome (HAS)
formal: Tonic pupil with absent or reduced tendon reflexes, from damage to ciliary ganglion and dorsal root ganglion neurons; usually young women, benign, with sectoral iris palsy and light-near dissociation.
simple: A harmless condition with one large, slowly reacting pupil and reduced knee and ankle reflexes.

name: Horizontal gaze palsy
formal: Loss of conjugate eye movement to one side from a lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus in the pons, or the frontal eye field; may be isolated or part of a brainstem syndrome.
simple: Inability to move both eyes together toward one side, caused by damage in the brainstem or brain.

name: Horner syndrome
formal: Oculosympathetic palsy with ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from a lesion along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway; causes include carotid dissection, Pancoast tumour and lateral medullary stroke.
simple: A drooping eyelid, small pupil and reduced sweating on one side of the face, from damage to nerves that run from brain to eye.

name: HTLV-1 associated myelopathy
formal: Chronic progressive spastic paraparesis from HTLV-1 infection with thoracic cord inflammation, causing leg weakness, bladder dysfunction and mild sensory loss; endemic in Japan, Caribbean and South America.
simple: Slowly worsening stiffness and weakness of the legs with bladder problems, caused by a virus infecting the spinal cord.
th: ขาแข็งเกร็งอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ ร่วมปัญหาปัสสาวะ จากไขสันหลังอักเสบเรื้อรังจากเชื้อ HTLV-1
tempoNote: Insidious, slowly progressive over years; occasionally rapid in the first 2 years
feat: Slowly worsening spastic paraparesis, legs much more than arms
Early bladder urgency, frequency and incontinence; constipation; erectile dysfunction
Low back pain and leg dysaesthesia with only mild sensory signs
Brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, sometimes with brisk jaw jerk
Associated: uveitis, infective dermatitis, Strongyloides, adult T-cell leukaemia
inv: HTLV-1 serology (ELISA) confirmed by western blot or PCR in blood and CSF
CSF: mild lymphocytosis, oligoclonal bands, raised neopterin/CXCL10, intrathecal antibody
MRI spine: thoracic cord atrophy, occasionally T2 signal in active cases
Exclude compression, B12/copper deficiency, MS, HSP

case.who: 52-year-old woman who once received a blood transfusion abroad
case.story: Over 4 years her legs stiffened; she now walks with a stick and has urgency incontinence and low back ache.
case.exam: Spastic gait, mild hip flexor weakness, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with clonus, bilateral Babinski, vibration slightly reduced at toes; arms normal.
case.tests: MRI thoracic cord thin without compression; HTLV-1 antibody positive with western blot; CSF 12 lymphocytes, oligoclonal bands, high proviral load.
case.q: Which other condition must be screened for before giving steroids?
case.a: Strongyloides stercoralis infection — HTLV-1 predisposes to hyperinfection, which corticosteroids can make fatal; treat with ivermectin first if positive.

det.patho: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus transmitted through breast milk, sexual contact, blood transfusion and needle-sharing; most carriers stay healthy, and only a few percent develop HAM/TSP. Infected CD4 T cells crossing into the cord provoke a cytotoxic CD8 response with bystander tissue damage, mainly in the thoracic lateral columns. High proviral load is a risk factor.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the 40s–50s, more often in women. Gait stiffness, leg weakness and bladder dysfunction dominate, with back pain and paraesthesias out of proportion to sensory signs. Arms are mildly involved at most. Endemic areas include southern Japan, the Caribbean, South America, parts of Africa, Iran and Aboriginal Australia; cases in Thailand are uncommon and usually linked to travel or migration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a progressive spastic paraparesis plus HTLV-1 antibodies in serum and CSF (confirmed), after excluding other myelopathies. CSF often shows mild pleocytosis and intrathecal antibody synthesis; CSF/blood proviral load ratio and neopterin help gauge activity. MRI typically shows thoracic atrophy without compression.
det.treatment: No antiviral is proven. Steroids (oral or pulsed) may help in early or rapidly progressive disease after Strongyloides is excluded; interferon-alpha and mogamulizumab are options in some countries. Most care is symptomatic: antispasticity drugs (baclofen, tizanidine), bladder management, physiotherapy and walking aids. Counsel about avoiding breastfeeding and safe sex to limit transmission.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many need walking aids within a decade, with a minority of rapid progressors.
pearls: Spastic paraparesis with early bladder symptoms and few sensory signs: test HTLV-1.
Screen for Strongyloides before starting steroids.
Check for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma in carriers with lymphocytosis or skin lesions.
det.thd: HAM/TSP เป็นไขสันหลังอักเสบเรื้อรังจากเชื้อ HTLV-1 ซึ่งติดต่อทางนมแม่ เพศสัมพันธ์ และเลือด ผู้ป่วยมีขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ หลายปี ปัสสาวะกลั้นไม่อยู่ และปวดหลัง ส่วนความรู้สึกเสียเพียงเล็กน้อย วินิจฉัยด้วยแอนติบอดี HTLV-1 ในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง และ MRI พบไขสันหลังส่วนอกฝ่อ รักษาตามอาการ อาจใช้ steroid ในระยะแรกหลังตัด Strongyloides

ddx.pt: Brain and cord lesions on MRI with typical distribution; HTLV-1 negative
Family history, very slow course, bladder involvement later; normal CSF
Low B12 with prominent posterior column loss and neuropathy

aN: ham | ham tsp | tropical spastic paraparesis | htlv 1 myelopathy

name: HTLV-1 infection
formal: Infection with the human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 retrovirus, transmitted via breastfeeding, sex and blood; most carriers are asymptomatic, with risk of HAM and adult T-cell leukaemia.
simple: A long-term viral infection that usually causes no symptoms but can lead to spinal cord disease or a blood cancer in a few people.

name: Human herpesvirus and myelitis
formal: Spinal cord inflammation caused by herpesviruses such as VZV, HSV-2, CMV and EBV, producing acute or subacute myelopathy, often in immunocompromised patients, with CSF pleocytosis and PCR positivity.
simple: Inflammation of the spinal cord triggered by herpes-family viruses, causing weakness, numbness and bladder or bowel problems.

name: Human prion disease
formal: Group of transmissible neurodegenerative diseases from misfolded prion protein: sporadic, genetic, acquired or variant CJD, GSS and fatal familial insomnia, with rapid dementia and myoclonus.
simple: Rare, fatal brain diseases caused by abnormally folded proteins that destroy brain tissue and cause rapid dementia.

name: Human T-lymphocyte type 1 infection
formal: Retroviral infection causing HTLV-1-associated myelopathy (tropical spastic paraparesis), adult T-cell leukaemia, and sometimes myositis or neuropathy.
simple: A virus infection that can slowly damage the spinal cord and cause stiff, weak legs, or leukaemia in a few carriers.
more: Serology and CSF antibodies or PCR confirm it; myelopathy treated with steroids and symptomatic care. Most carriers stay symptom-free.

name: Hunter disease
formal: X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis II from iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, causing coarse features, hydrocephalus, cognitive decline, dysostosis multiplex and carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: An inherited condition in boys where the body cannot break down certain sugars, leading to coarse features, skeletal problems and, in severe forms, brain damage.

name: Huntington sine chorea
formal: Genetically confirmed Huntington disease presenting with cognitive, psychiatric or hypokinetic-rigid features but without chorea, as in the juvenile Westphal variant or late disease.
simple: Huntington disease in which the typical jerky movements are absent, so it shows up as stiffness, slowness or thinking and mood changes.

name: Huntington’s disease
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder of huntingtin with progressive chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance, due to striatal neuronal loss; onset usually in midlife.
simple: An inherited brain disease that gradually causes jerky involuntary movements, memory and thinking problems, and mood changes.
more: Diagnosis by HTT CAG repeats of 36 or more (full penetrance 40 or more) with caudate atrophy on MRI; genetic counselling and predictive testing protocols are crucial. Tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine for chorea, antidepressants, and supportive care.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่น — การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกไม่ตั้งใจ (chorea) บุคลิกเปลี่ยน ความคิดเสื่อม
feat: Chorea, motor impersistence (milkmaid grip), slow saccades
Psychiatric change: irritability, depression, obsessive behaviour
Subcortical dementia
Autosomal dominant with anticipation (paternal)
inv: HTT CAG repeat (≥40 full penetrance) with genetic counselling
MRI caudate atrophy

case.story: Family notice fidgeting and temper outbursts; his father died in a nursing home with 'dancing movements'.
case.exam: Flowing irregular movements of face and fingers, cannot keep tongue protruded, delayed saccade initiation.
case.tests: HTT CAG 44 repeats.
case.q: Name the inheritance pattern and the phenomenon seen in successive generations.
case.a: Autosomal dominant with anticipation — earlier onset, especially via paternal transmission.

ddx.pt: Young, liver disease, Kayser–Fleischer rings, low caeruloplasmin
HD phenocopy with JPH3 expansion, African ancestry
Childhood onset, non-progressive, no dementia

det.patho: An expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4 produces huntingtin with a long polyglutamine tract that is toxic to neurons, especially medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; 36–39 repeats show reduced penetrance and 40 or more are fully penetrant. Larger repeats give earlier onset, and repeats tend to expand through the father, explaining anticipation and juvenile (Westphal) cases.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the 30s–50s with a combination of motor, cognitive and psychiatric change, any of which may come first. Early motor signs are fidgety restlessness, slowed saccade initiation and motor impersistence, evolving to chorea, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and gait instability. Psychiatric features include depression, irritability, apathy, obsessive behaviour and a high suicide risk. Cognitive decline affects speed, planning and multitasking before memory. Juvenile HD often presents with rigidity, bradykinesia and seizures rather than chorea.
det.diagnosis: Confirm with genetic testing for HTT CAG repeat length in a symptomatic person; predictive testing of at-risk relatives must follow a formal counselling protocol. MRI shows caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns, but this is supportive, not diagnostic. Where testing is negative, consider phenocopies: C9orf72 expansion, HDL2, SCA17, neuroacanthocytosis, Wilson disease, and acquired chorea from drugs, thyroid disease, lupus or polycythaemia.
det.treatment: No therapy slows the disease yet; antisense and other huntingtin-lowering strategies remain under study. Chorea that causes harm or distress can be treated with tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine/valbenazine (watch for depression) or with antipsychotics, which also help agitation. Treat depression and irritability actively and screen for suicidality. Speech and swallow therapy, nutritional support (high calorie needs), physiotherapy, social care and genetic counselling for the family are essential.
det.prognosis: Death typically occurs 15–20 years after motor onset, usually from aspiration, falls or complications of immobility.
pearls: Motor impersistence — inability to sustain a grip or tongue protrusion — is often more reliable than chorea itself.
Always ask about suicidal thoughts; risk peaks around diagnosis and when independence is lost.
A negative family history does not exclude HD: misattributed paternity, early parental death or intermediate-allele expansion can hide it.
det.thd: Huntington's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากการขยายของ CAG repeat ในยีน HTT ทำให้เซลล์ใน caudate และ putamen ตาย อาการมีสามด้านคือ การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกแบบ chorea ความผิดปกติทางจิตใจ เช่น ซึมเศร้า หงุดหงิด และความคิดช้าลงจนสมองเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน (40 repeats ขึ้นไปแสดงโรคแน่นอน) โดยต้องให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการ เช่น tetrabenazine และดูแลด้านจิตเวชและครอบครัว

name: Huntington’s disease look like-2 disease
formal: Phenocopy of Huntington disease with chorea, psychiatric and cognitive features but a negative huntingtin test; causes include HDL1 to 4 and other genetic disorders.
simple: A condition that looks like Huntington disease but is caused by a different gene or cause.

name: Huntington’s disease-like 2 (HDL2)
formal: Autosomal dominant triplet repeat disorder from a CTG/CAG expansion in JPH3, resembling Huntington disease with chorea, dementia and acanthocytes; almost exclusively in people of African ancestry.
simple: An inherited disease that closely mimics Huntington disease, with movement problems and dementia, mostly seen in people of African descent.

name: Huntington’s disese
formal: Misspelling of Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder causing chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance from striatal degeneration.
simple: An inherited brain disease that gradually causes jerky involuntary movements, memory and thinking problems, and mood changes.

name: Hurler-Scheie syndrome
formal: Intermediate form of mucopolysaccharidosis I from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, with corneal clouding, joint stiffness, valvular disease and carpal tunnel syndrome, but milder or absent intellectual impairment.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder that causes joint stiffness, cloudy eyes and heart problems, milder than the severe infant form.

name: Hurst disease
formal: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis, a fulminant post-infectious demyelinating disease with perivascular haemorrhage and necrosis, causing rapid fever, coma and seizures; a hyperacute ADEM variant.
simple: A rare, very rapid and severe brain inflammation with bleeding, usually after an infection.

name: Hyaline body myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with subsarcolemmal hyaline inclusions of myosin, caused by MYH7, with slowly progressive scapuloperoneal or proximal weakness.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease with glassy protein clumps seen in muscle biopsies, causing slowly progressive weakness.
more: Biopsy shows hyaline bodies reactive for slow myosin; MYH7 testing; supportive care.

name: Hydrocephalic parkinsonism
formal: Gait disorder with bradykinesia and rigidity predominantly in the legs in patients with hydrocephalus, due to ventricular enlargement compressing frontal-subcortical pathways; may improve after shunting.
simple: Slow, shuffling walking and stiffness caused by fluid build-up in the brain, which can improve after the fluid is drained.

name: Hydrocephalus
formal: Excess CSF within the ventricles from obstructed flow, impaired absorption or rarely overproduction, producing raised pressure, headache, vomiting and papilloedema, or gait and cognitive decline in normal pressure form.
simple: A build-up of fluid inside the brain that raises pressure and can cause headache, vomiting and problems with walking or thinking.

name: Hydrogen sulphide poisoning
formal: Toxic gas exposure inhibiting cytochrome oxidase, causing rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure and, in survivors, basal ganglia damage and parkinsonism or cognitive sequelae.
simple: Poisoning by a rotten-egg smelling gas that can cause sudden collapse, seizures and lasting brain damage.

name: Hyperacute stroke
formal: Earliest phase of ischaemic stroke, within roughly six hours of onset, when thrombolysis or thrombectomy can salvage penumbra; imaging may show early ischaemic change or a hyperdense vessel.
simple: The very first hours after a stroke begins, when urgent treatment can save the most brain tissue.

name: Hyperekplexias
formal: Startle disorders, usually hereditary from glycine receptor or transporter mutations, with exaggerated startle, stiffening and falls to unexpected stimuli, and neonatal stiffness; treated with clonazepam.
simple: Conditions in which a sudden noise or touch causes an exaggerated startle and stiffening, sometimes with falls.

name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES)
formal: Persistent eosinophilia with end-organ damage, which can cause neuropathy, mononeuritis, myopathy, encephalopathy and cardiac thrombosis.
simple: A condition where very high levels of one type of white blood cell damage organs such as nerves and heart.
more: Diagnosed by sustained eosinophil count over 1500 with organ involvement after excluding other causes; treated with steroids, hydroxyurea or imatinib or mepolizumab.

name: Hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome (OMIM 600886)
formal: Autosomal dominant disorder from mutations in the iron-responsive element of the L-ferritin gene, causing high serum ferritin without iron overload and early bilateral cataracts.
simple: An inherited condition with very high blood ferritin without too much iron and cataracts at a young age.
more: Distinguished from iron overload by normal transferrin saturation; genetic test confirms. Treat cataracts surgically; venesection is not helpful and can cause anaemia.

name: Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (hyperPP)
formal: Autosomal dominant sodium or calcium channel muscle disease with episodes of flaccid weakness during raised serum potassium, often triggered by rest after exercise or potassium intake, with myotonia.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium rises, often after rest following exercise.
th: อ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ เริ่มในวัยเด็ก กระตุ้นด้วยการพักหลังออกกำลังหรือกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง — โรค SCN4A
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to a few hours, often daily; onset in first decade
feat: Brief attacks of flaccid limb weakness, frequently in the morning or during rest after exercise
Provoked by potassium-rich food, fasting, cold, stress; eased by mild exercise or carbohydrate
Serum potassium high or high-normal in attacks (can be normal)
Mild myotonia or paramyotonia (eyelid lag), and later a fixed proximal myopathy in some
inv: Potassium during an attack; ECG
Long exercise test: post-exercise fall in CMAP amplitude; EMG may show myotonia
SCN4A genetic testing; exclude secondary hyperkalaemia (renal, adrenal, drugs)

case.story: Several times a week, after resting following football, his legs go weak for 30–60 minutes; eating bananas seems to bring attacks on. His father had similar episodes as a child.
case.exam: Between attacks strength is normal; lid lag after looking down; mild grip myotonia.
case.tests: K 5.6 mmol/L during an attack; long exercise test shows a 45% CMAP decline; SCN4A variant confirmed.
case.q: What are the first-line measures?
case.a: Frequent carbohydrate-rich low-potassium meals, avoiding fasting and cold, mild exercise at onset, inhaled salbutamol to abort attacks, and a thiazide or acetazolamide for prevention.

det.patho: Gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the skeletal-muscle sodium channel, impair inactivation so that a modest rise in extracellular potassium leaves the membrane persistently depolarised and inexcitable. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. The same gene causes paramyotonia congenita and some potassium-aggravated myotonias, and phenotypes overlap.
det.clinical: Attacks begin in infancy or childhood and are typically short and frequent. Weakness affects limbs more than face, rarely the respiratory muscles. Rest after exercise, fasting, cold, potassium intake and anaesthesia provoke attacks, while light activity can abort them. Myotonia, paramyotonia of the eyelids, and a slowly progressive fixed proximal weakness in middle age may accompany the disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, potassium during attacks (raised in many but not all), exclusion of secondary hyperkalaemia, and genetic confirmation of SCN4A. The long exercise test (prolonged exercise then serial CMAPs) shows a delayed decrement; EMG often reveals myotonic discharges between attacks. Provocative potassium loading is no longer recommended outside specialist settings.
det.treatment: Lifestyle: frequent carbohydrate-rich meals, avoid potassium-rich foods, fasting, cold and strenuous exercise followed by rest. Acute attacks may resolve with light exercise, glucose, or inhaled beta-agonist. Preventive therapy uses kaliuretic diuretics (thiazides) or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide). Anaesthetists must be informed—avoid potassium-containing fluids and depolarising relaxants and keep the patient warm.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen after middle age, but a permanent proximal myopathy can develop. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Short, frequent attacks in childhood favour hyperPP; long attacks in adolescence favour hypoPP.
Potassium can be normal in an attack — the name reflects sensitivity, not always the level.
Ask about anaesthesia: suxamethonium and potassium-rich fluids can provoke severe weakness.
det.thd: HyperPP เกิดจาก mutation ของยีน SCN4A (sodium channel ของกล้ามเนื้อ) ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ ตั้งแต่เด็ก มักเกิดขณะพักหลังออกกำลังหรือหลังกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง ระหว่างอาการโพแทสเซียมสูงหรือปกติ อาจมี myotonia ร่วม วินิจฉัยด้วย long exercise test และตรวจยีน รักษาโดยกินคาร์โบไฮเดรตบ่อย หลีกเลี่ยงโพแทสเซียม ใช้ thiazide หรือ acetazolamide ป้องกัน

ddx.pt: Longer attacks (hours–days), low K, carbohydrate provokes rather than relieves
Attacks with ventricular arrhythmia, long QU and dysmorphic features
Cold- and exercise-worsened stiffness dominates; weakness is secondary

name: Hyperkinetic syndromes
formal: Movement disorders with excess involuntary movement, including chorea, dystonia, tremor, tics, myoclonus and athetosis, from dysfunction of basal ganglia circuits.
simple: A group of conditions in which the body makes too many unwanted movements, such as jerks, twists, tremors or tics.

name: Hyperosmolar non-ketotic state (HONK)
formal: Hyperglycaemic emergency in type 2 diabetes with severe dehydration, serum osmolality above 320 and minimal ketosis, causing confusion, seizures, focal deficits and coma.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and dehydration that can cause confusion, seizures and coma.

name: Hypertensive encephalopathy
formal: Acute encephalopathy from severe hypertension exceeding cerebral autoregulation, with headache, visual loss, seizures and confusion, and vasogenic oedema on MRI, as in PRES.
simple: Brain swelling caused by extremely high blood pressure, leading to headache, vision problems, seizures and confusion.

name: Hyperthermic catatonia
formal: Catatonia with fever and autonomic instability, overlapping with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and lethal catatonia; features stupor, rigidity and tachycardia and needs urgent benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A serious state of immobility or agitation with high fever and unstable vital signs, needing urgent hospital treatment.

name: Hypnic headache
formal: Rare primary headache of older adults that wakes patients from sleep at consistent times with moderate pain lasting 15 to 240 minutes; responds to caffeine or lithium.
simple: A rare headache in older people that wakes them from sleep at the same time each night.

name: Hypnogenic dyskinesias
formal: Abnormal involuntary movements arising from sleep, such as paroxysmal nocturnal dystonia, that are often frontal lobe seizures and appear in stereotyped episodes at night.
simple: Unusual movements that happen during sleep, sometimes caused by seizures in a part of the brain.

name: Hypnogenic paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Old term for paroxysmal dystonic or hyperkinetic attacks arising from sleep, now largely recognised as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy, often linked to CHRNA4 and related genes.
simple: Short, sudden episodes of abnormal movements during sleep that are usually due to frontal lobe seizures.
more: Video-EEG confirms an epileptic basis; carbamazepine often works. Differentiate from parasomnias and from true paroxysmal dyskinesias.

name: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (hypoPP)
formal: Channelopathy from calcium or sodium channel mutations causing episodes of flaccid weakness with low serum potassium, often after carbohydrate meals or rest following exercise; treated with potassium and acetazolamide.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium is low, often after carbohydrate-rich meals or rest after exercise.

feat: Flaccid weakness of limbs, sparing face and breathing, with low potassium during the attack
Triggers: carbohydrate-rich meals, rest after exercise, stress, cold

Late fixed proximal myopathy can develop
inv: Potassium during the attack; ECG (U waves, arrhythmia)
Thyroid function; urine potassium to exclude renal loss
Long exercise test on NCS; CACNA1S / SCN4A genetics

case.story: Woke at 5 a.m. unable to lift his arms or legs after a large rice-and-sweets dinner; normal the day before. Recent weight loss and tremor.
case.exam: Symmetric flaccid quadriparesis, absent reflexes, normal sensation and cranial nerves, fine tremor, tachycardia.
case.tests: K 1.9 mmol/L; ECG U waves; TSH suppressed, free T4 high.
case.q: How does this change long-term treatment?
case.a: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — attacks stop once the patient is euthyroid; beta-blockers help meanwhile. Give potassium cautiously to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia.

ddx.pt: Days not hours, sensory symptoms, normal potassium
Brief attacks with high or normal K, triggered by rest after exercise or fasting; myotonia
Ocular/bulbar fatigable weakness

aN: hypopp | hypokalemic periodic paralysis | hypokpp | cacna1s | thyrotoxic periodic paralysis

det.patho: Primary hypoPP is an autosomal dominant channelopathy, mostly from CACNA1S (calcium channel) and less often SCN4A (sodium channel) variants that create an abnormal leak current through the voltage-sensor region. When serum potassium falls, affected fibres depolarise paradoxically, sodium channels inactivate and the membrane becomes inexcitable. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, frequent in Asian men, reflects thyroid hormone driving Na/K-ATPase activity with a genetic susceptibility (e.g. KCNJ18), shifting potassium into cells.
det.clinical: Attacks of flaccid weakness usually begin on waking or after rest following exertion or a carbohydrate load, and may last from hours to a day or more. Proximal limbs are hit hardest; bulbar, ocular and respiratory muscles are generally spared, although severe hypokalaemia can threaten cardiac rhythm. Reflexes drop during the episode and sensation is normal. Primary forms start in childhood or adolescence, with attack frequency often waning after mid-life while a permanent proximal myopathy may emerge. A first attack in an adult man, especially with weight loss, tremor or palpitations, should prompt a thyroid screen.
det.diagnosis: Document a low potassium during an attack, since values between attacks are normal in primary disease. Check thyroid function, and measure urinary potassium and acid–base status to exclude renal or gastrointestinal loss (secondary hypokalaemic paralysis). The long exercise test on nerve conduction shows a delayed decline in CMAP amplitude in many patients, though a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis. Genetic testing of CACNA1S and SCN4A confirms primary disease; distinguish from Andersen–Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2) by looking for arrhythmia and dysmorphic features.
det.treatment: During an attack, give oral potassium chloride in modest repeated doses with ECG and potassium monitoring; reserve IV potassium for patients who cannot swallow or have arrhythmia, using non-glucose diluent. Overcorrection is common because potassium returns from cells as the attack resolves. Prevention includes avoiding high-carbohydrate meals and abrupt rest after strenuous exercise, plus carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) or potassium-sparing diuretics. In thyrotoxic paralysis, non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol) helps acutely and restoring euthyroidism stops attacks; acetazolamide is not useful there.
det.prognosis: Attacks are rarely fatal when potassium and rhythm are watched, but a fixed proximal myopathy can accumulate over decades. Thyrotoxic attacks cease once thyroid function is normal.
pearls: Normal potassium between attacks does not exclude hypoPP — test during the episode.
Adult Asian man with first attack: think thyrotoxicosis first.
Beware rebound hyperkalaemia after aggressive potassium replacement.
SCN4A-related hypoPP may worsen with acetazolamide; genotype guides choice.

name: Hypokalemia/Potassium disorders
formal: Disturbed serum potassium, with hypokalaemia causing weakness, cramps and rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia causing weakness, arrhythmia and paralysis.
simple: Too low or too high potassium in the blood, which can cause muscle weakness, cramps and heart rhythm problems.
more: Investigate with ECG, renal function and drug history; correct the underlying cause and replace or lower potassium according to severity.

name: Hypokalemic myopathy
formal: Acquired proximal myopathy with severe hypokalaemia, from diuretics, licorice, renal tubular acidosis or hyperaldosteronism, with raised CK and sometimes rhabdomyolysis.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by a low level of potassium in the blood.
more: Corrected by potassium replacement and treating the cause; usually fully reversible.

name: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 2
formal: Autosomal dominant periodic paralysis from SCN4A mutations, with attacks of flaccid weakness with low potassium, often with tubular aggregates on biopsy.
simple: An inherited condition with attacks of muscle weakness linked to low potassium, caused by a sodium channel gene change.
more: Provoked by carbohydrate meals or rest after exercise; treat with potassium, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide and trigger avoidance.

name: Hypokinetic (Parkinsonian) syndromes
formal: Syndromes with paucity of movement, bradykinesia and rigidity, mainly Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonisms, drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism, from basal ganglia dopaminergic dysfunction.
simple: Conditions with slowed or reduced movement and stiffness, of which Parkinson disease is the commonest.

name: Hypophysitis
formal: Inflammation of the pituitary, lymphocytic, granulomatous or secondary to checkpoint inhibitors, causing headache, visual disturbance and hypopituitarism, with an enlarged gland and stalk thickening on MRI.
simple: Swelling of the pituitary gland that can cause headache, vision trouble and low hormone levels.

name: Hypothyroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness, cramps, delayed reflex relaxation, and mounding with raised CK in hypothyroidism, from impaired glycogenolysis and mitochondrial function.
simple: Muscle weakness, cramps, and aching caused by an underactive thyroid.
more: Thyroid function tests confirm the cause; thyroxine replacement normalises strength over months.

tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months as hypothyroidism worsens
feat: Proximal weakness, muscle aches, cramps and stiffness, worse in cold
Slow relaxation phase of tendon reflexes ('hung-up' ankle jerk)
Muscle mounding (myoedema) when percussed
Occasional muscle enlargement (Hoffmann syndrome in adults)
Systemic signs: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, bradycardia
inv: TSH and free T4
CK often raised, sometimes many times normal
EMG: normal or mildly myopathic; nerve studies may show coexisting carpal tunnel or neuropathy

case.who: 50-year-old woman with prior radioactive iodine for Graves
case.story: Missed follow-up; over 4 months tired, cold, gaining weight, with aching thighs and painful cramps climbing stairs.
case.exam: Puffy face, dry skin, HR 54; mild hip flexor weakness; ankle jerks contract briskly but relax very slowly; tapping the deltoid raises a ridge.
case.tests: TSH 86 mIU/L, free T4 low; CK 2,400 U/L.
case.q: Does she need a muscle biopsy?
case.a: Usually no — replace thyroid hormone and recheck CK and strength; biopsy is reserved for failure to improve once euthyroid.

det.patho: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows muscle metabolism: reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity, impaired glycogen breakdown and slowed calcium reuptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Slow calcium handling explains delayed relaxation of reflexes and myoedema. Membrane leakiness raises CK.
det.clinical: Most patients have aches, cramps, fatigue and mild proximal weakness rather than severe paralysis. Delayed reflex relaxation is a classic sign. Rarely there is marked muscle hypertrophy with stiffness (Hoffmann syndrome), or rhabdomyolysis, especially with exercise or statins. Carpal tunnel syndrome and a mild sensorimotor neuropathy may coexist.
det.diagnosis: High TSH with low free T4 explains the picture; CK may be strikingly high and can trigger an unnecessary myositis work-up. Always check TSH in any unexplained raised CK or myopathy. EMG and biopsy are needed only when weakness persists after correction.
det.treatment: Levothyroxine replacement, started cautiously in older patients or those with heart disease, resolves the myopathy. Hold or review statins until euthyroid. Symptoms and CK improve over weeks to months.
det.prognosis: Very good; weakness and CK normalise with adequate replacement, though recovery may take several months.
pearls: Check TSH before labelling a high CK as myositis.
Slow-relaxing ankle jerk is a bedside clue to hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism amplifies statin muscle toxicity.

aN: myxedema myopathy | hypothyroid myopathy | hoffmann syndrome | kocher debre semelaigne syndrome

name: Hypothyroidism
formal: Thyroid hormone deficiency with neuromuscular manifestations including myopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, polyneuropathy, myoedema, and delayed relaxation of reflexes.
simple: An underactive thyroid gland, which can cause tiredness, weakness, muscle pain, and nerve compression.
more: Diagnosed by high TSH with low free T4; levothyroxine replacement usually reverses neuromuscular complications.

name: Hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)
formal: Brain injury from inadequate oxygen and blood flow, classically after cardiac arrest or perinatal asphyxia, causing coma, seizures, myoclonus and watershed or deep grey matter infarction.
simple: Brain damage from a lack of oxygen and blood flow, for example after a cardiac arrest or a difficult birth.

name: Hysterical hyperekplexia
formal: Functional startle disorder with exaggerated, non-habituating startle responses and abnormal posturing that lack the features of genetic hyperekplexia and are inconsistent with distraction.
simple: A psychologically driven, exaggerated startle reaction to sudden stimuli that is not due to structural brain disease.

name: Hysterical tremor
formal: Functional tremor with variable frequency and amplitude, entrainment to voluntary rhythm, distractibility and co-contraction, often with a sudden onset and suggestibility.
simple: A tremor from a functional nervous system disorder that changes with attention and has no structural cause.

name: Iatrogenic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
formal: Prion disease transmitted by medical procedures, such as contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater grafts or human growth hormone, with long incubation before progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: A rare form of CJD passed on by contaminated medical equipment or tissue products, appearing years after exposure.

name: ICCA syndrome
formal: Familial syndrome linking infantile convulsions with later paroxysmal choreoathetosis, autosomal dominant, from PRRT2 mutation; benign infantile seizures respond well to carbamazepine.
simple: An inherited condition in which a baby has seizures and later in childhood or adulthood has episodes of writhing movements.

name: Ideational/conceptual apraxia
formal: Apraxia from failure of the concept of an action, so patients misuse objects and cannot sequence multi-step tasks, due to dominant parietal or diffuse lesions as in Alzheimer disease.
simple: Loss of understanding of how to use objects or plan a sequence of actions, even though muscles work normally.

name: Ideomotor apraxia
formal: Apraxia with impaired performance of skilled movements to command or imitation, with intact object use in context, due to dominant parietal or premotor lesions or the corpus callosum.
simple: Difficulty carrying out learned gestures, such as waving goodbye, on request even though the person understands and has normal strength.

name: IDH-mutant diffuse glioma
formal: WHO-defined astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, typically young adults, with favourable prognosis; oligodendroglioma also has 1p19q codeletion.
simple: A slow-growing type of brain tumour in younger adults that carries a particular genetic change and has a better outlook.

name: IDH-mutant gliomas
formal: Diffuse glioma family with IDH mutation, including astrocytomas with ATRX and TP53 changes and 1p19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, associated with longer survival than IDH-wildtype tumours.
simple: A group of brain tumours with a specific gene change that tend to grow more slowly and respond better to treatment.

name: IDH-wildtype glioblastoma
formal: The most aggressive primary adult brain tumour, with necrosis and microvascular proliferation and no IDH mutation; median survival about 15 months despite surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide.
simple: The most common and aggressive primary brain cancer in adults, which is hard to treat.

name: Idiopathic axonal neuropathies
formal: Distal, mostly sensory length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy of unknown cause in older adults, slowly progressive, with normal evaluation for secondary causes.
simple: A slowly worsening nerve problem in the feet and hands of older people for which no cause can be found.

name: Idiopathic axonal neuropathy (IAN)
formal: Slowly progressive, mainly sensory distal axonal neuropathy in older people, with no identified cause after exhaustive work-up, diagnosed by exclusion.
simple: A slowly worsening nerve problem causing numbness and tingling in the feet, with no cause found.

name: Idiopathic basal ganglia calcification (IBGC)
formal: Familial or sporadic Fahr disease with bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate and thalamus, causing parkinsonism, dementia and psychiatric features; genes include SLC20A2, PDGFB and XPR1.
simple: A condition in which calcium builds up in deep brain areas, leading to movement, thinking and mood problems.

name: Idiopathic choreic syndromes
formal: Choreic disorders with no secondary cause, including benign hereditary chorea and senile chorea, as well as unexplained sporadic chorea, after genetic and metabolic exclusion.
simple: Jerky, dance-like movements for which doctors cannot find a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic copper toxicosis syndromes
formal: Copper overload disorders without a Wilson gene defect, such as Indian childhood cirrhosis and Tyrolean copper toxicosis, with hepatic copper accumulation and liver failure from environmental and genetic factors.
simple: Rare conditions in which too much copper builds up in the liver in children, causing liver damage.
more: Liver copper is high but ceruloplasmin is often normal. Treat with copper chelation like penicillamine and avoid copper-rich water and utensils.

name: Idiopathic cranial dystonias
formal: Primary focal dystonias of cranial muscles, such as blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and Meige syndrome, of unknown origin and usually in middle age.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the eyes, face or jaw that start without a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic hypersomnia
formal: Chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, sleep inertia and no cataplexy, with normal sleep apnoea testing and mean sleep latency below eight minutes.
simple: Constant, heavy daytime sleepiness despite long nights of sleep, without a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
formal: Heterogeneous autoimmune muscle diseases, including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotising myopathy and inclusion body myositis, with proximal weakness and raised creatine kinase.
simple: A group of conditions in which the immune system attacks muscles, causing weakness and sometimes muscle pain.

name: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy
formal: Autoimmune muscle diseases including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotizing myopathy and inclusion body myositis, causing proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A group of conditions where the immune system attacks muscles, causing weakness and sometimes skin rashes.
more: Diagnosis by CK, EMG, MRI, antibodies and biopsy; treat with steroids, immunosuppressants or IVIG; screen for cancer in dermatomyositis.

name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
formal: Raised intracranial pressure with normal imaging and CSF content, typical in overweight young women, causing headache, papilloedema and visual loss; treated with weight loss, acetazolamide or shunting.
simple: High pressure around the brain with no tumour, causing headaches and risk to vision, most often in young women with obesity.

feat: Daily headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus
Bilateral papilloedema; sixth nerve palsy may occur (false-localising)
Typically women of childbearing age with recent weight gain
Threat is permanent visual field loss
inv: MRI with MR venography to exclude mass and venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus: raised opening pressure, normal CSF contents
Formal visual fields and OCT

case.story: Three months of headache and brief greying of vision on standing; hears a whooshing in her ears.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, enlarged blind spots, mild left abduction deficit.
case.tests: MRI/MRV normal apart from empty sella; LP opening pressure 38 cmH2O, normal cell count and protein.
case.q: What is the most important outcome to protect?
case.a: Vision — treat with weight loss and acetazolamide and monitor fields; escalate urgently if fields deteriorate.

ddx.pt: Venous filling defect on MRV
Disc drusen or crowded discs without true oedema; normal pressure
Normal fundi and pressure

aN: iih | idiopathic intracranial hypertension | pseudotumor cerebri | benign intracranial hypertension | pseudotumour cerebri

det.patho: Raised CSF pressure without mass, hydrocephalus or venous thrombosis; the mechanism likely involves impaired CSF drainage, venous sinus stenosis that feeds a pressure loop, and metabolic or hormonal factors linked to obesity (adipose-derived androgens and cortisol). It predominantly affects women of reproductive age with obesity, especially after recent weight gain. Drugs such as tetracyclines, retinoids and growth hormone can provoke a secondary form.
det.clinical: Daily headache, transient visual obscurations lasting seconds, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia from sixth nerve palsy and neck or back pain are typical. Papilloedema is usually bilateral; vision loss begins peripherally (enlarged blind spot, nasal field loss) and central acuity is affected late. Fulminant IIH progresses to severe visual loss within weeks. Headache often persists even after pressure normalises, partly from coexisting migraine or medication overuse.
det.diagnosis: Modified Dandy criteria/Friedman criteria require papilloedema, a non-focal exam apart from sixth nerve palsy, normal brain parenchyma on MRI, normal CSF composition and opening pressure ≥25 cmH2O in adults (lateral decubitus, relaxed). Supportive MRI signs are an empty sella, flattened posterior globes, distended optic nerve sheaths and transverse sinus stenosis. MRV is mandatory to exclude CVT. Distinguish true papilloedema from pseudopapilloedema (drusen) with OCT or ultrasound.
det.treatment: Weight loss of about 5–15% is disease-modifying; bariatric surgery is effective in suitable patients. Acetazolamide is first-line drug therapy, with topiramate as an alternative that also helps headache. Monitor visual fields and OCT closely. Threatened vision needs urgent CSF diversion (shunt), optic nerve sheath fenestration or venous sinus stenting. Treat the headache separately and avoid medication overuse.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise, but permanent visual field loss occurs in a meaningful minority; relapse is linked to weight regain.
pearls: Always do MRI with MRV before calling it idiopathic.
Sixth nerve palsy in raised ICP is a false-localising sign.
Vision, not headache, is what you are protecting.

name: Idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia (ILOCA)
formal: Sporadic progressive cerebellar ataxia starting after about age 40 with no family history and no identified cause, after excluding genetic, toxic, immune, vitamin and paraneoplastic causes.
simple: A balance and coordination problem beginning in later life with no known cause, in someone without a family history.
more: MRI shows cerebellar atrophy. Some cases are probable MSA-C or have genetic causes, so search carefully; treatment is supportive.
nN: idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia iloca
aN: iloca | idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia

name: Idiopathic late-onset ataxia
formal: Progressive cerebellar ataxia developing after age 40 with no identified genetic or acquired cause, often sporadic and including undiagnosed cases later classified as MSA-C.
simple: A balance and coordination problem that begins later in life without a known cause.

name: Idiopathic PD
formal: Sporadic Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity and postural instability from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra with Lewy body pathology, responsive to levodopa.
simple: The usual form of Parkinson disease with slowness, tremor and stiffness, in which no single cause is found.
more: Diagnosis is clinical with levodopa response, and DaT scan if unclear. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and deep brain stimulation in selected patients.

name: Idiopathic perineuritis
formal: Rare inflammatory neuropathy affecting nerve perineurium, causing painful, patchy sensorimotor deficits, with perineurial inflammation on biopsy and no systemic cause.
simple: A rare inflammation of the nerve sheath that causes pain and patchy weakness without a clear cause.
more: Biopsy shows perineurial inflammation; corticosteroids are often effective.

name: Idiopathic recurring stupor
formal: Rare recurrent episodes of unexplained stupor with elevated endogenous benzodiazepine-like activity, reversed by flumazenil, with normal EEG and structural imaging.
simple: Repeated episodes of unexplained drowsiness and unresponsiveness that may be caused by natural sedative-like substances in the body.

name: Idiopathic scoliosis
formal: Lateral spinal curvature of unknown cause, usually in adolescent girls, defined by Cobb angle above 10 degrees; neurological screening is needed to exclude syringomyelia and other spinal causes.
simple: A sideways curve of the spine appearing in childhood or teens without a known cause.

name: Idiopathic sensory neuropathy
formal: Sensory polyneuropathy with no found cause after evaluation, causing distal numbness and tingling.
simple: Numbness or tingling in the feet and hands for which no cause can be found.
more: Exclude treatable causes; treat symptoms; the course is usually slowly progressive.

name: Idiopathic torsion dystonia
formal: Primary generalised dystonia, often DYT1 (TOR1A) mutation, with childhood onset limb dystonia that spreads, especially in Ashkenazi Jewish families, without other neurological features.
simple: An inherited condition in which muscles twist the body into abnormal postures, usually starting in childhood.
more: Normal MRI and DAT-SPECT; DYT1 is a GAG deletion in TOR1A with autosomal dominant inheritance and about 30 percent penetrance. Treat with anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl, botulinum toxin, and DBS of globus pallidus internus gives marked benefit.

name: Imipramine akathisia
formal: Akathisia induced by imipramine or other tricyclic antidepressants, with inner restlessness and inability to sit still, probably from altered dopaminergic and serotonergic transmission.
simple: Intense restlessness and inability to stay still caused by a tricyclic antidepressant medicine.

name: Immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)
formal: Neurotoxicity after CAR-T or bispecific T-cell therapy, with aphasia, encephalopathy, tremor, seizures and cerebral oedema, related to cytokine release and endothelial dysfunction; treated with steroids.
simple: Confusion, speech trouble and seizures that can occur after certain cancer immune cell treatments.
nN: immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome icans
aN: icans | immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome

name: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity following CAR-T or T-cell engager therapy, ranging from word-finding difficulty to seizures and fatal cerebral oedema, usually with cytokine release syndrome.
simple: Brain side effects such as confusion and speech problems after certain cell-based cancer treatments.

name: Immune mediated necrotising myopathy
formal: Autoimmune myopathy with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies and necrotic muscle fibres with little inflammation, causing subacute proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase; may follow statin use.
simple: A muscle disease in which the immune system damages muscle, causing weakness and often linked to statin medicines.

No rash; weakness continues after stopping a statin (unlike toxic statin myopathy)

case.story: Three months of rising difficulty standing from a chair; the statin was stopped 6 weeks ago without improvement.
case.exam: Hip flexors and deltoids 3/5, neck flexors weak, no rash, reflexes normal.
case.tests: CK 9,800 U/L; anti-HMGCR positive; biopsy: necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation.
case.q: What treatment is usually needed?
case.a: Immunotherapy — steroids plus a steroid-sparing agent and often IVIG; stopping the statin alone is not enough.

aN: imnm | necrotizing autoimmune myopathy | nam | anti hmgcr myopathy | anti srp myopathy | statin myopathy autoimmune

det.patho: IMNM is an autoimmune myopathy in which antibodies (anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR) and complement target muscle fibres, causing widespread necrosis with little lymphocytic infiltration. Anti-HMGCR disease is linked to statin exposure in older adults, although it also occurs in statin-naive younger patients; HLA-DRB1*11:01 increases risk. A seronegative form shows the strongest cancer association. It is classified alongside dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome and inclusion body myositis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness develops over weeks to months, often severe, with neck flexor weakness, dysphagia and myalgia. Extramuscular features are uncommon, though anti-SRP disease may involve the heart and lungs and is often more aggressive. Younger patients, especially children with anti-HMGCR disease, may present slowly and resemble limb-girdle dystrophy. Unlike self-limited statin myotoxicity, weakness and high CK persist after stopping the statin.
det.diagnosis: CK is typically very high. Test anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies; a positive HMGCR antibody with a typical picture may make biopsy unnecessary. Biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres, sparse inflammation and sarcolemmal complement deposition. Muscle MRI shows oedema and helps choose a biopsy site. Screen for cancer, especially in seronegative and anti-HMGCR cases, and assess cardiac and pulmonary function.
det.treatment: Start early, combined immunotherapy: corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate), with IVIG frequently added and effective, particularly for anti-HMGCR disease. Rituximab is used in refractory or anti-SRP disease. Stop the statin and avoid re-exposure; PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe are lipid-lowering alternatives. Physiotherapy and swallowing therapy support recovery.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve, but relapses on tapering and residual weakness are common; younger patients and those with anti-SRP antibodies tend to do worse.
pearls: Persistent weakness with very high CK after stopping a statin = test anti-HMGCR.
Necrosis with little inflammation on biopsy does not mean non-immune.
Children with slow anti-HMGCR myopathy may be misdiagnosed as LGMD.
det.thd: IMNM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้เซลล์กล้ามเนื้อตายเป็นจำนวนมาก โดยมีเซลล์อักเสบน้อย สัมพันธ์กับแอนติบอดี anti-HMGCR (มักมีประวัติใช้ยาสแตติน) หรือ anti-SRP ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน CK สูงมาก และอาการไม่ดีขึ้นแม้หยุดยาสแตติน การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจแอนติบอดี MRI และชิ้นเนื้อ ร่วมกับตรวจคัดกรองมะเร็ง การรักษาคือสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และมักให้ IVIG ร่วมด้วย ส่วนรายที่ดื้อยาใช้ rituximab

name: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
formal: Paradoxical worsening of an infection or onset of inflammation after antiretroviral recovery of the immune system in HIV, such as with cryptococcal meningitis, TB or PML.
simple: A worsening of infection symptoms when the immune system recovers after starting HIV treatment.

name: Immune-mediated encephalitis
formal: Brain inflammation due to autoimmune or paraneoplastic mechanisms, such as anti-NMDA receptor or LGI1 antibodies, with seizures, memory loss, psychiatric change and movement disorders.
simple: The immune system attacking the brain, causing confusion, seizures and memory or behaviour changes.

name: Immune-mediated neurological diseases
formal: Neurological disorders from immune attack on the nervous system, such as multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis and CIDP.
simple: Conditions in which the body's own immune system damages the brain, nerves or muscles.

name: Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD)
formal: Fibro-inflammatory disease with IgG4-positive plasma cells, causing hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, orbital pseudotumour and cranial neuropathies; responds to steroids and rituximab.
simple: An immune condition causing swollen, scarred tissues that can affect the brain coverings, pituitary, eye sockets and nerves.
nN: immunoglobulin g4 related disease igg4 rd
aN: igg4 rd | immunoglobulin g4 related disease

name: Impulsive behavior disorders
formal: Impulse control disorders such as pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating, frequently dopamine agonist related in Parkinson disease.
simple: Strong urges to do things like gamble, shop or overeat that are hard to resist, often triggered by Parkinson treatment.
more: Screen at each visit and lower or stop the dopamine agonist; cognitive behavioural therapy can help. Symptoms usually improve after the drug is adjusted.

name: Inclusion body myositis (IBM)
formal: Late-onset inflammatory myopathy with asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and poor response to immunotherapy.
simple: A slowly progressing muscle disease in older people, causing weak grip and thigh muscles and falls.
more: Diagnose from biopsy with rimmed vacuoles, p62 or TDP-43 aggregates, and positive anti-cN1A antibodies; CK is mildly raised and EMG shows mixed myopathic and neurogenic changes. Dysphagia is frequent; supportive care and exercise are the main management.

case.story: Three years of falls on stairs and difficulty gripping a golf club.
case.exam: Wasted forearms with weak finger flexors, quadriceps 3/5, knee jerks reduced, sensation normal.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; biopsy: rimmed vacuoles with endomysial CD8 T cells.
case.q: Which two muscle groups give the diagnosis away at the bedside?
case.a: Deep finger flexors and quadriceps.
