aN: ibm | inclusion body myositis | sibm | sporadic inclusion body myositis

det.patho: A slowly progressive myopathy of older adults combining cytotoxic CD8 T-cell inflammation with degenerative features — rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates (TDP-43, p62) and mitochondrial abnormalities. Antibodies against cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A) are found in a proportion of patients. It is the most common acquired myopathy after 50, more frequent in men, and does not respond to standard immunotherapy, suggesting the degenerative process is not simply driven by inflammation.
det.clinical: Weakness develops over years, typically asymmetric, with selective involvement of deep finger flexors (weak grip, difficulty turning keys) and quadriceps (knees buckling, falls on stairs). Ankle dorsiflexors and facial muscles may be involved, and dysphagia affects over half. Wasting of the medial forearm and thigh is a visual clue. Sensation is normal, but a mild neuropathy can coexist, causing confusion with motor neuron disease.
det.diagnosis: CK is normal or moderately raised (usually under 15 times the upper limit). EMG shows myopathic and often neurogenic-looking units with fibrillations. Muscle MRI or ultrasound highlights selective flexor digitorum profundus and quadriceps involvement with relative rectus femoris sparing. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation invading non-necrotic fibres, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates and mitochondrial changes; anti-cN1A is supportive but not specific (also seen in Sjögren and SLE). The ENMC 2011 criteria are commonly used.
det.treatment: No drug has proven effective; corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressants do not halt progression. Management centres on physiotherapy and safe exercise, falls prevention with knee-ankle orthoses and walking aids, occupational therapy for grip, and swallowing assessment with dilatation or cricopharyngeal myotomy for severe dysphagia. IVIG may help dysphagia in some reports. Patients should be offered clinical trials where available.
det.prognosis: Slow progression over years; many need a walking aid within 10–15 years, but life expectancy is near normal unless dysphagia causes aspiration.
pearls: Older man, weak finger flexors and quadriceps, poor steroid response = IBM.
Steroid-refractory polymyositis should prompt reconsideration of IBM.
det.thd: IBM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเรื้อรังในผู้ที่อายุเกิน 50 ปี มีทั้งการอักเสบจาก CD8 T cell และการเสื่อมที่พบ rimmed vacuoles ในชิ้นเนื้อ อาการค่อย ๆ อ่อนแรงหลายปีแบบไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง เด่นที่กล้ามเนื้องอนิ้วมือ (กำไม่แน่น) และ quadriceps (เข่าทรุด หกล้ม) และกลืนลำบาก CK สูงเล็กน้อย ตรวจแอนติบอดี anti-cN1A, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ และตัดชิ้นเนื้อช่วยยืนยัน โรคนี้ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์และยากดภูมิ การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน และดูแลการกลืน

name: Index brainstem reticular myoclonus
formal: Cortical-subcortical myoclonus arising from the brainstem reticular formation, producing generalised jerks with startle-like characteristics, often after hypoxic brain injury or in hyperekplexia.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks involving the whole body that originate in the brainstem, often after brain injury.

name: Index classical essential tremor
formal: Common postural and kinetic tremor, mostly of the hands, slowly progressive, often familial, improved by alcohol and responsive to propranolol or primidone.
simple: A very common tremor of the hands that appears with action, often runs in families and improves with alcohol.

name: Index globoid cell leucodystrophy (Krabbe’s disease)
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal disease from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination with irritability, spasticity, seizures and optic atrophy, usually in infancy.
simple: An inherited disease where nerves lose their insulating coating, leading to stiffness, seizures and developmental loss, most often in babies.
nN: index globoid cell leucodystrophy krabbe disease
aN: krabbe disease | index globoid cell leucodystrophy

name: Index heavy metal poisoning
formal: Neurotoxicity from lead, mercury, arsenic, manganese or thallium, producing encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy, tremor or parkinsonism depending on the agent and exposure.
simple: Nerve and brain damage caused by poisoning with metals such as lead, mercury or arsenic.

name: Index hemidystonia
formal: Dystonia affecting one half of the body, usually symptomatic of contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesions, such as stroke, trauma or perinatal injury.
simple: Twisting muscle spasms on one side of the body, usually from damage to the opposite side of the brain.

name: Index palatal myoclonus/tremor
formal: Rhythmic palatal movements at 1 to 3 Hz from hypertrophic olivary degeneration after Guillain-Mollaret triangle lesions, either symptomatic with ear click or essential.
simple: A rhythmic jerking of the soft palate, often with a clicking sound in the ear, usually after damage in the brainstem.

name: Index pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
formal: Autosomal recessive NBIA from PANK2 mutation, with childhood dystonia, rigidity, retinopathy and the eye-of-the-tiger sign in the globus pallidus on MRI.
simple: An inherited childhood disease with iron build-up in the brain, causing stiffness and twisting movements.

name: Index progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia
formal: Syndrome of myoclonus, seizures and progressive neurological decline, including Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, or myoclonic ataxia (Ramsay Hunt).
simple: A group of inherited disorders with muscle jerks, seizures and worsening coordination and thinking.
nN: index progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia

name: Index restless legs syndrome (RLS)
formal: Sensorimotor disorder with urge to move the legs at rest, worse at night and relieved by movement, associated with iron deficiency and dopaminergic dysfunction; treated with gabapentinoids or iron.
simple: An irresistible urge to move the legs, especially in the evening or at rest, relieved by movement.

name: Index subcortical dementia
formal: Dementia from basal ganglia, thalamus and white matter disease, with slowed thinking, apathy, executive dysfunction and movement abnormalities, as in Parkinson, Huntington disease and HIV.
simple: Memory and thinking problems with slowed thinking and mood change, caused by damage to deep brain structures.

name: Index systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody
formal: Systemic autoimmune disease with antiphospholipid antibodies, causing stroke, seizures, chorea, myelitis, cognitive dysfunction and cerebral venous thrombosis through vasculopathy and thrombosis.
simple: An immune disease that can lead to strokes, seizures and thinking problems, in part through blood clots in brain vessels.
nN: index systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody

name: Indian childhood cirrhosis
formal: Infantile copper-associated liver disease of rural India with progressive cirrhosis and marked hepatic copper deposits, linked to copper-contaminated milk in brass vessels with a genetic susceptibility.
simple: A fatal childhood liver disease from too much copper in the diet seen in rural India, historically.
more: Liver biopsy shows copper and Mallory bodies. Early chelation (penicillamine) and stopping copper exposure help; it is now rare after public health changes.

name: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive PLA2G6-related disorder with onset in infancy of psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy, with axonal spheroids on biopsy.
simple: An inherited disease starting in infancy in which a child loses skills and develops weak muscles, vision problems and later stiffness.
more: Diagnosed by PLA2G6 testing; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and a characteristic clock-hand sign in the thin cord. Biopsy of skin or conjunctiva shows spheroids; prognosis is poor and care is supportive.

name: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (INAD
formal: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, PLA2G6-associated, with early psychomotor regression, hypotonia, tetraparesis, visual failure and cerebellar atrophy; iron accumulation in globus pallidus later.
simple: An inherited disease starting in infancy in which a child loses skills and develops weak muscles, vision problems and later stiffness.

name: Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Haltia-Santavuori disease)
formal: Santavuori-Haltia disease, a CLN1 PPT1-related lysosomal storage disorder with onset before 2 years of microcephaly, myoclonus, visual failure and flat EEG, with granular osmiophilic deposits.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing loss of skills, seizures, blindness and early death, from build-up of waste material in brain cells.
nN: infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis haltia santavuori disease
aN: haltia santavuori disease | infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis

name: Infantile onset spinocerebellar ataxia (IOSCA)
formal: Finnish autosomal recessive disorder from C10orf2 (Twinkle) variants with infantile ataxia, athetosis, ophthalmoplegia, sensory neuropathy, deafness and epilepsy.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing worsening balance, abnormal movements, deafness and nerve damage beginning in infancy.
more: Confirmed by genetic testing and MRI showing cerebellar atrophy. Treatment is supportive, and affected individuals often lose mobility in adolescence.

name: Infantile Pompe disease
formal: Severe lysosomal glycogen storage disease from GAA deficiency, with hypotonia, cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly in the first months of life; treated with enzyme replacement.
simple: An inherited disorder in babies where sugar stores build up in muscles and the heart, causing floppiness and heart enlargement.

name: Infantile spasms
formal: Epileptic spasms in infancy, typically with hypsarrhythmia on EEG and developmental regression (West syndrome); causes include tuberous sclerosis and hypoxic injury; treated with ACTH or vigabatrin.
simple: A serious type of seizure in babies, with sudden clusters of jerks and developmental delay, which needs prompt treatment.

name: Infectious intracranial aneurysms (IIAs)
formal: Mycotic aneurysms of cerebral arteries, usually distal, from septic emboli in infective endocarditis, which may cause subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage.
simple: Weak bulges in brain arteries caused by infection that can burst and bleed into the brain.

name: Infective endocarditis
formal: Infection of heart valves producing septic emboli to the brain, with ischaemic stroke, mycotic aneurysm, abscess, meningitis and haemorrhage as neurological complications.
simple: An infection of the heart valves that can send clots or germs to the brain and cause strokes or abscesses.

name: Infective vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of cerebral blood vessels caused by infection such as VZV, syphilis, tuberculosis or fungi, leading to ischaemic stroke or aneurysm and cranial neuropathy.
simple: Brain blood vessel inflammation caused by an infection, which can lead to stroke.

name: Infiltrative optic neuropathy
formal: Visual loss from optic nerve infiltration by lymphoma, leukaemia, carcinoma, sarcoidosis or granuloma, with optic disc swelling or pallor, often with a sluggish course.
simple: Loss of vision caused by cancer cells or inflammatory tissue growing into the optic nerve.

name: Inflammatory bowel disease
formal: Chronic inflammatory gut disease, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, with extra-intestinal neurological associations such as peripheral neuropathy, stroke, venous thrombosis and demyelination.
simple: Long-term gut inflammation, such as Crohn disease, that can also be linked to nerve problems and blood clots.
more: Neurological syndromes include natalizumab progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and demyelination during anti-TNF therapy. Evaluate for B12 and copper deficiency or vasculitis; treat the gut disease and associated thromboembolism risk.

name: Inflammatory disease of orbit
formal: Idiopathic orbital inflammation, or orbital pseudotumour, causing painful proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, responsive to corticosteroids; differential includes IgG4 disease and thyroid orbitopathy.
simple: Painful swelling inside the eye socket that causes a bulging eye and double vision, usually improving with steroids.

name: Inflammatory myopathies
formal: Group of immune-mediated muscle diseases such as polymyositis, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis causing proximal weakness, elevated CK and inflammatory infiltrates.
simple: A group of muscle conditions caused by inflammation, leading to weakness, usually in the shoulders and hips.
more: Check myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, SRP, NT5c1A), EMG with irritable myopathy, MRI and biopsy. Treat PM and DM with steroids plus methotrexate or azathioprine and IVIG; IBM is resistant and screen for malignancy in DM.

name: Inflammatory myopathy
formal: Acquired muscle disease with inflammatory infiltrates, such as dermatomyositis, polymyositis or inclusion body myositis, giving progressive proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A muscle disease with inflammation that causes weakness, usually of the shoulders and hips.

name: Inflammatory neuropathies
formal: Immune-mediated nerve diseases such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and CIDP, with demyelination causing weakness, areflexia and sensory loss, treatable with IVIG, plasma exchange or steroids.
simple: Conditions in which the immune system attacks nerves, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Infratentorial haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding in the posterior fossa, such as cerebellar or brainstem haemorrhage, causing vomiting, ataxia, coma and risk of hydrocephalus and herniation; may need surgical decompression.
simple: Bleeding in the lower part of the brain, around the cerebellum or brainstem, which can quickly become life-threatening.

name: Inherited ataxia syndromes
formal: Group of genetic cerebellar disorders, including spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia and episodic ataxias, with progressive gait and limb incoordination and dysarthria.
simple: A group of inherited conditions causing poor balance and coordination that worsen over time.

name: Inherited Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (iCJD)
formal: Genetic prion disease caused by PRNP mutations, with CJD-like rapid dementia, myoclonus and ataxia, with autosomal dominant inheritance.
simple: A rare inherited form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease that runs in families and causes fast-progressing dementia.

name: Inherited leukodystrophies, adult-onset
formal: Genetic white matter disorders presenting in adulthood, including ALSP, adrenomyeloneuropathy, Alexander disease and CADASIL-like disorders, with spastic gait, ataxia and cognitive decline.
simple: Inherited diseases of the brain's white matter that begin in adulthood and cause stiffness, imbalance and memory problems.

name: Inherited muscle disorders
formal: Genetic myopathies, including muscular dystrophies, congenital and metabolic myopathies and channelopathies, with progressive weakness and often elevated creatine kinase.
simple: Inherited conditions that weaken and waste muscles over time.

name: Inherited neuromyotonia and paroxysmal ataxia
formal: Episodic ataxia type 1, from KCNA1 mutation, with brief ataxia attacks lasting seconds to minutes, interictal myokymia and neuromyotonia, triggered by startle or exercise.
simple: An inherited condition with short attacks of unsteadiness and muscle twitching, set off by sudden movement or fright.

name: Inherited neuropathies
formal: Genetic peripheral nerve diseases, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth, hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies and hereditary sensory neuropathies, causing slowly progressive weakness and sensory loss.
simple: Inherited conditions that damage the nerves in the arms and legs, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Inherited neuropathy
formal: Genetic peripheral neuropathy, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, with slowly progressive distal weakness, foot deformities, and reduced reflexes.
simple: An inherited condition affecting nerves to the feet and hands, causing weakness, numbness and high-arched feet.

name: Inherited peripheral nerve diseases
formal: Genetic disorders of peripheral nerves such as CMT, HNPP and familial amyloid neuropathy, causing slowly progressive weakness and sensory loss, often with foot deformities.
simple: Inherited conditions that damage nerves in the arms and legs, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Inherited prion diseases
formal: Genetic prion disorders from PRNP mutation, including familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease and fatal familial insomnia, with rapidly progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: Rare inherited brain diseases from faulty prion protein that cause dementia, imbalance and sleep problems.

name: Initiation tremor
formal: Tremor that appears at the start of voluntary movement, as in Holmes tremor or primary orthostatic tremor variants, due to cerebellar outflow disturbance or other basal ganglia lesions.
simple: A tremor that shows up at the start of a movement and often settles once the movement is under way.

name: Insomnia
formal: Chronic difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with daytime impairment; may be primary or secondary to psychiatric, medical or neurological disease, medicines or sleep disorders.
simple: Ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep that affects how a person feels and functions in the daytime.

name: Insulin neuritis
formal: Acute painful small fibre neuropathy with autonomic features after rapid glycaemic correction in poorly controlled diabetes, such as treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.
simple: Severe nerve pain and autonomic symptoms that can follow a sudden fall in blood sugar after starting diabetes treatment.

name: Intention tremor
formal: Tremor on goal-directed movement that increases toward the target, characteristic of cerebellar outflow lesions in the dentate-rubro-thalamic pathway, seen in multiple sclerosis, stroke and toxins.
simple: A tremor that gets worse as the hand approaches a target, such as touching the nose, usually from cerebellar damage.

name: Intermittent ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia syndromes with attacks of incoordination between normal intervals, due to channelopathies or metabolic disorders; episodic ataxia types 1 and 2 are common.
simple: Conditions in which attacks of poor balance and coordination come and go.

name: Intermittent metabolic ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia from inborn errors of metabolism, such as maple syrup urine disease, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, urea cycle defects and Hartnup disease, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: Attacks of unsteady walking caused by inherited metabolic disorders, often brought on by infection or a high-protein meal.

name: Internal carotid artery (ICA) disease
formal: Stenosis or occlusion of the ICA, usually atherosclerotic at the bifurcation, causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or hemispheric stroke; also dissection, treated with endarterectomy or stenting.
simple: Narrowing or blockage of the main neck artery to the brain, which can cause temporary vision loss or stroke.

name: Internal carotid artery disease
formal: Stenosis, occlusion or dissection of the internal carotid artery causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or stroke through emboli or haemodynamic failure.
simple: Narrowing or blockage of the main neck artery to the brain, which can cause temporary vision loss or stroke.

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
formal: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from MLF lesions; commonly multiple sclerosis in young adults and brainstem stroke in older patients.
simple: Poor inward movement of one eye when looking sideways, caused by damage in a brainstem pathway.

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia of abduction
formal: Posterior or Lutz INO with weakness of abduction, rather than adduction, due to dysfunction of the contralateral side or lesions of paramedian pontine fibres, a variant of internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
simple: A rare eye movement problem in which the eye cannot move outward properly, due to damage to a brainstem pathway.

name: Interstitial lung disease (ILD)
formal: Diffuse parenchymal lung disease commonly associated with antisynthetase syndrome and other inflammatory myopathies, causing dyspnoea and restrictive physiology.
simple: Scarring or inflammation of the lungs, often seen alongside autoimmune muscle disease, causing breathlessness.
more: Diagnosed with HRCT and lung function tests; treated with steroids and immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; strongly affects prognosis in myositis.

name: Intracerebral haematoma
formal: Focal collection of blood within the brain parenchyma, typically from hypertensive vasculopathy, amyloid angiopathy, trauma or vascular malformation, with sudden deficit and mass effect.
simple: A pocket of blood inside the brain tissue that causes sudden weakness or other deficits.

name: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic stroke from rupture of a vessel in the parenchyma, most often hypertensive deep bleed or amyloid lobar bleed, with sudden headache, deficit and reduced consciousness.
simple: A stroke caused by bleeding inside the brain, often linked to high blood pressure.

case.story: Sudden left arm and leg weakness and headache while lifting a box; vomited twice; drowsier over 2 hours.
case.exam: BP 220/120, GCS 13, dense left hemiplegia and hemisensory loss, eyes deviated to the right.
case.tests: CT: 30 mL right putaminal haematoma with intraventricular extension.
case.q: Name the likely mechanism and two immediate management priorities.
case.a: Hypertensive deep ICH. Lower systolic BP promptly and safely, correct any coagulopathy, and monitor for hydrocephalus/expansion (neurosurgical review).

ddx.pt: Same bedside picture; CT shows no blood
Lobar bleeds in older patients with microbleeds/superficial siderosis on SWI
Younger patient, atypical site; flow voids or nidus on angiography

aN: ich | intracerebral hemorrhage | hemorrhagic stroke | brain bleed

det.patho: Rupture of a small penetrating artery bleeds into brain parenchyma; chronic hypertension damages deep perforators (lipohyalinosis), whereas amyloid angiopathy weakens cortical vessels in older people. Other causes include anticoagulants, vascular malformations, tumours, venous thrombosis, sympathomimetic drugs and haemorrhagic transformation of infarcts. ICH is relatively more common in Asian populations than in Western ones, and the haematoma often grows during the first hours.
det.clinical: Onset is sudden with a focal deficit, often accompanied by headache, vomiting, very high BP and progressive drowsiness. Site predicts the syndrome: putamen (hemiplegia, gaze toward lesion), thalamus (sensory loss, downward gaze deviation), pons (coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia), cerebellum (vertigo, ataxia, inability to stand). Cerebellar haematomas can rapidly compress the brainstem or block CSF. Deterioration in the first day usually reflects expansion, intraventricular extension or hydrocephalus.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT confirms the bleed; estimate volume with the ABC/2 method and look for ventricular blood and hydrocephalus. A spot sign on CTA marks risk of expansion. Check coagulation, platelets and anticoagulant use. In young patients, lobar bleeds, normotensive patients or unusual locations, look for an underlying lesion with CTA, MRI with SWI, and catheter angiography when needed. The ICH score helps communicate severity but should not by itself drive withdrawal of care.
det.treatment: Lower systolic BP early and smoothly toward about 140 mmHg, avoiding large swings. Reverse anticoagulation at once: vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors. Platelet transfusion is not helpful for antiplatelet-associated ICH unless surgery is planned. Cerebellar haematomas over about 3 cm or with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus need neurosurgery; external ventricular drainage treats obstructive hydrocephalus. Provide stroke-unit care, treat seizures if they occur (no routine prophylaxis), and use intermittent pneumatic compression for DVT prevention.
det.prognosis: Thirty-day mortality is around 40%; volume, GCS, age, intraventricular blood and infratentorial site predict poor outcome.
pearls: Deep bleed + hypertension = arteriolopathy; lobar bleed in the elderly = think CAA.
Cerebellar haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency even if the patient looks well.
Do not give platelets routinely for antiplatelet-related ICH.
det.thd: เลือดออกในเนื้อสมองจากหลอดเลือดเล็กแตก สาเหตุหลักคือความดันสูง (ตำแหน่งลึก เช่น putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) และ CAA ในผู้สูงอายุ (ตำแหน่ง lobar) อาการคล้าย stroke ตีบแต่มักปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ความดันสูงมาก และซึมลง วินิจฉัยด้วย CT ประเมินปริมาตรและหา spot sign การรักษาคือลดความดันซิสโตลิกไปประมาณ 140 แก้ฤทธิ์ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดทันที และส่งศัลยแพทย์เมื่อเลือดออกใน cerebellum ขนาดใหญ่หรือมี hydrocephalus

name: Intracranial epidural abscess
formal: Collection of pus between dura and skull, from sinusitis, otitis, trauma or surgery, causing fever, headache and subtle focal signs; needs drainage and antibiotics.
simple: A pocket of pus between the skull and the brain's outer covering, usually after a sinus or ear infection or surgery.

name: Intracranial haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding within the cranium, including epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral and intraventricular, from trauma, vascular rupture or coagulopathy, with raised pressure and focal deficits.
simple: Bleeding inside the skull, which can press on the brain and cause headache, weakness or loss of consciousness.

name: Intradural extramedullary (ID-EM) tumours
formal: Spinal tumours inside the dura but outside the cord, such as meningioma and schwannoma, causing slowly progressive radicular pain and myelopathy; usually resectable.
simple: Slow-growing tumours near the spinal cord that press on nerves or the cord, usually removable by surgery.

name: Intradural spinal tumours
formal: Tumours within the dural sac of the spine, either extramedullary such as meningioma and schwannoma, or intramedullary such as ependymoma and astrocytoma, causing pain and myelopathy.
simple: Growths inside the spinal canal that can press on the spinal cord and nerve roots.

name: Intramedullary abscess
formal: Rare pyogenic infection within the spinal cord, often from haematogenous spread or dermal sinus, with fever, pain and rapid myelopathy; needs MRI and drainage.
simple: A rare pus-filled infection inside the spinal cord that causes fever, back pain and rapid weakness.

name: Intramedullary spinal tumours
formal: Tumours arising within the cord, most often ependymoma or astrocytoma, and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, dissociated sensory loss and myelopathy; treated by microsurgical resection.
simple: Tumours that grow inside the spinal cord, causing pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Intravascular cerebral B cell lymphoma
formal: Intravascular large B cell lymphoma with neoplastic cells within small vessels, causing multifocal infarcts, dementia and encephalopathy; diagnosis often needs biopsy.
simple: A rare lymphoma growing inside tiny brain vessels, causing multiple small strokes and confusion.

name: Intraventricular haemorrhage
formal: Blood within the cerebral ventricles from germinal matrix bleeding in premature infants or extension of intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, risking hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding into the brain's fluid-filled chambers, which can block fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus.

name: Intrinsic cord tumours
formal: Tumours originating within the spinal cord, especially ependymoma, astrocytoma and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, segmental sensory loss and myelopathy.
simple: Tumours growing inside the spinal cord itself, causing back pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Ipsiversive seizures
formal: Focal seizures with head and eye version toward the side of the epileptic focus, an uncommon pattern in semiology compared with contraversive turning; lateralising value is debated.
simple: Seizures in which the head and eyes turn toward the same side as the seizure's starting point.

name: Iris hamartomas
formal: Lisch nodules, benign pigmented iris hamartomas that are a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1 and appear in childhood.
simple: Small harmless bumps on the coloured part of the eye that are a sign of neurofibromatosis type 1.

name: Iron akathisia
formal: Akathisia related to iron deficiency, overlapping with restless legs syndrome and responding to iron replacement; low ferritin is linked to reduced dopamine function.
simple: Inner restlessness and the need to move, linked to low iron stores and improved by iron treatment.

name: Iron deficiency
formal: Reduced body iron stores, linked to restless legs syndrome, akathisia, breath-holding spells, pica and cognitive effects in children; ferritin below 50 is relevant in RLS.
simple: Not having enough iron in the body, which can cause tiredness and is linked to restless legs.

name: Isaacs’ syndrome
formal: Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with muscle stiffness, fasciculation, myokymia and cramps, from VGKC complex antibodies (CASPR2), sometimes with thymoma; responds to immunotherapy.
simple: A condition in which overactive nerves cause constant muscle twitching, stiffness and cramps.
more: Diagnose with EMG showing neuromyotonic, myokymic or doublet discharges that persist during sleep and nerve block, with anti-CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies. Treat with carbamazepine, phenytoin, plasma exchange or IVIG.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทำงานเกิน — กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น แข็ง ตะคริว เหงื่อออกมาก สัมพันธ์แอนติบอดี CASPR2 และ thymoma
feat: Continuous rippling (myokymia), stiffness, cramps and slow relaxation after contraction
Excess sweating; may have insomnia, confusion or seizures (Morvan overlap)
Associated with thymoma and other tumours
inv: EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges that persist during sleep and after nerve block
CASPR2 (and LGI1) antibodies; CT chest for thymoma

case.story: Months of muscle stiffness, painful cramps and constant twitching under the skin of the calves; he sweats heavily and sleeps poorly.
case.exam: Visible undulating myokymia in both calves, slow hand opening after a firm grip, normal strength and reflexes.
case.tests: EMG: doublet and multiplet neuromyotonic discharges persisting in sleep; CASPR2 antibodies positive; CT chest: anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What is the likely mediastinal mass and why look for it?
case.a: Thymoma — CASPR2-associated neuromyotonia can be paraneoplastic, and treating the tumour helps.

ddx.pt: Axial rigidity with co-contraction; anti-GAD; EMG continuous normal motor units
Fasciculations with progressive weakness and UMN signs
Prominent memory loss and seizures (LGI1) without peripheral hyperexcitability

aN: acquired neuromyotonia | isaacs syndrome | caspr2 neuromyotonia | peripheral nerve hyperexcitability | continuous muscle fibre activity

det.patho: Acquired neuromyotonia arises from hyperexcitability of motor axons, usually distal. Antibodies against proteins of the voltage-gated potassium channel complex — chiefly CASPR2 at the juxtaparanode — reduce potassium currents, so axons fire repetitively and spontaneously. A paraneoplastic origin, especially thymoma, is found in a substantial minority. Combined central involvement (Morvan syndrome) indicates a broader autoimmune process.
det.clinical: Patients describe continuous twitching, rippling, stiffness, cramps and slow relaxation after a grip; symptoms persist during sleep. Hyperhidrosis and other autonomic features are common, and neuropathic pain or paraesthesia may occur. Insomnia, agitation, hallucinations, dysautonomia and weight loss suggest Morvan syndrome. A coexisting myasthenia gravis raises suspicion of thymoma.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges (high-frequency bursts with decrementing amplitude), and after-discharges following nerve stimulation. Test for CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies with cell-based assays; many patients remain seronegative. Image the chest for thymoma and screen for other tumours, such as lung cancer. Distinguish from cramp-fasciculation syndrome, stiff-person syndrome and hereditary forms (e.g. KCNA1).
det.treatment: Symptomatic control uses sodium-channel blocking drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or lamotrigine. Plasma exchange, IVIG, corticosteroids and rituximab are used for antibody-positive or disabling disease. Remove a thymoma if present. Morvan syndrome often needs more aggressive immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Non-paraneoplastic disease often improves with treatment and may remit; outcome in paraneoplastic cases depends on the tumour.
pearls: Twitching that continues during sleep and after nerve block points to peripheral nerve hyperexcitability.
Thymoma links Isaacs, Morvan and myasthenia gravis — image the chest.
det.thd: Isaacs’ syndrome คือภาวะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายถูกกระตุ้นง่ายเกินไป มักเกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่นตลอดเวลา แข็ง เป็นตะคริว และเหงื่อออกมาก แม้ขณะหลับ EMG พบ myokymic และ neuromyotonic discharges ต้องตรวจหาเนื้องอก thymoma เสมอ รักษาอาการด้วยยากลุ่ม sodium-channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine และใช้ภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัดเช่น plasma exchange หรือ IVIG ในรายที่รุนแรง

name: Ischaemic ocular syndromes
formal: Disorders of reduced ocular blood flow from carotid disease, with amaurosis fugax, central retinal artery occlusion, ischaemic optic neuropathy and ocular ischaemic syndrome with painful eye.
simple: Eye problems caused by poor blood flow to the eye, from temporary vision loss to permanent damage.

name: Ischaemic stroke
formal: Focal brain infarction from arterial occlusion due to large vessel atherosclerosis, cardioembolism or small vessel disease, with sudden focal deficit; treated with thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
simple: A stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, causing sudden weakness, speech or vision problems.

name: Isolated cerebral angiitis
formal: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system, an inflammatory vasculitis confined to cerebral vessels, with headache, strokes and cognitive change; diagnosed by angiography or biopsy.
simple: Inflammation limited to the blood vessels of the brain, causing headaches, strokes and confusion.

name: Isolated sleep paralysis
formal: Brief inability to move or speak on falling asleep or waking, with full awareness, from REM atonia intruding into wakefulness; not accompanied by narcolepsy.
simple: Being unable to move or speak for a short time when falling asleep or waking up, while fully aware.

name: Isolated thalamic degeneration (pure thalamic atrophy)
formal: Rare degenerative disease with neuronal loss limited to thalamic nuclei, causing cognitive decline, ataxia and sleep disturbance, sometimes with familial or prion-like mechanisms such as fatal insomnia.
simple: A rare brain condition in which only the thalamus shrinks, causing memory problems and balance and sleep trouble.
more: Diagnosis is by imaging or pathology. No treatment, and prion testing should be considered when sleep failure and dysautonomia are present.
nN: isolated thalamic degeneration pure thalamic atrophy
aN: pure thalamic atrophy | isolated thalamic degeneration

name: Isolated vertigo
formal: Vertigo as the only symptom without other neurological signs; causes include BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere disease, and rarely posterior circulation stroke.
simple: A spinning sensation that is the only symptom, often from a problem in the inner ear.

name: Isolated ‘primary’ angiitis of CNS
formal: Primary angiitis of the CNS, a rare vasculitis restricted to brain and spinal cord vessels, causing headaches, stroke and cognitive change, confirmed by biopsy.
simple: Rare inflammation of blood vessels in the brain and spinal cord without disease elsewhere in the body.

name: Isometric tremor
formal: Tremor from voluntary muscle contraction against a rigid object, such as in primary orthostatic tremor or functional tremor, without movement.
simple: A shaking that occurs when muscles tighten against something without moving, such as gripping a bar.

name: Isovaleric acidaemia (IVA)
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, with sweaty-feet odour, vomiting, lethargy and coma, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: An inherited condition in which the body cannot break down part of protein, causing vomiting and drowsiness and a sweaty-feet smell.

name: Issacs’ syndrome
formal: Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome with continuous muscle fibre activity, myokymia, cramps and delayed relaxation, often autoimmune (CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies).
simple: A condition where nerves fire too much, causing constant twitching, stiffness and cramps.
more: Neuromyotonic discharges on EMG; test for CASPR2 antibodies and thymoma. Treat with carbamazepine or phenytoin, and immunotherapy for autoimmune cases.

name: Jacksonian motor partial seizures
formal: Focal motor seizures with march of clonic jerking from a distal body part up the limb, caused by a lesion in the contralateral primary motor cortex; may be followed by Todd paralysis.
simple: Seizures starting with jerking in one hand or foot that spreads up the limb as the seizure moves across the brain.

name: Jansky-Bieschowsky disease (late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis CLN2 with seizures, ataxia and regression between ages 2 and 4, caused by TPP1 deficiency; treated with cerliponase alfa enzyme replacement.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing seizures, loss of skills and vision, from a faulty enzyme in brain cells.
nN: jansky bieschowsky disease late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
aN: late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | jansky bieschowsky disease

name: Japanese B encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis in Asia, with fever, seizures, parkinsonism and flaccid paralysis; vaccine preventable and often leaves persistent deficits.
simple: A brain infection spread by mosquitoes in Asia that causes fever, seizures and confusion.

name: Japanese encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis in Asia, with fever, headache, seizures, parkinsonian features, and thalamic lesions on MRI; vaccine preventable and often leaves sequelae.
simple: A brain infection spread by mosquitoes in Asia that causes fever, seizures and confusion.

name: Jaw tremor
formal: Rhythmic tremor of the jaw, from Parkinson disease, essential tremor, drug-induced causes such as antipsychotics (rabbit syndrome), dystonic tremor or functional movement disorder.
simple: A shaking of the jaw, which can occur with Parkinson disease or as a drug side effect.

name: JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV-GCN)
formal: JC virus infection of cerebellar granule neurons in immunosuppressed patients, with progressive ataxia and cerebellar atrophy, a variant of PML.
simple: A cerebellar infection by a common virus in people with weak immune systems, causing worsening balance problems.
nN: jc virus granule cell neuronopathy jcv gcn
aN: jcv gcn | jc virus granule cell neuronopathy

name: Jerking stiff man syndrome
formal: Stiff-person-like syndrome with painful spasms and prominent startle-induced jerks, often with brainstem involvement and glycine receptor antibodies, as in PERM.
simple: A rare condition with muscle stiffness, painful spasms and sudden jerks, often set off by noise or touch.

name: Joubert syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive ciliopathy with hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and the molar tooth sign on MRI, with hypotonia, abnormal breathing and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited condition of the brain in which a part of the cerebellum is underdeveloped, causing poor muscle tone and delayed development.

name: Jugular foramen syndrome
formal: Combined lesion of cranial nerves IX, X and XI at the jugular foramen, causing dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness; typically from glomus tumours or skull base disease.
simple: Damage to three cranial nerves leaving the skull, causing trouble swallowing, hoarse voice and weak shoulder.

name: Juvenile Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease starting in childhood or adolescence, with rigidity, dystonia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with large CAG repeat expansions inherited paternally.
simple: Huntington disease that starts in childhood or the teens, causing stiffness, seizures and learning decline.

name: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Genetic generalised epilepsy starting in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks, generalised tonic-clonic seizures and sometimes absences, with polyspike-wave on EEG; responds to valproate and levetiracetam.
simple: An epilepsy of teenagers with sudden arm jerks, mostly in the morning, often triggered by sleep loss.

Absence seizures in some

case.story: First convulsion after an all-night party; admits she has jerked and spilled her coffee most mornings for a year.
case.exam: Normal.
case.tests: EEG: generalised polyspike-wave discharges with photic stimulation.
case.q: Which common antiseizure drug class may worsen her seizures?
case.a: Sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine/phenytoin; valproate (if not of childbearing concern), levetiracetam or lamotrigine are preferred.

ddx.pt: Aura, lateralised features, focal EEG/MRI abnormality
Eyes closed, side-to-side movements, long duration, normal EEG during event

aN: jme | janz syndrome | impulsive petit mal

det.patho: JME is a common idiopathic generalised epilepsy with complex polygenic inheritance; first-degree relatives often have generalised epilepsies. Imaging and network studies suggest altered thalamo-frontal connectivity, though routine MRI is normal. Onset is usually between 12 and 18 years, and it accounts for roughly 5–10% of all epilepsies.
det.clinical: The hallmark is brief bilateral myoclonic jerks of the arms, mostly within an hour or two of waking, with preserved awareness; patients often regard them as clumsiness. Most patients also have generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often provoked by lack of sleep, alcohol or stress, and some have absence seizures. Photosensitivity is common. Because the jerks go unreported, the diagnosis is frequently missed until the first convulsion — direct questioning about morning jerks is essential.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EEG showing generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges on a normal background, often triggered by photic stimulation or sleep deprivation. A sleep-deprived EEG improves yield. MRI is normal and is not required in a typical case. Focal-looking EEG asymmetries are common and should not redirect the diagnosis to focal epilepsy if the clinical picture fits.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medication is used: valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in women and girls who could become pregnant because of teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks; levetiracetam and lamotrigine (which can sometimes worsen myoclonus) are common alternatives, with topiramate or perampanel as further options. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and pregabalin may aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures. Counsel about regular sleep, alcohol limits and driving regulations.
det.prognosis: Seizures are usually well controlled with treatment, but the condition is typically lifelong, with high relapse rates after drug withdrawal.
pearls: Always ask a teenager with a first convulsion whether they drop things or jerk in the morning.
Sodium-channel blockers can make JME worse.
Plan contraception and pregnancy counselling before choosing a drug for a young woman.

name: Juvenile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Childhood or adolescent onset neuroaxonal dystrophy with progressive dystonia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline and iron accumulation, as in PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration.
simple: A rare inherited disease starting in childhood or teens that causes stiffness, movement problems and loss of skills.

name: Juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Spielmeyer-Vogt-Sjögren disease)
formal: Batten disease, CLN3, a lysosomal storage disorder starting at age 4 to 7 with visual loss, then seizures, dementia and parkinsonism, with vacuolated lymphocytes.
simple: An inherited childhood disease that first causes loss of vision, followed by seizures and loss of skills.
nN: juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis spielmeyer vogt sjogren disease
aN: spielmeyer vogt sjogren disease | juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis

name: Juvenile neuronopathic Gaucher’s disease
formal: Neuronopathic Gaucher disease with onset in childhood, causing supranuclear gaze palsy, myoclonic seizures and ataxia, plus organomegaly, from glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder in children that affects the brain, causing abnormal eye movements, seizures and balance problems.

name: Juvenile parkinsonism
formal: Early onset parkinsonism before age 21, often from PARK genes such as parkin or PINK1, with dystonia and good levodopa response, and also in Wilson disease or Huntington disease.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness, slowness and tremor beginning in childhood or the teens.

name: Juvenile segmental SMA
formal: Focal lower motor neuron disease affecting one limb with asymmetric wasting, usually self-limited, as in monomelic amyotrophy (Hirayama or Sobue).
simple: A rare condition where muscles of one arm or leg waste away in young people and then the disease stops on its own.
more: EMG shows anterior horn cell loss in a segment; MRI may show cord flexion changes. A neck collar may help; typically plateaus within 1-5 years.

name: Juvenile-onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease with onset before age 20, with rigidity, bradykinesia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with CAG repeats over 60.
simple: Huntington disease that starts in childhood or teens, causing stiffness, seizures and learning decline.

name: Kallmann syndrome
formal: Genetic disorder with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia from failed migration of GnRH neurons; may include mirror movements, renal agenesis and hearing loss.
simple: An inherited condition causing absent sense of smell and delayed puberty.

name: Kanner’s disease
formal: Early infantile autism as originally described by Kanner, a neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired social interaction, language delay and repetitive behaviours.
simple: The original name for classic autism, a developmental condition affecting communication, social interaction and behaviour.

name: Karak syndrome
formal: Rare autosomal recessive neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation from PLA2G6 or related variants, with childhood onset dystonia, spasticity, cognitive loss and cerebellar atrophy first reported in Pakistan.
simple: A rare inherited disease where iron collects in the brain, causing stiffness, dystonia and mental decline in children.
more: MRI shows iron in the globus pallidus and cerebellar atrophy. Care is supportive, and the disease is progressive.

name: Katayama syndrome
formal: Acute schistosomiasis with fever, urticaria and eosinophilia occurring several weeks after exposure, sometimes with encephalopathy or cord involvement from egg migration.
simple: A feverish illness caused by schistosome worms in people newly infected, which can rarely affect the brain or spinal cord.

name: Kearns–Sayre syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial disorder from large mtDNA deletion with onset before age 20: progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction block, often with ataxia and raised CSF protein.
simple: A mitochondrial disease with drooping eyelids, restricted eye movement, retinal changes and heart rhythm problems.
more: Diagnose from the clinical triad, muscle biopsy with ragged red fibres, and a large single mtDNA deletion in muscle. Monitor ECG and pacemaker as needed, and screen for diabetes, hypoparathyroidism and short stature; prognosis is poor.

Salt-and-pepper pigmentary retinopathy, usually with only mild visual loss
Cardiac conduction block that can progress suddenly to complete heart block
Cerebellar ataxia, raised CSF protein, short stature, hearing loss
Endocrine problems: diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, delayed puberty

Fundoscopy; CSF protein (often >1 g/L); serum lactate

MRI brain: symmetric T2 change in subcortical white matter, basal ganglia and brainstem

case.story: Droopy eyelids since age 12, now clumsy when walking; fainted twice at school this month.
case.exam: Short stature, bilateral ptosis and near-complete ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, mild limb ataxia.
case.tests: ECG: bifascicular block; Holter shows intermittent complete heart block. CSF protein 1.4 g/L. Muscle shows a 5 kb mtDNA deletion.
case.q: What is the most urgent management step?
case.a: Prophylactic permanent pacemaker (or ICD as advised by cardiology) — sudden death from heart block is the main preventable risk.

det.patho: KSS is caused by a large single mtDNA deletion (classically about 5 kb) that is almost always sporadic, arising during early embryonic development. The deleted mtDNA is spread widely through tissues, which explains the multisystem nature. Pearson syndrome (marrow and pancreas failure in infancy) can evolve into KSS in survivors.
det.clinical: The defining triad is onset before 20, PEO and pigmentary retinopathy, with at least one of heart block, cerebellar ataxia or CSF protein above 1 g/L. Many also have deafness, short stature, diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, renal tubular disease and cognitive decline. Syncope in a young person with ptosis is a red flag for advancing conduction disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical criteria plus detection of a large mtDNA deletion, best in muscle (blood may also show it in KSS more often than in CPEO). Serial ECG and Holter are mandatory. Low CSF folate is common and is worth measuring because it is treatable.
det.treatment: Early pacemaker or ICD prevents sudden death and should be considered even for lesser blocks. Replace calcium, vitamin D and hormones as needed; manage diabetes and hearing. Folinic acid is given when CSF folate is low. Coenzyme Q10 is often used but evidence is weak.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with death often in early to mid adulthood from cardiac or multisystem failure; pacing has improved survival.
pearls: Triad: under 20, PEO, pigmentary retinopathy; plus heart block, ataxia or CSF protein >1 g/L.
Sporadic deletion: recurrence risk for siblings is low.
Check CSF folate — cerebral folate deficiency responds to folinic acid.
det.thd: Kearns–Sayre syndrome เกิดจาก mtDNA deletion ขนาดใหญ่ที่มักไม่ถ่ายทอด เริ่มก่อนอายุ 20 ปี มีหนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ จอประสาทตาเสื่อมแบบมีเม็ดสี และอาจมี heart block เดินเซ หรือโปรตีนในน้ำไขสันหลังสูง สิ่งสำคัญที่สุดคือตรวจ ECG/Holter และใส่ pacemaker แต่เนิ่น ๆ เพื่อป้องกันเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน

ddx.pt: Onset after 20 without retinopathy or the full multisystem picture
Myotonia, distal weakness, cataract and CTG expansion; ophthalmoplegia uncommon
Fatigable fluctuating ptosis and diplopia without retinopathy or heart block

aN: kss | kearns sayre syndrome | oculocraniosomatic syndrome

name: Kennedy’s disease
formal: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy from an androgen receptor CAG expansion, with proximal weakness, fasciculations, bulbar signs, gynaecomastia and sensory neuropathy in men.
simple: An inherited disease in men that causes slowly worsening muscle weakness, twitching and swallowing problems.
more: Diagnosed by AR gene CAG repeat testing (more than 38 repeats); CK is raised and EMG shows chronic denervation with reduced sensory action potentials. Management is supportive; the disease is slowly progressive and lifespan is near normal.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีน AR ในผู้ชาย — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและกล้ามเนื้อพูด/กลืน เต้นรอบปาก เต้านมโต
feat: Adult men; slowly progressive proximal and bulbar weakness
Perioral and chin fasciculations on pursing the lips; cramps; postural tremor
Gynaecomastia, reduced fertility, diabetes (androgen insensitivity)
Mild sensory neuropathy (reduced sensory potentials) — unusual for a motor neuron disease
inv: Genetic test: expanded CAG tract in the AR gene (androgen receptor)
CK often moderately raised; EMG neurogenic; sensory potentials reduced

case.story: Ten years of thigh cramps and slow decline climbing stairs; recently nasal speech; breast enlargement for years.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, twitching of the chin when whistling, tongue wasting, reduced reflexes, mild distal vibration loss, gynaecomastia.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L; sural SNAP absent; AR CAG repeat 47.
case.q: Which two findings argue strongly against ALS?
case.a: Sensory nerve involvement and signs of androgen insensitivity (gynaecomastia), together with an X-linked family pattern and very slow course.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal muscular atrophy (X-linked SBMA), pp. 157–176

ddx.pt: UMN signs, faster progression, normal sensory studies
No sensory or endocrine features; SMN1 deletion
Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or fasciculation

aN: sbma | spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy | x linked bulbospinal neuronopathy | kennedy disease

det.patho: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is X-linked and caused by an expanded CAG repeat (generally 38 or more) in the androgen receptor gene. The mutant receptor, when bound by testosterone, enters the nucleus, misfolds and aggregates, damaging lower motor neurons, dorsal root ganglion cells and muscle. Partial loss of receptor function produces signs of androgen insensitivity. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic because of lower androgen levels.
det.clinical: Men develop symptoms in their 30s to 50s, often preceded by years of cramps, tremor or gynaecomastia. Proximal limb weakness, facial and tongue weakness with chin fasciculations on lip pursing, dysarthria and dysphagia progress slowly. Laryngospasm episodes may occur. Reduced sensation and absent sensory responses, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, reduced fertility, and metabolic abnormalities (diabetes, fatty liver, dyslipidaemia) complete the picture.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the AR CAG repeat is diagnostic. Supportive findings are a raised CK (often moderately high), neurogenic EMG with fasciculations, and reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials. It is frequently misdiagnosed as ALS; the absence of UMN signs, sensory involvement, endocrine signs and X-linked family history should prompt testing.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy in most countries; androgen-reduction strategies have been studied with limited benefit. Management is supportive with speech and swallowing therapy, physiotherapy, respiratory monitoring, treatment of diabetes and dyslipidaemia, and genetic counselling. Testosterone supplementation should be avoided.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow and life expectancy is near normal, though late aspiration pneumonia can occur.
pearls: Gynaecomastia plus bulbar and limb LMN signs in a man = test the androgen receptor gene.
Absent sensory potentials in a 'motor neuron disease' argue against ALS.
Daughters of an affected man are obligate carriers; his sons are unaffected.
det.thd: Kennedy's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากการขยายตัวของ CAG repeat ในยีน androgen receptor พบในผู้ชายวัยกลางคน มีอาการอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและกล้ามเนื้อพูดกลืน คางและริมฝีปากเต้น ร่วมกับเต้านมโตและมีบุตรยาก ตรวจพบการรับความรู้สึกเสียและ SNAP ลดลง ซึ่งช่วยแยกจาก ALS การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และโรคดำเนินไปช้า

name: Kinetic tremor
formal: Tremor during voluntary movement, including intention and action components, from cerebellar disease, drug effects or essential tremor.
simple: A tremor that occurs while moving a body part, such as reaching or writing.

name: Kjer’s optic neuropathy
formal: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy from OPA1 mutation, with childhood onset of slowly progressive bilateral central visual loss and temporal disc pallor, with blue-yellow colour defect.
simple: An inherited eye nerve disease causing slow, symmetric vision loss that starts in childhood.

name: Kleine–Levin syndrome
formal: Rare disorder of recurrent episodes of hypersomnia lasting days to weeks with cognitive change, hyperphagia and hypersexuality in adolescent boys; thought to involve hypothalamic dysfunction.
simple: A rare condition in which teenagers have repeated bouts of extreme sleepiness, strange behaviour and overeating.

name: Klinefelter’s disease
formal: Sex chromosome disorder, 47,XXY, with hypogonadism, tall stature and learning difficulties; associated with tremor, epilepsy and an increased risk of cerebral venous disease.
simple: A genetic condition in males with an extra X chromosome, causing small testes, tall height and learning problems.

name: Klippel–Feil syndrome
formal: Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae causing a short neck, low hairline and limited motion, with risk of cord compression, Chiari malformation and mirror movements.
simple: A condition from birth in which neck bones are fused, giving a short neck and limited motion.

name: Klüver–Bucy syndrome
formal: Bilateral anterior temporal lobe lesion syndrome with visual agnosia, hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity and memory loss; seen after herpes encephalitis, trauma or frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Behaviour changes with a compulsion to put objects in the mouth and loss of fear, caused by damage to both temporal lobes.

name: Korsakoff syndrome
formal: Amnestic syndrome from thiamine deficiency with severe anterograde amnesia, retrograde loss and confabulation, with damage to the mammillary bodies and thalamus; follows Wernicke encephalopathy.
simple: Severe memory loss, often with made-up stories to fill gaps, caused by a lack of vitamin B1, usually in heavy drinkers.

name: Kosaka–Shibayama disease
formal: Diffuse Lewy body disease variant described by Kosaka, with widespread cortical Lewy bodies, dementia and parkinsonism; an earlier term for dementia with Lewy bodies.
simple: An older name for a type of dementia with widespread Lewy bodies, causing memory trouble and Parkinson-like symptoms.

name: Krabbe disease
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination, irritability, spasticity, seizures and blindness; globoid cells on pathology.
simple: An inherited disease in which the brain's nerve coating breaks down, causing irritability, stiffness and seizures.
more: Diagnosed by low galactocerebrosidase activity in leucocytes and GALC mutations; MRI shows symmetric periventricular white matter and optic nerve change, with slowed nerve conduction. Early stem cell transplant helps if given before symptoms.

name: Krabbe’s disease (globoid cell leucodystrophy)
formal: Galactosylceramide lipidosis with globoid cell leucodystrophy: infant irritability, stiffness, seizures and optic atrophy, from GALC enzyme deficiency; later-onset forms exist.
simple: An inherited disease in which the brain's nerve coating breaks down, causing irritability, stiffness and seizures.

name: Kufor-Rakeb disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP13A2-related juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy and dementia, a PARK9 disorder.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease that starts in teens or twenties, with dementia and eye movement trouble.
more: Diagnosis by ATP13A2 mutation testing; MRI shows generalised or pallidal-pyramidal atrophy and iron accumulation in some. Usually levodopa-responsive at first with early motor complications; patients may show visual hallucinations.

name: Kufs’ disease (adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN4 or CLN6) with dementia, ataxia, seizures and movement disorders, without visual loss.
simple: A rare inherited adult disease causing seizures, memory loss and movement problems from waste build-up in brain cells.
nN: kufs disease adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
aN: adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | kufs disease

name: Kugelberg–Welander disease
formal: Juvenile-onset spinal muscular atrophy (SMA type III) from SMN1 deficiency, with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and loss of ambulation in some patients.
simple: An inherited condition causing slowly progressive weakness of hip and shoulder muscles in children and young adults.
more: Diagnose with SMN1 deletion, with copy number of SMN2 predicting severity; EMG shows chronic denervation and CK may be mildly raised. Treat with nusinersen, risdiplam or onasemnogene gene therapy, with scoliosis and respiratory care.

name: L-dopa responsive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism with a clear improvement in bradykinesia and rigidity on levodopa, typical of Parkinson disease and some genetic and dopa-responsive forms.
simple: Parkinson-type slowness and stiffness that improve well when levodopa is taken.
more: A good levodopa response supports Parkinson disease; if lost early, consider atypical causes. Treat with levodopa titration and adjuncts.

name: L-dopa-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus induced by levodopa in parkinsonism, often from drug peak dose or neuroplasticity, usually mild and reversible with dose reduction.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by levodopa medicine in people with Parkinson disease.

name: L-dopa-responsive dystonia
formal: Childhood-onset dystonia, often with diurnal fluctuation and sometimes parkinsonism, due to dopamine synthesis defects such as GCH1, TH or SPR variants, dramatically responsive to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited form of dystonia in children that improves dramatically with small doses of levodopa.
more: Diagnosed by CSF pterins and genetic tests, or a levodopa trial. Long-term low-dose levodopa works lifelong without causing dyskinesia.

name: Labyrinthitis
formal: Inflammation of the membranous labyrinth, usually viral or bacterial, with vertigo, hearing loss, nausea and tinnitus; differs from vestibular neuritis by cochlear involvement.
simple: Inner ear inflammation causing spinning dizziness, nausea and hearing loss.

name: Lacunar infarct
formal: Small deep infarct from occlusion of a penetrating artery in the basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule or pons, usually due to hypertensive small vessel disease.
simple: A tiny stroke deep in the brain caused by blockage of a small artery, often from high blood pressure.

name: Lacunar syndrome
formal: Clinical syndromes from small deep infarcts: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria-clumsy hand, with no cortical signs.
simple: A set of stroke patterns from small deep blockages that affect weakness or sensation without affecting thinking or speech.

name: Lafora body disease (EPM2B)
formal: Autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy with onset in adolescence and Lafora bodies, from mutations in EPM2A (laforin) or EPM2B (NHLRC1), with myoclonus, dementia and visual hallucinations.
simple: A severe inherited disease in teenagers causing seizures, muscle jerks and rapid loss of mental abilities.

name: Lafora disease
formal: Autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy with adolescent onset, seizures, visual hallucinations, myoclonus and dementia, with polyglucosan Lafora bodies on biopsy.
simple: A severe inherited disease in teenagers causing seizures, muscle jerks and rapid loss of mental abilities.

name: Laing distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal dominant distal myopathy from MYH7 variants, beginning with weakness of toe and ankle dorsiflexors and later finger extensors, with slender legs.
simple: An inherited condition where weakness begins in the feet and lower legs and later reaches the hands.
more: Diagnosed by MYH7 genetic testing and MRI; progress is slow, treatment is supportive with orthoses.

name: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)
formal: Presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder with antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels causing proximal weakness, areflexia and autonomic features; often paraneoplastic in small cell lung cancer.
simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and dry mouth, often linked to lung cancer.
more: Diagnosis uses electrodiagnosis with incremental response (greater than 100 percent) after exercise or high-rate stimulation, and P/Q-type VGCC antibodies. Search for small cell lung cancer; treat with 3,4-diaminopyridine, pyridostigmine and immunotherapy.
th: ภูมิต้านทานต่อช่องแคลเซียมที่ปลายประสาท — ต้นขาอ่อนแรง ปากแห้ง รีเฟล็กซ์ลดแต่ดีขึ้นหลังออกแรง มักสัมพันธ์มะเร็งปอดชนิด small cell
feat: Proximal leg weakness more than ocular/bulbar
Autonomic features: dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction
Reduced reflexes that transiently improve after brief exercise (facilitation)
About half are paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer)
inv: P/Q-type VGCC antibodies
Low CMAP amplitudes with >100% increment after 10 s exercise or high-rate stimulation
CT/PET chest for small-cell lung cancer

case.story: Three months of difficulty getting out of a chair and dry mouth; mild intermittent ptosis.
case.exam: Hip flexors 4−/5, knee jerks absent but appear after 10 seconds of contraction.
case.tests: CMAP amplitude doubles after exercise; VGCC antibody positive; CT: hilar mass.
case.q: Name the electrophysiological hallmark.
case.a: Post-exercise facilitation (increment) of a low baseline CMAP.

read.where: บทที่ 5 (LEMS) — ความไวของการตรวจ ตารางที่ 5.4 หน้า 75; แผนภูมิวินิจฉัย 5.1 หน้า 76

ddx.pt: Ocular-bulbar predominant, reflexes normal, decrement without large increment
High CK, myopathic EMG, no autonomic symptoms

aN: lems | lambert eaton myasthenic syndrome | lambert eaton | eaton lambert syndrome | myasthenic syndrome

det.patho: Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium entry into motor and autonomic nerve terminals, so fewer acetylcholine quanta are released. Repeated activation lets calcium accumulate, temporarily boosting release — the basis of facilitation. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, nearly always small-cell lung cancer; the rest are autoimmune, often in younger patients with HLA-B8-DR3.
det.clinical: Proximal leg weakness with difficulty rising and climbing stairs is the presenting complaint in most; ocular and bulbar symptoms are milder than in MG. Autonomic features — dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic symptoms — are characteristic. Reflexes are reduced or absent but may return briefly after sustained contraction. Paraneoplastic cases may also have cerebellar ataxia, and symptoms may precede detection of the tumour by months or years.
det.diagnosis: VGCC antibodies are positive in most cases. Electrodiagnosis shows low resting CMAP amplitudes, decrement at low-rate stimulation and an increment of more than 100% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or 50 Hz stimulation (60% is often used as a sensitive cut-off). The DELTA-P score estimates the likelihood of underlying SCLC. Screen with CT chest and FDG-PET, repeating periodically for at least two years if negative.
det.treatment: Treating the tumour often improves LEMS. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) is the first-line symptomatic drug, blocking potassium channels to prolong depolarisation; pyridostigmine adds little. Immunotherapy with prednisolone and azathioprine is used for persistent weakness, and IVIG or plasma exchange for severe disability. Avoid neuromuscular-blocking drugs and agents that impair transmission, and anticipate prolonged paralysis after anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the cancer in paraneoplastic cases; non-tumour LEMS is chronic but usually controllable.
pearls: Proximal leg weakness + dry mouth + low reflexes that improve after exercise = LEMS.
Look for small-cell lung cancer repeatedly, not just once.
Increment after brief exercise is the electrophysiological signature.
det.thd: LEMS เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อช่องแคลเซียมชนิด P/Q ที่ปลายประสาท ทำให้หลั่ง acetylcholine ได้น้อย ครึ่งหนึ่งสัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งปอดชนิด small cell อาการคือต้นขาอ่อนแรง ลุกจากเก้าอี้ลำบาก ปากแห้ง ท้องผูก รีเฟล็กซ์ลดลงแต่กลับมาชั่วคราวหลังเกร็งกล้ามเนื้อ วินิจฉัยด้วยแอนติบอดี VGCC และ EMG ที่ CMAP ต่ำแต่เพิ่มขึ้นมากกว่า 100% หลังออกแรง 10 วินาที ต้องค้นหามะเร็งปอดซ้ำเป็นระยะ รักษาด้วยการรักษามะเร็ง ยา amifampridine และยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน

name: Lance–Adams syndrome
formal: Chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus, often with intention myoclonus and ataxia, after cardiac arrest or asphyxia, usually with preserved intellect.
simple: Muscle jerks on movement and unsteadiness that persist after brain injury from lack of oxygen.

name: Large vessel vasculitis
formal: Vasculitis of large arteries such as giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis, with headache, jaw claudication, visual loss and stroke from stenosis or occlusion.
simple: Inflammation of the body's largest arteries that can cause headache, vision loss and stroke.

name: Large-fibre neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies affecting large myelinated fibres, with loss of vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia and areflexia, as in CIDP, B12 deficiency and ganglionopathies.
simple: Nerve damage affecting touch and position sense, leading to unsteadiness, especially in the dark.

name: Laryngo-pharyngeal dystonia
formal: Focal dystonia of the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, causing spasmodic dysphonia or dysphagia, often task-specific, or drug-induced.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms in the voice box or throat, affecting speech or swallowing.

name: Late infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Neuroaxonal dystrophy beginning at 2 to 3 years with psychomotor regression, ataxia, optic atrophy and seizures, with axonal spheroids on biopsy, often PLA2G6-related.
simple: A rare inherited childhood disease with loss of skills, unsteadiness and vision problems.

name: Late onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease beginning after age 50 with milder chorea and slower decline, often with smaller CAG expansions and no family history.
simple: Huntington disease that starts late in life and tends to progress more slowly.

name: Late-onset cerebellar degenerations
formal: Sporadic or hereditary cerebellar atrophy starting after age 40, such as MSA-C, alcohol-related, autoimmune or SAOA, causing progressive ataxia.
simple: Gradual loss of balance and coordination in older age due to degeneration of the cerebellum.

name: Late-onset nemaline myopathy
formal: Adult-onset myopathy with nemaline rods, sometimes associated with monoclonal gammopathy or HIV, causing rapidly progressive proximal and axial weakness.
simple: A form of muscle disease starting in adulthood, with rod-like structures in muscle, causing weakness that can progress quickly.
more: Screen for monoclonal gammopathy; treat the underlying clone, for example with chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อมี nemaline rods เริ่มในผู้ใหญ่แบบเป็นเอง มักสัมพันธ์กับ monoclonal gammopathy — ค่อนข้างรักษาได้
tempoNote: Weakness develops over months (sometimes weeks) after age 40
feat: Progressive proximal and axial weakness — prominent neck extensor weakness ('dropped head')
Respiratory muscle involvement and dysphagia may occur early
Normal or mildly raised CK; no family history
Associated monoclonal gammopathy in about half; also HIV
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains; HIV test
EMG: myopathic, often with fibrillations; pulmonary function tests
Muscle biopsy: nemaline rods on Gomori trichrome / electron microscopy without inflammation

case.story: Six months of difficulty keeping his head up while driving a tuk-tuk, then trouble rising from a squat and breathlessness lying flat.
case.exam: Severe neck extensor weakness, symmetric hip and shoulder weakness, mild facial weakness, normal sensation and reflexes.
case.tests: CK 280 U/L; IgG-kappa paraprotein; FVC 55% predicted; biopsy shows many fibres with nemaline rods.
case.q: Why does the paraprotein matter for treatment?
case.a: SLONM with MGUS often responds to clone-directed therapy — high-dose melphalan with autologous stem-cell transplant or daratumumab-based regimens — and IVIG; untreated it can cause respiratory failure.

det.patho: Nemaline rods are aggregates of Z-disc material, mainly α-actinin, within muscle fibres. In the sporadic late-onset form the cause is probably acquired and immune-related, as about half of patients carry a monoclonal protein and response to clone-directed therapy suggests a pathogenic role. HIV and other inflammatory states are also associated.
det.clinical: Patients over 40 develop subacute weakness of proximal limbs, neck and trunk; head drop and camptocormia are typical. Bulbar, facial and respiratory muscles can be involved, sometimes leading to ventilatory failure as the first presentation. Course without treatment is relentless, and patients with a paraprotein tend to progress faster.
det.diagnosis: SLONM should be considered in any adult with new progressive axial and proximal myopathy, especially with head drop or respiratory weakness. Serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains are mandatory. Biopsy shows rods in a variable proportion of fibres with little inflammation; EMG is myopathic, often irritable. Exclude congenital nemaline myopathy, myositis, MG, Pompe disease and ALS.
det.treatment: Patients with a monoclonal protein have the best responses to high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell transplantation or modern anti-plasma-cell therapy (for example daratumumab-based regimens). IVIG can stabilise or improve some patients. Patients without a paraprotein may respond to immunotherapy but evidence is limited. Respiratory monitoring and non-invasive ventilation are essential.
det.prognosis: Untreated, many die from respiratory failure within a few years; with clone-directed treatment a substantial proportion improve or stabilise.
pearls: Dropped head plus a paraprotein in a middle-aged adult: think SLONM and biopsy.
A treatable myopathy hiding behind 'MGUS' — always check immunofixation in unexplained adult myopathy.
Rods can be missed on routine H&E; ask for trichrome staining or EM.
det.thd: SLONM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 ปี กล้ามเนื้อคอ ลำตัว และต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงในหลายเดือน มักคอตก และอาจหายใจล้มเหลว ประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ monoclonal gammopathy ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ nemaline rods วินิจฉัยต้องตรวจ immunofixation ทุกราย ผู้ที่มี paraprotein ตอบสนองดีต่อการรักษาที่มุ่ง plasma cell clone เช่น เคมีบำบัดร่วม stem-cell transplant หรือ daratumumab ร่วมกับ IVIG

ddx.pt: Quadriceps and finger flexor weakness, rimmed vacuoles, slow course
Adult-onset proximal and respiratory weakness with low acid α-glucosidase on dried blood spot
Fatigable ptosis/diplopia, positive antibodies and decrement on RNS
