name: McArdle’s disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type V from myophosphorylase deficiency causing exercise intolerance, cramps, contractures, second-wind phenomenon and myoglobinuria with flat lactate response.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles cannot use stored sugar, causing cramps and fatigue with exercise.

name: McLeod syndrome
formal: X-linked neuroacanthocytosis from XK gene mutation with Kell antigen weakness, causing chorea, tics, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, raised CK and acanthocytes, in adulthood.
simple: A rare X-linked disorder causing involuntary movements, muscle and heart problems and unusual blood cells, starting in adulthood.
more: Diagnosis by absent Kx antigen with weak Kell antigens on blood typing, XK gene sequencing; blood transfusion carries risk of anti-Kx antibodies, so avoid unmatched transfusion. Treat symptomatically; cardiac surveillance for arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

name: Measles encephalitis
formal: Neurological complications of measles: acute postinfectious demyelinating encephalitis, immunosuppressed inclusion body encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later.
simple: Brain inflammation caused by measles infection, which can occur during illness, soon after, or many years later.

name: Median neuropathy
formal: Focal neuropathy of the median nerve, most commonly carpal tunnel syndrome, causing thenar weakness and sensory loss in the lateral three and a half fingers.
simple: Damage to the median nerve, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, causing hand numbness and weakness.
more: Nerve conduction confirms it; treat with splints, steroid injection or carpal tunnel release.

name: Mediterranean myoclonus
formal: Historical term for Unverricht-Lundborg disease, an autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutations with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, seizures and mild decline.
simple: An older name for an inherited condition with jerking muscle movements and seizures, common around the Mediterranean.

name: Medium vessel vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of medium-sized arteries, such as polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease, causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, and visceral and skin ischaemia.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels that can damage nerves, skin and organs, causing pain, numbness or strokes.

name: Medulloblastoma
formal: Malignant embryonal posterior fossa tumour of childhood, arising in cerebellar vermis, with hydrocephalus, ataxia and vomiting; molecular groups include WNT, SHH, group 3 and 4, with CSF seeding.
simple: A fast-growing brain cancer in children arising in the back of the brain, causing poor balance, headaches and vomiting.

name: Meige’s syndrome (Breughel’s syndrome)
formal: Cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia, usually in older adults, with sensory tricks and response to botulinum toxin.
simple: A movement disorder causing involuntary eye squeezing together with jaw and mouth spasms.
more: Usually an idiopathic disorder, sometimes secondary to dopamine blockers; treat with botulinum toxin injections to orbicularis oculi, with oral trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam or tetrabenazine as alternatives. Rarely DBS is used for refractory cases.

name: MELAS syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial disease (commonly m.3243A>G) with encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes that do not follow vascular territories, plus seizures, migraine, deafness and diabetes.
simple: An inherited mitochondrial energy disorder causing stroke-like episodes, seizures, migraines and muscle weakness.

name: Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome
formal: Rare granulomatous disorder with recurrent orofacial swelling, relapsing facial palsy and fissured tongue.
simple: A rare condition with repeated swelling of the lips and face, facial weakness and a furrowed tongue.

name: Membranous lipodystrophy
formal: Nasu-Hakola disease, a recessive disorder from TYROBP or TREM2 mutations with polycystic bone lesions, fractures, and presenile frontal dementia with white matter change.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing bone cysts and fractures in adulthood followed by early dementia.
more: Diagnosis with imaging and genetic testing; no specific treatment is available. Course is progressive and care is supportive.

name: Meniere’s disease
formal: Inner ear disorder with recurrent vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness attributed to endolymphatic hydrops.
simple: An inner ear problem causing attacks of spinning dizziness, ringing in the ear and hearing loss that comes and goes.

name: Meningiomas
formal: Common extra-axial, usually benign, dural-based tumours from arachnoid cap cells, with dural tail enhancement; present with seizures, focal deficits or cranial nerve compression; associated with NF2 and radiation.
simple: Usually slow-growing, non-cancerous tumours of the brain or spinal cord coverings that press on the brain and cause headaches, seizures or weakness.

name: Meningitis
formal: Inflammation of the leptomeninges due to bacteria, viruses, fungi or non-infectious causes, with fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia; diagnosed by CSF analysis.
simple: Infection or inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, causing fever, bad headache and a stiff neck.

name: Meningococcal meningitis
formal: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis with fever, neck stiffness, petechial or purpuric rash and meningococcaemia; risk of shock, deafness and epidemic spread.
simple: A dangerous bacterial infection of the brain coverings causing fever, stiff neck and a purple rash, needing urgent antibiotics.

name: Meningoencephalitis
formal: Infection or inflammation of both meninges and brain parenchyma, with headache, fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal deficits.
simple: Inflammation of both the brain and its covering layers, usually from infection.
more: CSF analysis, MRI, and PCR for pathogens; treat with antimicrobials such as aciclovir and supportive care; early treatment improves outcome.

name: Meningovascular syphilis
formal: Form of neurosyphilis from endarteritis of small and medium arteries months to years after infection, causing strokes in young adults with prodromal headache and cranial neuropathies.
simple: Syphilis infection affecting the brain coverings and blood vessels, which can cause strokes in younger people.

name: Menkes kinky-hair disease
formal: X-linked ATP7A defect of copper transport causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, developmental regression, kinky hair, connective tissue problems and early death.
simple: An inherited disease in infant boys with brittle, kinky hair, seizures and developmental loss due to poor copper handling.
more: Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin; early copper-histidinate injections can help in some. Prognosis is poor and most affected children die in early childhood.

name: Menkes’ disease
formal: X-linked copper transport defect (ATP7A) causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, kinky hair, neurodegeneration, connective tissue abnormalities and low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.
simple: An inherited problem of copper handling in baby boys causing seizures, brittle kinky hair and severe developmental problems.

name: Mercury neurotoxicity
formal: Toxicity from inorganic or organic mercury causing tremor, erethism, ataxia, paraesthesias, visual field constriction and, in infants, acrodynia or developmental harm (Minamata disease).
simple: Nerve damage from mercury poisoning, causing tremor, mood changes, numbness and poor coordination.

name: Metabolic encephalopathies
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement such as hepatic, uraemic, hypoglycaemic or electrolyte disturbance, causing fluctuating consciousness, asterixis and myoclonus.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by body chemistry problems such as liver or kidney failure, leading to confusion and drowsiness.

name: Metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement such as hepatic, uraemic, hypoglycaemic or electrolyte disturbance, causing fluctuating consciousness, asterixis and myoclonus.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by a body chemistry problem such as liver or kidney failure, leading to confusion and drowsiness.

name: Metabolic muscle diseases
formal: Inherited disorders of glycogen, lipid or purine metabolism affecting muscle energy supply, with exercise intolerance, cramps, recurrent myoglobinuria or fixed weakness.
simple: Inherited problems in how muscles make energy, causing tiring, cramps and sometimes muscle breakdown with exercise.
more: Investigate with forearm exercise test, CK, acylcarnitine profile, lactate, muscle biopsy and gene panels; avoid fasting and strenuous exercise. Treatment depends on the defect: carbohydrate loading, carnitine, or enzyme replacement where available.

name: Metabolic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus resulting from systemic metabolic disturbance such as uraemia, hepatic failure, hypoxia or hyponatraemia, often multifocal with asterixis.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by body chemistry problems such as kidney or liver failure.

name: Metabolic neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies caused by metabolic disease such as diabetes, uraemia, hypothyroidism or porphyria, usually length-dependent axonal sensorimotor.
simple: Nerve damage in the hands and feet caused by body chemistry problems such as diabetes or kidney failure.
more: Nerve conduction shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, and treatment relies on addressing the underlying disorder, including glycaemic control and dialysis. Check B12, thyroid and monoclonal protein; pain is managed symptomatically.

name: Metabolic syndrome
formal: Cluster of central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose tolerance that increases risk of stroke, diabetes and cardiovascular disease; also linked to neuropathy and cognitive decline.
simple: A group of conditions, including belly fat, high blood pressure and raised sugar and cholesterol, that raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
more: Diagnosis from waist, blood pressure, lipids and glucose measurements. Treat with lifestyle change, weight loss and drugs for each component.

name: Metachromatic leucodystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency causing sulfatide accumulation, with progressive demyelination, motor regression, ataxia, neuropathy and dementia; late-infantile, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited lysosomal disease that gradually destroys myelin in the brain and nerves, causing loss of movement and thinking skills.

name: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency causing sulfatide accumulation, with progressive demyelination, motor regression, ataxia, neuropathy and dementia; late-infantile, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited lysosomal disease that gradually destroys myelin in the brain and nerves, causing loss of movement and thinking skills.
more: Diagnosed by low leucocyte arylsulfatase A activity and ARSA mutations, with raised urinary sulfatides; MRI shows confluent periventricular T2 hyperintensity with a tigroid pattern. Stem cell transplant in early disease; gene therapy for late-infantile.

name: Metastatic spinal cord tumours
formal: Epidural or intradural spread of cancer (lung, breast, prostate) causing back pain, myelopathy and cord compression; an oncological emergency needing steroids, radiotherapy or surgery.
simple: Cancer that has spread to the spine and presses on the spinal cord, causing back pain, leg weakness and numbness.

name: Methyl bromide-induced myoclonus
formal: Toxic action myoclonus and ataxia after inhalational exposure to the fumigant methyl bromide, with seizures and encephalopathy; resembles Lance-Adams syndrome.
simple: Jerking muscle movements and poor balance caused by breathing in a pesticide gas called methyl bromide.

name: Methylmalonic acidaemia (MMA)
formal: Inherited disorder of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or cobalamin metabolism, causing recurrent ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, basal ganglia infarction and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited condition where the body cannot break down some proteins, leading to acid build-up, vomiting, lethargy and brain damage.

name: Methylphenidate akathisia
formal: Drug-induced motor restlessness and inability to stay still related to stimulant methylphenidate, a form of medication-induced movement disorder.
simple: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving caused by the medicine methylphenidate.

name: MGUS neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, often IgM with anti-MAG antibodies causing distal demyelinating sensory ataxic neuropathy and tremor.
simple: Nerve damage associated with an abnormal protein in the blood that is not cancer, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Serum immunofixation, anti-MAG antibodies, and nerve conduction studies; rituximab for IgM; IVIG or steroids in IgG or IgA forms.
ab: monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance neuropathy
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมร่วมกับ MGUS — โปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลปริมาณน้อยโดยยังไม่เป็นมะเร็ง ชนิด IgM มักเป็น anti-MAG ชนิด IgG/IgA อาจคล้าย CIDP
feat: MGUS = M-protein < 30 g/L, marrow plasma cells < 10%, no myeloma-related organ damage
IgM type: distal demyelinating, often anti-MAG
IgG/IgA type: either CIDP-like (treat as CIDP) or slowly progressive axonal (often no treatment)
Becomes commoner with age, so the link to the neuropathy may be coincidental
inv: Immunofixation, free light chains, haematology review to exclude myeloma/lymphoma
Repeat M-protein measurement every 6–12 months

case.story: Three years of slowly spreading numbness in both feet; walks normally and has no other symptoms.
case.exam: Stocking loss of pinprick to mid-shin, reduced ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: IgG-kappa band 6 g/L, normal free light chain ratio, normal blood count, calcium and creatinine; marrow plasma cells 4%; NCS: length-dependent axonal neuropathy.
case.q: Does the paraprotein need treatment for the neuropathy?
case.a: Usually not — a slowly progressive axonal IgG MGUS neuropathy is monitored (M-protein every 6–12 months); treatment is reserved for CIDP-like or disabling forms.

ddx.pt: Umbrella term — includes malignant causes
Lambda paraprotein with sclerotic bone lesions and high VEGF
IgM with anti-MAG antibodies, sensory ataxia and tremor

aN: mgus | monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance neuropathy | igg mgus neuropathy | iga mgus neuropathy | igm mgus neuropathy

det.patho: MGUS is a premalignant clonal plasma-cell or B-cell disorder present in about 3% of people over 50 and more in older age. When neuropathy and MGUS coexist the link may be causal (IgM with anti-MAG or anti-ganglioside activity) or coincidental. IgM MGUS carries a risk of progression to Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma, and non-IgM MGUS to myeloma or AL amyloidosis, at roughly 1% per year overall.
det.clinical: IgM MGUS usually produces a distal demyelinating, sensory-predominant neuropathy with ataxia. IgG or IgA MGUS is associated with either a CIDP-like syndrome with proximal weakness or a slowly progressive axonal neuropathy indistinguishable from idiopathic neuropathy of the elderly. New pain, autonomic symptoms or systemic features should prompt a search for amyloid or malignancy.
det.diagnosis: MGUS requires an M-protein below 30 g/L, fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no end-organ damage (no hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia or bone lesions) or lymphoma features. Characterise the neuropathy carefully with NCS, test anti-MAG when IgM, and exclude other causes such as diabetes, B12 deficiency and alcohol. Haematological follow-up with periodic M-protein levels and blood counts is advised.
det.treatment: CIDP-like IgG/IgA MGUS neuropathy is treated like CIDP with IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange. IgM anti-MAG disease is managed as anti-MAG neuropathy. Mild axonal neuropathy needs symptomatic treatment (neuropathic pain agents, foot care) rather than immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients have slowly progressive disability; the main long-term risk is haematological transformation, which needs lifelong surveillance.
pearls: MGUS is common in older adults — finding it does not prove it caused the neuropathy.
Check the M-protein isotype: IgM points to anti-MAG; IgG/IgA with demyelination points to a CIDP-like disorder.
det.thd: MGUS คือภาวะที่มีโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลปริมาณน้อยในเลือด โดยยังไม่เข้าเกณฑ์มะเร็ง พบได้บ่อยในผู้สูงอายุ จึงอาจเกี่ยวข้องหรือไม่เกี่ยวข้องกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมก็ได้ ชนิด IgM มักเป็น anti-MAG ทำให้ชาและเดินเซ ส่วนชนิด IgG/IgA อาจคล้าย CIDP หรือเป็นแบบแอกซอนช้าๆ การรักษาแบบ CIDP ใช้ IVIG หรือสเตียรอยด์ ส่วนแบบแอกซอนรักษาตามอาการ และต้องติดตามระดับโปรตีนเพราะมีโอกาสกลายเป็นมะเร็งเม็ดเลือดประมาณ 1% ต่อปี

name: Microangiopathy
formal: Small-vessel endothelial injury with thrombosis, hemolysis and ischaemia, as in thrombotic microangiopathy, CNS cerebral small vessel disease or diabetic microangiopathy.
simple: Damage to the smallest blood vessels, leading to clots and poor blood supply to organs.
more: Management depends on type, such as plasma exchange for TTP and complement inhibitors for atypical HUS; control of diabetes and hypertension for chronic forms.

name: Micronutrient deficiency
formal: Deficiency of vitamins or trace elements such as B12, thiamine, copper, vitamin E or folate, causing neuropathy, myelopathy, ataxia or encephalopathy.
simple: Lack of small amounts of vitamins or minerals the body needs, which can damage nerves and the brain.

name: Microscopic polyangiitis
formal: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (usually MPO-ANCA) with necrotising glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage and mononeuritis multiplex or, less often, CNS involvement.
simple: An inflammatory disease of small blood vessels that can damage kidneys, lungs and nerves.
more: Diagnose with MPO-ANCA, urine sediment, and biopsy of kidney or nerve; treat with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, and plasma exchange in severe cases. Relapse is common; maintenance with azathioprine or rituximab.

name: Midbrain tremor
formal: Holmes tremor: slow, large-amplitude rest, postural and intention tremor from lesions of the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
simple: A slow, large shaking of the arm present at rest and on movement, usually after damage to the midbrain.

name: Migraine
formal: Primary headache disorder of recurrent unilateral pulsating attacks with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, with or without aura, from trigeminovascular activation and cortical spreading depression.
simple: A common condition causing repeated severe throbbing headaches, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
th: ไมเกรน — ปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ ข้างเดียว คลื่นไส้ กลัวแสงเสียง เป็นซ้ำ ๆ 4–72 ชั่วโมง
tempoNote: Attacks of 4–72 h, recurrent
feat: Unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe headache worsened by activity
Nausea, photophobia and phonophobia
Aura in a third: spreading visual or sensory symptoms over 5–60 min
Triggers: sleep change, menstruation, fasting, stress
inv: Clinical diagnosis; imaging only for red flags (SNOOP4)

case.story: Since her teens, monthly throbbing right-sided headaches with vomiting; she lies in a dark room. Sometimes a zigzag light expands across her vision for 20 minutes beforehand.
case.exam: Normal, including fundi.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What features of the visual aura distinguish it from a TIA?
case.a: Positive phenomena that gradually spread over minutes and resolve, followed by headache; TIA causes sudden negative loss.

ddx.pt: Bilateral pressing, mild–moderate, no nausea
Strictly orbital, 15–180 min, restless, autonomic signs
Daily headache with papilloedema
Thunderclap first-ever severe headache

aN: migraine without aura | common migraine | migraine headache | sick headache

det.patho: Migraine is a genetically influenced brain disorder of sensory processing. Activation of the trigeminovascular system releases CGRP and other neuropeptides, sensitising meningeal nociceptors and central pain pathways; aura corresponds to cortical spreading depolarisation. The hypothalamus and brainstem probably drive the premonitory phase. It affects roughly 15% of people, with a threefold female predominance during reproductive years.
det.clinical: Attacks can include a premonitory phase (yawning, food cravings, neck stiffness), aura in about a third, the headache phase and a postdrome of fatigue. Aura is typically visual (scintillating zigzags or scotoma), sometimes sensory or speech-related, developing gradually and lasting 5–60 minutes. Chronic migraine means headache on 15 or more days a month with migraine features on at least eight; medication overuse often drives this. Red flags (SNOOP4) include systemic symptoms, neurological deficit, sudden onset, onset after 50, positional or Valsalva-triggered pain, and a change in pattern. Vestibular migraine, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura are recognised variants.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows ICHD-3 clinical criteria: at least five attacks of 4–72 hours with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe or activity-worsened pain, plus nausea or photophobia and phonophobia. A headache diary clarifies frequency and medication use. Neuroimaging is not needed with a typical history and normal examination; image when red flags are present or the aura is atypical (motor weakness, prolonged, or always on the same side). First-ever aura after 50 should be evaluated as possible TIA.
det.treatment: For acute attacks, give an NSAID or paracetamol early, with an antiemetic, and use a triptan for moderate-severe attacks; gepants and lasmiditan are alternatives when triptans are contraindicated. Limit acute treatment to fewer than 10–15 days a month to avoid medication-overuse headache. Prevention is offered for frequent or disabling attacks: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, flunarizine or valproate (not in people who could become pregnant), and for refractory cases CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants or onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine. Regular sleep, meals, exercise and treatment of comorbid anxiety, depression or sleep disorders support any drug plan.
det.prognosis: Migraine often eases after menopause and with age, but it remains a leading cause of disability in young adults; migraine with aura carries a small increase in ischaemic stroke risk, enhanced by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraception.
pearls: Aura spreads over minutes (march); TIA symptoms appear all at once.
Ask about painkiller days per month in every patient with frequent headache.
Combined oestrogen contraception should be avoided in migraine with aura.
det.thd: ไมเกรนเป็นโรคของสมองที่ไวต่อสิ่งกระตุ้น เกี่ยวข้องกับระบบ trigeminovascular และสาร CGRP อาการคือปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ ข้างเดียว 4–72 ชั่วโมง คลื่นไส้ กลัวแสงเสียง บางรายมี aura เห็นแสงซิกแซกค่อย ๆ ขยายก่อนปวด วินิจฉัยจากประวัติตามเกณฑ์ ICHD-3 ส่งภาพสมองเมื่อมี red flags การรักษาเฉียบพลันใช้ NSAID หรือ triptan ไม่ควรกินยาแก้ปวดเกิน 10–15 วันต่อเดือน ถ้าเป็นบ่อยให้ยาป้องกัน เช่น propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate หรือยากลุ่ม CGRP

name: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)
formal: Head injury with brief altered consciousness, amnesia or GCS 13 to 15, causing concussion symptoms such as headache, dizziness, cognitive slowing; most recover within weeks.
simple: A mild head injury, often called concussion, causing headache, dizziness and trouble concentrating.

name: Miller Fisher syndrome
formal: Variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies after infection.
simple: A variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome causing weak eye movements, poor balance and absent reflexes.
more: Anti-GQ1b IgG is positive in most cases; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation. Prognosis is excellent with spontaneous recovery over weeks to months, and IVIG is used in severe cases; Bickerstaff encephalitis is the central overlap variant.
th: GBS ชนิดหนึ่ง — กลอกตาไม่ได้ เดินเซ รีเฟล็กซ์หาย สัมพันธ์แอนติบอดี GQ1b พยากรณ์ดี
feat: Triad: external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia
Often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
May overlap with GBS limb weakness or Bickerstaff encephalitis (drowsiness, upgoing plantars)
Usually recovers well over weeks to months
inv: Anti-GQ1b IgG (and GT1a)
CSF albuminocytological dissociation (may be delayed)
MRI brain to exclude a brainstem lesion

case.story: A week after a sore throat she developed double vision and staggering gait over 3 days.
case.exam: Bilateral ophthalmoparesis, mild ptosis, truncal and limb ataxia, absent reflexes, normal power.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; anti-GQ1b IgG positive.
case.q: Why are the eye muscles particularly vulnerable to this antibody?
case.a: GQ1b is abundant at the paranodes of the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nerves.

ddx.pt: Confusion, alcohol/malnutrition, reflexes usually preserved
Descending paralysis with dilated pupils, no ataxia
Fatigable, reflexes and coordination normal
Chronic course with IgM paraprotein and cold agglutinins

aN: mfs | fisher syndrome | anti gq1b syndrome | ophthalmoplegia ataxia areflexia

det.patho: After an infection (often respiratory, sometimes Campylobacter or Haemophilus influenzae), cross-reactive IgG is produced against GQ1b and GT1a. GQ1b is concentrated in the paranodal regions of the nerves to the extraocular muscles and in muscle spindle afferents and dorsal root ganglion neurons, explaining ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia. Antibody binding at nerve terminals may also contribute. It accounts for a larger share of GBS spectrum disorders in East Asia.
det.clinical: Diplopia is usually the first symptom, followed within days by unsteady gait. Ptosis, facial or bulbar weakness and pupillary abnormalities may accompany it. Overlap with limb-weakness GBS or with Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (drowsiness, hyperreflexia) occurs and these form one anti-GQ1b spectrum. Incomplete forms include acute ophthalmoparesis without ataxia or acute ataxic neuropathy. Respiratory failure is uncommon unless it overlaps with GBS.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by anti-GQ1b IgG in most cases. CSF protein may be normal in the first week. Nerve conduction may show reduced sensory amplitudes or be normal. MRI brain is important to exclude brainstem stroke, Wernicke encephalopathy or tumour. Also consider botulism, myasthenia and diphtheria.
det.treatment: Pure MFS usually recovers well without immunotherapy; IVIG has not been proven to change outcome, though many clinicians treat severe or overlapping cases. Monitor for evolving limb or respiratory weakness, which would prompt standard GBS treatment. Supportive care includes prism or patch for diplopia, fall prevention and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully over 3–6 months; recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia after infection: send anti-GQ1b and get an MRI brain.
Drowsiness or extensor plantars suggests Bickerstaff encephalitis on the same spectrum.
det.thd: Miller Fisher syndrome เป็น GBS ชนิดหนึ่ง เกิดหลังการติดเชื้อ ร่างกายสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ GQ1b ซึ่งพบมากที่เส้นประสาทกลอกตา จึงมีอาการเห็นภาพซ้อน กลอกตาไม่ได้ เดินเซ และรีเฟล็กซ์หาย การวินิจฉัยอาศัยอาการและตรวจ anti-GQ1b ควรทำ MRI สมองเพื่อแยกโรคก้านสมอง ส่วนใหญ่หายเองได้ดีภายในไม่กี่เดือน แต่ต้องเฝ้าระวังกรณีที่มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงหรือหายใจลำบากร่วมด้วย

name: Minamata disease
formal: Methylmercury poisoning from contaminated fish, causing cerebellar ataxia, constriction of visual fields, sensory disturbance, dysarthria and hearing loss, with fetal exposure producing congenital disease.
simple: A mercury poisoning from eating contaminated fish that causes clumsiness, numbness, tunnel vision and hearing loss.
more: Diagnosed from exposure history and blood or hair mercury levels. Chelation is of limited use; prevention by avoiding exposure is key and damage is mostly permanent.

name: Minipolymyoclonus
formal: Small, irregular, multifocal finger and hand twitching seen in anterior horn cell disease and some neuropathies, as visible tremulous movements without joint displacement.
simple: Tiny irregular twitches of the fingers or hands, seen in some nerve and spinal cord diseases.

name: Mitochodrial encephalomyopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disorder affecting brain and muscle with seizures, stroke-like episodes, myopathy, exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis; syndromes include MELAS, MERRF and Kearns-Sayre.
simple: A group of inherited energy-production diseases affecting the brain and muscles, causing weakness, seizures and developmental problems.

name: Mitochondrial ataxia syndromes
formal: Ataxia syndromes arising from mitochondrial DNA or nuclear POLG-related defects, often with neuropathy, epilepsy, ophthalmoplegia and, sometimes, NARP or SANDO phenotypes.
simple: Inherited energy-production problems that cause poor balance and clumsiness along with other nerve problems.

name: Mitochondrial cytopathy
formal: General term for disease from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, affecting high-energy tissues such as brain, muscle, heart and eye, with variable multisystem presentations.
simple: An illness where the cell's energy factories do not work properly, affecting organs such as brain and muscle.

name: Mitochondrial disease
formal: Heterogeneous disorders of mitochondrial or nuclear DNA affecting oxidative phosphorylation, with multisystem presentations including myopathy, encephalopathy, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and diabetes.
simple: Inherited conditions in which the cell's energy-making parts fail, causing problems in muscles, brain and other organs.
more: Investigate lactate and pyruvate, muscle biopsy (ragged-red fibres), MRI, and mtDNA or nuclear gene panel; heteroplasmy affects phenotype and maternal inheritance for mtDNA. Management is supportive: avoid valproate and aminoglycosides, give CoQ10.

name: Mitochondrial disorders
formal: Heterogeneous disorders of mitochondrial or nuclear DNA affecting oxidative phosphorylation, with multisystem presentations including myopathy, encephalopathy, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and diabetes.
simple: Inherited conditions in which the cell's energy-making parts fail, causing problems in muscles, brain and other organs.

name: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disorder affecting brain and muscle with seizures, stroke-like episodes, myopathy, exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis; syndromes include MELAS, MERRF and Kearns-Sayre.
simple: A group of inherited energy-production diseases affecting the brain and muscles, causing weakness, seizures and developmental problems.

name: Mitochondrial encephalopathy
formal: Brain dysfunction from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, with seizures, developmental regression, stroke-like episodes, movement disorders and raised lactate; examples include Leigh disease and MELAS.
simple: Brain disease caused by faulty cell energy production, leading to seizures, developmental setbacks and movement problems.

name: Mitochondrial myopathies
formal: Primary muscle diseases from mitochondrial dysfunction, with exercise intolerance, proximal weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibres on biopsy.
simple: Muscle diseases caused by faulty cell energy production, causing weakness and tiredness with exercise.
more: Diagnosed with serum lactate, CK, biopsy showing ragged-red and COX-deficient fibres, and mitochondrial DNA or nuclear gene sequencing. Treatment is supportive; exercise training may help, and aminoglycosides and valproate should be avoided in some syndromes.

name: Mitochondrial myopathy
formal: Primary muscle disease from mitochondrial dysfunction, with exercise intolerance, proximal weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibres on biopsy.
simple: A muscle disease caused by faulty cell energy production, causing weakness and tiredness with exercise.

name: Mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes (MELAS)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder, mainly from m.3243A>G in MT-TL1, with stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, seizures, myopathy and deafness.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing stroke-like episodes, seizures, muscle weakness and hearing loss.
more: Diagnosed by genetic testing, lactate and MRI; treatment is supportive, with L-arginine for acute episodes and avoidance of valproate.
ab: Mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes
mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes

tempoNote: Attacks evolve over hours to days on a background of slowly accumulating deficits; onset usually before 40
feat: Stroke-like episodes in a young person: hemianopia, aphasia or cortical blindness, often with headache, vomiting and seizures
Lesions favour the occipital and parietal cortex and do not obey arterial territories
Short stature, sensorineural hearing loss and diabetes in the patient or maternal relatives
Exercise intolerance or mild proximal weakness; cardiomyopathy may coexist
Stepwise cognitive decline after repeated episodes
inv: MRI: cortical/subcortical T2 and DWI change crossing vascular borders, with mixed diffusion signal that can migrate over weeks; MR spectroscopy lactate peak
Serum and CSF lactate (raised), glucose, ECG and echo, audiogram
mtDNA testing for m.3243A>G (urine sediment or muscle preferred over blood because blood heteroplasmy falls with age)
Muscle biopsy if genetics negative: ragged-red fibres, COX-positive strongly SDH-reactive vessels

case.story: Severe headache and vomiting, then a focal seizure; next morning he cannot see on the right. His mother is deaf and has diabetes.
case.exam: Short, thin build; right homonymous hemianopia, bilateral hearing aids, mild proximal weakness.
case.tests: MRI: swollen left occipital cortex with DWI change spilling beyond the PCA territory; MRA normal. Lactate 4.8 mmol/L.
case.q: What genetic test fits best, and which sample should be sent?
case.a: MELAS — test for m.3243A>G, ideally on urine epithelial cells or muscle, as blood can give a false-negative result.

det.patho: Most cases stem from the m.3243A>G point change in the mitochondrial tRNA-Leu gene, inherited through the mother with variable heteroplasmy. Faulty oxidative phosphorylation causes an energy crisis in neurons and in the smooth muscle and endothelium of small vessels, and nitric oxide depletion may impair vasodilatation. Stroke-like lesions are thought to be metabolic and partly vascular rather than embolic or atherothrombotic.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in childhood or early adult life, although first episodes after 40 are recognised. Attacks begin with headache, vomiting or seizures and leave a cortical deficit that may improve over weeks; recurrent attacks cause cumulative cognitive and visual loss. The same mutation can produce only diabetes and deafness (MIDD) in relatives, so family history must be taken across the maternal line. Look for cardiomyopathy, WPW, renal tubular problems, gut dysmotility and short stature.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when a young person has a stroke with cortical, non-territorial lesions and normal vessels. MRI and MRS (lactate doublet) support it; serum lactate is raised in most but not all. Genetic confirmation is key, and urine sediment gives higher yield than blood. Exclude encephalitis, venous thrombosis, vasculitis, PRES and status-related cortical change.
det.treatment: During an attack, give IV L-arginine where available and treat seizures aggressively, since status worsens the energy failure. Avoid valproate, which can precipitate liver failure and worsen mitochondrial function; take care with metformin and prolonged propofol. Long-term care includes L-arginine or citrulline prophylaxis (evidence moderate), cardiac and diabetes surveillance, hearing aids or cochlear implants, and genetic counselling for maternal relatives.
det.prognosis: Course is progressive with accumulating disability; many patients develop dementia, and median survival after first stroke-like event is limited to roughly a decade or two.
pearls: Cortical lesion not respecting arterial borders plus normal MRA in a young patient: think MELAS.
Blood can miss the mutation; send urine or muscle.
Do not use valproate for MELAS seizures.

name: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE)
formal: Autosomal recessive TYMP deficiency causing thymidine accumulation, with gut dysmotility, cachexia, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy.
simple: An inherited disease causing severe gut movement problems, weight loss, nerve damage and eye muscle weakness.
more: Diagnosed by raised plasma thymidine and deoxyuridine and low leucocyte thymidine phosphorylase activity; MRI shows diffuse leukoencephalopathy. Allogeneic stem cell or liver transplant corrects the enzyme defect but is risky; nutritional support.

name: Mitochondrial neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies due to mitochondrial dysfunction, as in POLG disorders, MNGIE or NARP, usually axonal sensorimotor and combined with other multisystem features.
simple: Nerve damage in the limbs caused by faulty cell energy production, often seen with other mitochondrial problems.

name: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive fatty-acid beta-oxidation defect (HADHA or HADHB) causing neonatal cardiomyopathy, hypoglycaemia, recurrent rhabdomyolysis and peripheral neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disorder in burning long-chain fats, leading to heart, muscle and nerve problems.
more: Elevated hydroxyacylcarnitines on screening; management with avoiding fasting, MCT oil and triheptanoin; prognosis variable.

name: Mixed connective tissue disease
formal: Autoimmune overlap syndrome with high-titre anti-U1 RNP, combining features of lupus, scleroderma and myositis, and sometimes trigeminal neuropathy.
simple: An autoimmune disease with features of several others like lupus and scleroderma, including joint pain, rashes and muscle weakness.
more: Diagnosis by anti-U1 RNP antibody; treat with steroids, hydroxychloroquine or immunosuppressants.

name: Miyoshi distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal recessive dysferlinopathy (DYSF) with early distal posterior calf weakness, markedly raised CK and inflammatory features on biopsy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that begins with weak calf muscles in young adults.
more: Genetic testing of DYSF or dysferlin protein studies; no specific therapy, so physiotherapy and avoiding eccentric exercise.

name: Mobile spasms (myorhythmia)
formal: Slow, rhythmic 1 to 4 Hz repetitive movements of face, limbs or palate, often from brainstem lesions; seen in Whipple disease with oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: Slow repeating rhythmic movements, often of the jaw or limbs, usually from a brainstem problem.

name: Moebius syndrome
formal: Congenital facial diplegia with abducens palsy from brainstem cranial nerve nuclei hypoplasia, causing expressionless face, inability to abduct eyes and sometimes limb anomalies.
simple: A rare condition from birth where facial muscles and eye movements to the side are weak, giving a face with little expression.

name: MOG-associated optic neuritis (MOG-ON)
formal: Optic neuritis in MOG antibody-associated disease, often bilateral with marked disc swelling, long optic nerve involvement, steroid-responsive but relapsing.
simple: Inflammation of the optic nerve linked to an antibody against MOG, causing vision loss and eye pain.
nN: mog associated optic neuritis mog on
aN: mog on | mog associated optic neuritis

name: Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome
formal: X-linked deafness-dystonia-optic neuronopathy syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with childhood sensorineural deafness, then dystonia, visual loss and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare X-linked condition causing early deafness, followed by movement problems, vision loss and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by TIMM8A sequencing; MRI is often normal early, and females are mildly affected carriers. Some have contiguous gene deletion with BTK deficiency; therapy is supportive, with hearing aids or cochlear implants and symptomatic dystonia treatment.

name: Mollaret’s meningitis
formal: Recurrent benign aseptic lymphocytic meningitis with large Mollaret cells in CSF, often caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 reactivation, with self-limited attacks.
simple: Repeated attacks of viral meningitis that go away by themselves, often caused by a herpes virus.

name: Monge’s disease
formal: Chronic mountain sickness: excessive erythrocytosis with hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension at high altitude, causing headache, dizziness and cognitive slowing.
simple: A long-term illness in people living at high altitude where too many red blood cells cause headache, tiredness and dizziness.

name: Monoamine disorders
formal: Inherited disorders of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin synthesis or metabolism, such as tyrosine hydroxylase or AADC deficiency, with hypotonia, oculogyric crises, dystonia and autonomic features.
simple: Inherited disorders of brain chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin, causing floppiness, abnormal movements and developmental delay in infants.
more: Diagnosed by CSF neurotransmitter metabolites and genetics. Treatment with levodopa, dopamine agonists or gene therapy depends on type.

name: Monoballism
formal: Violent flinging movements of a single limb caused by a basal ganglia lesion, typically contralateral subthalamic nucleus stroke; a restricted form of hemiballism.
simple: Wild flinging movements of just one limb, usually from a small stroke in a deep brain area.

name: Monoclonal gammopathy
formal: Presence of a clonal plasma cell paraprotein, such as MGUS, associated with demyelinating neuropathy (anti-MAG IgM), POEMS, amyloidosis and other neuropathies.
simple: A blood condition where abnormal immune cells make one abnormal protein, which can sometimes cause nerve damage.

name: Monomelic polyneuropathies
formal: Asymmetric sensorimotor neuropathy confined to one limb, such as monomelic amyotrophy or focal neuropathy of a limb, usually with a slow or self-limiting course.
simple: Nerve disease affecting only one arm or leg.
more: Workup includes EMG and MRI; treatment depends on cause, with immunotherapy for immune cases.

name: Mononeuropathies
formal: Focal disorders of a single peripheral nerve from entrapment, compression, trauma, or ischaemia, such as median at the wrist or peroneal at the fibular head.
simple: Damage to a single nerve, causing weakness or numbness in the area it supplies.
more: Nerve conduction studies and ultrasound locate the lesion; splinting, avoiding compression, steroid injection, or surgical decompression depending on cause.

name: Mononeuropathy
formal: Focal injury of a single peripheral nerve by compression, entrapment, trauma, ischaemia or infiltration, with deficits in its distribution.
simple: Damage to a single nerve, causing numbness, weakness or pain in the area it supplies.
more: Electrodiagnosis localises the lesion; entrapments are managed with splinting, injection or surgery.

name: Monoradiculopathies
formal: Disorder of a single spinal nerve root, usually from disc herniation or foraminal stenosis, producing dermatomal pain or sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reduced reflex.
simple: Pinching or irritation of one nerve root near the spine, causing pain, numbness or weakness in the area that nerve supplies.
more: Confirmed by MRI and EMG; most cases improve with conservative care, while persistent deficits or cord compromise may need steroid injection or surgical decompression.

name: Mood disorders
formal: Psychiatric conditions including major depression and bipolar disorder, with persistent disturbance of affect; common comorbidities of epilepsy, stroke, Parkinson disease and dementia.
simple: Conditions such as depression and bipolar disorder where mood is persistently very low or very high.

name: Morvan syndrome
formal: Autoimmune syndrome with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, autonomic dysfunction, insomnia and encephalopathy, linked to CASPR2 antibodies and sometimes thymoma.
simple: An autoimmune condition causing muscle twitching and cramps, severe insomnia, sweating and confusion.

name: Motor neuron degeneration (MND)
formal: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations and spasticity, as in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
simple: Gradual loss of the nerve cells controlling muscles, leading to weakness, wasting and stiffness.

name: Motor neuron disease
formal: Progressive neurodegeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, most commonly ALS, causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations, bulbar dysfunction and respiratory failure without sensory loss.
simple: A disease where the nerves controlling muscles slowly die, causing progressive weakness, muscle wasting and trouble speaking, swallowing and breathing.
more: Diagnose by El Escorial criteria, EMG showing widespread acute and chronic denervation, and exclusion of mimics with MRI and labs. Riluzole and edaravone modestly prolong survival; non-invasive ventilation and gastrostomy help; median survival 3 to 5 years.

name: Motor neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies predominantly affecting motor axons, such as multifocal motor neuropathy, distal hereditary motor neuropathy, or lead and dapsone toxicity.
simple: Nerve disorders that mainly cause muscle weakness with little numbness.

name: Motor neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy predominantly affecting motor axons, such as multifocal motor neuropathy, distal hereditary motor neuropathy, or lead and dapsone toxicity.
simple: A nerve disorder that mainly causes muscle weakness with little numbness.

name: Motor tics
formal: Sudden, brief, repetitive stereotyped movements, such as blinking or head jerks, preceded by premonitory urge and temporarily suppressible; core feature of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Quick, repeated, involuntary movements such as eye blinking or head jerking that a person can sometimes hold back briefly.

name: Moyamoya disease
formal: Progressive steno-occlusive disease of distal ICA and proximal circle of Willis vessels, with fragile collaterals giving the puff of smoke angiographic appearance; causes ischaemic or haemorrhagic strokes.
simple: A disease where brain arteries narrow and tiny fragile vessels form to compensate, causing strokes in children and adults.
more: Diagnosis by MRA or catheter angiography; RNF213 variants are a susceptibility locus in East Asians. Treat with revascularisation (STA-MCA bypass or indirect synangiosis); children present with TIAs on crying or hyperventilation, so avoid hypocapnia.

name: MtDNA depletion syndrome
formal: Group of disorders with reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number from nuclear gene defects such as TK2, POLG, and DGUOK, causing myopathic, hepatocerebral, or encephalomyopathic phenotypes.
simple: Inherited conditions where cells have too few mitochondrial DNA copies, causing weakness, liver or brain disease.
more: Muscle biopsy with mtDNA quantification and gene panels; nucleoside therapy for TK2 deficiency; otherwise supportive; severity ranges widely.

name: Muckle–Wells syndrome
formal: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome from NLRP3 mutation with recurrent fever, urticaria, sensorineural deafness and amyloidosis; aseptic meningitis and papilloedema may occur.
simple: An inherited inflammatory condition causing recurrent fever, rash, joint pain and hearing loss.

name: Multi-infarct dementia
formal: Vascular cognitive impairment from multiple cortical or subcortical infarcts, with stepwise decline, focal signs, pseudobulbar features and executive dysfunction.
simple: Memory and thinking decline caused by a series of small strokes that damage the brain over time.

name: Multi/minicore myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with multiple small cores on oxidative stains, due to SEPN1 or RYR1 mutations, with axial weakness, scoliosis, rigid spine, and respiratory failure.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weak trunk and neck muscles, scoliosis, and breathing problems.
more: Biopsy shows minicores; genetic confirmation; supportive care, including ventilation monitoring, scoliosis surgery.

name: Multibacillary leprosy
formal: Leprosy with many skin lesions and high bacillary load (lepromatous, borderline types), causing symmetrical nerve thickening, sensory loss and neuropathy; treated with multidrug therapy.
simple: A more widespread form of leprosy with many bacteria, causing skin patches and numbness from nerve damage.

name: Multifocal cortical myoclonus
formal: Cortical myoclonus affecting multiple body parts with sensorimotor cortex hyperexcitability and giant SEPs, seen in encephalopathy, post-hypoxia and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks in several parts of the body that arise from overactive brain cortex.

name: Multifocal mononeuropathy
formal: Involvement of multiple individual peripheral nerves, mononeuritis multiplex, from vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, or sarcoidosis, with asymmetric patchy weakness and sensory loss.
simple: Damage to several separate nerves at different places, causing patchy numbness and weakness.

name: Multifocal motor acquired motor axonopathy
formal: Immune-mediated pure motor neuropathy with conduction block, asymmetric distal weakness, and anti-GM1 antibodies in some patients.
simple: An immune condition causing slowly worsening weakness in the hands or feet without numbness.
more: Nerve conduction shows motor conduction block; IVIG is first-line, whereas steroids and plasma exchange are ineffective or harmful.

name: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN)
formal: Immune-mediated pure motor neuropathy with asymmetric distal arm weakness, motor conduction block, and often anti-GM1 IgM antibodies, without sensory loss.
simple: An immune-related nerve condition causing slowly progressive weakness of the hands and arms, with no numbness.
more: Nerve conduction shows multifocal conduction block; IVIG is first-line treatment; steroids are ineffective or may worsen it.

det.patho: MMN is an immune neuropathy of motor axons in which IgM antibodies, often against GM1, bind at or near the nodes and activate complement, causing focal conduction block. Why motor fibres are selectively targeted is uncertain; motor and sensory axons differ in ganglioside composition and ion-channel properties. Ongoing block leads to secondary axonal loss over years. It affects men more often, usually with onset between 20 and 50.
det.clinical: Weakness begins in one hand or forearm, following the territory of an individual nerve (often radial, ulnar or median), and spreads slowly to other nerves over years. Strength may be lost well before obvious wasting. Cramps, fasciculations and cold-worsened weakness are common, reflexes are variable, and sensation stays normal. There are no bulbar or upper motor neuron signs, and legs are affected less than arms.
det.diagnosis: The core finding is motor conduction block at sites away from common entrapment points, with normal sensory conduction through the same segment; the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline defines definite and probable block. IgM anti-GM1 is present in roughly half. Nerve ultrasound or MRI of the brachial plexus may show focal enlargement. CSF protein is normal or only mildly raised. The main mimic is lower motor neuron-predominant ALS; also exclude Lewis–Sumner syndrome and HNPP.
det.treatment: IVIG is first-line: a loading course of 2 g/kg followed by individualised maintenance infusions (intravenous or subcutaneous) at the lowest effective dose and interval. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange are generally ineffective and may worsen weakness. Cyclophosphamide is rarely used because of toxicity. Complement-targeted agents are under clinical study. Track grip strength and functional scores to adjust dosing.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with IVIG, but many need long-term infusions and slow axonal loss can still accumulate. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Asymmetric hand weakness with no sensory loss and no UMN signs: look for conduction block before diagnosing ALS.
Steroids can make MMN worse — unlike CIDP.
A negative anti-GM1 test does not exclude MMN.
det.thd: MMN เป็นโรคเส้นประสาทสั่งการอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มักพบในชายวัยทำงาน อ่อนแรงมือหรือแขนตามเส้นประสาทแต่ละเส้นแบบไม่สมมาตร มีตะคริวและกล้ามเนื้อเต้นได้ แต่ไม่มีอาการชาและไม่มี UMN signs การตรวจไฟฟ้าพบ conduction block ในเส้นประสาทสั่งการ ส่วน sensory ปกติ และประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ IgM anti-GM1 รักษาด้วย IVIG ซึ่งได้ผลดีแต่มักต้องให้ต่อเนื่อง ไม่ควรใช้สเตียรอยด์เพราะอาจทำให้อาการแย่ลง

name: Multifocal myoclonus
formal: Myoclonic jerks involving multiple body regions, often from metabolic, hypoxic or neurodegenerative encephalopathies.

name: Multifocal neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy with multiple nerve involvement, as in multifocal motor neuropathy, MADSAM, vasculitis or hereditary pressure palsies, giving asymmetric deficits.

more: Investigate with nerve conduction and biopsy; therapy depends on the cause, such as IVIG for immune neuropathies.

name: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
formal: Glutaric aciduria type II, a disorder of electron transfer flavoprotein or ETF-QO affecting fatty acid and amino acid oxidation, with hypoglycaemia, myopathy and encephalopathy; riboflavin-responsive in late forms.
simple: An inherited disorder of fat and protein breakdown causing low blood sugar, muscle weakness and sometimes brain problems, which can improve with riboflavin.

name: Multiple cervical radiculopathies
formal: Compression or irritation of more than one cervical nerve root, commonly from cervical spondylosis, with neck and arm pain, weakness and possible myelopathy.
simple: Pinched nerves at several levels in the neck, causing arm pain, numbness and weakness.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it; managed with physiotherapy, medications and decompression surgery if progressive.

name: Multiple cranial neuropathies (MCNs)
formal: Involvement of two or more cranial nerves from skull base disease, carcinomatous or infectious meningitis, cavernous sinus lesions, sarcoidosis, Lyme or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.
simple: Damage to several nerves of the head and face at once, causing problems such as double vision, facial weakness or hearing loss.

name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
formal: Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating and neurodegenerative CNS disease with relapsing-remitting or progressive course, optic neuritis, myelitis and brainstem syndromes with periventricular lesions.
simple: A long-term disease where the immune system attacks the covering of nerves in the brain and spinal cord, causing vision, strength and balance problems.
more: Diagnose with MRI brain and spine (McDonald criteria), CSF oligoclonal bands and evoked potentials. Use high-dose steroids for relapses and disease-modifying therapy such as interferon, ocrelizumab, natalizumab or fingolimod to reduce relapses.

det.patho: An immune-mediated disease in which autoreactive T and B cells cross the blood–brain barrier and cause focal inflammatory demyelination with axonal injury, alongside a slower compartmentalised process (smouldering lesions, microglial activation) that drives progression. Risk is shaped by genetics (HLA-DRB1*15:01), Epstein–Barr virus infection, low vitamin D, smoking and obesity in youth. It is commoner in women and at higher latitudes, and less common in Thailand than in Western countries.
det.clinical: Most patients start with relapsing-remitting disease: optic neuritis with painful eye movement, partial myelitis, brainstem syndromes such as INO, or cerebellar symptoms, evolving over days and recovering over weeks. Fatigue, heat sensitivity, Lhermitte sign, bladder urgency, depression and cognitive slowing are common. Many later enter secondary progressive MS; about one in ten has primary progressive disease from onset, often as a spastic paraparesis. Red flags for another diagnosis include fever, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy and very extensive cord lesions.
det.diagnosis: The McDonald criteria (2017, with later revisions recognising optic nerve lesions and central vein sign) require dissemination in space and time with no better explanation. MRI shows ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions; new enhancing lesions or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands satisfy dissemination in time. In Asian patients, test for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG before diagnosing MS. Exclude B12 deficiency, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, infection and small vessel disease.
det.treatment: Relapses that impair function are treated with high-dose methylprednisolone (typically 1 g IV per day over 3–5 days), with plasma exchange for severe steroid-unresponsive attacks. Disease-modifying therapies range from moderate efficacy (interferons, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) to high efficacy (S1P modulators, natalizumab, anti-CD20 antibodies such as ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine); early high-efficacy treatment is increasingly favoured. Ocrelizumab is approved for primary progressive MS. Monitor for PML, infections and lymphopenia, and address spasticity, bladder, fatigue, mood and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Disease course is highly variable; early effective therapy has substantially reduced long-term disability, and life expectancy is only modestly reduced.
pearls: Bilateral INO in a young adult is MS until proven otherwise.
Always test AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG in suspected MS — some MS drugs worsen NMOSD.
Oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time under McDonald 2017.
det.thd: MS เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายปลอกประสาทในสมอง ไขสันหลัง และเส้นประสาทตา เกิดเป็นครั้ง ๆ ต่างตำแหน่งต่างเวลา พบในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาวมากกว่า อาการเช่น optic neuritis, myelitis บางส่วน, INO, ชา และอ่อนเพลีย วินิจฉัยตาม McDonald criteria ด้วย MRI และ oligoclonal bands ในน้ำไขสันหลัง และในคนเอเชียต้องตรวจ AQP4-IgG และ MOG-IgG แยกก่อนเสมอ รักษาอาการกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone ขนาดสูง และป้องกันระยะยาวด้วยยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน (DMT) โดยปัจจุบันนิยมเริ่มยาประสิทธิภาพสูงเร็ว

det.patho: MSA is an alpha-synucleinopathy in which the protein accumulates mainly inside oligodendrocytes as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, leading to neuronal loss in the striatonigral system, the olivopontocerebellar circuits and central autonomic nuclei. Degeneration of brainstem and spinal autonomic neurons causes preganglionic autonomic failure. Onset is usually in the sixth decade and the disease is sporadic.
det.clinical: Patients present with parkinsonism (MSA-P, commoner in Western series) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C, relatively commoner in East Asia), together with prominent autonomic failure. Urinary urgency, incomplete emptying and erectile dysfunction often precede motor symptoms by years; symptomatic orthostatic hypotension can cause syncope. Other clues are night-time inspiratory stridor, sleep apnoea, disproportionate antecollis, Pisa syndrome, jerky postural tremor, cold violaceous hands and emotional incontinence. Levodopa responsiveness is poor or transient and may provoke facial dystonia. Progression is noticeably faster than in PD, with walking aids needed within a few years.
det.diagnosis: The 2022 MDS criteria define clinically established and clinically probable MSA based on autonomic dysfunction plus parkinsonism and/or cerebellar syndrome, supported by MRI markers and red flags. Document orthostatic hypotension (a fall of at least 20/10 mmHg, ideally with a blunted heart-rate rise) and measure post-void residual volume. MRI may show putaminal atrophy with a hypointense rim and hyperintense lateral margin, pontine cruciform hyperintensity, and middle cerebellar peduncle or pontine atrophy. Cardiac MIBG uptake is usually preserved, unlike PD and DLB. Exclude fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome, SCAs and other secondary ataxias in MSA-C.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive. For orthostatic hypotension use non-drug measures first (fluids, salt, head-up tilt at night, compression garments) then midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa. Bladder symptoms need urodynamic assessment; clean intermittent catheterisation is often required because of high residual volumes. A levodopa trial is worth doing, and CPAP or tracheostomy may be needed for stridor. Botulinum toxin, physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy and palliative care input are central.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 7–10 years from symptom onset; sudden death at night, aspiration and infections are major causes of mortality.
pearls: Early urogenital and orthostatic failure in a patient with parkinsonism or ataxia: think MSA.
Nocturnal stridor is a red flag for sudden death — refer for airway assessment.
A normal cardiac MIBG scan favours MSA over PD/DLB because MSA is a preganglionic failure.
det.thd: MSA เป็นโรคเสื่อมจาก alpha-synuclein ที่สะสมในเซลล์ oligodendrocyte ทำให้มีอาการพาร์กินสัน (MSA-P) หรือเดินเซ (MSA-C) ร่วมกับระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวตั้งแต่ต้น เช่น ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ปัสสาวะค้าง หย่อนสมรรถภาพทางเพศ เสียงหายใจดังตอนนอน MRI อาจเห็น hot cross bun sign ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เช่น แก้ความดันตก สวนปัสสาวะเป็นระยะ และดูแลทางเดินหายใจ

name: Multiplex mononeuropathy
formal: Mononeuritis multiplex, with asymmetric involvement of separate nerves, often due to vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, or infections.
simple: Several different nerves are damaged one after another, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve and muscle biopsy, and vasculitis work-up; treat with immunosuppression for vasculitis.

name: Multisystem atrophy
formal: Alternative term for multiple system atrophy, an alpha-synucleinopathy with parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure.
simple: Another name for multiple system atrophy, a progressive brain disease with stiffness, balance problems and blood pressure problems.

name: Multisystem mitochondrial disorders
formal: Mitochondrial diseases affecting several organs, such as brain, muscle, heart, eye, ear and endocrine glands, from mtDNA or nuclear DNA mutations.
simple: Energy-production diseases of the cell that affect many organs of the body at once.

name: Multivitamin malabsorption syndromes
formal: Conditions such as coeliac disease, short bowel or bariatric surgery causing multiple vitamin deficiencies (B12, E, thiamine, copper), leading to neuropathy, myelopathy and ataxia.
simple: Gut problems that stop the body absorbing vitamins, leading to nerve and balance problems.

name: Munchausen syndrome
formal: Factitious disorder in which a person deliberately feigns or induces illness to assume the sick role without external gain; can present with neurological symptoms such as seizures or weakness.
simple: A mental health condition in which someone makes up or causes illness so as to receive medical care.
more: Diagnosis requires excluding real disease and finding inconsistent history. Management is supportive psychiatric care; confrontation is often unhelpful.

name: Muscle-specific kinase myasthenia gravis (MuSK MG)
formal: Autoimmune myasthenia with anti-MuSK antibodies, prominent bulbar, facial, neck and respiratory weakness, muscle atrophy and poor response to cholinesterase inhibitors.
simple: A type of myasthenia gravis causing weakness of the face, throat and neck, often responding poorly to usual medicines.

name: Muscle–eye–brain disease (MEB)
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, eye malformations and severe developmental delay, from defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMGNT1).
simple: A severe inherited condition from birth that affects muscle, eyes and brain.
more: Autosomal recessive; MRI shows brain malformation and CK is high; care is supportive, with limited survival in severe cases.

name: Muscular dystrophies
formal: Inherited progressive myopathies with muscle fibre degeneration, elevated CK and dystrophic biopsy, including Duchenne, Becker, limb-girdle and facioscapulohumeral types.
simple: Inherited conditions in which muscles gradually become weaker and waste away.
more: Diagnosed by CK, EMG, muscle imaging, biopsy with dystrophin, sarcoglycan or merosin immunostaining, and genetic testing. Corticosteroids help Duchenne; management is supportive with cardiac and respiratory surveillance and physiotherapy.

name: Muscular dystrophy
formal: Group of inherited primary muscle diseases with progressive degeneration and weakness, raised CK and dystrophic biopsy changes; caused by mutations in genes for muscle structural or membrane proteins.
simple: Inherited conditions in which muscles gradually break down and become weaker over time.
more: Diagnosis by CK, biopsy and genetic testing; patterns include Duchenne, limb-girdle, myotonic and facioscapulohumeral. Care is supportive with steroids, respiratory and cardiac care; some have gene-targeted therapy.

name: Muscular dystrophy (MDC) 1C
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy from FKRP mutations causing alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylation, with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and respiratory or cardiac involvement.
simple: An inherited muscle disease from early life causing weakness, large calves and breathing trouble.
more: Autosomal recessive; very high CK; monitor respiration and heart; management supportive.

name: Musicians occupational cramps
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia in musicians affecting hands or embouchure, with loss of motor control during playing but normal other activities.
simple: Involuntary cramping or curling of the hand or lips that only occurs when playing a musical instrument.

name: Myasthenia
formal: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder with fatigable weakness caused by antibodies to AChR, MuSK or LRP4, often with ocular and bulbar symptoms.
simple: A condition where the immune system blocks nerve signals to muscles, causing weakness that worsens with activity.
more: Diagnosis with antibodies, repetitive stimulation or single-fibre EMG; treat with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy, IVIG and complement or FcRn inhibitors.

name: Myasthenia gravis (MG)
formal: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease with antibodies to acetylcholine receptors, MuSK or LRP4, causing fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and limb weakness; associated with thymoma.
simple: An autoimmune disease causing muscle weakness that worsens with activity, often affecting the eyelids, eyes, face and swallowing.
more: Diagnose with repetitive nerve stimulation showing decrement, single-fibre EMG with increased jitter, and antibody testing; CT chest for thymoma. Treat with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy and rescue IVIG or plasma exchange in crisis.

det.patho: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic proteins at the neuromuscular junction — the acetylcholine receptor in about 85% of generalised cases, MuSK or LRP4 in a minority — reduce the safety factor of transmission. AChR antibodies are complement-fixing IgG1/3, whereas MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement. The thymus is central: thymic hyperplasia in early-onset disease and thymoma in about 10–15%. Incidence peaks in young women and in older men.
det.clinical: Fatigable weakness is the core feature: ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day, then bulbar weakness (nasal speech, chewing fatigue, dysphagia), neck flexor and proximal limb weakness. About half start with ocular symptoms and most of those generalise within two years. MuSK-MG favours bulbar, neck and respiratory muscles with tongue atrophy. Myasthenic crisis — respiratory or severe bulbar failure — is often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or drugs such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and beta-blockers.
det.diagnosis: Antibody testing comes first (AChR, then MuSK and LRP4 if negative); about half of purely ocular cases are seronegative. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decrement above 10%, and single-fibre EMG jitter is the most sensitive test but not specific. The ice pack test supports ocular MG at the bedside. Image the chest for thymoma and check thyroid function. Exclude LEMS, botulism, mitochondrial myopathy, thyroid eye disease and brainstem lesions.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine relieves symptoms. Most generalised patients need immunotherapy: prednisolone (start low and increase slowly to avoid early worsening) plus azathioprine or mycophenolate to spare steroids. Thymectomy benefits AChR-positive generalised patients aged roughly 18–65 and is mandatory for thymoma. Refractory disease options include rituximab (especially MuSK-MG), complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) and FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab). Crisis is treated with ventilatory support and IVIG or plasma exchange, with temporary withdrawal of pyridostigmine if intubated.
det.prognosis: With modern therapy most patients achieve minimal manifestations and near-normal life expectancy; crisis mortality is now low.
pearls: Pupils are never involved in MG; if they are, think of a third nerve lesion or botulism.
High-dose steroids can transiently worsen MG — start low or admit.
Know the drugs to avoid: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium, some beta-blockers.
det.thd: MG เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ acetylcholine receptor (หรือ MuSK, LRP4) ที่รอยต่อเส้นประสาทกับกล้ามเนื้อ อาการเด่นคืออ่อนแรงที่แย่ลงเมื่อใช้งานหรือช่วงเย็น เช่น หนังตาตก เห็นภาพซ้อน เสียงขึ้นจมูก กลืนลำบาก แต่รูม่านตาและความรู้สึกปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจแอนติบอดี RNS ที่พบ decrement และ CT ทรวงอกหา thymoma รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine สเตียรอยด์ ยากดภูมิ ผ่าตัด thymectomy และยาใหม่ เช่น complement inhibitor หรือ FcRn blocker ส่วน crisis ให้ IVIG หรือ plasma exchange

name: Myasthenia gravis-like syndrome
formal: Neuromuscular junction disorders mimicking myasthenia, including Lambert-Eaton syndrome, drug-induced myasthenia, botulism and congenital myasthenic syndromes, with fatigable weakness.
simple: A group of conditions that cause muscle weakness that worsens with activity, similar to myasthenia gravis.
more: Repetitive nerve stimulation, antibodies (VGCC, AChR) and drug history differentiate them. Treat the cause with 3,4-diaminopyridine, immunotherapy or withdrawal of the drug.

name: Myasthenic crisis
formal: Life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenia gravis with respiratory or bulbar failure needing ventilation, often precipitated by infection or drugs; treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A dangerous worsening of myasthenia gravis in which breathing or swallowing muscles become too weak.

name: Myelitis
formal: Inflammation of the spinal cord causing motor, sensory and sphincter dysfunction; causes include MS, NMOSD, MOG disease, infections and post-infectious or paraneoplastic disease.
simple: Inflammation of the spinal cord that can cause weakness, numbness and bladder problems.

name: Myeloneuropathy
formal: Combined spinal cord and peripheral nerve disorder with spastic gait and neuropathy, seen in B12 or copper deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1 and nitrous oxide toxicity.
simple: A condition where both the spinal cord and the nerves in the limbs are damaged, causing stiff, weak and numb legs.

name: Myelopathy
formal: Disorder of the spinal cord with upper motor neuron signs, sensory level and sphincter disturbance, caused by compression (spondylosis), inflammation, vascular, infective or metabolic disease.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord causing weakness, numbness and bladder or bowel problems.
more: Investigate with MRI of the spine, CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands, AQP4 and MOG antibodies), B12, copper, HIV and syphilis serology, and urgent decompression for compressive lesions. Prognosis depends on the cause and the severity at presentation.

name: Myoadenylate deaminase (MAD) deficiency
formal: Common metabolic myopathy from AMPD1 variants with exercise intolerance and cramps, though often asymptomatic, and absent histochemical activity.
simple: An enzyme shortage in muscle that can cause tiredness or cramps with exercise, though many people have no symptoms.
more: Diagnosed by absent AMPD1 staining or genetic testing; the ischaemic forearm test shows low ammonia rise; reassurance and graded exercise.

name: Myocardial infarction (MI)
formal: Acute heart muscle necrosis from coronary occlusion; neurologically relevant as a cause of cardioembolic stroke, hypoxic brain injury and syncope.
simple: A heart attack, when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked; it can lead to stroke or brain injury.

name: Myocarditis
formal: Inflammation of heart muscle, relevant to neurology as a source of cardioembolic stroke and association with myopathies, Duchenne and some autoimmune diseases.
simple: Inflammation of the heart muscle, which can cause strokes if clots form.

name: Myoclonic dystonia
formal: Early-onset disorder with alcohol-responsive myoclonic jerks and dystonia of neck and arms, often from SGCE mutation (DYT11), sometimes with anxiety or alcohol use.
simple: An inherited condition with sudden jerks and twisting postures of the neck and arms, often improving with alcohol.

name: Myoclonic encephalopathy
formal: Disorder with myoclonus and encephalopathy from metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative causes, or opsoclonus-myoclonus in childhood.
simple: A brain condition with muscle jerks and reduced alertness caused by various illnesses or poisons.

name: Myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infants with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus, ataxia and irritability, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma or post-infectious.
simple: A rare childhood illness with jerking limbs, rapid chaotic eye movements and poor balance, sometimes linked to a tumour.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy syndromes dominated by myoclonic seizures, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and progressive myoclonic epilepsies, with generalised spike-wave discharges.
simple: A kind of epilepsy in which the main seizures are sudden muscle jerks.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERRF)
formal: Mitochondrial disease (m.8344A>G) with myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, ataxia and myopathy showing ragged-red fibres; lipomas and deafness may occur.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing muscle jerks, seizures, poor coordination and muscle weakness.
more: Diagnose by MT-TK m.8344A>G testing in blood or muscle, raised lactate, and EEG with generalised spike-wave and photosensitivity; MRI may show cerebellar atrophy. Treat seizures with levetiracetam, avoiding valproate.
ab: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres
nN: myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres merrf

name: Myoclonic seizures
formal: Brief, shock-like involuntary jerks from cortical epileptic discharge, often generalised, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: Sudden, very brief muscle jerks caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

name: Myoclonic-astatic epilepsy (Doose syndrome)
formal: Childhood generalised epilepsy with myoclonic, atonic and myoclonic-atonic seizures causing sudden falls, with generalised spike-wave EEG, variable cognitive outcome and links to SLC2A1 or SCN1A variants.
simple: A childhood epilepsy with sudden jerks and drop attacks causing falls, that may affect learning.

name: Myoclonus (PERM)
formal: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus: brainstem and spinal inflammatory disease with stiffness, spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia, linked to glycine receptor antibodies.
simple: A rare autoimmune disease causing muscle stiffness, spasms and jerks from inflammation in the brainstem and spinal cord.
more: Check glycine receptor antibodies, and CSF pleocytosis; MRI often normal. Treat with high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasmapheresis, and symptomatic benzodiazepines or baclofen; screen for tumours, and outcome is variable, with some fatal.

name: Myoclonus dystonia
formal: Early-onset inherited disorder with alcohol-responsive myoclonic jerks and dystonia of neck and arms, often from SGCE mutation (DYT11).
simple: An inherited condition with sudden jerks and twisting postures of the neck and arms, often improving with alcohol.
more: Diagnosis by SGCE gene testing, which is maternally imprinted so inherited paternally; EEG normal and EMG with brief myoclonic bursts. Treat with benzodiazepines, valproate, zonisamide or botulinum toxin; DBS to GPi is highly effective in severe cases.

name: Myoclonus epilepsy
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with action myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures and ataxia, from conditions such as Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora disease, MERRF and sialidosis.
simple: A group of rare seizure disorders with sudden muscle jerks, seizures and gradual loss of coordination.
more: Genetic testing confirms the type (CSTB, EPM2A, mitochondrial). Treat with valproate, levetiracetam, piracetam and avoid phenytoin; prognosis varies.

name: Myoclonus epilepsy and ragged-red fibre syndrome (MERRF)
formal: Mitochondrial disease (m.8344A>G) with myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, ataxia and myopathy showing ragged-red fibres; lipomas and deafness may occur.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing muscle jerks, seizures, poor coordination and muscle weakness.
