Urinary urgency/incontinence
Subcortical cognitive slowing
Arm swing and upper limbs relatively preserved (unlike Parkinson’s disease)
inv: MRI: ventriculomegaly (Evans index > 0.3), tight high convexity sulci, enlarged Sylvian fissures (DESH)
High-volume lumbar tap test or external lumbar drainage with timed gait

case.story: One year of increasingly 'stuck' walking and two falls, then urgency incontinence and slowness of thought.
case.exam: Wide-based shuffling gait with start hesitation, arms swing normally, no rest tremor.
case.tests: MRI: Evans index 0.36 with tight convexity sulci; 30% faster 10-m walk after a 40 mL tap.
case.q: What does the positive tap test predict?
case.a: Likely improvement with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.

ddx.pt: Asymmetric rest tremor and bradykinesia of the arms; levodopa response
White matter disease without disproportionate ventriculomegaly; no tap response
Memory-led decline with gait preserved until late

aN: nph | normal pressure hydrocephalus | inph | idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus | hakim syndrome

det.patho: Communicating hydrocephalus in older adults in which CSF dynamics are disturbed while lumbar opening pressure remains normal or mildly raised. Idiopathic NPH probably reflects impaired CSF absorption and reduced intracranial compliance, often with coexisting small vessel disease; secondary NPH follows SAH, meningitis or head injury. Ventricular enlargement stretches periventricular fibres serving leg control, bladder and frontal circuits.
det.clinical: Gait disturbance comes first and dominates: broad-based, short, shuffling, 'magnetic' steps with poor turning and start hesitation, but arm swing and upper-limb movement are relatively preserved. Cognitive slowing, apathy and inattention follow, and urinary urgency progresses to incontinence. The full triad is present in only some patients. Comorbid Parkinson disease, vascular disease and Alzheimer pathology often coexist and limit shunt response.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows ventriculomegaly (Evans index >0.3) with a disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space pattern: tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures (DESH), and a narrow callosal angle. Confirm likely shunt-responsiveness with a high-volume tap test (30–50 mL) or extended lumbar drainage, measuring gait speed and cognition before and after. A negative tap test does not exclude benefit. Exclude obstructive hydrocephalus and other causes of gait apraxia.
det.treatment: Ventriculoperitoneal (or lumboperitoneal) shunting with an adjustable valve is the definitive treatment. Gait improves most reliably; cognition and continence less so. Complications include over-drainage with subdural collections, infection and shunt blockage, so follow-up is needed. Physiotherapy and management of comorbidities support recovery.
det.prognosis: Most carefully selected patients improve after shunting, especially those with a short history and gait-led presentation; benefit may wane over years.
pearls: Gait first, then cognition, then bladder — reversed order argues against NPH.
Normal arm swing and no rest tremor separate NPH from Parkinson disease.
DESH on MRI predicts a good shunt response.
det.thd: NPH คือโพรงน้ำในสมองขยายในผู้สูงอายุโดยความดันน้ำไขสันหลังปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อย อาการเด่นเรียงลำดับคือเดินลำบากแบบเท้าติดพื้น ก้าวสั้น ฐานกว้าง ตามด้วยคิดช้าและกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่อยู่ ส่วนแขนยังแกว่งปกติ ไม่สั่น MRI พบ Evans index >0.3 และ DESH การทำ tap test ระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง 30–50 มล. แล้วเดินดีขึ้นช่วยทำนายว่าจะตอบสนองต่อการผ่าตัดใส่ VP shunt

name: Norrie’s disease
formal: X-linked NDP mutation disorder with congenital blindness from retinal dysplasia, progressive deafness and intellectual disability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in boys causing blindness from birth, later hearing loss and learning problems.

name: Northern epilepsy
formal: Progressive epilepsy with mental retardation (EPMR) from CLN8 mutation in Finland, with seizures starting in childhood and cognitive decline.
simple: An inherited childhood epilepsy from Finland with seizures and gradual decline in thinking skills.

name: Nosocomial meningitis
formal: Hospital-acquired meningitis, usually after neurosurgery, shunts or drains; caused by Gram-negative bacilli or staphylococci, with atypical presentation and need for broad empirical cover.
simple: A brain-lining infection caught during a hospital stay, often after brain surgery or a drain, and caused by hospital-type germs.

name: NREM arousal disorders
formal: Parasomnias from slow wave sleep including sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals, with partial arousal and amnesia, common in childhood.
simple: Sleep problems such as sleepwalking and night terrors in which a person partly wakes up and does not remember.
more: Diagnosed clinically and polysomnography if atypical. Treat triggers such as poor sleep and sleep apnoea; safety measures and sometimes clonazepam.

name: Nucleoside neuropathies
formal: Painful distal axonal sensory neuropathy from nucleoside analogue antiretroviral and antiviral drugs (ddI, ddC, d4T), via mitochondrial toxicity.
simple: Nerve damage with burning and numbness in the feet, caused by some HIV drugs.
more: Withdraw the drug; symptom control with neuropathic pain medications; improvement may take months.

name: Numb chin syndrome
formal: Mental neuropathy with numbness of the chin and lip from inferior alveolar or mental nerve involvement; an ominous sign of metastatic or haematological malignancy, or dental or mandibular disease.
simple: Numbness of the chin and lower lip from damage to a facial nerve, which can be an early warning of cancer spread.

name: Nummular headache
formal: Primary headache with chronic focal pain in a small coin-shaped scalp area of 1-6 cm, with stable location and often paroxysmal exacerbations; benign, may respond to gabapentin or indomethacin.
simple: A long-lasting headache felt in one small round patch of the scalp, about the size of a coin.

name: Nutritional and toxic optic neuropathies
formal: Bilateral symmetric painless visual loss with centrocaecal scotomas from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, or toxins such as methanol, ethambutol and tobacco; mitochondrial vulnerability of papillomacular fibres.
simple: Slowly worsening vision in both eyes caused by poor diet or poisons that damage the nerves carrying signals from the eyes.

name: Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD)
formal: Psychiatric disorder of intrusive obsessions and repetitive compulsions linked to cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit dysfunction; associated with tics, Tourette syndrome and basal ganglia disease.
simple: A condition with unwanted repeated thoughts and rituals that a person feels driven to carry out, even though they know they are excessive.
more: Treat with high-dose SSRIs and exposure and response prevention; augment with antipsychotics, and consider DBS for refractory disease. Neuroimaging is usually normal; rule out secondary causes such as PANDAS and structural lesions.

name: Obsessive–compulsive personality disorders (OCPD)
formal: Personality disorder marked by perfectionism, rigidity, orderliness and control, without true obsessions or compulsions, and ego-syntonic unlike OCD.
simple: A lasting personality style with extreme perfectionism and a need for order and control that interferes with relationships and flexibility.

name: Obstetrically related plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injuries related to childbirth, such as Erb palsy from shoulder dystocia or maternal lumbosacral trunk compression.
simple: Nerve injury connected with childbirth, either in the baby (arm weakness) or in the mother (leg weakness).
more: Most recover spontaneously; severe infant cases may need microsurgical repair.

name: Obstructive hydrocephalus
formal: Ventricular dilatation from blockage of CSF flow within the ventricular system, for example aqueduct stenosis or a posterior fossa mass, causing raised intracranial pressure.
simple: A build-up of fluid in the brain because a blockage stops it draining, causing headache, vomiting and drowsiness.

name: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS)
formal: Recurrent upper airway collapse in sleep causing hypoxaemia, fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence; risk factor for stroke, hypertension and arrhythmia; treated with CPAP.
simple: Breathing repeatedly stops or becomes shallow during sleep because the throat closes, leading to loud snoring and daytime tiredness.
nN: obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome osahs
aN: osahs | obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome

name: Obturator neuropathy
formal: Injury to the obturator nerve (L2-4) from pelvic surgery, hernia, labour or tumour, causing weak hip adduction and sensory loss over the medial thigh.
simple: Damage to a nerve in the pelvis causing weakness pulling the leg inward and numbness on the inner thigh.

name: Occupational cramp
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia such as writer's cramp or musician's dystonia, with abnormal posturing triggered by a repetitive skilled movement; linked to impaired sensorimotor plasticity.
simple: Cramping or twisting of the hand or arm that occurs only during a repeated skilled task such as writing or playing an instrument.

name: Ocular apraxia
formal: Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital (Cogan) or acquired from bilateral frontoparietal lesions.
simple: Difficulty deliberately moving the eyes to look sideways, so the person turns the head to shift gaze.

name: Ocular ischaemic syndrome
formal: Chronic hypoperfusion of the eye from severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis or occlusion, causing visual loss, orbital pain, venous stasis retinopathy and neovascularisation.
simple: Reduced blood flow to the eye from a badly narrowed neck artery, causing vision loss and eye pain.

name: Ocular motor apraxia
formal: Deficit of voluntary horizontal saccade initiation with intact reflexive eye movements, congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cerebral lesions; head thrusts are typical.
simple: Trouble starting eye movements on command, so the person jerks the head to look to the side.

name: Ocular myasthenia
formal: Myasthenia gravis limited to ptosis and diplopia, often AChR antibody positive, with possible generalization within two years.
simple: A form of myasthenia affecting only eye muscles, causing droopy eyelids and double vision.
more: Diagnosed by ice-pack test, antibodies and single-fibre EMG; treat with pyridostigmine or low-dose prednisolone.

name: Oculomotor (IIIrd) nerve palsy
formal: Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia with eye down and out, and mydriasis from lesion of the third nerve; pupil-involving cases suggest compressive causes such as posterior communicating aneurysm, pupil-sparing suggests diabetic ischaemia.
simple: Damage to the third eye nerve causing a drooping eyelid, an eye turned down and outward, and often a large pupil.

name: Oculomotor apraxia
formal: Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex eye movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cortical lesions.
simple: Difficulty starting voluntary sideways eye movements, so the person turns the head to look at things.

name: Oculopalatal tremor
formal: Pendular vertical ocular oscillations with synchronous palatal tremor following brainstem or cerebellar lesion, with hypertrophic olivary degeneration within the Guillain-Mollaret triangle.
simple: Rhythmic eye wobbling together with a rhythmic movement of the soft palate, usually after a stroke in the brainstem.

name: Oculopharyngeal dystrophy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and limb weakness caused by GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1, with intranuclear inclusions.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in middle age with drooping eyelids and trouble swallowing.

name: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness due to GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1; common in French Canadian families.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing drooping eyelids and swallowing difficulty from midlife.
more: Diagnosed with GCG trinucleotide expansion (more than 10 repeats) in PABPN1; biopsy shows intranuclear filamentous inclusions and rimmed vacuoles. Treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy for dysphagia and ptosis surgery; disease progresses slowly.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมชนิดหนังตาตกและกลืนลำบากในผู้ใหญ่อายุมาก ยีนเด่น (PABPN1)
feat: Onset after 40–50: slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and dysphagia
Later proximal limb weakness; ophthalmoparesis mild, diplopia rare
Autosomal dominant; patients tilt the head back to see
inv: PABPN1 GCN repeat expansion
CK normal or mildly raised; swallow assessment

case.story: Eyelids have drooped over 10 years; now chokes on solid food. His mother had the same.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis with frontalis overactivity, mild upgaze limitation, mild hip weakness.
case.tests: PABPN1 expansion; no fatigability on sustained upgaze.
case.q: What helps the dysphagia?
case.a: Cricopharyngeal myotomy or dilatation after swallow assessment; ptosis surgery for the eyelids.

ddx.pt: Fatigable and fluctuating, antibody positive
Marked ophthalmoplegia, mitochondrial DNA changes, ragged-red fibres
Myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction

det.patho: OPMD is usually autosomal dominant and caused by a short expansion of the GCN trinucleotide repeat in PABPN1, lengthening a polyalanine tract. The mutant protein forms intranuclear filamentous inclusions in muscle fibres and impairs RNA processing. Founder populations include French-Canadians and Bukhara Jews, but it occurs worldwide.
det.clinical: Bilateral ptosis and dysphagia begin after age 40–50 and progress slowly over years. Patients compensate by tilting the head back and contracting the frontalis. Mild ophthalmoparesis, tongue weakness, dysphonia and proximal limb weakness appear later; diplopia is uncommon. Aspiration pneumonia, weight loss and social isolation are the major complications.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the PABPN1 repeat expansion confirms the diagnosis. CK is normal or mildly elevated, and muscle biopsy (rarely needed) shows rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions. Videofluoroscopy assesses swallowing safety. Distinguish from myasthenia gravis (fluctuation, antibodies), mitochondrial CPEO (marked ophthalmoplegia) and myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: Ptosis is managed with levator resection or frontalis sling surgery when vision is obscured. Dysphagia may improve with cricopharyngeal myotomy, dilatation or botulinum toxin, along with diet modification and speech therapy; gastrostomy is used in advanced disease. Physiotherapy addresses limb weakness. Genetic counselling is offered to families.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually close to normal, but severe dysphagia and aspiration can shorten survival if not managed.
pearls: Late-onset ptosis + dysphagia + family history = OPMD; check the PABPN1 repeat.
Lack of fatigability helps separate OPMD from ocular-bulbar myasthenia.
det.thd: OPMD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่น จากการขยายตัวของ repeat ในยีน PABPN1 มักเริ่มหลังอายุ 40–50 ปี ด้วยหนังตาตกสองข้างและกลืนลำบากที่ค่อยๆ เป็นมากขึ้น ผู้ป่วยมักเงยหน้าเพื่อมอง ต่อมาอาจมีต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน และต้องแยกจาก myasthenia gravis ที่อาการเปลี่ยนแปลงตามความล้า การรักษาคือผ่าตัดแก้หนังตาตก และผ่าตัดหรือขยายหูรูดหลอดอาหารเพื่อช่วยการกลืน

name: Off period dyskinesias
formal: Dystonic or choreic movements during the low levodopa state in Parkinson disease, often painful foot dystonia in early morning; related to fluctuating dopaminergic stimulation.
simple: Twisting or painful muscle spasms that occur in Parkinson disease when the medicine has worn off.

name: Off-dystonia
formal: Painful dystonic posturing, typically of the foot, during wearing-off of levodopa in Parkinson disease or early morning; responds to improved dopaminergic coverage.
simple: Painful cramping or twisting of a foot or leg in Parkinson disease when the medicine wears off, often in the morning.

name: Olanzapine akathisia
formal: Drug-induced restlessness with inner urge to move after olanzapine, due to dopamine receptor blockade; managed by dose reduction, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines or anticholinergics.
simple: Feeling unable to sit still, caused as a side effect of the antipsychotic medicine olanzapine.

name: Olfactory groove meningioma
formal: Slow-growing anterior skull base tumour causing anosmia, frontal lobe behaviour change and Foster Kennedy syndrome; often large at diagnosis.
simple: A slow-growing tumour under the front of the brain that can cause loss of smell and personality change.

name: Oligodendroglial α-synucleinopathy
formal: Multiple system atrophy, characterised by glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes, producing parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure.
simple: A progressive brain disease caused by an abnormal protein in support cells, causing stiffness, imbalance and blood pressure and bladder problems.
more: Diagnosed by clinical criteria and MRI; no disease-modifying therapy. Treat orthostatic hypotension and urinary symptoms; survival is about 6 to 10 years.

name: Oligodendrogliomas
formal: Diffuse glioma with IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion, typically frontal, calcified and presenting with seizures; better chemosensitivity and prognosis than astrocytoma.
simple: A type of brain tumour, often in the frontal lobe, that commonly causes seizures and tends to grow slowly.

name: Olivoponto-cerebellar atrophy
formal: Neurodegenerative cerebellar syndrome with loss of inferior olive, pontine nuclei and Purkinje cells, a pattern of multiple system atrophy or hereditary ataxias.
simple: Shrinking of parts of the brainstem and cerebellum causing progressive unsteadiness and poor coordination.
more: Neuropathological diagnosis of loss of olivary, pontine and cerebellar neurons; MRI shows the hot cross bun sign in MSA-C. Genetic testing for SCA mutations and autonomic tests help differentiate; treatment is supportive.

name: Olivopontocerebellar atrophy (OPCA)
formal: Neurodegeneration of inferior olives, pons and cerebellum causing progressive ataxia; sporadic form is multiple system atrophy with cerebellar predominance, also familial SCAs.
simple: Progressive shrinking of brainstem and cerebellum causing worsening balance and clumsiness.
more: MRI shows the hot cross bun sign and atrophy of cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncles and pons; autonomic testing is needed. Sporadic cases have the MSA-C phenotype; consider SCA genetic testing for familial cases, and treatment is symptomatic.

name: One and a half syndrome
formal: Pontine lesion involving the PPRF or abducens nucleus and ipsilateral MLF, causing ipsilateral gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia so only abduction of the contralateral eye remains.
simple: A brainstem problem leaving one eye unable to move sideways and the other able to move only outward.

name: Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)
formal: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis and slowly worsening eye movement paralysis, usually mitochondrial DNA deletion or POLG-related disease; part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome.
simple: Slowly worsening weakness of the eye muscles causing drooping lids and limited eye movement, usually due to a mitochondrial problem.

name: Opioid toxicity
formal: Overdose causing coma, miosis and respiratory depression via mu receptor agonism; reversed by naloxone; chronic use may cause leukoencephalopathy and myoclonus.
simple: Too much opioid medicine or drug, causing deep drowsiness, tiny pupils and slow breathing that can be fatal.

name: OPMD (oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy)
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy due to GCN expansions in PABPN1, with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness, and intranuclear inclusions.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in later life that causes droopy eyelids, trouble swallowing and weak legs.
more: Diagnosed by PABPN1 repeat testing. Treatment is eyelid surgery, cricopharyngeal myotomy for swallowing and supportive care; more common in French-Canadian and Bukhara Jewish populations.

name: Opportunistic infections
formal: CNS infections in immunocompromised hosts such as HIV, with toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, PML, CMV and TB; present with subacute focal deficits, headache or encephalopathy.
simple: Infections of the nervous system that mainly occur when the immune system is weak, such as in advanced HIV.

name: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome (OMS)
formal: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus, ataxia and irritability; paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma in children, breast or lung cancer in adults) or parainfectious and immune-mediated.
simple: A condition with rapid, random jerking eye movements and muscle jerks, often linked to an immune reaction to cancer.

name: Opsoclonus-myoclonus (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
formal: Childhood opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, often paraneoplastic with neuroblastoma, with irritability and sleep disturbance; treated with immunotherapy and tumour removal.
simple: A rare childhood illness with dancing eye movements, jerks and unsteadiness, often triggered by a hidden tumour.
nN: opsoclonus myoclonus myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
aN: myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy | opsoclonus myoclonus

name: Opsoclonus–myoclonus syndrome
formal: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma, small cell lung or breast cancer) or post-infectious; probable cerebellar disinhibition.
simple: Constant random eye jerking with muscle jerks and poor balance, often caused by an immune reaction to a cancer.

name: Optic and optochiasmal gliomas
formal: Pilocytic low-grade astrocytomas of optic nerve or chiasm, frequent in neurofibromatosis type 1, causing visual loss, proptosis and endocrine dysfunction.
simple: Slow-growing tumours of the vision pathway that can cause vision loss and are common in neurofibromatosis.

name: Optic atrophy plus syndrome
formal: Inherited optic atrophy with additional neurological features such as deafness, ataxia or neuropathy, as in OPA1 or mitochondrial disease.
simple: Inherited loss of the optic nerve that comes with other problems like deafness or poor coordination.

name: Optic gliomas
formal: Low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas of the optic pathway, linked to NF1, in children causing progressive visual loss, proptosis and optic atrophy.
simple: Slow-growing tumours of the optic nerve, mostly in children, that can reduce vision.

name: Optic neuritis
formal: Acute inflammatory optic neuropathy with painful subacute monocular visual loss, dyschromatopsia and RAPD; commonly first presentation of multiple sclerosis, also NMO and MOG disease.
simple: Inflammation of the eye nerve causing pain on eye movement and blurred, dull vision, often linked to multiple sclerosis.

name: Optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica (NMO-ON)
formal: Severe, often bilateral or longitudinally extensive optic neuritis with AQP4 antibodies, poor recovery and risk of blindness; needs early steroids or plasma exchange.
simple: A severe form of optic nerve inflammation linked to neuromyelitis optica, which can cause lasting vision loss.
ab: Optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica
nN: optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica nmo on
aN: nmo on | optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica

name: Optic neuropathy
formal: Damage to the optic nerve from inflammation, ischaemia, compression, toxins or inheritance, causing visual loss, colour desaturation, RAPD and a visual field defect.
simple: Damage to the nerve connecting the eye to the brain, causing reduced vision and dull colours.

name: Optic pathway glioma (OPG)
formal: Pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve, chiasm or tract, usually in childhood and associated with NF1, causing visual loss, proptosis, precocious puberty or hypothalamic signs.
simple: A usually slow-growing tumour along the vision pathway in children that can affect sight and hormones.

name: Optic perineuritis
formal: Inflammation of optic nerve sheath with eye pain, visual loss and ring enhancement around the nerve on MRI; responds well to corticosteroids, may follow infection or autoimmune disease.
simple: Swelling of the covering around the eye nerve causing pain and blurred vision, which usually improves with steroids.

name: Orbicularis oculi cranial dystonias
formal: Benign essential blepharospasm, focal cranial dystonia with involuntary bilateral eyelid closure; may combine with oromandibular dystonia (Meige syndrome); treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Involuntary squeezing shut of the eyelids caused by overactive eye muscles.

name: Orbital inflammatory syndromes
formal: Idiopathic or IgG4-related inflammation of orbital tissues causing pain, proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia; diagnosis of exclusion, responsive to steroids.
simple: Swelling and inflammation behind the eye that can cause pain, bulging of the eye and double vision.

name: Orbital pseudotumour
formal: Idiopathic non-infectious orbital inflammation with painful proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and chemosis, rapidly responsive to corticosteroids; excludes thyroid eye disease, lymphoma and infection.
simple: A non-cancerous swelling behind the eye causing pain, bulging and double vision, which usually responds to steroids.

name: Organic acidaemias
formal: Inherited disorders of amino acid or fatty acid catabolism, such as methylmalonic or propionic acidaemia, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and basal ganglia injury.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot break down certain proteins, causing acid build-up and brain problems.

name: Organic acidurias
formal: Group of inherited metabolic diseases such as propionic, methylmalonic and glutaric aciduria with accumulation of organic acids, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy, and basal ganglia injury.
simple: Inherited disorders in which the body cannot break down certain protein parts, causing acid build-up and brain injury.
more: Urine organic acid analysis and newborn screening diagnose them. Treat with protein restriction, carnitine and emergency fluids; early treatment improves outcome.

name: Organic solvents, neurological toxicity
formal: Chronic or acute exposure to toluene, n-hexane or related solvents causing encephalopathy, cerebellar ataxia, leukoencephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy.
simple: Nerve and brain damage caused by breathing or touching industrial solvents such as glue or paint thinner.

name: Organophosphate poisoning
formal: Cholinesterase inhibition producing cholinergic crisis with muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS features and intermediate syndrome with proximal weakness.
simple: Poisoning by pesticides that overstimulates nerves, causing sweating, small pupils, weakness and breathing failure.
more: Treat with atropine, pralidoxime, decontamination and ventilatory support; delayed neuropathy can follow.

tempoNote: Cholinergic crisis in minutes–hours; intermediate syndrome day 1–4; delayed neuropathy 2–3 weeks later
feat: Muscarinic excess: pinpoint pupils, sweating, salivation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea
Nicotinic effects: fasciculations, then weakness; CNS: confusion, seizures, coma
Intermediate syndrome: neck flexor, proximal and respiratory muscle weakness 1–4 days later
OP-induced delayed neuropathy: distal motor-predominant axonal neuropathy with later spasticity
Garlic or solvent smell; history of farm work or self-poisoning
inv: Red-cell acetylcholinesterase (or plasma butyrylcholinesterase) activity — supportive, do not delay treatment
Serial neck-flexion strength, single-breath count / vital capacity for intermediate syndrome
NCS/EMG weeks later if distal weakness develops

case.story: Drank an insecticide after a family argument; brought in drooling, vomiting and short of breath.
case.exam: Pupils 1 mm, wet crackles, HR 48, diffuse fasciculations; responsive to voice.
case.tests: Plasma cholinesterase markedly reduced; SpO2 88% on room air.
case.q: On day 3, after atropine is tapered, he cannot lift his head and breathing becomes shallow. What is this?
case.a: Intermediate syndrome — postsynaptic NMJ failure needing ventilatory support; atropine does not reverse it. Watch neck flexion and vital capacity daily.

det.patho: Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. Over hours the bond can 'age' and become permanent, which limits the benefit of oximes given late. Intermediate syndrome reflects persistent postsynaptic nicotinic dysfunction, while the delayed neuropathy follows inhibition of neuropathy target esterase and causes distal axonal degeneration in long motor fibres of nerves and spinal cord.
det.clinical: The acute phase combines secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, fasciculation and altered consciousness; death is mostly from respiratory failure. Intermediate syndrome appears after the cholinergic phase seems controlled, with weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs, cranial muscles and diaphragm. Weeks later some patients develop cramping calves, foot drop and distal weakness, and long-term pyramidal signs can emerge as the spinal cord tracts are involved. Thailand sees many cases from agricultural exposure and intentional ingestion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical—toxidrome plus exposure history—and treatment should not wait for laboratory results. Red-cell or plasma cholinesterase levels support the diagnosis and help follow recovery, though they correlate imperfectly with severity. Repetitive nerve stimulation may show decrement or repetitive CMAPs in intermediate syndrome. Delayed neuropathy is confirmed by NCS showing reduced motor amplitudes.
det.treatment: Secure the airway, decontaminate the skin, and give atropine in doubling boluses until the chest is clear, heart rate above about 80 and systolic pressure adequate, then maintain by infusion. Pralidoxime may help if given early; evidence is mixed. Benzodiazepines treat seizures and agitation. Monitor neck flexion and respiratory capacity for intermediate syndrome and ventilate early; delayed neuropathy is managed with rehabilitation and orthoses.
det.prognosis: Mortality depends on the compound and amount ingested and is lower with prompt atropinisation and ventilation. Intermediate syndrome usually resolves within 1–3 weeks; delayed neuropathy recovers slowly and incompletely, especially if spasticity develops.
pearls: Endpoints for atropine are dry chest and adequate heart rate, not pupil size.
Neck flexion weakness after the crisis settles is the warning sign of intermediate syndrome.
Fasciculations plus miosis plus wet lungs in a farm worker should trigger this diagnosis immediately.

Known MG, no muscarinic secretions or miosis, normal cholinesterase
Ascending weakness with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation; no cholinergic signs

aN: op poisoning | organophosphorus poisoning | anticholinesterase insecticide poisoning | cholinergic crisis

name: Orgasmic sex headache
formal: Primary headache of explosive onset at orgasm, lasting minutes to hours; must exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; usually benign.
simple: A sudden severe headache at the moment of sexual climax, usually harmless but needing a check for serious causes.

name: Orofacial apraxia
formal: Inability to perform voluntary mouth and face movements on command with preserved automatic movements, from left frontal or opercular lesions, often with Broca aphasia.
simple: Difficulty making face and mouth movements on request, such as blowing or sticking out the tongue, although they happen automatically.

name: Orofacial chorea
formal: Involuntary irregular movements of lips, tongue and jaw, as in Huntington disease or tardive dyskinesia, or after levodopa or neuroleptics.
simple: Irregular uncontrolled movements of the mouth, lips and tongue.

name: Orofacial dyskinesia
formal: Involuntary repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing, as in tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers, edentulous states or levodopa.
simple: Uncontrolled chewing, lip-smacking or tongue movements, often a side effect of some medicines.
more: Review drug history and dental status; stop or reduce the neuroleptic and consider switching to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are effective in tardive forms; spontaneous orofacial dyskinesia occurs in older people.

name: Orofacial tremor
formal: Rhythmic movement of lips, jaw or tongue, for example rabbit syndrome from antipsychotics, or tremor in Parkinson disease.
simple: Rhythmic shaking of the lips, jaw or tongue.

name: Orolingual dyskinesia
formal: Repetitive involuntary movements of tongue, lips and jaw, such as chewing, lip smacking and tongue protrusion, typical of tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers or edentulous states.
simple: Repeated involuntary tongue, lip and jaw movements such as chewing or smacking.
more: Treat by withdrawing the offending drug if feasible, with VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) as first-line; may persist for years.

name: Orolingual tremors
formal: Rhythmic tremor of tongue and perioral muscles, seen in parkinsonism, essential tremor, drug-induced syndromes or other basal ganglia disease.
simple: Rhythmic shaking of the tongue and mouth.

name: Oromandibular dystonia
formal: Focal cranial dystonia with involuntary jaw, lip and tongue contractions causing jaw opening, closing or deviation; worsened by speaking or eating, relieved by sensory tricks; treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the jaw, lips and tongue that make speaking and eating difficult.

name: Orthostatic hypotension (OH)
formal: Sustained fall in blood pressure of at least 20/10 mmHg within three minutes of standing, from autonomic failure, hypovolaemia or drugs; seen in Parkinson disease, MSA and neuropathy.
simple: A drop in blood pressure on standing up that causes dizziness or fainting.

name: Orthostatic myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks of the legs and trunk on standing that improve on walking or sitting, causing unsteadiness; often cortical and seen in neurodegenerative disease.
simple: Sudden jerks in the legs when standing that make a person unsteady, easing when they sit.

name: Orthostatic tremor
formal: Very fast (13–18 Hz) tremor of the legs and trunk that appears only when standing still and eases on walking or sitting; felt as unsteadiness rather than visible shaking.
simple: A fast shaking of the legs when standing still that makes a person feel unsteady but stops when they walk or sit.

name: Oscillatory myoclonus
formal: Repetitive rhythmic myoclonic jerks, as in some cortical or spinal forms, or stimulus-triggered; considered between myoclonus and tremor.
simple: Repeated rhythmic muscle jerks.

name: Osler-Rendu-Weber disease
formal: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant vascular disorder (ENG, ACVRL1) with mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations, causing stroke and brain abscess.
simple: An inherited disease with fragile abnormal blood vessels, causing nosebleeds and sometimes strokes or brain abscess.
more: Curacao criteria and genetic testing; screen for pulmonary and cerebral AVMs. Treat with embolisation, bevacizumab and iron replacement.

name: Osmotic demyelination
formal: Pontine and extrapontine demyelination after rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, locked-in state and parkinsonism.
simple: Brain damage after sodium levels in the blood are corrected too quickly, causing weakness and speech problems.

name: Osteoid osteoma
formal: Benign bone tumour with a nidus, causing nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; in the spine may cause painful scoliosis and radiculopathy.
simple: A small non-cancerous bone growth causing night pain that aspirin-like drugs relieve, sometimes in the spine.

name: Osteosarcoma, spinal
formal: Rare primary malignant bone tumour of the spine, causing pain and cord or root compression, often after radiation or in Paget disease.
simple: A rare cancer of the spine bone that may press on the nerves.

name: Otosclerosis
formal: Bone remodelling of the otic capsule that fixes the stapes and causes progressive conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and paracusis; Schwartz sign on otoscopy.
simple: Abnormal bone growth in the middle ear that stops sound passing and gradually causes hearing loss.

name: Otosyphilis
formal: Syphilitic involvement of cochlea and labyrinth causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo; part of neurosyphilis, treated with penicillin and steroids.
simple: Syphilis infection of the inner ear that causes hearing loss, ringing and dizziness.

name: Overlap myositis
formal: Inflammatory myopathy occurring with another connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or lupus; often anti-synthetase, PM-Scl or Ku antibodies.
simple: Muscle inflammation occurring together with another autoimmune disease.

name: Pachymeningitis
formal: Thickening and inflammation of the dura causing headache and cranial neuropathies, from IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, TB or infection.
simple: Inflammation of the thick outer covering of the brain causing headache and nerve problems.

name: Paediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
formal: MS beginning before age 18, with a higher relapse rate than adult-onset but slower progression; needs distinction from ADEM and MOG disease.
simple: Multiple sclerosis that starts in childhood or teenage years.

name: Paget’s disease
formal: Disordered bone remodelling with bone enlargement causing deafness, spinal stenosis, cranial neuropathies and platybasia; raised alkaline phosphatase; treated with bisphosphonates.
simple: A bone disease in which bones grow too large and weak, which can squeeze nerves and cause deafness.

name: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome
formal: Persistent leg pain with involuntary writhing toe movements, due to nerve root, nerve or spinal lesion; treated symptomatically with gabapentin or nerve blocks.
simple: Pain in the legs with toes that move on their own in a writhing way.
nN: painful legs and moving tes syndrome

name: Painful neuropathies
formal: Peripheral nerve disorders in which neuropathic pain dominates, typically burning or shooting, from small-fibre involvement; causes include diabetes, toxins, amyloid, HIV and inherited channelopathies.
simple: Nerve damage that causes burning, stabbing or electric-shock-like pain, often in the feet and hands.
more: Work up includes glucose, B12, skin biopsy and nerve conduction studies. Treatment targets the cause and uses duloxetine, gabapentinoids or tricyclics; topical agents help some people.

name: Painful ophthalmoplegia
formal: Orbital or cavernous sinus pain with ocular motor palsies, as in Tolosa-Hunt syndrome, aneurysm, diabetes, tumour or infection; steroids respond in idiopathic cases.
simple: Eye pain together with weak eye movements, often caused by inflammation or pressure behind the eye.

name: Painful sensory neuropathies
formal: Predominantly small-fibre sensory neuropathies with burning pain, allodynia and autonomic features, often with normal conduction studies; causes include diabetes, impaired glucose tolerance, Fabry disease and SCN9A variants.
simple: Damage to the small sensory nerves that makes the feet and hands burn, tingle or hurt, sometimes from light touch.
more: Skin biopsy for intra-epidermal nerve fibre density is useful. Manage underlying disease and use neuropathic pain drugs; the course is usually chronic but not disabling for movement.

name: Painful sensory neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy dominated by burning, stabbing pain from small-fibre dysfunction, from diabetes, toxins, or idiopathic causes.
simple: Nerve damage causing burning or stabbing pain, mostly in the feet.
more: Skin biopsy for fibre density; treat with duloxetine, pregabalin, gabapentin, or tricyclics, and address the cause.

name: Palatal myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic soft palate contractions, 1-3 Hz, persistent during sleep; symptomatic form follows brainstem lesion with olivary hypertrophy, essential form causes ear click.
simple: Rhythmic jerks of the soft palate at the back of the mouth, sometimes heard as a clicking in the ear.

name: Palatal myoclonus/tremor
formal: Rhythmic soft palate movements, either symptomatic with olivary hypertrophy after brainstem lesion or essential with ear click; classified as palatal tremor.
simple: Rhythmic jerking of the soft palate, either after a brainstem injury or without a clear cause.

name: Palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic soft palate movement of 1-3 Hz; symptomatic after brainstem or cerebellar lesion with hypertrophic olivary degeneration, or essential with ear click.
simple: Regular rhythmic jerking of the soft palate that may cause a clicking noise in the ear.

name: Pallidoluysian atrophy (PLA)
formal: Degeneration of the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, as in DRPLA, producing chorea, ataxia, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia.
simple: Loss of cells in deep brain areas that control movement, causing jerks, imbalance and dementia.
more: Genetic testing for atrophin-1 CAG repeats in DRPLA is typical. Treatment is symptomatic and the disease is progressive.

name: Pallidoluysian dentate atrophy (PLDA)
formal: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, a CAG repeat disorder of ATN1 with progressive ataxia, choreoathetosis, myoclonic epilepsy and dementia, more frequent in Japan.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease with clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia, seen mostly in Japan.
more: Autosomal dominant with anticipation; confirm by ATN1 repeat testing. MRI shows brainstem and cerebellar atrophy; treat symptomatically.

name: Pallidonigral atrophy (PNA)
formal: Rare degeneration of the globus pallidus and substantia nigra producing parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, sometimes with pyramidal signs, described pathologically.
simple: A rare brain degeneration affecting two movement centres, causing stiffness and slowness.
more: Diagnosis made at autopsy; treatments have limited effect and care is supportive.

name: Pallidonigroluysian atrophy (PNLA)
formal: Rare neurodegeneration of the pallidum, substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus with parkinsonism, dystonia or chorea, possibly with pyramidal signs and dementia.
simple: A rare brain disease with cell loss in three deep movement-control areas, causing stiffness and slow movement.
more: Definitive diagnosis is pathological; some cases overlap with PSP. Treatment is symptomatic.

name: Pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration (PPD/S)
formal: Rare juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, dystonia and early onset, often from PLA2G6 or ATP13A2 variants, with levodopa responsiveness at first.
simple: A rare early-onset condition combining parkinsonism and stiff, brisk limb reflexes from spinal cord pathway involvement.
more: Genetic testing identifies causes (e.g. PARK9 Kufor-Rakeb). Levodopa helps initially but dyskinesia and decline occur.
nN: pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration ppd s
aN: ppd | s | pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration

name: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
formal: Autosomal recessive PANK2 disorder with iron accumulation in globus pallidus (eye-of-the-tiger sign), causing dystonia, parkinsonism, retinopathy and acanthocytes.
simple: An inherited brain disease with iron build-up causing stiffness, twisting movements and sometimes vision problems.

name: Pantothenate kinase-associated parkinsonism
formal: Atypical late-onset PANK2 disease with parkinsonism, gait freezing, speech disorder and psychiatric features; pallidal iron accumulation on MRI.
simple: A later-onset form of an inherited iron-storage brain disease causing stiffness, slowness and speech problems.

name: Paraballism
formal: Bilateral ballistic flinging movements of both legs, usually from bilateral basal ganglia or subthalamic lesions, or less commonly spinal causes.
simple: Wild flinging movements of both legs, usually after damage to deep brain areas.

name: Paralysis agitans
formal: Historical term for Parkinson disease, meaning shaking palsy, referring to rest tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia.
simple: An old name for Parkinson disease.

name: Paralysis, sleep
formal: Temporary inability to move or speak while falling asleep or waking, with preserved awareness from REM atonia intrusion; common in narcolepsy and sleep deprivation.
simple: Waking up unable to move or speak for a short time, which can feel frightening but is harmless.

name: Paramnesias
formal: Distortions of memory with false recognition or recall such as déjà vu, confabulation or reduplicative paramnesia; seen in temporal lobe epilepsy and frontal or right hemispheric lesions.
simple: Memory distortions in which a person believes a false memory or feels wrongly familiar with something.

name: Paramyotonia
formal: Sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with cold-induced myotonia that worsens with exercise and may cause episodes of weakness.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles become stiff in the cold and stiffness worsens with repeated use.
more: Cooling EMG test and genetic testing; mexiletine is effective.

name: Paramyotonia congenita
formal: Autosomal dominant SCN4A sodium channelopathy with cold-induced myotonia worsening with exercise, and episodic weakness; mexiletine helpful.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles stiffen in the cold and with repeated use.
more: Cold provocation with EMG shows a drop in compound muscle amplitude; the common mutation is T1313M or R1448C in SCN4A. Avoid cold and potassium loading; mexiletine or acetazolamide reduces attacks.
th: กล้ามเนื้อคลายช้าแบบที่แย่ลงเมื่อทำซ้ำและเมื่อเย็น — ใบหน้า มือ เปลือกตา (SCN4A)
feat: Paradoxical myotonia: stiffness increases with repeated action
Cold provokes stiffness and then weakness of face, eyelids and hands
Eyelid myotonia (slow opening after forced closure); may overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis
inv: EMG myotonia; cooling worsens findings
SCN4A genetic testing

case.story: In cold weather her face stiffens and she cannot open her eyes quickly after squeezing them shut; in winter her hands become weak.
case.exam: Eyelid myotonia increasing with repeated closures, mild grip myotonia that worsens with repetition.
case.tests: EMG myotonic discharges; SCN4A variant.
case.q: Which bedside feature separates this from myotonia congenita?
case.a: Worsening (not improving) with repetition, and cold sensitivity.

ddx.pt: Warm-up phenomenon, muscle hypertrophy
Episodes of flaccid weakness with high K; may overlap

aN: paramyotonia | eulenburg disease | scn4a myotonia | paradoxical myotonia

det.patho: Autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SCN4A impair fast inactivation of the skeletal muscle sodium channel, particularly at low temperatures. Persistent inward sodium current produces repetitive firing (myotonia) and, with more sustained depolarisation, inexcitability and weakness. Some variants overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin in infancy or childhood and mainly affect the face, eyelids, tongue and hands. Stiffness becomes worse rather than better with repeated movement (paradoxical myotonia) and is provoked by cold, leading to weakness that can last hours after rewarming. Eyelid myotonia after forced closure is a typical bedside sign. Some patients also have episodic flaccid weakness, particularly after potassium intake or rest following exercise.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history of cold sensitivity and paradoxical myotonia is very suggestive. EMG shows myotonic discharges; on short exercise testing with cooling, CMAP amplitude falls progressively, unlike chloride channel myotonia. SCN4A testing confirms the diagnosis. CK may be mildly elevated.
det.treatment: Keep the body and hands warm and avoid triggers such as cold water swimming. Mexiletine is effective for cold-induced stiffness; acetazolamide or thiazide-type diuretics may reduce weakness episodes in overlap patients. As with other myotonias, avoid depolarising muscle relaxants and monitor temperature during anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: The course is non-progressive and life expectancy is normal; quality of life is mainly affected in cold climates or occupations.
pearls: Paradoxical myotonia (worse with repetition) plus cold sensitivity = SCN4A.
Test eyelid opening after repeated forced closures.
Ask about episodic weakness: overlap with hyperPP is common.
det.thd: Paramyotonia congenita เกิดจากยีน SCN4A ทำให้ช่องโซเดียมของกล้ามเนื้อปิดไม่สนิทโดยเฉพาะเมื่อเย็น อาการเด่นคือใบหน้า เปลือกตา และมือแข็งเกร็งมากขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำหรือโดนอากาศเย็น ตามด้วยอ่อนแรงได้ ต่างจาก myotonia congenita ที่ดีขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำ ตรวจ EMG ร่วมกับทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเย็น และตรวจยีน SCN4A รักษาด้วยการรักษาความอบอุ่นและ mexiletine

name: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Autonomic neuropathy related to cancer, commonly anti-Hu or ganglionic AChR antibodies, causing gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and pseudo-obstruction.
simple: Nerve damage affecting automatic body functions caused by the immune response to a cancer.
more: Search for tumour, e.g. small cell lung cancer; treat tumour and immunotherapy; prognosis often poor.

name: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD)
formal: Subacute pancerebellar syndrome with Purkinje cell loss due to onconeural antibodies such as anti-Yo, Hu or Tr, associated with ovarian, breast, lung cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma.
simple: Rapidly worsening balance and coordination caused by the immune system attacking the cerebellum in response to a cancer.

name: Paraneoplastic encephalitis
formal: Immune-mediated limbic or diffuse encephalitis with memory loss, seizures and psychiatric features associated with tumour and antibodies such as anti-Hu, Ma2 or NMDA receptor.
simple: Brain inflammation caused by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer, causing memory loss, seizures and confusion.

name: Paraneoplastic neurological disorders (PND)
formal: Immune-mediated nervous system syndromes remote from cancer, with onconeural antibodies; includes encephalomyelitis, cerebellar degeneration, neuropathy and Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
simple: Nerve and brain problems caused by the body's immune response to a cancer elsewhere in the body.

name: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus–myoclonus (POM)
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus with ataxia associated with neuroblastoma in children and breast, lung or other tumours in adults, with anti-Ri antibodies in some.
simple: Wild eye movements and muscle jerks caused by the immune system reacting to a cancer.

name: Paraneoplastic sensorimotor polyneuropathy
formal: Subacute or chronic sensorimotor neuropathy associated with underlying cancer, often lung, lymphoma, or myeloma, via immune or paraproteinaemic mechanisms.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness and weakness as a remote effect of a hidden cancer.
more: Investigate with antibodies and cancer screening; treat the tumour and use immunotherapy.

name: Paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy/ganglionopathy
formal: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) related dorsal root ganglionopathy with asymmetric sensory loss, ataxia, and pain, typically with small-cell lung cancer.
simple: Immune damage to sensory nerve cells in a ganglion, causing numbness and balance loss, often with a lung cancer.
more: Check anti-Hu antibodies and search for tumour; treat the tumour; immunotherapy is rarely beneficial.

name: Paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome
formal: Stiff-person variant with progressive rigidity and spasms associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies and breast or lung cancer.
simple: A rare condition of muscle stiffness and spasms triggered by the body's immune response to cancer.

name: Paraneoplastic syndrome
formal: Remote effects of malignancy on the nervous system or other organs from immune mechanisms or secreted factors, with antibodies such as Hu, Yo, Ri and CV2.
simple: Symptoms caused not by a tumour itself but by the body's immune response to it.
more: Test for onconeural antibodies (anti-Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, Ma2) and screen for tumour with CT, PET and mammography. Treat the tumour and give immunotherapy, but prognosis is poor; neurological syndromes often precede detection of the cancer.

name: Paraplegia
formal: Paralysis of both legs from thoracic or lumbar cord, cauda equina or cerebral lesion, with sensory level and sphincter disturbance; causes include trauma, myelitis and tumour.
simple: Weakness or paralysis of both legs, usually caused by spinal cord injury or disease.

name: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy occurring with a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) produced by a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population — most often MGUS, sometimes myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, lymphoma, AL amyloidosis, cryoglobulinaemia or POEMS; mechanisms include antibody binding to nerve antigens and deposition of immunoglobulin or amyloid.
simple: Nerve damage that comes with an abnormal single type of antibody protein in the blood, made by an overgrown family of blood cells; sometimes that family is a cancer, so it must be looked for.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด — ต้องตรวจหาโรคเม็ดเลือดชนิด plasma cell/B cell ที่ซ่อนอยู่
feat: Usually a slowly progressive distal sensory-predominant polyneuropathy in older adults
Three clinical patterns: distal demyelinating (often IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like (often IgG/IgA), or length-dependent axonal
The neuropathy may appear years before the blood disorder declares itself
Red flags for malignancy: weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, anaemia, renal failure, autonomic failure
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (more sensitive than electrophoresis alone) and serum free light chains
Urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation
NCS to define demyelinating vs axonal pattern
Haematology referral: bone marrow, skeletal survey; anti-MAG if IgM; VEGF if POEMS suspected; fat pad biopsy for amyloid

case.story: Two years of numb feet climbing to the ankles and unsteadiness in the dark; recently losing weight.
case.exam: Stocking sensory loss, reduced vibration at the knees, absent ankle jerks, mild toe extensor weakness.
case.tests: Serum immunofixation: IgG-lambda band; free light chain ratio abnormal; skeletal survey: lytic lesions.
case.q: What does the skeletal survey change about the label 'MGUS neuropathy'?
case.a: Lytic bone lesions point to multiple myeloma rather than MGUS — treatment targets the malignancy.

Proximal and distal weakness without M-protein
