det.patho: A clone of plasma cells or B cells secretes a single immunoglobulin (M-protein). Nerve injury can arise because the M-protein acts as an autoantibody (anti-MAG, anti-ganglioside), because light chains form amyloid deposits, because cryoglobulins cause vasculitis, through cytokines such as VEGF in POEMS, or through direct infiltration. In many older patients with an IgG or IgA band the M-protein is incidental, since MGUS is common in the elderly. IgM gammopathies are proportionally more often truly linked to neuropathy.
det.clinical: Most patients have a slowly worsening distal sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy. Three main patterns guide work-up: distal acquired demyelinating (typical of IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like with proximal weakness, and length-dependent axonal. Red flags for a serious underlying disorder include weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, autonomic failure, painful small-fibre neuropathy, rapid progression, renal impairment and skin changes.
det.diagnosis: Screen any unexplained neuropathy with serum electrophoresis plus immunofixation and serum free light chains; electrophoresis alone misses small bands. Characterise the neuropathy with NCS. Then tailor tests: anti-MAG for IgM, VEGF and bone imaging for lambda bands with demyelination, fat pad or nerve biopsy for amyloid, cryoglobulins and hepatitis C for vasculitic pictures. Refer to haematology for marrow examination and staging.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the mechanism. CIDP-like IgG/IgA cases are treated as CIDP. Anti-MAG disease is treated with rituximab when disabling. Malignant causes (myeloma, Waldenström, AL amyloid, POEMS) require haematological therapy directed at the clone. Slow axonal neuropathy with an incidental MGUS usually needs only symptomatic care and monitoring.
det.prognosis: Outlook depends on the underlying disorder, ranging from a benign course with MGUS to serious systemic disease with amyloidosis or POEMS.
pearls: Immunofixation and free light chains are more sensitive than SPEP — order them together.
A lambda paraprotein with a demyelinating neuropathy is POEMS until proven otherwise.
An IgG MGUS in an elderly patient may be a bystander; do not over-attribute.
det.thd: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด ซึ่งสร้างจากกลุ่มเซลล์พลาสมาหรือ B cell ที่เจริญผิดปกติ กลไกมีหลายแบบ เช่น โปรตีนทำหน้าที่เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อเส้นประสาท หรือสะสมเป็นอะไมลอยด์ ควรตรวจ immunofixation และ free light chain ในผู้ป่วยเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ และส่งปรึกษาโลหิตวิทยาเพื่อหาโรคมะเร็ง การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น แบบคล้าย CIDP รักษาเหมือน CIDP ส่วนแบบที่เป็นมะเร็งต้องรักษาตัวโรคเลือด

name: Parasagittal meningioma
formal: Meningioma along the superior sagittal sinus causing focal seizures and contralateral leg weakness from parasagittal motor cortex involvement.
simple: A slow-growing brain-lining tumour near the midline that can cause seizures and leg weakness.

name: Parasitic neurological infections
formal: CNS infection by helminths or protozoa such as neurocysticercosis, toxoplasmosis, malaria and schistosomiasis, producing seizures, mass lesions and meningitis.
simple: Nervous system infections caused by parasites, such as tapeworm cysts in the brain.

name: Parasomnias
formal: Abnormal sleep behaviours, either NREM (sleepwalking, night terrors) or REM (REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmares), reflecting incomplete state dissociation.
simple: Unusual behaviours during sleep such as sleepwalking, talking or acting out dreams.

name: Parathyroid disorders
formal: Hyper- or hypoparathyroidism causing calcium disturbance, with neuromuscular irritability, tetany, seizures, basal ganglia calcification and proximal myopathy.
simple: Problems with the glands controlling calcium, which can cause muscle cramps, weakness and seizures.
more: Check serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, with CT or MRI showing basal ganglia calcification. Neuromuscular signs improve with correction of calcium: calcium and calcitriol for hypoparathyroidism, parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism.

name: Parathyroid-induced myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness and wasting from primary hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia, with normal CK, reversible after treatment.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and hips caused by an overactive parathyroid gland or low vitamin D.

name: Parenchymal CNS tuberculosis
formal: Tuberculoma or abscess of brain or spinal cord from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, causing focal deficits and seizures with ring-enhancing lesions.
simple: Tuberculosis forming lumps within the brain or spinal cord, causing weakness or seizures.

name: Parinaud syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with impaired upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and lid retraction, from pineal tumour, hydrocephalus or midbrain stroke.
simple: A problem with looking upward and abnormal pupils, caused by damage to the top of the brainstem.

name: Parinaud’s syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and Collier sign, typically from pineal region tumour or hydrocephalus.
simple: Trouble looking upward with abnormal pupils, caused by pressure on the back of the midbrain.

name: Parkin disease
formal: Autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease from PRKN mutations, with dystonia, slow progression, good levodopa response and usually no Lewy bodies.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease starting in young adults, caused by a change in the parkin gene.

name: Parkinsonian rigidity
formal: Lead-pipe or cogwheel increased resistance to passive movement of limbs, a cardinal sign of parkinsonism from nigrostriatal dopamine loss.
simple: Stiffness of the arms and legs when someone moves them, a typical sign of Parkinson disease.

name: Parkinsonian-dementia syndromes
formal: Disorders combining parkinsonism and cognitive decline, including Parkinson disease dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, PSP and corticobasal degeneration.
simple: Illnesses that cause both movement slowness or stiffness and memory or thinking problems.

name: Parkinsonism
formal: Clinical syndrome of bradykinesia with rest tremor, rigidity or postural instability; due to Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism, vascular disease or drugs.
simple: A set of symptoms including slowness, stiffness and shaking, from Parkinson disease or other causes.
more: Evaluate with levodopa trial, MRI, DAT-SPECT, and drug history; atypical features include early falls, poor levodopa response, and autonomic failure. Treatment depends on cause, and drug-induced parkinsonism often resolves in weeks to months after withdrawal.

name: Parkinsonism-plus syndromes
formal: Atypical parkinsonian disorders such as MSA, PSP and corticobasal degeneration, with poor levodopa response, early falls, autonomic failure or gaze palsy.
simple: Parkinson-like illnesses with extra problems such as early falls or blood pressure trouble, which respond poorly to treatment.

name: Parkinsonism–dementia complex of Guam (PDC)
formal: Western Pacific tauopathy with parkinsonism and dementia, linked to ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex, with neurofibrillary tangles; possible environmental cycad toxin link.
simple: A rare illness on the island of Guam causing Parkinson-like symptoms and dementia.
nN: parkinsonism dementia complex of guam pdc
aN: pdc | parkinsonism dementia complex of guam

name: Parkinson’s disease (PD)
formal: Neurodegenerative synucleinopathy with nigrostriatal dopamine loss causing bradykinesia, rest tremor and rigidity, with non-motor symptoms; levodopa-responsive.
simple: A brain disease causing slowness, stiffness and tremor because cells that make dopamine are lost.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by DAT-SPECT showing reduced striatal uptake; MRI excludes secondary causes. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors and amantadine; DBS for motor fluctuations; LRRK2.
th: โรคพาร์กินสัน — เคลื่อนไหวช้า สั่นขณะพัก แข็งเกร็ง เริ่มข้างเดียว ตอบสนองดีต่อยาเลโวโดปา
feat: Bradykinesia with decrement plus rest tremor and/or rigidity
Asymmetric onset that stays asymmetric
Prodrome: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression
Clear, sustained levodopa response; later motor fluctuations and dyskinesia
inv: Clinical diagnosis (MDS criteria)
Dopamine transporter SPECT if uncertain (vs essential or drug-induced tremor)
MRI to look for atypical features if red flags

case.story: Two years of a shaking right hand at rest, smaller handwriting and slowness doing up buttons; his wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep.
case.exam: Right pill-rolling rest tremor, decrementing finger taps on the right, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: None required; marked improvement on levodopa.
case.q: Which sleep symptom is a prodromal clue?
case.a: REM sleep behaviour disorder (dream enactment) — a synucleinopathy marker.

ddx.pt: Bilateral postural/action tremor, no bradykinesia, alcohol responsive
Early falls backwards, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, poor levodopa response
Early severe autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, poor levodopa response
Symmetric, dopamine blocker exposure, normal DAT scan
Lower-body gait disorder with incontinence and ventriculomegaly

aN: pd | parkinson disease | idiopathic parkinson disease | paralysis agitans | ipd

det.patho: Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, and pigmented dopaminergic cells of the substantia nigra pars compacta die off, starving the dorsal putamen of dopamine. Pathology probably begins years earlier in the olfactory bulb and lower brainstem (and possibly the gut), which explains the non-motor prodrome. Most cases are sporadic; monogenic forms (LRRK2, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1) and GBA variants as a risk factor account for a minority. Age is the dominant risk factor, with a modest male excess.
det.clinical: Motor onset is typically one-sided, with slowness and fatiguing of repetitive movements, a 4–6 Hz resting tremor and lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity. Patients describe small handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial expression and a shuffling gait with less arm swing. Non-motor problems — smell loss, constipation, dream enactment, mood change, pain, urinary urgency and later orthostasis and cognitive decline — often matter more for quality of life. After some years on levodopa, wearing-off, peak-dose dyskinesia and freezing of gait appear. Red flags pointing elsewhere include early falls, early dementia, early severe autonomic failure, rapid progression, symmetric onset and a poor drug response.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on the 2015 MDS criteria: establish parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity), then weigh supportive features against absolute exclusions and red flags. A convincing, sustained response to dopaminergic therapy strongly supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss but cannot separate PD from MSA or PSP; it is mainly useful against essential tremor, dystonic tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism. Routine MRI is normal; order it if atypical signs are present. Skin biopsy or CSF seed amplification assays for alpha-synuclein are emerging biomarkers, mostly in research or specialist use.
det.treatment: Start symptomatic treatment when symptoms impair function; levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor is the most effective drug, while dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives in younger or milder patients. Warn every patient on agonists about impulse control disorders and sudden sleep attacks. Fluctuations are managed by fractionating levodopa, adding COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, amantadine for dyskinesia, and rescue apomorphine or inhaled levodopa. Advanced options include deep brain stimulation (STN or GPi) and continuous levodopa or apomorphine infusion. Exercise, physiotherapy, speech therapy and treatment of non-motor symptoms are integral; avoid typical antipsychotics and metoclopramide, and never stop levodopa abruptly.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow over 10–20 years, with life expectancy only modestly reduced; falls, dementia and dysphagia drive late disability and death.
pearls: Tremor that is absent when the hands are held out but returns after a few seconds (re-emergent tremor) is still a Parkinsonian rest tremor.
Abrupt levodopa withdrawal can cause a hyperpyrexic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Strictly symmetric onset, early falls or no levodopa benefit should make you rethink the diagnosis.
det.thd: โรคพาร์กินสันเกิดจากเซลล์สร้างโดปามีนใน substantia nigra ตายลงพร้อมการสะสมของโปรตีน alpha-synuclein อาการหลักคือเคลื่อนไหวช้าที่เริ่มข้างเดียว ร่วมกับสั่นขณะพักหรือเกร็ง และมีอาการนำ เช่น จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น ท้องผูก ละเมอตามความฝัน การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการทางคลินิกตามเกณฑ์ MDS ส่วน DAT scan ช่วยเมื่อแยกจาก essential tremor หรือยาที่ทำให้เกิดอาการ ยาหลักคือ levodopa และเมื่อโรคก้าวหน้าอาจใช้ DBS หรือยาแบบให้ต่อเนื่อง

name: Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD)
formal: Dementia developing after at least a year of established Parkinson disease, with attention and executive deficits, hallucinations and Lewy body pathology.
simple: Memory and thinking decline that develops in someone who has had Parkinson disease for some time.

name: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI)
formal: Cognitive decline in Parkinson disease not interfering with daily function, with executive or visuospatial deficits; risk factor for later dementia.
simple: Mild thinking and memory problems in a person with Parkinson disease that do not yet affect daily life.
ab: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment
nN: parkinson disease with mild cognitive impairment pd mci
aN: pd mci | parkinson disease with mild cognitive impairment

name: Paroxysmal (nonepileptic) movement disorders
formal: Episodic attacks of dyskinesia without loss of consciousness or EEG epileptiform activity, including kinesigenic, nonkinesigenic and exertional dyskinesias, episodic ataxias and hypnogenic forms.
simple: Sudden short episodes of abnormal movements such as twisting or jerking that are not seizures.
more: Classified by trigger and duration; genes include PRRT2, MR-1 and SLC2A1. Treatment is trigger avoidance and drugs such as carbamazepine or acetazolamide depending on subtype.

name: Paroxysmal choreoathetosis
formal: Episodic attacks of chorea, athetosis or dystonia, either kinesigenic, non-kinesigenic or exercise-induced, often genetic channelopathies or PRRT2 mutations.
simple: Short attacks of twisting or writhing movements that come and go.

name: Paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Episodic involuntary movements, dystonia or chorea with normal examination between attacks, classified as kinesigenic, non-kinesigenic or exercise-induced.
simple: Sudden short episodes of abnormal movements with normal movement in between.
more: PKD (PRRT2 mutations) responds to carbamazepine or phenytoin; PNKD (MR-1) responds poorly to medication and is triggered by alcohol, caffeine. Video recording is helpful; interictal exam and EEG are normal.

name: Paroxysmal dystonia
formal: Episodic dystonic attacks, genetic or secondary, with preserved consciousness; includes kinesigenic, nonkinesigenic and exercise-induced forms.
simple: Short episodes of muscle twisting or cramping that come and go.

name: Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia
formal: Dystonic attacks triggered by prolonged exercise lasting 5-30 minutes, often from SLC2A1 (GLUT1) mutations; may respond to ketogenic diet.
simple: Attacks of muscle twisting in the legs set off by long exercise.
more: Examine for GLUT1 deficiency with CSF glucose, lactate and SLC2A1 testing; PED can also result from PRRT2, ATP1A3 or dopa-responsive dystonia genes. Ketogenic diet or modified Atkins is effective, and avoidance of triggers helps.

name: Paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia
formal: Episodic dystonia or choreoathetosis after prolonged exercise lasting 5 to 30 minutes, often from SLC2A1 (GLUT1) variants, with epilepsy or hemolytic anaemia in some.
simple: Attacks of twisting or jerky movements of the legs triggered by prolonged exercise such as walking or running.
more: Lumbar puncture may show low CSF glucose; ketogenic diet is effective in GLUT1 deficiency and acetazolamide sometimes helps.

name: Paroxysmal hypnic dyskinesia
formal: Nocturnal episodes of dystonic or choreic movements arising from NREM sleep, likely frontal lobe epilepsy mimic and responsive to carbamazepine.
simple: Short attacks of abnormal movements that wake a person from sleep, probably a form of sleep seizure.

name: Paroxysmal hypnic dystonia
formal: Nocturnal dystonic attacks from NREM sleep, now regarded as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy responsive to carbamazepine.
simple: Brief episodes of twisting movements out of sleep, now thought to be a type of seizure.

name: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
formal: Brief attacks of dystonia or chorea triggered by sudden movement, due to PRRT2 mutations, with excellent response to low-dose carbamazepine.
simple: Brief attacks of abnormal movements set off by suddenly starting to move, which respond well to a seizure medicine.

name: Paroxysmal kinesiogenic dyskinesia (PKD)
formal: Brief attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting seconds, triggered by sudden movement, linked to PRRT2 variants, starting in childhood or adolescence, with a usually benign course.
simple: Short episodes of involuntary movements triggered by suddenly starting to move, such as getting up quickly.
more: Dramatic response to low-dose carbamazepine or phenytoin; many remit in adulthood. Genetics reveal PRRT2 in most families.

name: Paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia
formal: Attacks of dystonia and chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, stress or fatigue, caused by MR-1 (PNKD) mutations.
simple: Longer attacks of abnormal movements triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress.

name: Paroxysmal nonkinesiogenic dyskinesia (PNKD)
formal: Attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, fatigue or stress and not movement, from MR-1 variants, autosomal dominant.
simple: Longer episodes of abnormal movements triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress rather than movement.
more: Avoid triggers; clonazepam or benzodiazepines work better than carbamazepine. Prognosis is good and may improve with age.

name: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity
formal: Episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating and dystonia after severe brain injury, from disconnection of autonomic control; treated with beta-blockers, gabapentin, bromocriptine.
simple: Episodes of racing heart, high blood pressure, sweating and fever after serious brain injury.

name: Parry–Romberg syndrome
formal: Progressive hemifacial atrophy affecting skin, fat, muscle and bone, with trigeminal neuralgia, migraine or epilepsy; related to linear scleroderma.
simple: A rare condition where one side of the face slowly shrinks, sometimes with headaches or seizures.

name: Partial spinal cord syndrome
formal: Incomplete cord lesion patterns such as Brown-Séquard, anterior or central cord syndromes, with characteristic motor and sensory distributions below the lesion.
simple: Spinal cord damage that affects only part of the cord, so some movement or feeling is lost and some is kept.

name: Paucibacillary leprosy
formal: Tuberculoid or indeterminate leprosy with few skin patches and nerve thickening, causing sensory loss and mononeuropathy; strong cell-mediated response.
simple: A milder form of leprosy with few skin patches and numb areas.

name: PCOM artery aneurysm
formal: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm, often causing painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement, or subarachnoid haemorrhage when ruptured.
simple: A bulge in a brain artery that can press on a nerve to the eye or bleed.

name: Peak-dose dyskinesias
formal: Choreiform or dystonic movements during peak plasma levodopa levels in treated Parkinson disease, related to pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation; amantadine may help.
simple: Involuntary wriggling movements when medicine levels are highest in Parkinson disease.

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease (PMD)
formal: X-linked hypomyelinating leukodystrophy from PLP1 mutations, with nystagmus, hypotonia, spasticity and developmental delay in infancy.
simple: An inherited condition in boys where nerve insulation fails to form properly, causing abnormal eye movements and delayed development.
more: PLP1 duplication is the most common cause (also point mutations and null); MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination; sequencing or MLPA. Treatment is supportive with antispasticity and seizure management; milder spastic paraplegia SPG2 allelic.

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher-like disease (PMLD)
formal: Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy clinically like PMD but without PLP1 mutation, often due to GJC2 (connexin 47) mutations, with nystagmus and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited disorder similar to Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease with poorly formed nerve insulation.

name: Penicillamine dermatopathy
formal: Skin complications of penicillamine such as elastosis perforans serpiginosa, pemphigus and cutis laxa-like change, occurring during treatment of Wilson disease and other conditions.
simple: Skin damage, including wrinkling, blistering and fragile skin, caused by penicillamine treatment.
more: Diagnosed from drug history and skin biopsy. Switch to trientine or reduce dose; some lesions heal slowly or leave scars.

name: Penicillin cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus and encephalopathy from high-dose penicillin, especially in renal failure, due to GABA-A antagonism by beta-lactams.
simple: Muscle jerks and confusion caused by very high levels of penicillin antibiotic.

name: Periarteritis nodosa
formal: Necrotising medium-vessel vasculitis causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke and renal involvement; associated with hepatitis B.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels that can damage nerves and organs.

name: Periodic paralysis
formal: Channelopathy causing episodic flaccid weakness, hypo- or hyperkalaemic, triggered by rest after exercise or carbohydrate meals, from CACNA1S or SCN4A mutations.
simple: Attacks of temporary muscle weakness, usually inherited and linked to potassium levels.

name: Perioperative plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injury from surgical positioning, traction, tourniquets or retractors during an operation.
simple: Nerve network injury occurring during or after surgery, from stretch or pressure.
more: Most are neurapraxic and recover over weeks to months; EMG and imaging guide prognosis.

name: Peripheral myoclonus
formal: Myoclonic jerks arising from peripheral nerve, plexus or root lesions, such as hemifacial spasm or spinal root disease.
simple: Muscle jerks that start from a damaged nerve outside the brain and spinal cord.

name: Peripheral neuropathies
formal: Disorders of peripheral nerves producing sensory loss, weakness and autonomic features; axonal or demyelinating, with causes such as diabetes, toxins, immune and inherited disease.
simple: Damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, causing numbness, tingling and weakness.

name: Peripheral neuropathy
formal: Dysfunction of peripheral nerves causing distal sensory loss, weakness and areflexia, from diabetes, alcohol, drugs, vitamin deficiency, immune or hereditary causes.
simple: Damage to nerves in the hands and feet, causing numbness, tingling, pain or weakness.

name: Peripheral vertigo
formal: Vestibular spinning sensation from labyrinth or vestibular nerve disease such as BPPV, neuritis or Menière disease, with horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation.
simple: Spinning dizziness caused by a problem in the inner ear or its nerve.

name: Peritonitis
formal: Inflammation of the peritoneum, usually bacterial infection; neurologically relevant as shunt infection and abdominal complication of ventriculoperitoneal shunts.
simple: Infection or inflammation of the lining of the abdomen, causing severe belly pain and fever.
more: Diagnose from abdominal tenderness, fever and leucocytosis; ascitic neutrophils over 250 per mm3 define spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and coagulase-negative staphylococci typify shunt infection. Treat with antibiotics and shunt externalisation.

name: Peroneal neuropathies
formal: Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck, causing foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of foot, from compression, trauma or weight loss.
simple: Damage to a nerve near the knee causing a dropped foot and numbness on the top of the foot.

case.story: After losing 15 kg and sitting cross-legged for hours at a meditation retreat, her right foot slaps when she walks.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, normal inversion, numb dorsum of foot, normal ankle jerk.
case.tests: Peroneal motor conduction block across the fibular head; normal L5 paraspinals.
case.q: Which muscle test separates this from an L5 radiculopathy?
case.a: Ankle inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve, L5) — preserved in peroneal neuropathy, weak in L5 radiculopathy.

ddx.pt: Back pain, weak inversion and hip abduction, abnormal paraspinal EMG
Recurrent palsies, family history, PMP22 deletion
Bilateral, symmetric, pes cavus, lifelong

aN: peroneal neuropathy | fibular neuropathy | common peroneal palsy | foot drop at fibular head | crossed leg palsy

det.patho: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, where it is easily compressed or stretched. Weight loss removes the protective fat pad, and habitual leg crossing, squatting, kneeling, tight casts or prolonged immobility compress the nerve. The deep branch tends to be more affected than the superficial branch. Space-occupying lesions such as intraneural ganglion cysts arise from the superior tibiofibular joint.
det.clinical: Foot drop develops suddenly or over days, causing a steppage or slapping gait and tripping. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion are weak, whereas inversion, plantar flexion and the ankle jerk are spared. Sensory loss covers the lateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot, and a Tinel sign may be present at the fibular neck. Pain is uncommon with compression; marked pain should raise concern for ganglion cyst, tumour or vasculitis.
det.diagnosis: Examine ankle inversion and hip abduction carefully: weakness of either points to L5 radiculopathy or sciatic or plexus lesions. NCS show conduction block or slowing across the fibular head, or reduced amplitudes with axon loss. EMG of short head of biceps femoris (sciatic innervated) is normal in peroneal neuropathy and abnormal in sciatic lesions, and paraspinals are normal. Imaging with ultrasound or MRI is indicated without a clear compressive cause, or when progressive.
det.treatment: Remove the cause: stop leg crossing and squatting, pad the knee, adjust casts, and address weight loss. An ankle-foot orthosis improves gait and prevents falls during recovery, with physiotherapy to avoid Achilles contracture. Surgery is reserved for ganglion cysts, masses, lacerations or lack of recovery after several months; tendon transfer may help in permanent foot drop.
det.prognosis: Compressive lesions with predominant conduction block usually recover well within weeks to months. Severe axonal injury recovers slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Preserved inversion separates peroneal palsy from L5 radiculopathy.
Short head of biceps femoris on EMG separates peroneal from sciatic lesions.
Recurrent or bilateral pressure palsies: test for HNPP.
