name: Peroxisomal disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic diseases with impaired peroxisome function, such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and Zellweger spectrum, with very-long-chain fatty acid elevation.
simple: Inherited diseases where small cell structures cannot break down certain fats, damaging the brain and nerves.
more: Diagnose by raised plasma very long chain fatty acids, phytanic and pristanic acids, plasmalogens and bile acid intermediates, with PEX or ABCD1 gene testing. Treatment is supportive; Refsum responds to diet and X-ALD to transplantation.

name: Perry syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant DCTN1-related parkinsonism with depression, weight loss and central hypoventilation, with TDP-43 pathology.
simple: A rare inherited illness with Parkinson-like symptoms, depression, weight loss and breathing problems.

name: Persistent akathisia
formal: Chronic restlessness with inner urge to move persisting after dopamine blocker withdrawal; part of tardive syndromes.
simple: A lasting feeling of restlessness and need to move, remaining after stopping a medicine.

name: Personality disorder
formal: Enduring maladaptive pattern of inner experience and behaviour present from adolescence or early adulthood, causing distress or impairment; differentiate from frontal lobe personality change.
simple: A lifelong pattern of thinking and behaving that is very different from what is expected and causes difficulties in life and relationships.

name: Phaeochromocytoma
formal: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal medulla causing episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension; associated with VHL, MEN2 and NF1.
simple: A rare tumour of the adrenal gland releasing adrenaline-like hormones, causing pounding headaches, sweating and high blood pressure.

name: Phenobarbitone chorea
formal: Chorea caused by phenobarbitone and other antiepileptic drugs, reversible on drug withdrawal.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by the seizure medicine phenobarbitone.

name: Phonic tics
formal: Vocal tics such as throat clearing, sniffing, grunts or coprolalia, simple or complex, features of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Repeated sounds made involuntarily, like throat clearing or grunts.

name: Phosphate disorders
formal: Hypophosphataemia or hyperphosphataemia, with hypophosphataemia causing proximal myopathy, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory weakness, especially in refeeding.
simple: Too low or too high phosphate in the blood, which can lead to weakness and breathing problems.
more: Treat cause and replace phosphate carefully; watch for refeeding syndrome.

name: Phosphatidate phosphatase 1 deficiency
formal: LPIN1 deficiency causing recurrent childhood rhabdomyolysis triggered by fasting or infection, with myoglobinuria and raised CK.
simple: An inherited muscle condition in which illness or fasting causes muscle breakdown and dark urine.

name: Photosensitive myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Photoparoxysmal generalised epilepsy triggered by flickering light, with myoclonic jerks and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often in adolescents.
simple: Seizures and jerks triggered by flashing or flickering lights.

name: Phrenic nerve neuropathies
formal: Injury or dysfunction of the phrenic nerve, causing hemidiaphragm paralysis and dyspnoea, from surgery, trauma, neuralgic amyotrophy or tumour.
simple: Damage to the nerve controlling the diaphragm, causing breathlessness.

name: Phylloquinone (vitamin K) deficiency
formal: Impaired clotting factor synthesis causing bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage in newborns, from malabsorption, antibiotics or warfarin.
simple: Low vitamin K, which causes poor blood clotting and bleeding, including in the brain of newborns.

name: Physiological myoclonus
formal: Normal myoclonic jerks such as hiccups, sleep starts and hypnic jerks, without disease.
simple: Harmless muscle jerks like hiccups or twitching as you fall asleep.

name: Physiological tremor
formal: Low-amplitude, high-frequency postural tremor of 8-12 Hz present in everyone, enhanced by anxiety, caffeine, drugs and thyrotoxicosis.
simple: A fine normal tremor that everyone has, which can become more noticeable with stress, caffeine or some medicines.

name: Pick’s disease
formal: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with 3R tau Pick bodies and ballooned neurons, with personality change, disinhibition and language impairment.
simple: A type of dementia that damages the front and side of the brain, causing personality and language changes.
more: MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy; FDG-PET shows frontotemporal hypometabolism. Pick bodies are tau-positive and argyrophilic, and there is no disease-modifying treatment; use SSRIs and non-drug measures for behaviour.

name: Pill-rolling tremor
formal: Characteristic parkinsonian rest tremor of 4-6 Hz of thumb and fingers, resembling rolling a pill, which diminishes on action.
simple: A tremor in the thumb and finger that looks like rolling a pill, typical of Parkinson disease.

name: Pilocytic astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 1 astrocytoma with biphasic pattern and Rosenthal fibres, often cerebellar in children, with BRAF alterations and cyst with mural nodule; good prognosis.
simple: A slow-growing brain tumour, mainly in children, often in the cerebellum and often curable with surgery.

name: Pineal region tumours
formal: Germ cell tumours, pineocytoma, pineoblastoma and others causing Parinaud syndrome and obstructive hydrocephalus; markers AFP and hCG in germ cell types.
simple: Tumours near the pineal gland deep in the brain that can cause hydrocephalus and trouble looking up.

name: Pituitary disorders
formal: Disorders of hormone excess or deficiency from the pituitary, including adenomas, apoplexy and hypopituitarism, with endocrine and visual field effects.
simple: Problems of the pituitary gland, which controls many hormones, sometimes causing vision changes.
more: Investigate with morning cortisol, prolactin, IGF-1, TSH, pituitary-protocol MRI and visual fields. Treat with transsphenoidal surgery, cabergoline for prolactinoma and hormone replacement; apoplexy needs urgent steroids and decompression.

name: Pituitary tumours
formal: Mostly benign adenomas causing hormone excess or deficiency and bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression; prolactinoma most common.
simple: Usually non-cancerous growths of the pituitary gland that disturb hormones and may affect vision.

name: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration
formal: Autosomal recessive PLA2G6 disorder (infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, NBIA) with regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy, cerebellar atrophy and iron deposition; also adult dystonia-parkinsonism.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing loss of skills in young children, with stiffness and vision problems.

name: PLAN/NBIA-2
formal: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration (infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy and related) with brain iron accumulation, psychomotor regression, hypotonia, spasticity and optic atrophy, with early childhood onset.
simple: A rare inherited childhood disease with iron deposits in the brain and gradual loss of movement and skills.
more: MRI shows cerebellar atrophy and pallidal iron; autosomal recessive PLA2G6 mutations. No cure and treatment is supportive.

name: Plasmocytoma
formal: Solitary plasma cell tumour of bone or soft tissue, affecting skull base or spine with cord or nerve root compression; may progress to myeloma.
simple: A single growth of abnormal plasma cells in bone that can press on nerves or the spinal cord.

name: Plectin deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive PLEC deficiency causing epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy, and sometimes myasthenic features.
simple: An inherited condition with skin blistering and muscle weakness caused by a missing structural protein.
more: Diagnosis with skin and muscle immunostaining and PLEC genetics; supportive care, with some myasthenic cases improving on pyridostigmine.

name: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas (PXAs)
formal: Superficial temporal lobe astrocytoma in young people with seizures, BRAF V600E mutation and mostly good prognosis.
simple: A rare, usually slow-growing brain tumour near the surface, causing seizures in young people.

name: Plexiform neurofibromas
formal: Diffuse nerve sheath tumours pathognomonic of NF1 involving multiple fascicles, with risk of malignant transformation; MEK inhibitors can shrink them.
simple: Large soft nerve tumours seen in neurofibromatosis that can grow along nerves and sometimes turn cancerous.

name: Plexopathies
formal: Disorders of brachial or lumbosacral plexus from trauma, tumour, radiation, inflammation or diabetes, with patchy weakness and sensory loss across several nerve roots.
simple: Damage to a network of nerves in the shoulder or pelvis, causing weakness, numbness and pain.
more: Diagnose with EMG and MRI of brachial or lumbosacral plexus, with neuralgic amyotrophy preceded by acute pain, and radiation plexopathy appearing years after treatment. Treatment depends on the cause and includes steroids, analgesia and rehabilitation.

name: Plexopathy
formal: Lesion of brachial or lumbosacral plexus from trauma, neoplasm, radiation or neuralgic amyotrophy, with multi-root deficits.
simple: Damage to a nerve network at the shoulder or hip causing arm or leg weakness and numbness.
more: Diagnose with EMG, nerve conduction and MRI plexus imaging, with CSF protein often raised in neuralgic amyotrophy or radiation injury. Treat the cause: analgesia, physiotherapy, immunotherapy for inflammatory forms and surgery for traumatic lesions.

name: Pneumococcal meningitis
formal: Bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, most common in adults, with fever, neck stiffness and encephalopathy; treat with ceftriaxone, vancomycin and dexamethasone.
simple: A serious brain-lining infection caused by pneumococcus bacteria, needing urgent antibiotics.

name: POEMS syndrome
formal: Plasma cell dyscrasia with polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein and skin changes, driven by VEGF; treated with radiotherapy or myeloma-directed therapy.
simple: A rare condition linked to abnormal blood cells that causes nerve damage, enlarged organs, hormone problems and skin changes.
th: POEMS — เส้นประสาทเสื่อม อวัยวะโต ต่อมไร้ท่อผิดปกติ โปรตีนโมโนโคลนอล (lambda) ผิวหนังเปลี่ยน VEGF สูงมาก มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น CIDP
feat: Progressive distal, then proximal, demyelinating-axonal neuropathy with prominent weakness
Organomegaly, endocrinopathy, lambda M-protein, skin changes (hyperpigmentation, haemangiomas, clubbing)
Sclerotic bone lesions, Castleman disease, papilloedema, oedema/ascites, thrombocytosis
Often initially treated as CIDP without benefit
inv: Immunofixation (lambda light chain almost always) — small bands are easy to miss
Plasma/serum VEGF (markedly raised)
CT/PET-CT for sclerotic lesions; endocrine panel

case.story: Treated for CIDP for a year with IVIG and steroids, yet worsening; now has darker skin and ankle swelling.
case.exam: Distal and proximal leg weakness, areflexia, hepatomegaly, gynaecomastia, cherry haemangiomas, papilloedema.
case.tests: Small IgA-lambda band; VEGF 1,100 pg/mL; CT: sclerotic lesion in the pelvis.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment if the sclerotic lesion is solitary?
case.a: Radiotherapy to the plasmacytoma; disseminated disease is treated with chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation.

read.where: POEMS syndrome; VEGF testing; treatment (radiotherapy, stem cell transplant)

ddx.pt: No systemic features, normal VEGF, responds to IVIG
No bone lesions, organomegaly or raised VEGF
Painful small-fibre and autonomic neuropathy; amyloid on biopsy

aN: pems | crow fukase syndrome | osteosclerotic myeloma | takatsuki syndrome

det.patho: POEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome of a small plasma-cell clone that almost always produces a lambda light chain. The clone drives very high levels of VEGF and other cytokines, which increase vascular permeability and cause oedema, organomegaly, skin changes and endoneurial microangiopathy. The neuropathy combines demyelination with prominent axonal loss and tends to be motor-predominant.
det.clinical: Patients usually present with a progressive, symmetric, distal-to-proximal sensorimotor neuropathy that is often misdiagnosed as CIDP and fails IVIG. Systemic clues include hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, endocrine disturbance (hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes), hyperpigmentation, glomeruloid haemangiomas, white nails, clubbing, peripheral oedema, ascites, pleural effusion, papilloedema, thrombocytosis and polycythaemia. Neuropathic pain and weight loss are frequent. Untreated disease progresses to wheelchair dependence and cardiorespiratory complications.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires polyneuropathy and a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder (both mandatory), at least one major criterion (sclerotic bone lesions, Castleman disease, raised VEGF) and at least one minor criterion. NCS show uniform slowing and more severe axonal loss than typical CIDP, with less temporal dispersion. Use immunofixation (small bands are easily missed), serum or plasma VEGF, and CT or PET-CT for sclerotic lesions; bone marrow biopsy may show lambda-restricted clonal plasma cells.
det.treatment: One to a few sclerotic lesions without marrow disease are treated with targeted radiotherapy. Widespread disease or marrow involvement is treated with systemic therapy such as lenalidomide-dexamethasone or high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation. Avoid neurotoxic drugs such as bortezomib and thalidomide where possible, given the neuropathy. Supportive care includes orthoses, physiotherapy and management of oedema and endocrine deficits; VEGF is used to monitor response.
det.prognosis: With effective therapy most patients stabilise and neurological recovery continues slowly over 1–3 years; long-term survival is good.
pearls: IVIG-refractory 'CIDP' with a lambda band: check VEGF and look for sclerotic bone lesions.
Thrombocytosis and polycythaemia are useful laboratory hints.
Neurological improvement lags behind the haematological response by months.
det.thd: POEMS เป็นกลุ่มอาการจากเซลล์พลาสมาผิดปกติที่สร้าง lambda light chain และกระตุ้นให้ VEGF สูงมาก ทำให้เส้นประสาทเสื่อมแบบอ่อนแรงเด่น ร่วมกับอวัยวะโต ต่อมไร้ท่อผิดปกติ ผิวคล้ำ บวม และมีรอยโรคกระดูกแบบ sclerotic มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น CIDP ที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ IVIG การวินิจฉัยใช้ immunofixation ระดับ VEGF และ CT/PET หารอยโรคกระดูก การรักษาคือฉายรังสีหากรอยโรคมีจำนวนน้อย หรือให้ยาเคมีบำบัดร่วมกับปลูกถ่ายเซลล์ต้นกำเนิดหากโรคกระจาย

name: POLG disorders
formal: Mitochondrial DNA replication disorders from POLG variants, with phenotypes including Alpers-Huttenlocher, MIRAS, SANDO, progressive external ophthalmoplegia and myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: A family of inherited energy-production diseases causing seizures, liver failure, nerve damage, eye muscle weakness and ataxia.
more: Confirmed by POLG sequencing; avoid valproate. Treatment is supportive; severity varies from childhood fatal to adult-onset forms.

name: Poliomyelitis
formal: Enteroviral infection of anterior horn motor neurons causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis; prevented by vaccination.
simple: A virus infection that damages nerves controlling muscles, causing paralysis; prevented by vaccine.
more: Diagnose from acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis with CSF pleocytosis and stool or throat viral isolation; EMG shows denervation. No specific treatment exists, so care is supportive. Eradication relies on oral or inactivated vaccine.

name: Poliomyeloradiculitis
formal: Viral infection involving anterior horn cells and nerve roots, causing flaccid paralysis and radicular pain, as in polio or enterovirus infections.
simple: A viral infection of spinal nerve cells and roots causing weakness and pain.

name: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
formal: Necrotising vasculitis of medium arteries causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, hypertension and renal infarcts; hepatitis B associated.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized arteries that can damage nerves, kidneys and other organs.
more: Diagnose from nerve and muscle biopsy or angiography showing aneurysms, with raised inflammatory markers; ANCA is usually negative. Treat with steroids plus cyclophosphamide, with antivirals and plasma exchange for hepatitis B related disease.

name: Polycystic ovarian syndrome
formal: Endocrine disorder with anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries; relevance to neurology includes valproate exposure and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
simple: A common hormone condition causing irregular periods, excess hair growth and cysts on the ovaries.

name: Polyglutamine tract disorders
formal: CAG repeat expansion diseases, including Huntington disease, SCAs, SBMA and DRPLA, with toxic gain of function and anticipation.
simple: Inherited brain diseases caused by a repeated stretch in a gene, including Huntington disease.

name: Polymyositis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with subacute symmetric proximal weakness, raised CK, endomysial CD8 T-cell infiltrate and steroid response.
simple: A muscle inflammation causing weakness in the shoulders and hips, treated with immune-suppressing drugs.
more: Biopsy shows CD8 T cells invading non-necrotic fibres expressing MHC class I; EMG shows myopathic units with spontaneous activity. It is a diagnosis of exclusion needing rule-out of inclusion body myositis; add methotrexate or azathioprine.

name: Polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP)
formal: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with progressive or relapsing symmetric weakness and sensory loss over more than 8 weeks; responds to steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A long-lasting immune attack on nerves that causes weakness and numbness, treatable with immune therapies.
more: Supportive criteria include raised CSF protein, nerve conduction showing demyelination and, if unclear, nerve ultrasound or biopsy. Maintenance IVIG or subcutaneous immunoglobulin is often needed; steroid dependence and relapses are common.

name: Polyradiculopathies
formal: Disorder of multiple nerve roots, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome, CIDP, infiltration or CMV, causing weakness, areflexia and sensory change.
simple: Damage to several nerve roots at once, causing weakness and numbness.
more: Diagnosis by CSF, MRI and nerve studies; treat the cause, such as IVIG for immune types.

name: Polyradiculopathy
formal: Disorder of multiple nerve roots, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome, CIDP, infiltration or CMV, causing weakness, areflexia and sensory change.
simple: Damage to several nerve roots at once, causing weakness and numbness.
more: Diagnosis by CSF, MRI and nerve studies; treat the cause, such as IVIG for immune types.

name: Pompe disease
formal: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency with lysosomal glycogen storage causing myopathy, respiratory weakness and cardiomyopathy; enzyme replacement therapy.
simple: An inherited disease where sugar stores build up in muscles, causing weakness and breathing problems.
more: Diagnose by low acid alpha-glucosidase activity in dried blood spot and GAA testing; biopsy shows vacuoles with PAS-positive glycogen and EMG shows myotonic discharges. Alglucosidase or avalglucosidase alfa slows decline; early infant treatment is crucial.
th: โรคปอมเป (ขาดเอนไซม์ GAA) — ผู้ใหญ่มีต้นขาอ่อนแรงและหายใจไม่ไหวตั้งแต่ระยะแรก รักษาด้วยเอนไซม์ทดแทน
feat: Late-onset form: limb-girdle and axial (paraspinal) weakness
Early diaphragm weakness — orthopnoea, morning headache, respiratory failure out of proportion
Infantile form: floppy baby with cardiomyopathy and macroglossia
inv: Dried blood spot GAA enzyme activity, then GAA gene testing
CK mildly raised; EMG myotonic discharges in paraspinals; supine vs sitting FVC drop

case.story: Slowly harder to climb stairs over years; now sleeps propped on three pillows and wakes with headaches.
case.exam: Hip and trunk flexor weakness, paradoxical abdominal movement when lying flat, mild Beevor sign.
case.tests: CK 650 U/L; FVC falls 30% supine; low GAA activity, biallelic GAA variants.
case.q: What does the supine FVC drop indicate?
case.a: Diaphragmatic weakness — a hallmark of Pompe; start enzyme replacement and assess for night-time ventilation.

ddx.pt: Respiratory failure usually later; normal GAA
Subacute, inflammatory biopsy, steroid responsive
Fatigable ocular/bulbar features, antibodies

aN: pompe | acid maltase deficiency | gsd ii | glycogen storage disease type ii | gaa | late onset pompe

det.patho: Autosomal recessive deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) leads to glycogen accumulation inside lysosomes and autophagic build-up in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. Residual enzyme activity determines the phenotype: near-absent activity causes the infantile cardiomyopathic form, while partial activity gives late-onset disease. The intronic c.-32-13T>G variant is common in Caucasian late-onset patients; different variants prevail in Asia.
det.clinical: Infantile-onset Pompe presents in the first months with hypotonia, feeding difficulty, macroglossia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and early death if untreated. Late-onset disease can appear from childhood to late adulthood as a slowly progressive limb-girdle pattern with striking axial and abdominal weakness, scoliosis and early diaphragm involvement. Orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness or unexplained respiratory failure may be the presenting complaint. Some patients have only raised CK, and basilar or other intracranial aneurysms are reported.
det.diagnosis: Screen with GAA enzyme activity in a dried blood spot, confirmed in lymphocytes or fibroblasts and by biallelic GAA variants. CK is normal to moderately raised. EMG may show myopathic units with myotonic or complex repetitive discharges, particularly in paraspinal muscles. A fall in vital capacity of more than about 10–25% from sitting to supine indicates diaphragmatic weakness. Muscle MRI shows paraspinal and posterior thigh involvement; biopsy may show vacuoles but can be non-diagnostic, so enzyme testing should not be skipped.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant GAA (alglucosidase alfa, or newer avalglucosidase alfa or cipaglucosidase alfa with miglustat) is given intravenously every two weeks. Respiratory surveillance with sitting/supine FVC and sleep studies guides nocturnal non-invasive ventilation. Physiotherapy, scoliosis management and nutrition matter. Infants need cardiology input, and CRIM-negative infants may require immune tolerance induction to prevent antibody neutralisation.
det.prognosis: ERT has transformed infantile survival and stabilises or slows decline in many late-onset patients, though response varies. Respiratory failure remains the main cause of death in adults.
pearls: Respiratory failure out of proportion to limb weakness: test GAA.
Always measure supine as well as sitting FVC in a suspected myopathy.
Dried blood spot GAA is cheap and should precede biopsy.
det.thd: Pompe เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ GAA ในไลโซโซม ทำให้ไกลโคเจนสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อ ชนิดทารกมีกล้ามเนื้อปวกเปียกและหัวใจโต ชนิดผู้ใหญ่มีต้นขา/ลำตัวอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ และกะบังลมอ่อนแรงตั้งแต่ต้น (หายใจลำบากเมื่อนอนราบ ปวดหัวตอนเช้า) วินิจฉัยด้วย dried blood spot GAA และยีน GAA ตรวจ FVC ท่านั่งเทียบท่านอน รักษาด้วยเอนไซม์ทดแทนทุก 2 สัปดาห์ร่วมกับเครื่องช่วยหายใจกลางคืนเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Porphyria
formal: Heme biosynthesis enzyme disorder; acute porphyrias cause abdominal pain, neuropathy, seizures and psychosis; triggered by drugs, fasting and hormones.
simple: An inherited metabolic problem causing attacks of belly pain, nerve problems and confusion.
more: Diagnose acute attacks by raised urine porphobilinogen and delta-aminolevulinic acid, then confirm with enzymology or gene testing. Treat with IV hemin and glucose and avoid precipitants; the neuropathy is mainly motor axonal and mimics GBS.

name: Position-sensitive and -specific postural tremor
formal: Postural tremor appearing only in specific limb positions or tasks, such as primary writing tremor or position-specific tremor, related to essential tremor or dystonia.
simple: A tremor that occurs only when holding the arm or hand in a particular position.
nN: position sensitive and specific postural tremor

name: Positive myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus due to sudden muscle contraction, in contrast to negative myoclonus with brief lapse of muscle tone such as asterixis.
simple: A sudden brief jerk caused by a muscle contracting abruptly.

name: Post Lyme syndrome
formal: Persistent fatigue, pain and cognitive complaints after treated Lyme disease; not due to ongoing infection and no benefit from prolonged antibiotics.
simple: Lasting tiredness, aches and poor concentration that continue after Lyme disease has been treated.

name: Post pump chorea
formal: Choreoathetosis after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass in children, related to hypoxic-ischaemic injury of basal ganglia and cerebellum.
simple: Writhing movements in children after heart surgery using a bypass machine.

name: Post stroke movement disorders (PSMD)
formal: Hyperkinetic or hypokinetic movement disorders after stroke, including hemichorea-hemiballism, dystonia, tremor, myoclonus and parkinsonism, often from basal ganglia or thalamic infarcts or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal movements such as jerking, tremor or twisting that develop after a stroke.
more: MRI localises the lesion; treatment is tetrabenazine, antipsychotics, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin depending on type; many settle over months.

name: Post-anoxic action myoclonus
formal: Lance-Adams syndrome, intention myoclonus of limbs after hypoxic brain injury in survivors, responsive to valproate, levetiracetam or clonazepam.
simple: Jerking when trying to move, appearing in survivors of cardiac arrest or oxygen loss to the brain.

name: Post-anoxic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus after cardiac arrest: acute status myoclonus carries a poor prognosis, whereas chronic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams) occurs in survivors.
simple: Muscle jerks after the brain loses oxygen, for example after a cardiac arrest.

name: Post-concussion syndrome
formal: Persistent headache, dizziness, fatigue, cognitive and mood symptoms after mild traumatic brain injury beyond weeks to months; multifactorial.
simple: Headache, dizziness and poor concentration lasting for weeks or months after a mild head injury.

name: Post-dural puncture headache
formal: Orthostatic headache after lumbar puncture from CSF leak and intracranial hypotension; treated with fluids, caffeine, epidural blood patch.
simple: A headache that is worse sitting up and eases lying down, after a spinal tap.

name: Post-herpetic neuralgia
formal: Neuropathic pain persisting more than 3 months after herpes zoster rash, with allodynia; treated with gabapentinoids, tricyclics or lidocaine patches.
simple: Long-lasting nerve pain in the area where shingles occurred.

name: Post-infectious myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following infection, sometimes due to immune-mediated encephalitis such as opsoclonus-myoclonus or brainstem encephalitis.
simple: Muscle jerks that appear after an infection.

name: Post-intensive care syndrome
formal: New or worsened physical weakness, cognitive impairment and psychiatric problems after critical illness, including critical illness neuromyopathy.
simple: Weakness, memory problems and low mood that persist after a stay in intensive care.

name: Post-polio syndrome
formal: Late progressive weakness, fatigue and pain decades after poliomyelitis, from motor unit overuse and attrition of surviving motor neurons.
simple: New muscle weakness and tiredness appearing many years after recovery from polio.
more: Diagnosis needs a history of prior polio, new weakness after stable years and exclusion of other causes; EMG shows large reinnervated motor unit potentials. Management includes pacing, orthotics and ventilatory support; IVIG has not shown consistent benefit.
th: อ่อนแรงและล้าใหม่ในผู้ที่เคยเป็นโปลิโอเมื่อหลายสิบปีก่อน — เกิดหลังช่วงอาการคงที่ยาวนาน
tempoNote: Decades after acute polio (often 30+ years); slow, sometimes stepwise
feat: Childhood paralytic (or even non-paralytic) polio, then many years of stable function
New weakness and wasting — in old polio limbs and in limbs that seemed unaffected
Fatigue is the most disabling complaint; muscle and joint pain, cold intolerance
Sometimes new swallowing or breathing difficulty
Sensation and reflexes in unaffected limbs are normal
inv: EMG: chronic neurogenic change with large motor units, ± new denervation; normal sensory studies
Exclude mimics: radiculopathy, entrapment, ALS, myopathy, thyroid disease (MRI spine, bloods)
Respiratory function and sleep study if night-time symptoms

case.story: Had polio aged 3 with a weak right leg, worked normally for 50 years; over 2 years increasingly tired by afternoon, and now the left leg also gives way.
case.exam: Wasted right leg with absent knee jerk; mild new left quadriceps weakness, no fasciculation, normal sensation, no UMN signs.
case.tests: EMG: large-amplitude long-duration motor units in both legs with a few fibrillations; MRI lumbar spine shows only mild degeneration.
case.q: What must be excluded before calling this post-polio syndrome?
case.a: Other treatable causes of new weakness — compressive radiculopathy, entrapment, myopathy, thyroid disease — and ALS. PPS is a diagnosis of exclusion; management is paced rehabilitation and energy conservation.

ddx.pt: UMN signs and relentless spread; no remote polio with long stable interval
No history of polio; progression is faster and generalizes
Root pain, dermatomal sensory loss and imaging correlate

aN: pps | post poliomyelitis syndrome | late effects of polio

det.patho: After acute poliomyelitis, surviving motor neurons sprout extra terminal branches to adopt orphaned muscle fibres, creating giant motor units. Over decades these overstretched units cannot maintain all their terminals, so distal axonal branches drop out and new weakness appears. Normal ageing loss of motor neurons, overuse and possibly low-grade inflammation contribute. It affects a substantial proportion of polio survivors, mainly those who had paralytic disease.
det.clinical: After at least 15 years of neurological stability, patients notice new fatigue, slowly progressive weakness, muscle and joint pain, and reduced endurance. Weakness may also affect muscles that seemed spared, because subclinical denervation was widespread. Cold intolerance, sleep-disordered breathing, dysphagia and falls are common. Progression is slow, often with plateaus.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion based on a history of paralytic polio with partial recovery, a long stable period, and new weakness or fatigue lasting at least a year without another cause. EMG confirms chronic denervation with large motor units and normal sensory studies. Exclude radiculopathy, entrapment neuropathy, myopathy, thyroid disease, anaemia, depression, sleep apnoea and ALS. Respiratory function tests and polysomnography are needed if hypoventilation is suspected.
det.treatment: Management is rehabilitative: pacing activity, energy conservation, individually tailored non-fatiguing exercise, orthoses, mobility aids and weight control. Treat sleep-disordered breathing with nocturnal non-invasive ventilation and manage swallowing difficulties with speech therapy. IVIG has shown only modest effects and is not routine. Anaesthetists should be warned about respiratory weakness and sensitivity to sedatives.
det.prognosis: Decline is usually slow, and life expectancy is generally not shortened unless there is significant respiratory involvement.
pearls: PPS is not reactivation of the virus; it is late failure of oversized motor units.
Overwork worsens symptoms — pacing beats strengthening to exhaustion.
det.thd: Post-polio syndrome เกิดในผู้ที่เคยป่วยเป็นโปลิโอเมื่อหลายสิบปีก่อน เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการที่เหลือรอดต้องแตกแขนงไปเลี้ยงกล้ามเนื้อจำนวนมาก เมื่อเวลาผ่านไปจึงเสื่อมจนเกิดอ่อนแรงใหม่ อาการเด่นคืออ่อนล้า อ่อนแรงช้าๆ ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ และอาจหายใจหรือกลืนลำบาก การวินิจฉัยต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่นออกก่อน เช่น รากประสาทถูกกด หรือ ALS การรักษาเน้นฟื้นฟู ออกกำลังพอดี จัดสรรพลังงาน และใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจตอนกลางคืนเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Post-synaptic CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes with defects at the postsynaptic membrane, such as acetylcholine receptor or rapsyn mutations, causing fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited muscle weakness that worsens with activity, caused by a fault in how nerve signals are received by muscles.

name: Post-traumatic cervical dystonia
formal: Neck dystonia developing days to months after neck or head trauma, often with pain and sometimes a peripheral origin, with abnormal sustained head postures.
simple: A twisting or tilting of the head and neck that starts after an injury.
more: Treat with botulinum toxin injections and physiotherapy; many have persistent pain, and spontaneous improvement is less likely.

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD)
formal: Psychiatric disorder after trauma with intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood or cognition lasting beyond one month.
simple: A mental health condition after a frightening event with flashbacks, nightmares and feeling on edge.

name: Post-traumatic tics
formal: Tics appearing after head injury or other trauma, sometimes functional, with abrupt onset.
simple: Repeated sudden movements or sounds that start after an injury.

name: Post-traumatic tremor
formal: Rest, postural or kinetic tremor after head trauma, commonly from midbrain or cerebellar injury, including rubral tremor of Holmes.
simple: Shaking that starts after a head injury.

name: Postencephalic parkinsonism (PEP)
formal: Parkinsonism following encephalitis lethargica of 1916-1930s, with oculogyric crises and sleep disturbance, without Lewy bodies.
simple: Parkinson-like illness appearing after a brain infection called sleeping sickness.

name: Postencephalitic parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism following encephalitis lethargica, with oculogyric crises, behavioural changes and tau pathology without Lewy bodies.
simple: Parkinson-like illness appearing years after sleeping sickness encephalitis.
more: Historical complication of the 1918 influenza epidemic; MRI shows substantia nigra gliosis. Levodopa responses are often initially good with sensitivity to dyskinesias; now rare, with similar syndromes after other encephalitides.

name: Posterior circulation aneurysms
formal: Aneurysms of vertebral, basilar and posterior cerebral arteries, with subarachnoid haemorrhage or brainstem compression; higher rupture risk and technically difficult treatment.
simple: Bulges in blood vessels at the back of the brain that can bleed or press on the brainstem.

name: Posterior communicating (PCOM) artery aneurysms
formal: Aneurysms at the internal carotid-posterior communicating junction, commonly causing painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.
simple: A bulge in a brain artery that can press on a nerve to the eye, causing a droopy lid and large pupil.

name: Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (PION)
formal: Ischaemic optic neuropathy of the retrobulbar optic nerve with sudden visual loss and normal disc, after surgery, hypotension, anaemia or giant cell arteritis.
simple: Sudden vision loss from poor blood supply to the back part of the eye nerve, with a normal-looking eye exam.

name: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)
formal: Clinico-radiological syndrome with headache, seizures, visual loss and confusion, with posterior vasogenic oedema; triggered by hypertension, eclampsia or immunosuppressants.
simple: A brain swelling condition causing headache, seizures and vision loss, usually reversible when treated.
th: สมองบวมจากความดันสูงหรือยาบางชนิด — ปวดศีรษะ ตามัว ชัก ซึม มักหายได้ถ้ารักษาเร็ว
tempoNote: Hours to days
feat: Headache, visual disturbance (including cortical blindness), seizures and confusion
Triggers: severe hypertension, eclampsia, renal failure, calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy
Usually reversible with control of the trigger
inv: MRI FLAIR: symmetric parieto-occipital subcortical vasogenic oedema
BP, renal function, magnesium, drug levels

case.story: Severe headache, flashing lights then inability to see, followed by a generalised seizure.
case.exam: BP 190/115, proteinuria, pupils reactive but she cannot count fingers.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral occipital FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion.
case.q: Why do the pupils still react?
case.a: The visual loss is cortical (occipital oedema); the anterior visual pathway and pupillary reflex arc are intact.

ddx.pt: Venous filling defect on venography
Restricted diffusion in an arterial (often PCA) territory
Immunosuppressed, subacute progressive, asymmetric; not reversible with BP control

aN: pres | posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome | reversible posterior leukencephalopathy | rpls | hypertensive encephalopathy

det.patho: Failure of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction allow fluid to leak into the brain, producing vasogenic oedema with a posterior predominance, where sympathetic vascular innervation is sparser. Triggers include abrupt severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, renal failure, sepsis, autoimmune disease and drugs such as calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy and anti-VEGF agents. BP may be only modestly raised in drug-related cases.
det.clinical: Patients develop headache, altered awareness, visual disturbances ranging from blurring to cortical blindness, and seizures, which may become status epilepticus. Focal deficits are less common. Onset is over hours to days. Atypical forms involve the frontal lobes, brainstem, cerebellum or basal ganglia, and some cases bleed or develop restricted diffusion, which predicts permanent damage.
det.diagnosis: MRI FLAIR shows largely symmetric subcortical and cortical oedema in parieto-occipital regions, usually without restricted diffusion. Look for the trigger: BP, renal function, magnesium, drug levels, pregnancy status, and signs of sepsis. Exclude CVT with venography and consider infarction, encephalitis and PML when the course or imaging is unusual. Repeat imaging after treatment helps confirm reversibility.
det.treatment: Lower BP in a controlled way (roughly 20–25% in the first hours) with titratable IV agents, and treat seizures with standard antiseizure drugs. In eclampsia give magnesium sulfate and arrange delivery. Stop or reduce the culprit drug where possible. Correct fluid and electrolyte disturbances; long-term antiseizure treatment is usually unnecessary once the syndrome resolves.
det.prognosis: Clinical and radiological recovery within days to weeks is the rule; haemorrhage, extensive oedema or infarction carry a risk of lasting deficit.
pearls: Cortical blindness with brisk pupils = occipital pathology such as PRES.
Normotension does not exclude PRES in patients on tacrolimus or chemotherapy.
The name misleads: it is not always posterior and not always reversible.
det.thd: PRES คือสมองบวมแบบ vasogenic จากการที่หลอดเลือดสมองคุมความดันตัวเองไม่ได้ มักพบบริเวณสมองส่วนหลัง (parieto-occipital) สาเหตุคือความดันสูงเฉียบพลัน ครรภ์เป็นพิษ ไตวาย หรือยา เช่น tacrolimus และยาเคมีบำบัด อาการคือปวดศีรษะ ตามัวจนถึงตาบอดจากสมอง ชัก และซึม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI FLAIR และต้องแยก CVT รักษาโดยลดความดันอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป คุมชัก หยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ และให้ magnesium ในครรภ์เป็นพิษ ส่วนใหญ่หายได้

name: Posthemiplegic dystonia
formal: Delayed dystonia in the hemiplegic limbs after stroke or perinatal injury, from basal ganglia lesion.
simple: Twisting muscle posture in a weak arm or leg that develops months after a stroke or early brain injury.

name: Postpartum neuropathy
formal: Peripheral nerve injury after delivery, such as femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, peroneal or obstetric palsy of lumbosacral trunk.
simple: Nerve damage in the leg or pelvis after childbirth, causing numbness or weakness.

name: Postsynaptic disorders related to CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes from defects in acetylcholine receptor subunits or rapsyn, DOK7, MUSK, with slow-channel or fast-channel kinetics.
simple: Inherited forms of myasthenia where the receptor on the muscle side of the junction is faulty.
more: Genetic testing; treatment depends on type, such as pyridostigmine, 3,4-DAP or salbutamol, and quinidine for slow channel.

name: Postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS)
formal: Orthostatic intolerance with sustained heart rate rise of 30 bpm or more on standing without hypotension, causing palpitations, fatigue and presyncope.
simple: A condition where the heart races when standing up, causing dizziness and tiredness.
th: ชีพจรเร็วขึ้นมากเมื่อลุกยืน มีใจสั่น มึนงง เหนื่อยง่าย แต่ความดันไม่ตก — พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อย
tempoNote: Symptoms recur daily on standing; often begins after a viral illness, surgery or pregnancy and lasts months to years
feat: Light-headedness, palpitations, tremulousness and fatigue within minutes of standing, relieved by lying
Heart rate rise of 30 bpm or more (40 in teens) within 10 minutes upright, without orthostatic hypotension
Worse in heat, after meals, after exertion and around menstruation
Brain fog, headache, exercise intolerance; acrocyanosis of legs when standing
Common associations: joint hypermobility, deconditioning, post-COVID, migraine
inv: Active stand test or tilt table: HR and BP every minute for 10 minutes
ECG, thyroid function, CBC/ferritin, cortisol if suspected, medication review
Selected cases: QSART/sweat test and skin biopsy for small fibre neuropathy, plasma catecholamines

case.story: Since dengue fever 6 months ago, she feels her heart racing and her vision greying when standing on the ward; she must sit after 5 minutes. Hot days are worst.
case.exam: Supine HR 72, BP 108/70; after 8 minutes standing HR 128, BP 112/74; feet purple-blue.
case.tests: ECG sinus tachycardia only; TSH, Hb and ferritin normal.
case.q: What first-line measures would you offer?
case.a: Education, 2–3 L fluid and extra salt daily, compression garments, avoiding triggers and a graded recumbent-to-upright exercise programme; drugs such as propranolol (low dose), ivabradine, fludrocortisone or midodrine are added if needed.

det.patho: PoTS is a syndrome with several overlapping mechanisms rather than one disease. These include patchy sympathetic denervation of leg vessels causing venous pooling, low blood volume, excess sympathetic drive (hyperadrenergic form), deconditioning and possibly autoimmunity. It often follows infection, trauma or pregnancy and is several times more common in women aged 15–50.
det.clinical: Symptoms of orthostatic intolerance appear within minutes upright and settle lying down. Fatigue, sleep disturbance, nausea, bloating and cognitive slowing are frequent, and anxiety is a consequence more often than a cause. Fainting is less common than near-fainting. Red flags for another diagnosis include true syncope with injury, weight loss, abnormal neurological examination or orthostatic hypotension.
det.diagnosis: Criteria require a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 bpm (40 bpm age 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing or tilt, chronic symptoms for at least 3 months, and absence of orthostatic hypotension. Exclude dehydration, anaemia, hyperthyroidism, medications (diuretics, vasodilators, stimulant withdrawal), adrenal insufficiency, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and prolonged bed rest. A normal resting ECG and echo are usually enough cardiac work-up.
det.treatment: Non-drug measures come first: fluids, salt, waist-high compression, head-up sleeping, small meals and a structured exercise plan that starts with rowing, swimming or recumbent cycling. Drugs are chosen by phenotype: low-dose propranolol or ivabradine to slow the rate, fludrocortisone or desmopressin for volume, midodrine for pooling, pyridostigmine in some. Treat iron deficiency and coexisting migraine or sleep problems.
det.prognosis: Many improve substantially over 1–5 years, particularly young people with a post-viral onset, but a minority stay limited.
pearls: The key number is the heart-rate rise, not the absolute rate, and BP must not fall.
Do the 10-minute stand test in clinic — it costs nothing.
Exercise reconditioning starts horizontal and moves upright over weeks.
det.thd: PoTS คือภาวะที่ชีพจรเพิ่มขึ้นอย่างน้อย 30 ครั้ง/นาทีภายใน 10 นาทีหลังยืน โดยความดันไม่ตก ผู้ป่วยมีใจสั่น มึนงง เหนื่อยง่าย มักเป็นหญิงอายุน้อยและอาจเริ่มหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส วินิจฉัยด้วย active stand test หรือ tilt table และต้องตัดภาวะขาดน้ำ โลหิตจาง ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ การรักษาหลักคือดื่มน้ำ เพิ่มเกลือ ใส่ถุงน่องรัด และฝึกออกกำลังกายทีละขั้น อาจเสริมยาตามกลไก

ddx.pt: Sustained BP fall ≥20/10 on standing with little HR rise in neurogenic forms
Transient loss of consciousness with abrupt BP/HR drop rather than sustained tachycardia
Widespread failure: OH, pupils, sicca, gut dysmotility and high α3-AChR antibody

aN: pots | postural tachycardia syndrome | postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome | orthostatic intolerance

name: Postural tremor
formal: Tremor appearing when a limb is held against gravity, seen in essential tremor, enhanced physiological tremor and drug-induced states.
simple: Shaking that occurs when holding the arms out.

name: Postural tremor in Parkinson’s disease
formal: Re-emergent or postural tremor in Parkinson disease, often with latency after posture adoption, and less levodopa responsive than rest tremor.
simple: Shaking when holding the arms out in someone with Parkinson disease.

name: Potassium aggravated myotonias (PAM)
formal: Sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with myotonia triggered by potassium intake or worsened after exercise, with no weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle stiffness that is made worse by foods rich in potassium.
more: Subtypes are myotonia permanens and acetazolamide-responsive myotonia; treat with mexiletine and acetazolamide.

name: Pott’s disease
formal: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, kyphosis (gibbus), cold abscess and cord compression.
simple: Tuberculosis of the spine that destroys vertebrae and can press on the spinal cord.

name: Pregnancy chorea gravidarum
formal: Chorea arising during pregnancy, often in women with prior rheumatic chorea, lupus or antiphospholipid antibodies; usually resolves after delivery.
simple: Jerky movements that appear during pregnancy and usually go away after the baby is born.

name: Preorgasmic sex headache
formal: Dull bilateral headache increasing with sexual excitement, sometimes a muscle contraction type; excluded secondary causes.
simple: A dull headache that builds up with sexual arousal.

name: Presynaptic CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes with presynaptic defects such as choline acetyltransferase deficiency, causing episodic apnoea and fatigable weakness.
simple: Inherited muscle weakness caused by faulty release of the chemical messenger from nerves.

name: Presynaptic disorders related to CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes with defective acetylcholine synthesis or release, such as CHAT, SLC5A7 or choline transporter defects, with episodic apnoea.
simple: Inherited forms of myasthenia where the nerve ending releases too little signal chemical.
more: Genetic confirmation; pyridostigmine and 3,4-DAP help, avoiding apnoea episodes.

name: Primary (AL) amyloidosis
formal: Plasma cell dyscrasia producing light chain amyloid, affecting heart, kidneys, and nerves, with neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction, macroglossia, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: A blood-cell disorder where abnormal proteins build up in organs and nerves.
more: Diagnosed by biopsy and mass spectrometry; treatment is daratumumab-based chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation; heart involvement determines prognosis.
th: อะไมลอยด์จากสายเบา (AL) — ปวดแสบปวดร้อนปลายเท้า ระบบอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว carpal tunnel ลิ้นโต หัวใจ/ไตผิดปกติ
feat: Painful small-fibre, length-dependent neuropathy (burning feet, loss of pain and temperature)
Autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea, impotence
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome
Systemic clues: weight loss, macroglossia, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, periorbital purpura
inv: Serum/urine immunofixation and free light chains
Abdominal fat pad aspirate (safer, less sensitive) or targeted tissue biopsy with Congo red
Echocardiography, NT-proBNP, troponin, urine protein
TTR gene testing to exclude hereditary amyloid

case.story: Burning feet for a year, light-headed on standing, chronic diarrhoea; had bilateral carpal tunnel release last year.
case.exam: Pinprick and temperature lost over both feet while vibration is largely spared, BP drop 40 mmHg on standing, enlarged tongue.
case.tests: Lambda free light chains raised; fat pad biopsy: Congo red positive; echo: thick ventricular walls.
case.q: Why might routine nerve conduction studies be nearly normal early on?
case.a: The neuropathy begins in small fibres, which standard NCS does not measure; skin biopsy or autonomic testing is more sensitive.

ddx.pt: TTR variant, family history, no light chain abnormality
Diabetes, slower, no organ infiltration
Demyelinating motor-predominant neuropathy, sclerotic bone lesions, high VEGF

aN: al | primary amyloidosis | al amyloidosis | light chain amyloidosis | amyloid neuropathy al

det.patho: A clonal plasma-cell population secretes misfolded immunoglobulin light chains (lambda more often than kappa) that aggregate as amyloid fibrils in tissues. In nerves, deposits in the endoneurium, vessel walls and dorsal root ganglia cause axonal degeneration, with small myelinated and unmyelinated fibres affected first. Heart, kidney, liver, gut and soft tissue are frequently involved, and cardiac involvement largely determines survival.
det.clinical: A painful, length-dependent small-fibre neuropathy with burning feet, loss of pain and temperature sensation and early autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, diarrhoea or constipation, early satiety) is typical. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome may precede the diagnosis by years. Systemic features include fatigue, weight loss, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, hepatomegaly, macroglossia and periorbital bruising. Progression is faster than in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.
det.diagnosis: Screen with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains. Tissue confirmation by Congo red staining (fat pad aspirate, bone marrow, or affected organ) is required, and the amyloid type must be determined by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry to exclude transthyretin amyloid. Stage cardiac disease with NT-proBNP, troponin, echocardiography and cardiac MRI. Standard NCS may be normal early; skin biopsy and autonomic testing are more sensitive.
det.treatment: Haematological therapy aims at rapid, deep suppression of the light chain clone; daratumumab combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone is the current first-line standard, with autologous stem cell transplantation for selected fit patients. Bortezomib can worsen neuropathy, so neurological status needs close monitoring. Supportive care includes neuropathic pain treatment, midodrine or droxidopa and compression for orthostatic hypotension, and careful fluid management.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is driven by cardiac stage and haematological response; neuropathy improves slowly, if at all, even after a good response.
pearls: Painful small-fibre neuropathy + autonomic failure + weight loss in an older adult: think AL amyloid.
Always type the amyloid — treating TTR amyloid with chemotherapy is a serious error.
Prior bilateral carpal tunnel release is an important historical clue.
det.thd: AL amyloidosis เกิดจากเซลล์พลาสมาผิดปกติสร้าง light chain ที่พับตัวผิดรูปและสะสมเป็นอะไมลอยด์ในเส้นประสาทและอวัยวะต่างๆ ผู้ป่วยมีอาการปวดแสบร้อนปลายเท้า ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว เช่น ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ท้องเสีย มักมี carpal tunnel ทั้งสองข้าง และอาจมีหัวใจหรือไตผิดปกติ การวินิจฉัยต้องตรวจ free light chain, immunofixation และยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red พร้อมแยกจากชนิด TTR การรักษาคือยาที่กดเซลล์พลาสมา เช่น daratumumab ร่วมกับ bortezomib และสเตียรอยด์ และพยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับการเป็นโรคที่หัวใจ

name: Primary (idiopathic) hypersomnia
formal: Chronic daytime sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, sleep inertia and no cataplexy, without another cause; diagnosed after excluding narcolepsy and sleep apnoea.
simple: Constant excessive sleepiness and very long, unrefreshing sleep without a known cause.

name: Primary antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
formal: Autoimmune thrombophilia with antiphospholipid antibodies, causing venous and arterial thrombosis, stroke, livedo, and pregnancy loss; treated with anticoagulation.
simple: An autoimmune condition making the blood clot too easily, causing stroke and pregnancy loss.

name: Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC)
formal: Autoimmune chronic cholestatic liver disease with anti-mitochondrial antibodies, associated with sensory neuropathy, Sjogren and fatigue.
simple: A long-term autoimmune disease destroying liver bile ducts, sometimes linked with nerve and dry eye problems.
more: Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid; liver transplantation in advanced disease.

name: Primary bone tumours
formal: Tumours arising in bone such as osteosarcoma, chordoma and Ewing sarcoma, causing local pain and neural compression of cord or root.
simple: Cancers that begin in bone, which may press on nearby nerves or spinal cord.

name: Primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL)
formal: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma confined to CNS, with periventricular homogeneously enhancing lesions, steroid-sensitive; treated with high-dose methotrexate.
simple: A cancer of immune cells that starts in the brain, often shrinking dramatically with steroids.

name: Primary dystonia
formal: Dystonia without other neurological abnormality or structural cause, often genetic such as DYT1, with sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures.
simple: Twisting and abnormal postures from overactive muscles, with no other cause found.

name: Primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 1 (HypoKPP 1)
formal: Autosomal dominant periodic paralysis from CACNA1S mutations causing flaccid attacks with low potassium, triggered by carbohydrate or rest after exertion.
simple: An inherited condition with attacks of muscle weakness linked to low potassium, from a calcium channel gene change.
more: Treat with potassium and acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide; avoid high carbohydrate meals; late fixed myopathy can occur.
nN: primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 1 hypokpp 1
aN: hypokpp 1 | primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 1

name: Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS)
formal: Pure upper motor neuron degeneration with progressive spasticity, pseudobulbar signs and no lower motor neuron findings for at least 3 years; slower than ALS.
simple: A slowly progressing disease causing stiffness and weakness through loss of upper motor neurons.

name: Primary mitochondrial diseases
formal: Disorders from mutations of mitochondrial or nuclear genes causing oxidative phosphorylation failure, such as MELAS, MERRF, Leigh and Kearns-Sayre syndromes.
simple: Inherited illnesses in which the cell's energy factories do not work, affecting the brain and muscles.

name: Primary optic nerve sheath meningiomas
formal: Meningioma of the optic nerve sheath causing slowly progressive painless vision loss, optic atrophy and optociliary shunt vessels; imaging shows tram-track sign.
simple: A slow-growing tumour around the eye nerve causing gradual vision loss.

name: Primary paroxysmal dyskinesia/ primary paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
formal: Idiopathic episodic dystonia or chorea triggered by sudden movement, PRRT2-related, responsive to low-dose carbamazepine.
simple: Short attacks of abnormal movements triggered by sudden movement, which respond well to a seizure medicine.
nN: primary paroxysmal dyskinesia primary paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia

name: Primary paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia
formal: Idiopathic dystonic attacks triggered by prolonged exercise lasting up to an hour, often due to GLUT1 deficiency.
simple: Attacks of muscle twisting brought on by long physical exercise.

name: Primary paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dystonic dyskinesia
formal: Idiopathic attacks of dystonia and chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine or stress, from PNKD gene mutation.
simple: Longer episodes of twisting movements triggered by alcohol, caffeine or stress.
nN: primary paroxysmal non kinesigenic dystonic dyskinesia

name: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA)
formal: Neurodegenerative language disorder with isolated progressive aphasia for at least two years; non-fluent, semantic and logopenic variants (the last often Alzheimer pathology).
simple: A condition where language ability slowly worsens while other mental abilities are preserved at first.
more: Diagnosis by Gorno-Tempini criteria with MRI patterns: left frontal insula in nonfluent, anterior temporal in semantic, and left posterior temporal and parietal in logopenic. Check CSF amyloid or amyloid PET for logopenic type.

name: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
formal: MS with steadily worsening disability from onset without relapses, typically a progressive myelopathy in older adults; ocrelizumab is licensed.
simple: A type of multiple sclerosis that gets steadily worse from the start, without relapses.

name: Primary spinal cord tumours
formal: Intradural intramedullary tumours such as ependymoma and astrocytoma, or extramedullary tumours like meningioma and schwannoma, causing myelopathy and radicular pain.
simple: Tumours that start in or around the spinal cord and cause pain, weakness and numbness.

name: Primary vasculitis
formal: Idiopathic inflammation of blood vessel walls, including giant cell arteritis, PAN and ANCA-associated vasculitis, with CNS or PNS involvement.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels that starts without another disease, and can harm nerves and brain.

name: Primitive neuroepithelial tumours (PNET)
formal: Embryonal small blue cell tumours of CNS, now classified under embryonal tumours, occurring in supratentorial brain or pineal region; aggressive in children.
simple: Aggressive tumours of immature nerve cells, mainly in children.

name: Prion disease
formal: Fatal neurodegenerative disorder caused by misfolded prion protein, including sporadic CJD, familial, variant and kuru, with rapid dementia, myoclonus and spongiform change.
simple: A rare, fast, fatal brain illness caused by abnormally folded proteins, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

name: Prodromal multiple sclerosis
formal: Early nonspecific symptoms such as pain, fatigue and mood or bladder disorders preceding clinical onset of MS, with increased healthcare use.
simple: Early vague symptoms that appear years before multiple sclerosis is diagnosed.

name: Progressive ataxia palatal tremor (PAPT)
formal: Sporadic or genetic progressive cerebellar ataxia with palatal tremor, without olivary hypertrophy, sometimes in Alexander disease or POLG.
simple: A slowly worsening balance disorder together with rhythmic palate movements.

name: Progressive ataxias
formal: Chronic cerebellar ataxias such as spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia, MSA-C and acquired causes with gradually worsening gait and coordination.
simple: Illnesses that cause increasing unsteadiness and clumsiness over time.

name: Progressive bulbar palsy (PBP)
formal: Motor neuron disease variant with lower motor neuron bulbar onset causing dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue wasting with fasciculation.
simple: A form of motor neuron disease starting with speech and swallowing difficulty.

name: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity
formal: Brainstem and spinal inflammatory disease with stiffness, spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia, associated with glycine receptor antibodies; stiff-person spectrum.
simple: A rare immune illness causing muscle stiffness, spasms and brainstem problems.

name: Progressive epilepsies
formal: Epilepsies with progressive neurological deterioration, including progressive myoclonic epilepsies and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, with myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and dementia.
simple: Seizure disorders in which the brain function gets worse with time, with jerks, seizures and loss of skills.
more: Diagnosed by EEG, MRI, enzyme and genetic tests. Valproate, levetiracetam, zonisamide and clonazepam control seizures but prognosis often poor.

name: Progressive epilepsy with mental retardation (EPMR)
formal: Northern epilepsy, autosomal recessive neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis CLN8 in Finland, with seizures from age 5-10 and slow cognitive decline.
simple: An inherited childhood seizure illness found in Finland, with slow decline in learning ability.
nN: progressive epilepsy with mental retardation epmr
aN: epmr | progressive epilepsy with mental retardation

name: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia
formal: Slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoparesis, mostly mitochondrial DNA deletions or POLG, sometimes with myopathy; part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome.
simple: Slowly worsening weakness of eye muscles with drooping eyelids, usually from a mitochondrial problem.
more: Muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibres and COX-negative fibres, and long-range PCR detects single large deletions in muscle DNA; CK is normal or mildly raised. Treatment is supportive, with ptosis surgery or crutches and cardiac monitoring for conduction block.

name: Progressive hemifacial atrophy
formal: Slowly progressive unilateral facial hemiatrophy of skin, fat, muscle and bone, often starting in youth; linked to localized scleroderma (Parry-Romberg), may accompany seizures or migraine.
simple: One side of the face slowly shrinks and thins over years, sometimes with headaches or seizures.

name: Progressive ischaemic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke with stepwise or gradual worsening of deficits over hours to days, from thrombus propagation, haemodynamic failure or small penetrating artery disease such as capsular warning syndrome.
simple: A stroke whose weakness or other problems keep getting worse over hours or days instead of staying stable.

name: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)
formal: Demyelinating infection of oligodendrocytes by reactivated JC polyomavirus in immunosuppressed patients (HIV, natalizumab); causes subacute multifocal deficits and non-enhancing white matter lesions.
simple: A brain infection from a common virus that wakes up when the immune system is weak, damaging the brain's wiring and causing slowly worsening problems.

name: Progressive muscular atrophy (PMA)
formal: Pure lower motor neuron form of motor neuron disease with progressive asymmetric weakness, wasting and fasciculations without upper motor neuron signs; some later develop ALS.
simple: A disease where the nerve cells controlling muscles slowly die, causing weakness, muscle shrinking and twitching.
more: Diagnose by EMG showing widespread denervation with normal sensory conduction and no conduction block; riluzole is used as in ALS. Survival tends to be longer than classical ALS; exclude multifocal motor neuropathy.
th: โรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการเสื่อมเฉพาะส่วนล่าง (LMN) — อ่อนแรง ลีบ กล้ามเนื้อเต้น ไม่มี UMN signs
feat: Progressive asymmetric weakness, wasting and fasciculations; reflexes reduced or absent
No upper motor neuron signs at presentation (some develop them later and become ALS)
Sensation normal
inv: EMG: widespread active and chronic denervation; normal sensory nerve studies; no conduction block
Exclude treatable mimics: MMN (anti-GM1, conduction block), Kennedy disease (AR repeat), SMA (SMN1), paraprotein, lead

case.story: One year of a weak left hand, then both arms; cramps and twitching.
case.exam: Asymmetric distal > proximal arm wasting with fasciculations, absent arm reflexes, no Hoffmann or Babinski, normal sensation.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in three regions; no conduction block; anti-GM1 negative; AR gene normal.
case.q: Why keep re-examining for UMN signs?
case.a: A proportion of PMA evolves into ALS; finding UMN signs changes prognosis and trial eligibility.

ddx.pt: UMN signs present
Weakness follows named nerves; motor conduction block; IVIG response
Gynaecomastia, perioral fasciculation, sensory neuropathy; AR CAG expansion

aN: pma | progressive muscular atrophy | lower motor neuron als | progressive spinal muscular atrophy adult

det.patho: PMA is a motor neuron disease that clinically involves only lower motor neurons. Autopsy and imaging studies show that many patients have subclinical corticospinal tract involvement and TDP-43 pathology identical to ALS, so PMA is now viewed as part of the ALS spectrum. It accounts for a small minority of adult-onset MND and is more common in men.
det.clinical: Asymmetric distal or proximal limb weakness with wasting, fasciculations and cramps spreads over months to years to other regions. Reflexes are reduced or absent and there are no UMN signs, at least initially. A proportion develop UMN signs within a few years and are reclassified as ALS. Bulbar and respiratory involvement occurs later in the course.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows active and chronic denervation in multiple regions with normal sensory studies and no conduction block. A careful search for treatable or distinct mimics is essential: MMN, Kennedy disease, adult SMA, hexosaminidase A deficiency, paraproteinaemic and lead neuropathy, and inclusion body myositis. Under the Gold Coast criteria, progressive LMN dysfunction in two regions can qualify as ALS.
det.treatment: Management follows ALS principles, including riluzole, multidisciplinary care, nutritional support, physiotherapy and planning for respiratory support. Patients should be offered clinical trial participation where available.
det.prognosis: Survival is often longer than in classic ALS, though it varies widely; early respiratory involvement predicts a poor outcome.
pearls: Keep re-examining for UMN signs — PMA often evolves into ALS.
Exclude MMN and Kennedy disease before labelling a pure LMN syndrome.

name: Progressive myoclonic ataxia
formal: Syndrome of action myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia and often infrequent seizures with preserved cognition (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), due to mitochondrial, storage or degenerative causes.
simple: A condition with sudden muscle jerks and poor balance and coordination that slowly worsen, usually with mostly normal thinking.

name: Progressive myoclonic ataxia associated with coeliac disease
formal: Progressive action myoclonus and ataxia occurring in the setting of coeliac disease, with gluten-related immune injury to the cerebellum; may be associated with refractory coeliac disease and cortical myoclonus.
simple: Muscle jerks and unsteadiness that slowly get worse in someone with coeliac disease, a gluten-triggered immune condition.
nN: progressive myoclonic ataxia associated with celiac disease

name: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies
formal: Group of genetic disorders (Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF, NCLs, sialidosis) combining myoclonus, generalized seizures and progressive neurological decline, often with ataxia and dementia.
simple: A group of inherited illnesses with muscle jerks, seizures and a slow loss of abilities over time.

name: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy (PME)
formal: Heterogeneous inherited syndrome of stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures and progressive cerebellar and cognitive deterioration, with a slow-wave EEG background and often polyspike discharges.
simple: An inherited condition with muscle jerks, seizures and gradual decline in movement and thinking.

name: Progressive myoclonus
formal: Persistent, worsening myoclonic jerks, typically cortical or reticular, within a progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disease.
simple: Sudden shock-like muscle jerks that become more frequent and disabling over time because of an underlying brain disease.

name: Progressive myoclonus epilepsy (progressive myoclonic encephalopathy)
formal: Inherited syndrome combining myoclonus, seizures and relentless neurological deterioration, caused by storage, mitochondrial or neurodegenerative diseases; onset usually in childhood or adolescence.
simple: An inherited disease causing muscle jerks and seizures along with steady worsening of brain function, usually starting in childhood or teenage years.
nN: progressive myoclonus epilepsy progressive myoclonic encephalopathy
aN: progressive myoclonic encephalopathy | progressive myoclonus epilepsy

name: Progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia
formal: Overlapping syndromes of action myoclonus with generalized seizures and cerebellar ataxia, seen in Unverricht-Lundborg disease, MERRF and related disorders.
simple: Conditions with jerks, seizures and balance problems that gradually worsen over time.
nN: progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia

name: Progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA)
formal: Variant of frontotemporal dementia with effortful, agrammatic speech and apraxia of speech, caused by degeneration of left inferior frontal and insular regions, often tau-related.
simple: A kind of dementia where speaking becomes slow, halting and full of grammar mistakes while understanding stays fairly good.

name: Progressive solitary sclerosis
formal: Rare progressive multiple sclerosis variant presenting with a single large demyelinating lesion, typically in the spinal cord or brainstem, causing steadily worsening disability.
simple: A rare form of multiple sclerosis where one main area of damage causes slowly worsening problems.

name: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP
formal: 4R tauopathy with early postural instability and falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity and frontal cognitive change; midbrain atrophy gives the hummingbird sign.
simple: A brain disease causing early falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.
th: โรคเสื่อมของสมองส่วนลึก — ล้มไปข้างหลังบ่อยตั้งแต่ต้น กลอกตาขึ้นลงไม่ได้ คอแข็ง ยาพาร์กินสันไม่ค่อยได้ผล
feat: Unexplained backward falls in the first year
Slow vertical saccades then vertical (down) gaze palsy; oculocephalic reflex preserved
Axial more than limb rigidity, upright posture, 'surprised' stare
Frontal dysexecutive syndrome, pseudobulbar dysarthria
inv: MRI: midbrain atrophy ('hummingbird' sign), reduced midbrain/pons ratio

case.story: Several unexplained backward falls; difficulty looking down at her plate and stairs.
case.exam: Slow vertical saccades with limited downgaze that overcomes on doll's-eye manoeuvre, axial rigidity, applause sign.
case.tests: MRI: midbrain tegmental atrophy.
case.q: What does preserved doll's-eye movement tell you?
case.a: The gaze palsy is supranuclear — the brainstem ocular motor nuclei and pathways from the vestibular system are intact.

ddx.pt: Asymmetric rest tremor, good levodopa response, falls late
Autonomic failure and cerebellar signs; hot cross bun sign
Asymmetric limb apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss

aN: psp | steele richardson olszewski syndrome | richardson syndrome

det.patho: PSP is a four-repeat tauopathy in which tau aggregates as tufted astrocytes, neurofibrillary tangles and coiled bodies in the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, midbrain and dentate nucleus. Loss of midbrain gaze centres (the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF) explains the vertical saccade failure. It is mostly sporadic, with MAPT H1 haplotype as a risk factor, and onset is usually after 60.
det.clinical: The classic Richardson phenotype brings backward falls within the first year, slowed then restricted vertical saccades, axial rigidity with an extended neck, a staring wide-eyed face and frontal dysexecutive change with apathy. Speech becomes slurred and spastic, swallowing worsens and patients may rush to stand impulsively (rocket sign). Other phenotypes present predominantly with parkinsonism (PSP-P, can respond partly to levodopa early), progressive gait freezing, speech/language disorder or a corticobasal syndrome. Examiners like to ask about the applause sign, preserved doll's-eye responses and the square-wave jerks seen on fixation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 MDS criteria combine four domains — ocular motor, postural instability, akinesia and cognitive dysfunction — at levels of certainty from suggestive to probable. Look carefully at the speed of vertical saccades before range becomes limited; slow downward saccades are an early and specific clue. MRI showing midbrain atrophy with relative pontine preservation (hummingbird or morning-glory appearance, low midbrain-to-pons ratio, raised MR parkinsonism index) supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT is abnormal and does not separate PSP from PD. Exclude mimics such as Niemann–Pick type C, Whipple disease, vascular parkinsonism and normal pressure hydrocephalus.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists; anti-tau antibodies have failed in trials. A levodopa trial (up to around 1 g/day) is reasonable, though benefit is small and brief. Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy and walking aids for falls, speech and swallow assessment with diet modification, prism glasses or reading aids, botulinum toxin for blepharospasm or apraxia of lid opening, and early advance care planning around feeding and aspiration.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 6–8 years from onset, with aspiration pneumonia and fall-related injury the usual causes of death.
pearls: Ask 'Does he fall backwards?' — early backward falls in a new parkinsonian patient point to PSP, not PD.
Vertical saccades slow down before their range shrinks — test speed, not only range.
Preserved oculocephalic movements prove the gaze palsy is supranuclear.
