name: Spinocerebellar degenerations
formal: Group of hereditary or sporadic degenerations of cerebellum and spinal tracts with progressive ataxia.
simple: Diseases where parts of the brain and spinal cord gradually degenerate, leading to unsteadiness.

name: Spirochete infection
formal: Neurological infection by spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum or Borrelia burgdorferi, causing meningitis, cranial neuropathy and neurosyphilis or neuroborreliosis.
simple: Infection with spiral-shaped bacteria such as those causing syphilis or Lyme disease, which can harm the nervous system.

name: Split hand syndrome
formal: Selective wasting of abductor pollicis brevis and first dorsal interosseous with preserved hypothenar muscles, typical for ALS.
simple: Wasting of the thumb-side hand muscles but not the little-finger side, typical in motor neuron disease.

name: Spondylodiscitis
formal: Infection of intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebrae with back pain and fever, risk of epidural abscess.
simple: Infection of the spine disc and bone causing back pain.

name: Spontaneous oro-facial chorea
formal: Chorea of mouth and face in the elderly without drug exposure, similar to edentulous dyskinesia.
simple: Involuntary mouth and face movements in older people without a clear cause.

name: Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (sCJD)
formal: Rapidly progressive prion disease with dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, cortical ribboning on DWI, periodic sharp waves and positive RT-QuIC.
simple: A rapidly progressing brain disease from abnormal proteins, causing quick loss of memory and movement control.

name: Sporadic hyperekplexia
formal: Exaggerated startle with stiffness and falls without GLRA1 mutation, may be symptomatic of brainstem lesions.
simple: An excessive startle reaction with stiffness and falls but no known gene cause.

name: Sporadic myopathy
formal: Muscle disease occurring without family history, such as sporadic inclusion body myositis or acquired inflammatory, toxic or endocrine myopathies, with proximal or distal weakness.
simple: Muscle weakness that appears without a family history and has an acquired cause.
more: Evaluate with CK, EMG, MRI and muscle biopsy. Treat the underlying cause; inclusion body myositis responds poorly to immunotherapy.

name: Sporadic prion disease
formal: Prion protein misfolding disease arising without mutation or exposure, mainly sporadic CJD.
simple: A brain disease from abnormal proteins that arises spontaneously, causing rapid dementia.

name: Sports concussion
formal: Mild traumatic brain injury in sport causing transient headache, confusion, amnesia and imbalance; repeated injury linked to chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
simple: A brain injury from a knock during sport that causes headache, confusion and memory problems.

name: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
formal: Malignancy of squamous epithelium whose head and neck forms spread perineurally to cranial nerves or metastasise to brain.
simple: A skin or mouth cancer that can spread along nerves to the brain.

name: St Louis encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus in the Americas causing fever, headache, confusion and SIADH, especially in the elderly.
simple: A mosquito-spread viral brain infection, most serious in older people.

name: Stabbing headache
formal: Primary stabbing headache with brief ice-pick pain in the head, lasting seconds, often in migraineurs.
simple: Very brief, sharp jabs of head pain like an ice pick.

name: Stargardt disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ABCA4 macular dystrophy with central visual loss in youth and yellow flecks.
simple: An inherited eye disease that causes loss of central vision in young people.

name: Startle epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy with seizures precipitated by sudden unexpected stimuli, typically in children with hemiplegia or brain damage.
simple: Seizures set off by a sudden noise or touch.

name: Statin myopathy
formal: Muscle toxicity from statins ranging from myalgia to necrotising immune-mediated myopathy with HMGCR antibodies and raised CK.
simple: Muscle pain or weakness caused by cholesterol-lowering statin medicines.
th: ปวดหรืออ่อนแรงกล้ามเนื้อจากยาลดไขมันกลุ่ม statin — ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดยา ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้นึกถึง anti-HMGCR myopathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months after starting or raising the dose; toxic form settles within weeks of stopping
feat: Aching, cramps or heaviness in thighs and calves, often symmetric
Spectrum: myalgia with normal CK → mild CK rise → true weakness → rarely rhabdomyolysis
Risk rises with high-intensity statin, CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles), fibrates, hypothyroidism, renal impairment, older age
Toxic form improves after withdrawal; persisting or worsening weakness with very high CK suggests immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
inv: CK at baseline and when symptomatic; TSH, renal and liver function
Anti-HMGCR antibody if weakness or high CK persists beyond 6–12 weeks off the drug
EMG/MRI thigh and muscle biopsy for persistent or atypical cases

case.who: 66-year-old man with diabetes and coronary stents
case.story: Atorvastatin was raised to 80 mg; a month later clarithromycin was added for pneumonia. He now has aching thighs and struggles to climb onto a songthaew.
case.exam: Mild symmetric hip flexor weakness, tender thighs, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: CK 4,800 U/L, TSH normal, creatinine slightly raised; urine dipstick heme negative.
case.q: What is the next step, and when would you test for anti-HMGCR?
case.a: Stop the statin and the interacting antibiotic, hydrate and follow CK. If weakness or CK fails to settle after about 2–3 months off the statin, check anti-HMGCR for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

det.patho: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, lowering not only cholesterol but also downstream products such as ubiquinone and prenylated proteins that muscle needs for energy and membrane repair. Toxicity is dose-related and amplified by high blood levels from drug interactions or a SLCO1B1 transporter variant. A separate, much rarer entity is an autoimmune necrotizing myopathy in which antibodies target HMG-CoA reductase itself and the disease continues after the drug is gone.
det.clinical: Most patients describe muscle aches without weakness and with normal or near-normal CK; true myopathy with proximal weakness is less common, and rhabdomyolysis is rare. Symptoms usually begin within the first months or after a dose increase or new interacting drug. Nocebo effects are frequent, so symptoms that vanish on rechallenge with placebo are well documented. Red flags are objective weakness, dark urine, CK above ten times normal, and progression after stopping.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on timing, CK and response to withdrawal. Check thyroid, renal and liver function, vitamin D and interacting drugs. If symptoms and CK resolve within weeks, the toxic form is likely. Persisting proximal weakness with high CK after withdrawal calls for anti-HMGCR serology, EMG (irritable myopathic pattern), MRI for oedema and a biopsy showing scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the statin and correct contributing factors. After recovery, options include a lower dose, a hydrophilic statin such as rosuvastatin or pravastatin, alternate-day dosing, or non-statin agents (ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid). Coenzyme Q10 has weak evidence. Anti-HMGCR myopathy needs immunotherapy—typically IVIG with steroids and a steroid-sparing agent—and permanent statin avoidance.
det.prognosis: Toxic myopathy recovers fully in nearly all patients within weeks to a few months. Anti-HMGCR myopathy is chronic and often needs long-term immunotherapy.
pearls: Normal CK with aches is usually not dangerous myopathy; weakness plus high CK is.
Getting worse after the statin is stopped is the clue to anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy.
Look for the interacting drug: macrolides, azole antifungals, gemfibrozil, ciclosporin, amiodarone.
det.thd: Statin ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อปวดหรืออ่อนแรงได้ โดยเฉพาะขนาดสูงหรือใช้ร่วมกับยาที่ยับยั้ง CYP3A4 ส่วนใหญ่ CK ปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อยและหายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์หลังหยุดยา หากอ่อนแรงต่อเนื่องและ CK สูงมากแม้หยุดยาแล้ว ต้องตรวจ anti-HMGCR เพราะอาจเป็น immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy ซึ่งต้องรักษาด้วยยากดภูมิ

Slow relaxation of reflexes, cold intolerance; raised TSH (also a statin risk factor)
No drug link; inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy and often other autoimmune features

name: Statokinetic dissociation
formal: Preservation of moving-object perception with failure to see static objects in a blind field, as in Riddoch phenomenon.
simple: Being able to see moving objects but not still ones in a blind part of vision.

name: Status cataplecticus
formal: Prolonged continuous cataplexy episodes in narcolepsy, usually after sudden stopping of antidepressants.
simple: Long periods of sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions in narcolepsy.

name: Status dysmyelinisatus
formal: Historic term for severe pallidal or striatal myelination abnormality with marbled appearance leading to athetosis.
simple: An old term for abnormal brain wiring in the basal ganglia, causing writhing movements.

name: Status dystonicus
formal: Life-threatening severe generalised dystonia with rhabdomyolysis and respiratory risk, needing ICU management.
simple: A severe, long-lasting episode of twisting spasms that can be life-threatening.

name: Status epilepticus
formal: Seizure lasting over 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery, a neurological emergency needing benzodiazepines and antiepileptics.
simple: A seizure that will not stop, or repeated seizures without waking, needing emergency treatment.
th: ชักต่อเนื่องเกิน 5 นาทีหรือชักซ้ำโดยไม่ฟื้น — ภาวะฉุกเฉิน ต้องให้ยาตามลำดับเวลา
tempoNote: Treat at 5 minutes; neuronal injury risk after ~30 minutes
feat: Continuous seizure ≥5 min or repeated seizures without recovery
Non-convulsive status may present as unexplained coma or confusion
Causes: antiseizure drug withdrawal, stroke, infection, metabolic, autoimmune encephalitis
inv: Glucose immediately; electrolytes, Ca/Mg, drug levels, toxicology
Continuous EEG if not waking up
CT/MRI and LP when cause unclear

case.story: Ran out of medication 3 days ago; convulsing for 10 minutes on arrival.
case.exam: Generalised tonic-clonic activity, SpO2 88%.
case.tests: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L.
case.q: Outline the first two drug steps.
case.a: IV benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam/diazepam, or IM midazolam if no access), then a second-line IV agent such as levetiracetam, valproate or fos/phenytoin; anaesthetic agents if refractory.

ddx.pt: Prolonged events with eyes closed, pelvic thrusting, normal lactate/EEG
Posturing in coma from brainstem compromise, no EEG seizure activity

aN: se | convulsive status | status epilepticus | gcse

det.patho: Status occurs when seizure-terminating mechanisms fail or seizure-sustaining mechanisms take over: GABA-A receptors are internalised while NMDA and AMPA receptors move to the synapse, so benzodiazepines lose potency the longer the seizure lasts. Prolonged seizures lead to excitotoxic neuronal injury, systemic hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and cardiorespiratory compromise. Time point t1 (5 minutes) marks when to treat and t2 (around 30 minutes) when lasting damage becomes likely.
det.clinical: Convulsive status is obvious, but subtle motor signs (eyelid or facial twitching) may be all that remain later. Non-convulsive status presents as confusion, behavioural change, aphasia or coma and is common in ICU and elderly patients. Common triggers include low antiseizure drug levels, alcohol withdrawal, stroke, CNS infection, metabolic derangement, toxins and autoimmune encephalitis. Refractory status persists despite benzodiazepine and a second-line drug; super-refractory status continues 24 hours after anaesthesia. NORSE describes new-onset refractory status in a previously healthy person.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of convulsive status is clinical; check capillary glucose at once. Send electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function, CK, blood gas, drug levels, toxicology and pregnancy test where relevant. Arrange urgent CT and, as indicated, MRI and lumbar puncture. Start continuous EEG if the patient does not wake within the expected time after convulsions stop, to detect non-convulsive status. Dissociative seizures, rigors and posturing in coma are key mimics.
det.treatment: Secure airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen, and correct hypoglycaemia; give IV thiamine before glucose if alcohol misuse or malnutrition is possible. At 5 minutes give a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam or diazepam, or IM midazolam/buccal midazolam pre-hospital), repeating once if needed. If seizures continue, load a second-line IV drug — levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin/phenytoin are similarly effective. Refractory status requires intubation and anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol or thiopental) titrated to EEG; treat the underlying cause in parallel, including immunotherapy for suspected autoimmune aetiology.
det.prognosis: Mortality is around 10–20% overall and higher in older patients, with acute symptomatic causes and refractory status; drug withdrawal-related status in known epilepsy has a better outlook.
pearls: Under-dosing benzodiazepines is the commonest treatment error — give a full dose early.
A patient who is not waking after convulsions stop may still be seizing: get an EEG.
Check glucose first and give thiamine where malnutrition or alcohol is possible.

name: Status marmoratus
formal: Perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury with marbled gliosis, leading to dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
simple: Brain injury around birth causing marbled scarring in deep brain areas and later movement problems.

name: Steal syndromes
formal: Haemodynamic diversion of blood from a vascular bed, e.g. subclavian steal causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
simple: Conditions where blood is diverted away from the brain or arm because of a narrowed artery.

name: Steele–Richardson–Olszewski disease
formal: Progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy, early falls and axial rigidity.
simple: A brain disease causing falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.
more: Pathology shows neurofibrillary tangles and tufted astrocytes in the midbrain and basal ganglia; levodopa response is poor. Treatment is supportive, with botulinum toxin for dystonia and swallowing assessment.

name: Steele–Richardson–Olszewski syndrome
formal: Progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy, early falls and axial rigidity.
simple: A brain disease causing falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.

name: Stereotypy
formal: Repetitive purposeless coordinated movements that are patterned, seen in autism, tardive syndromes and neurodegeneration.
simple: Repeated, patterned movements such as rocking or hand flapping.

name: Steroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness from chronic glucocorticoid excess with normal CK and type 2 fibre atrophy.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and shoulders caused by long-term steroid use.
more: CK is normal and EMG is usually normal, with biopsy showing type 2 fibre atrophy without inflammation; MRI is unremarkable. Treat by reducing or switching steroids, using a fluorinated-steroid-free regimen and exercise, with improvement over weeks to months.
th: กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงจากการใช้ steroid นาน ๆ — CK ปกติ
tempoNote: Chronic form develops over weeks to months of treatment; an acute form occurs with high-dose IV steroids in ICU
feat: Painless proximal weakness, legs before arms: trouble rising from chairs and climbing stairs
Cushingoid features: moon face, central obesity, skin thinning
Normal CK, normal sensation and reflexes
Higher risk with fluorinated steroids (dexamethasone) and doses above about 30 mg/day prednisolone
Acute ICU form (critical illness myopathy) with high-dose steroids ± neuromuscular blockers
inv: CK (normal) — helps separate from active myositis
EMG often normal or mildly myopathic without spontaneous activity
Muscle biopsy (rarely needed): type 2b fibre atrophy
Check potassium, thyroid, and vitamin D

case.story: CK fell from 6,000 to normal on prednisolone 60 mg daily for 3 months, but she now struggles more to stand from a squat.
case.exam: Cushingoid face, symmetric hip flexor weakness, no muscle tenderness, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 90 U/L; EMG without fibrillations; MRI thigh shows no oedema, only fatty atrophy.
case.q: Is her myositis relapsing, or is this steroid myopathy, and what should be done?
case.a: Normal CK, no fibrillations and no MRI oedema favour steroid myopathy; taper prednisolone while adding a steroid-sparing agent, and encourage resistance exercise.

det.patho: Glucocorticoids increase muscle protein breakdown through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway and reduce protein synthesis by inhibiting IGF-1 and mTOR signalling. Fast-twitch type 2 fibres are most affected, so atrophy rather than necrosis is the result. Fluorinated compounds carry the highest risk.
det.clinical: The chronic form develops gradually with proximal leg weakness, often accompanied by other steroid side effects. It is easy to confuse with a relapse of the condition being treated, especially myositis or myasthenia. The acute form arises within days of very high doses, often in ICU with sepsis, and can include rhabdomyolysis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by normal CK and a quiet EMG. In treated myositis, the absence of fibrillations and of MRI muscle oedema helps distinguish steroid myopathy from active inflammation; a trial of dose reduction is often decisive. Exclude hypokalaemia, thyroid dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency.
det.treatment: Reduce the steroid dose to the lowest effective level, switch to non-fluorinated agents, or use alternate-day dosing and steroid-sparing drugs. Resistance and aerobic exercise counteract atrophy. Ensure adequate protein intake and treat coexisting metabolic issues.
det.prognosis: Strength usually recovers over weeks to months after dose reduction.
pearls: Treated myositis getting weaker with normal CK: think steroids before escalating immunotherapy.
Dexamethasone is more myotoxic than equivalent prednisolone.
Exercise prevents and treats steroid myopathy.
det.thd: Steroid myopathy เกิดจากการใช้ corticosteroid ขนาดสูงหรือนาน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาต้นแขนอ่อนแรงโดยไม่ปวด CK ปกติ EMG มักปกติ ต้องแยกจากโรคเดิมกำเริบ เช่น myositis ซึ่งมี CK สูงและ EMG พบ fibrillation การรักษาคือลดขนาด steroid ใช้ยาลด steroid และออกกำลังกาย ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

ddx.pt: Raised CK, fibrillations on EMG and muscle oedema on MRI in active disease
Endogenous cortisol excess with the same myopathy but no exogenous steroid
Acute severe flaccid weakness in ICU with low CMAPs and loss of myosin

name: Steroid responsive encephalopathy
formal: Hashimoto encephalopathy or SREAT with confusion, seizures and anti-thyroid antibodies, dramatically responding to steroids.
simple: A brain inflammation linked to thyroid antibodies causing confusion and seizures that improves with steroids.

name: Stiff baby syndrome
formal: Hyperekplexia in infants with generalised hypertonia, exaggerated startle and apnoea, often GLRA1-related, relieved by clonazepam.
simple: A condition in newborns with very stiff muscles and an exaggerated startle.
more: Treat with clonazepam, and the Vigevano manoeuvre can abort attacks; consider shared pathogenic variants in GLRA1 and genetic testing. Attacks of apnoea can be fatal, and symptoms usually improve with age, although startle persists.

name: Stiff leg/stiff limb syndrome
formal: Autoimmune disorder with progressive limb or trunk stiffness and painful spasms, often asymmetric and confined to one limb; linked to anti-GAD or glycine receptor antibodies and spinal interneuron dysfunction.
simple: A condition where one leg or arm becomes stiff and goes into painful spasms because the immune system disturbs nerve signals in the spinal cord.

name: Stiff man syndrome
formal: Older name for stiff-person syndrome: progressive axial and proximal limb rigidity with superimposed spasms, startle-provoked, associated with anti-GAD65 antibodies and other autoimmune disease.
simple: A rare immune condition causing muscles in the trunk and legs to become stiff and to cramp painfully, often set off by sudden noise or touch.

name: Stiff-person spectrum disorders (SPSD)
formal: Umbrella term covering classic stiff-person syndrome, stiff-limb variants, progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, and paraneoplastic forms, united by autoantibodies and CNS hyperexcitability.
simple: A group of related rare immune conditions in which the nervous system causes muscle stiffness and spasms.

name: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS)
formal: Autoimmune CNS hyperexcitability disorder with fluctuating axial and limb rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms and lumbar hyperlordosis; anti-GAD65 antibodies are typical and it responds to benzodiazepines and baclofen.
simple: A rare immune disease making the back and leg muscles stiff and prone to painful spasms triggered by noise, touch or stress.
more: EMG shows continuous motor unit firing that stops with sleep or diazepam; also check anti-amphiphysin and anti-glycine antibodies, and screen for breast cancer or thymoma. Add IVIG, plasmapheresis or rituximab.
ab: progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
th: กล้ามเนื้อลำตัวแข็งเกร็งและกระตุกเป็นพักจากภูมิคุ้มกัน (anti-GAD) — ตกใจหรือเสียงดังกระตุ้น หลังแอ่น
feat: Fluctuating stiffness of trunk and proximal legs, exaggerated lumbar lordosis
Painful spasms triggered by noise, touch, emotion or sudden movement
Task-specific phobia (fear of open spaces or falling); often misdiagnosed as functional
Associations: type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, vitiligo; amphiphysin antibodies suggest breast cancer
inv: Anti-GAD65 at high titre (also glycine receptor, amphiphysin)
EMG: ongoing firing of normal motor units, with simultaneous contraction of opposing muscles, abolished by sleep or diazepam

case.story: Two years of a 'board-like' back and legs; a slammed door makes her fall rigidly. Labelled anxiety.
case.exam: Rigid paraspinal and abdominal muscles, hyperlordosis, stiff-legged gait, normal strength and sensation.
case.tests: Anti-GAD65 >2,000 IU/mL; EMG: co-contraction that melts with IV diazepam.
case.q: What symptomatic treatment usually helps first?
case.a: GABA-enhancing drugs — diazepam (often high doses) and baclofen; IVIG for disabling disease.

ddx.pt: No continuous motor unit activity; antibodies negative
Peripheral myokymia and cramps, neuromyotonic EMG; CASPR2
Wound, trismus, risus sardonicus, autonomic storms

aN: sps | stiff person syndrome | stiff man syndrome | anti gad syndrome | perm | progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus

det.patho: SPS is an autoimmune disorder of central inhibitory circuits: antibodies against GAD65 (the enzyme producing GABA), amphiphysin or the glycine receptor are associated with reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition of spinal and brainstem motor neurons. The result is continuous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles plus heightened startle-triggered spasms. It is rare, more common in women, and frequently coexists with other autoimmune conditions.
det.clinical: Onset is insidious in mid-adult life with aching stiffness of the lower back and abdomen, a fixed lumbar hyperlordosis and a slow, wide-based, stiff gait. Superimposed painful spasms are triggered by sudden noise, touch, cold or emotion and can cause falls 'like a statue'. Anxiety and fear of open spaces are common and secondary, often leading to a functional label. Variants include stiff-limb syndrome, and PERM with brainstem signs, myoclonus and encephalopathy. GAD antibodies may also accompany cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy or limbic encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Very high serum anti-GAD65 titres (far above those seen in type 1 diabetes) support the diagnosis; CSF GAD antibodies with intrathecal synthesis add weight. Surface EMG shows continuous normal motor unit firing in paraspinal and abdominal muscles with simultaneous agonist–antagonist activity that disappears in sleep or after IV diazepam. Amphiphysin antibodies demand a search for breast or small-cell lung cancer. Exclude tetanus, myelopathy, dystonia and neuromyotonia.
det.treatment: Symptomatic treatment centres on GABA-enhancing drugs: benzodiazepines (diazepam often in high divided doses) and baclofen, with gabapentin, pregabalin or levetiracetam as add-ons; intrathecal baclofen is used in refractory cases. Immunotherapy with IVIG has the best evidence; rituximab, plasma exchange and steroids are alternatives. Paraneoplastic cases need tumour treatment. Avoid abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can precipitate dangerous spasms.
det.prognosis: Course is variable and often progressive, with falls and disability; many patients improve partly with treatment. Paraneoplastic and PERM forms carry a worse outlook.
pearls: Board-like abdomen and hyperlordosis that melt under anaesthesia or sleep: think SPS.
Low-titre GAD is common in diabetes; SPS titres are usually very high.
Amphiphysin antibodies point to breast cancer.
det.thd: Stiff-person syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันต่อระบบยับยั้งในไขสันหลังและก้านสมอง (anti-GAD65, amphiphysin, glycine receptor) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหลังและท้องแข็งตลอด หลังแอ่น และกระตุกปวดเมื่อตกใจหรือถูกสัมผัส มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรควิตกกังวล วินิจฉัยด้วย anti-GAD ระดับสูงมาก และ EMG ที่เห็นกล้ามเนื้อหดตัวพร้อมกันต่อเนื่องซึ่งหายเมื่อหลับหรือให้ diazepam รักษาด้วย diazepam, baclofen และ IVIG

name: Strachan syndrome
formal: Syndrome of painful sensory neuropathy, optic neuropathy and sometimes spastic paraparesis, described in nutritionally deprived populations, probably related to deficiency of B vitamins and other nutrients.
simple: A condition from poor nutrition causing burning pain and numb feet, vision loss and sometimes stiff legs.

name: Striatocapsular infarction
formal: Infarct of the striatum and anterior internal capsule from occlusion of lenticulostriate branches or the MCA stem, causing contralateral hemiparesis with or without aphasia or neglect.
simple: A stroke in deep brain structures that causes weakness on one side of the body and sometimes trouble with speech.

name: Striatonigral degeneration (SND)
formal: Parkinsonian variant of multiple system atrophy with neuronal loss and gliosis in putamen and substantia nigra, causing akinetic-rigid syndrome with poor levodopa response and autonomic failure.
simple: A brain degeneration causing slowness and stiffness like Parkinson disease, but responding poorly to Parkinson medicines.
more: MRI shows reduced putaminal volume with T2 hypointensity of the posterolateral putamen and rim of hyperintensity; autonomic testing is helpful. Treat with levodopa trial (may produce orofacial dystonia), droxidopa, and supportive care.

name: Striatopallido-dentate calcification
formal: Bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate nuclei and other regions, producing parkinsonism, chorea, ataxia, dementia or psychiatric signs; idiopathic (Fahr) or secondary to hypoparathyroidism and genetic causes.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas that can cause movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.

name: Stroke
formal: Acute focal neurological deficit from cerebral ischaemia or haemorrhage; ischaemic subtypes include large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel and cryptogenic, managed by reperfusion and secondary prevention.
simple: Sudden loss of brain function when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bleeds, causing weakness, speech or vision problems.

name: Stroke-like migraine attacks
formal: Migraine with aura presenting with prolonged or severe focal deficits that mimic cerebral infarction, or occurring in conditions such as MELAS or SMART syndrome, requiring exclusion of true ischaemia.
simple: Migraine episodes whose symptoms, like weakness or speech trouble, look like a stroke but are caused by the migraine process.

name: Strychnine poisoning
formal: Convulsant poisoning from glycine receptor antagonism in the spinal cord, causing generalised muscle spasms, opisthotonos and risus sardonicus while consciousness is preserved; treated with benzodiazepines and supportive care.
simple: A poisoning that blocks calming signals in the spinal cord, causing violent painful muscle spasms while the person stays awake.

name: Sturge–Weber syndrome
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from somatic GNAQ mutation with facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma, hemiparesis and cognitive impairment; tram-track calcification on imaging.
simple: A birth condition with a facial birthmark and blood-vessel malformation on the brain surface, often causing seizures and eye pressure problems.

name: Stuve–Wiedemann syndrome
formal: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (LIFR mutation) with neonatal bowel, respiratory and feeding difficulties, bone dysplasia with bowing, autonomic dysfunction and sweating or temperature instability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in babies with bent bones, feeding and breathing trouble and unstable body temperature control.

name: Subacute combined degeneration
formal: Vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy affecting dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, with paraesthesias, sensory ataxia, spasticity and often neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia.
simple: Spinal cord damage from low vitamin B12 causing tingling, poor balance and weak stiff legs.

feat: Distal paraesthesia, loss of vibration and joint position sense, positive Romberg
Spastic weakness with extensor plantars yet absent ankle jerks (cord + nerve)
Cognitive change, macrocytic anaemia
Nitrous oxide abuse can precipitate it
inv: Serum B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine; full blood count
MRI spine: dorsal column T2 'inverted V'
Intrinsic factor/parietal cell antibodies

case.exam: Absent vibration to the iliac crests, Romberg positive, brisk knees, absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars.
case.tests: B12 borderline, MMA high; MRI: dorsal column hyperintensity C2–C6.

aN: scd | b12 deficiency myelopathy | subacute combined degeneration of the cord | cobalamin deficiency

det.patho: Vitamin B12 is needed for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis, particularly in the large myelinated fibres of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, beginning in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Peripheral nerves, optic nerves and the brain may also be affected. Common causes are pernicious anaemia, gastric surgery, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, metformin or proton pump inhibitor use, and nitrous oxide, which inactivates B12.
det.clinical: Symmetric tingling in the feet (sometimes the hands first) is followed by loss of vibration and joint position sense, sensory ataxia and Romberg positivity. Corticospinal involvement gives spastic leg weakness and extensor plantars, while a coexisting neuropathy may abolish ankle jerks. Cognitive change, depression, visual loss from optic neuropathy, and Lhermitte phenomenon can occur. Neurological damage may develop without anaemia or macrocytosis, especially if folate intake is high.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum B12 together with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, because B12 levels in the low-normal range may hide true deficiency; both metabolites rise in B12 deficiency, only homocysteine in folate deficiency. Look for the cause: intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies, gastrin, coeliac serology, diet and drug history, and nitrous oxide use. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity of the dorsal columns (inverted V on axial images). Check copper, which can produce an identical myelopathy, and consider nerve conduction studies.
det.treatment: Start parenteral hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin promptly, with frequent intramuscular injections in the first weeks for neurological involvement, then lifelong maintenance if the cause persists; high-dose oral B12 can be used for maintenance in many patients. Do not give folate alone, which can worsen the neurological picture. In nitrous oxide users, stop exposure and treat even if the B12 level looks normal. Physiotherapy helps recovery of gait.
det.prognosis: Improvement occurs over 6–12 months; the extent of recovery depends on severity and duration before treatment, and long-standing deficits may be permanent.
pearls: Normal haemoglobin does not exclude neurological B12 deficiency.
Recreational nitrous oxide is now a leading cause in young adults — ask directly.
Extensor plantars with absent ankle jerks: B12, copper, Friedreich ataxia, or combined cord and nerve disease.

name: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy
formal: Toxic myelopathy and optic neuropathy with abdominal symptoms and green tongue, caused by clioquinol; epidemic in Japan in the 1960s, causing sensory neuropathy, visual loss and paraparesis.
simple: A poisoning from an old anti-diarrhoea drug that caused stomach pain, numb legs and loss of vision.

name: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)
formal: Fatal progressive encephalitis from persistent defective measles virus after early childhood infection, with myoclonic jerks, cognitive decline, periodic EEG complexes and raised CSF measles antibodies.
simple: A rare, fatal brain infection years after measles, causing jerks, memory decline and loss of function.

name: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from ruptured saccular aneurysm, causing thunderclap headache, meningism and often reduced consciousness; complications include rebleeding, vasospasm and hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding around the brain surface, usually from a burst aneurysm, causing a sudden severe headache and neck stiffness.

det.patho: Most non-traumatic SAH comes from rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis, typically at the anterior communicating, posterior communicating or MCA bifurcation. Risk factors are smoking, hypertension, heavy alcohol use, family history and inherited conditions such as polycystic kidney disease. Blood in the subarachnoid space causes a sudden pressure surge, meningeal irritation and later arterial spasm. Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH is a benign venous variant.
det.clinical: The hallmark is a headache that is maximal within a minute, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, collapse or seizure. Neck stiffness may take hours to appear. Focal signs suggest the aneurysm site or a haematoma: painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy with PComm aneurysm. Complications follow a timeline: rebleeding (first day), hydrocephalus (early), delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (days 4–14), hyponatraemia and cardiac dysfunction. Severity is graded with the WFNS or Hunt–Hess scales.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset is nearly always positive when read by an expert; sensitivity drops after that. If CT is negative and the headache began more than 6 hours ago, perform LP at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia. CTA identifies most aneurysms; DSA remains the reference standard and guides treatment. Consider RCVS, CVT, pituitary apoplexy, arterial dissection and meningitis as alternative explanations.
det.treatment: Secure the aneurysm early, usually within 24 hours, by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping. Until then control BP, give analgesia, and reverse anticoagulation. Give oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days to reduce delayed ischaemia. Maintain euvolaemia, avoid hypotension, monitor sodium, and watch for neurological decline with transcranial Doppler or repeat imaging. Hydrocephalus needs CSF drainage; delayed ischaemia is treated by induced hypertension and endovascular therapy in selected cases.
det.prognosis: Overall case fatality approaches one third, with many survivors left with cognitive or mood problems; grade on admission is the strongest predictor.
pearls: Thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise; CT then LP if needed.
Nimodipine improves outcome but does not reliably prevent angiographic spasm.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is often cerebral salt wasting — do not fluid-restrict.

name: Subchoreic Huntington’s disease (status subchoreacticus)
formal: Late phase of Huntington disease with reduced chorea turning to rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonia in advanced or juvenile-onset cases; the title wording is nonstandard for an akinetic-rigid stage.
simple: A late stage of Huntington disease in which the jerky movements fade and the body becomes stiff and slow.

name: Subclavian steal syndrome
formal: Haemodynamic syndrome from proximal subclavian stenosis or occlusion causing retrograde vertebral flow, with arm claudication, blood pressure difference and posterior circulation symptoms on arm exercise.
simple: A blocked artery to the arm that steals blood from the brain's back circulation, causing dizziness or fainting when the arm is used.

name: Subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CARASIL)
formal: Autosomal recessive HTRA1-related small vessel disease with early leukoencephalopathy, alopecia, spondylosis and recurrent lacunar strokes leading to dementia in young adults.
simple: An inherited condition of small brain vessels causing early strokes, memory loss, hair loss and back problems.

name: Subcortical ischaemic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke in deep white matter, basal ganglia or internal capsule due to small-vessel disease, typically presenting as lacunar syndromes such as pure motor or sensory stroke.
simple: A stroke deep in the brain from blockage of a tiny vessel, often causing weakness or numbness on one side.

name: Subcortical-cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus generated by cortical hyperexcitability and relayed through subcortical pathways, producing multifocal jerks with cortical EEG correlates on back-averaging, in metabolic or degenerative disease.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks arising from overactive brain circuits involving the cortex and deeper brain areas.

name: Subcortical–nonsegmental myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus with subcortical generator and nonsegmental distribution, such as reticular reflex myoclonus or startle syndromes, lacking a consistent cortical EEG correlate.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks arising from deep brain regions, affecting widespread muscles rather than one body segment.

name: Subcortico-cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus in which cortical discharges drive subcortical structures, giving jerks with cortical spike precedence on EEG back-averaging; seen in post-hypoxic and progressive myoclonic conditions.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that begin with abnormal electrical activity in the brain's outer layer and spread to deeper brain areas.

name: Subcutaneous neurofibromas
formal: Benign nerve sheath tumours under the skin in neurofibromatosis type 1, appearing as soft, fleshy nodules along peripheral nerves, often multiple and sometimes painful.
simple: Soft lumps under the skin along nerves, typical of a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis.

name: Subdural and extradural haematoma
formal: Intracranial collections of blood in the subdural or epidural space, usually traumatic, causing raised pressure and focal signs; epidural lesions are arterial and lens shaped, subdural venous and crescentic.
simple: Blood collecting between the skull and the brain's coverings after head injury, which can press on the brain.

name: Subdural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood between dura and arachnoid from torn bridging veins, acute or chronic, particularly in elderly or anticoagulated patients, presenting with headache, confusion or hemiparesis.
simple: A slow or sudden bleed under the brain's outer covering, often after a minor head knock in older people.

name: Subhyaloid haemorrhage
formal: Retinal bleeding between the internal limiting membrane or hyaloid face and retina, often with subarachnoid haemorrhage (Terson syndrome) or raised pressure, causing sudden visual loss.
simple: A pool of blood in front of the retina that can suddenly blur vision, sometimes after a brain bleed.

name: Sudden adult cardiac death syndrome (SADS)
formal: Sudden death in adults with no structural cause on autopsy, often attributed to inherited arrhythmia such as channelopathy, sometimes with overlap with epilepsy-related deaths.
simple: An unexpected death in a young or healthy adult with no clear cause found, often due to a heart rhythm disorder.
nN: sudden adult cardiac death syndrome sads
aN: sads | sudden adult cardiac death syndrome

name: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
formal: Unexpected, non-traumatic death in a person with epilepsy, with or without a witnessed seizure, excluding status epilepticus; risk rises with frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, especially nocturnal.
simple: A sudden unexplained death in someone with epilepsy, mostly linked to poorly controlled seizures.

aN: sudep | sudden unexpected death in epilepsy

name: Sudeck’s atrophy
formal: Complex regional pain syndrome with patchy bone demineralisation after trauma or immobilisation, causing pain, swelling, temperature and skin changes and stiffness in the affected limb.
simple: A painful condition after injury where a limb swells, changes colour and becomes stiff and weak.

name: Sulphite oxidase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive inborn error of sulphite metabolism with neonatal intractable seizures, lens dislocation and severe encephalopathy; sulphite accumulates, with raised urinary S-sulphocysteine.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where a toxic substance builds up and causes severe seizures and brain damage in babies.

name: Super-refractory status epilepticus
formal: Status epilepticus persisting or recurring for 24 hours or more despite anaesthetic therapy, requiring continuous intravenous anaesthetics; causes include autoimmune encephalitis and cryptogenic FIRES.
simple: A seizure emergency that continues despite strong anaesthetic drugs for a day or more.

name: Superior orbital fissure syndrome
formal: Lesion at the superior orbital fissure involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI, causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis and forehead numbness, from tumour, trauma, inflammation or infection.
simple: Damage at the gap behind the eye that causes eye movement paralysis, drooping eyelid and forehead numbness.

name: Supranuclear gaze palsy (SGP)
formal: Gaze paralysis from lesions above the oculomotor nuclei, as in progressive supranuclear palsy, with preserved reflex movements on oculocephalic testing and impaired voluntary vertical gaze.
simple: Difficulty voluntarily moving the eyes, especially looking up or down, caused by problems in the brain rather than the eye muscles.

name: Supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
formal: Loss of voluntary eye movements with preserved reflex movements due to supranuclear lesions, typical of progressive supranuclear palsy and midbrain disease, often affecting vertical gaze first.
simple: Inability to move the eyes on command, though they still move reflexively, due to a brain rather than eye problem.

name: Supratentorial gliomas
formal: Primary brain tumours of the cerebral hemispheres, including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma in adults, presenting with seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: Tumours that grow from supporting brain cells in the upper brain, often causing seizures, headaches or weakness.

name: Surgical brachial plexopathies
formal: Iatrogenic injury to the brachial plexus from positioning, traction, retraction, sternotomy or regional anaesthesia, producing a patchy arm weakness and sensory deficit in the perioperative period.
simple: Damage to the nerve bundle supplying the arm that happens during or after an operation, causing arm weakness or numbness.
more: EMG and MRI or ultrasound localise the lesion. Most are neurapraxic and recover within weeks to months with physiotherapy; severe lesions may need nerve repair or transfer.

name: Susac’s syndrome
formal: Immune-mediated microangiopathy of brain, retina and cochlea causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions and low-frequency hearing loss; callosal snowball lesions on MRI.
simple: A rare immune disease harming tiny vessels in the brain, eyes and ears, causing confusion, vision loss and deafness.

name: Sydenham’s chorea
formal: Post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea in childhood, with rapid irregular movements, hypotonia, emotional lability and association with rheumatic fever; usually self-limiting over months.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements in children after a strep throat infection, linked to rheumatic fever.

name: Sympathetic algodystrophy
formal: Older term for complex regional pain syndrome with burning pain, autonomic and trophic changes after trauma or stroke, e.g. shoulder-hand syndrome.
simple: Severe burning limb pain with swelling and skin changes after an injury or stroke.

name: Symptomatic carotid stenosis
formal: Carotid stenosis causing ipsilateral transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax or stroke within recent months, for which endarterectomy or stenting is considered depending on degree of stenosis.
simple: Narrowing of the neck artery that has already caused a stroke or warning episode, so surgery or stenting may be needed.

name: Symptomatic choreic syndromes
formal: Chorea due to an underlying cause such as drugs, stroke, autoimmune disease or metabolic disorders rather than a primary hereditary chorea.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by another illness, drug or brain injury rather than inherited disease.

name: Symptomatic generalized myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus affecting the body widely, resulting from diffuse brain disorder such as metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative encephalopathy.
simple: Widespread sudden muscle jerks caused by a brain problem such as poisoning, low oxygen or metabolic disease.

name: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (sICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic infarct or thrombolysis-related bleed with neurological worsening, defined by haematoma and clinical deterioration within about 24-36 hours of treatment.
simple: A bleed in the brain after a stroke or clot-busting treatment that makes symptoms worse.

name: Symptomatic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus caused by an identifiable underlying disorder such as metabolic, post-anoxic, toxic or structural disease rather than essential or epileptic.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by another illness such as organ failure, brain injury or medication.

name: Symptomatic palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic palatal movements due to a lesion in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, often with inferior olive hypertrophy after brainstem stroke, with ear clicking and sometimes ocular oscillation.
simple: Rhythmic movements of the soft palate at the back of the mouth after brainstem damage, sometimes causing ear clicking.

name: Symptomatic startle syndromes
formal: Exaggerated startle responses secondary to brainstem or diffuse brain lesions or metabolic disease, distinct from hereditary hyperekplexia.
simple: Excessive jumping or stiffening when startled, caused by brain injury or illness.

name: Symptomatic tremors
formal: Tremors resulting from identifiable disease such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, drugs or metabolic causes, as opposed to essential tremor.
simple: Shaking caused by another disease, injury or drug rather than inherited or essential tremor.

name: Synaptic CMS
formal: Group of congenital myasthenic syndromes due to defects in synaptic proteins such as acetylcholinesterase, rapsyn or agrin pathway, causing fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited conditions of the nerve-muscle junction causing weakness that worsens with activity, starting in early life.

name: Synaptic disorders related to CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes from presynaptic, synaptic basal lamina or postsynaptic defects, with fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited disorders where signal passing at the nerve-muscle junction is faulty.
more: Genetic panel; treatments tailored, e.g. pyridostigmine, 3,4-DAP, salbutamol; avoid cholinesterase inhibitors in COLQ and DOK7.

name: Syndrome (CANVAS)
formal: Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome from biallelic RFC1 expansion, presenting with imbalance, sensory neuronopathy and bilateral vestibular loss, with chronic cough often.
simple: A late-onset inherited balance disorder with unsteady walking, numb feet and failing inner-ear function.
more: Diagnose by RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat expansion on repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot, with cerebellar vermis atrophy on MRI and absent sensory potentials on NCS. Late-onset, autosomal recessive; no disease-modifying therapy, so give rehabilitation.

name: Syndrome (ICANS)
formal: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome after CAR-T or bispecific antibody therapy, with confusion, aphasia, seizures or cerebral oedema, linked to cytokine release.
simple: Confusion, speech trouble or seizures that can follow certain immune cell cancer treatments.

name: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
formal: Hyponatraemia with concentrated urine from excess ADH release, seen with CNS disease, lung cancer or drugs; causes confusion, seizures and coma if severe, treated by fluid restriction.
simple: Low blood sodium caused by too much water-retaining hormone, which can lead to confusion and seizures.

name: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
formal: Hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine from non-suppressed ADH secretion in euvolaemic patients, caused by CNS disorders, malignancy or drugs and causing encephalopathy.
simple: Low blood sodium from too much water-retaining hormone, which may cause confusion or seizures.

name: Synthetic cannabinoids
formal: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists causing agitation, psychosis, seizures, stroke and acute kidney injury, with unpredictable potency compared with cannabis.
simple: Man-made drugs mimicking cannabis that can cause agitation, seizures and severe poisoning.

name: Syphilis
formal: Infection by Treponema pallidum that can invade the nervous system, causing meningitis, meningovascular disease, tabes dorsalis and general paresis; diagnosed by serology and treated with penicillin.
simple: A bacterial infection that can attack the brain and spinal cord years later, causing stroke, dementia or loss of coordination.

name: Syphilitic aortitis
formal: Inflammation and weakening of the aortic wall in tertiary syphilis, usually ascending aorta, risking aneurysm and aortic regurgitation; associated with neurosyphilis.
simple: Late syphilis damage to the main artery from the heart, which can widen and weaken it.

name: Syphilitic mesencephalitis
formal: Midbrain inflammation from syphilis with ocular motor abnormalities such as Argyll Robertson pupils and ptosis, within neurosyphilis.
simple: Syphilis infection of the upper brainstem causing small irregular pupils and eye movement problems.

name: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
formal: Autoimmune multisystem disease that can cause seizures, psychosis, stroke, chorea, myelitis, headache and neuropathy via antiphospholipid antibodies and vasculopathy.
simple: An immune disease affecting many organs that can also cause seizures, strokes, confusion and nerve damage.

name: Systemic vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of blood vessels of various sizes, which may involve CNS and peripheral nerves causing stroke, mononeuritis multiplex or encephalopathy.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessel walls throughout the body, which can damage the brain and nerves.

name: Takayasu’s arteritis (pulseless disease)
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous arteritis of the aorta and branches in young women, causing absent pulses, arm claudication, dizziness and stroke from stenosis.
simple: Inflammation of the body's main arteries in young women that narrows them, causing weak pulses, dizziness and strokes.

name: Takayasu’s disease
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous arteritis affecting the aorta and its branches, producing stenosis, aneurysm and reduced pulses with ischaemic cerebral or ocular symptoms.
simple: An inflammatory disease of the large arteries that can reduce blood flow to the arms and brain.

name: Tangier disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ABCA1 disorder with near-absent HDL, orange tonsils and recurrent or relapsing multifocal sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease with very low HDL cholesterol, enlarged orange tonsils and nerve problems.
more: ABCA1 genetics and lipid profile; neuropathy is often multifocal or syringomyelia-like; supportive therapy.

name: Tardive akathisia
formal: Persistent inner restlessness with an urge to move after long-term dopamine blocker exposure, often with dyskinesia; difficult to treat.
simple: A distressing feeling of needing to keep moving that develops after prolonged use of certain psychiatric medicines.

name: Tardive dyskinesia (TD)
formal: Late-onset involuntary orofacial and limb movements after prolonged dopamine receptor blocker exposure, treated with VMAT2 inhibitors or drug withdrawal.
simple: Involuntary mouth and body movements that develop after long use of certain antipsychotic drugs.
more: Diagnosis by exposure history; risk factors include age, female sex and duration; switch to clozapine or quetiapine when needed. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are FDA-approved; prevent with the lowest dose of antipsychotic, and monitor with AIMS.

name: Tardive dystonia
formal: Sustained abnormal postures and twisting after chronic dopamine antagonist exposure, often involving neck, trunk or face, and persistent after withdrawal.
simple: Painful twisting postures of the neck, face or trunk that develop after long use of certain psychiatric drugs.
more: Treat by switching to clozapine or quetiapine, botulinum toxin and VMAT2 inhibitors, and DBS of GPi for severe refractory cases. Young males and early onset are risk factors; anticholinergics may worsen the problem.

name: Tardive myoclonus
formal: Brief, shock-like involuntary jerks arising after prolonged exposure to dopamine blockers, forming part of tardive syndromes.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that appear after long use of certain antipsychotic medicines.

name: Tardive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism persisting or emerging late after prolonged neuroleptic exposure, sometimes persisting after withdrawal and needing differentiation from Parkinson disease.
simple: Slowness and stiffness like Parkinson disease that persist after long-term use of certain psychiatric drugs.

name: Tardive stereotypies
formal: Repetitive, purposeless, stereotyped movements such as rocking or lip smacking emerging after chronic dopamine blocker exposure.
simple: Repetitive purposeless movements, such as lip smacking or rocking, after long-term use of some psychiatric drugs.

name: Tardive syndromes
formal: Group of delayed-onset movement disorders from dopamine receptor blockers, including dyskinesia, dystonia, akathisia, tremor, myoclonus and stereotypies.
simple: A set of movement problems that appear after long-term use of certain psychiatric or stomach medicines.

name: Tardive tremor
formal: Postural or action tremor appearing late after prolonged dopamine receptor antagonist therapy.
simple: Shaking that develops after long use of certain psychiatric drugs.
more: Distinguish from Parkinson tremor by history of neuroleptic exposure and by DAT-SPECT being normal. Management is to reduce or stop the offending drug and consider propranolol or VMAT2 inhibitors.

name: Tarui disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type VII, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria and compensated haemolysis; avoidance of high-carbohydrate load before exercise.
simple: An inherited muscle energy disorder causing cramps, weakness and dark urine after intense exercise.
more: Diagnosis by muscle biopsy enzyme studies and genetic testing. Avoid strenuous exercise and high carbohydrate meals before activity; a ketogenic diet may help.

name: Task-specific tremor
formal: Tremor appearing only during a specific skilled task such as writing, a form of action tremor often with dystonic features.
simple: Shaking of the hand that only occurs when doing a particular task such as writing.

name: Tauopathies
formal: Neurodegenerative disorders characterised by tau protein accumulation, including Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration and frontotemporal dementias.
simple: Brain diseases in which an abnormal protein called tau builds up, causing memory, movement or behaviour problems.
more: Diagnosis uses MRI patterns, FDG-PET, CSF tau and amyloid, and tau-PET research; pathology confirms tau isoforms (3R, 4R, or both). Currently no disease-modifying therapy exists, though anti-tau trials are in progress; the genes MAPT and GRN are relevant.

name: Tay–Sachs disease
formal: Autosomal recessive HEXA deficiency causing GM2 ganglioside accumulation, with infantile regression, startle, macular cherry-red spot, seizures and early death.
simple: An inherited disease in babies in which a fatty substance builds up in the brain, causing loss of skills and early death.

name: Temporal arteritis
formal: Giant cell arteritis: granulomatous vasculitis of cranial arteries in people over 50, with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss risk and raised ESR; treated with steroids.
simple: Inflammation of arteries at the temples in older people, causing headache and jaw pain and risking sudden blindness.

name: Temporal lobe epilepsy
formal: Focal epilepsy from mesial or lateral temporal onset, commonly hippocampal sclerosis, with epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms and impaired awareness; may need surgery.
simple: Seizures starting in the temple area of the brain, often with odd feelings, staring and repetitive movements.

aN: tle | mesial temporal lobe epilepsy | mtle | complex partial seizures | focal impaired awareness seizures

det.patho: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy most often stems from hippocampal sclerosis — neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 and CA3 — frequently following prolonged febrile seizures or other early insults. Other causes include low-grade tumours, cavernomas, focal cortical dysplasia, post-encephalitic damage and autoimmune encephalitis. It is the commonest drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults.
det.clinical: Seizures often start with an aura that is in fact a focal aware seizure: rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu or jamais vu, fear, or an unpleasant smell or taste. These may evolve into impaired awareness with motionless staring, lip-smacking, chewing and fumbling hand automatisms, and contralateral dystonic arm posturing that helps lateralise. Seizures last 1–2 minutes and are followed by confusion; dominant-side onset may leave temporary language difficulty. Some seizures spread to bilateral tonic-clonic attacks. Memory complaints and mood disorders are common comorbidities.
det.diagnosis: A detailed witness account is central. MRI with an epilepsy protocol (thin coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus) detects hippocampal sclerosis and other lesions. Routine EEG may show anterior temporal spikes, but a normal interictal EEG does not exclude it; video-EEG telemetry captures typical events. In drug-resistant cases, pre-surgical evaluation adds neuropsychology, PET, functional MRI and sometimes intracranial EEG. New-onset adult TLE warrants consideration of autoimmune (e.g. LGI1) or neoplastic causes.
det.treatment: Focal-onset seizures respond to drugs such as lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide or zonisamide; choice depends on age, sex, comorbidity and interactions. Drug resistance is defined as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen drugs; at that point refer for surgical evaluation. Anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy offers seizure freedom to about two-thirds of suitable patients; laser ablation, vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation or deep brain stimulation are alternatives.
det.prognosis: About a third of patients remain drug-resistant; surgery in well-selected hippocampal sclerosis yields high seizure freedom and better quality of life.
pearls: Dystonic posturing of one hand usually points to seizure onset in the opposite temporal lobe.
Two failed drugs means refer for surgery — do not keep adding a third and fourth for years.
Late-onset TLE with memory loss and hyponatraemia: check LGI1 antibodies.

name: Tension-type headache (TTH)
formal: Most common primary headache with bilateral pressing, non-pulsatile mild to moderate pain lasting hours, without nausea or aura, and not worsened by activity.
simple: A common headache feeling like a tight band around the head, usually mild and without nausea.

name: Terminal tremor
formal: Tremor that increases in amplitude as the limb approaches a target, typical of cerebellar outflow lesions.
simple: Shaking that gets worse as the hand reaches for a target, caused by cerebellar damage.

name: Terson’s syndrome
formal: Vitreous haemorrhage associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure, causing visual loss.
simple: Bleeding in the eye jelly that occurs with brain bleeds, causing blurred vision.

name: Thalamocortical seizures
formal: Generalised epileptic seizures arising from abnormal thalamocortical oscillation, as in absence epilepsy with spike-wave discharges.
simple: Seizures caused by abnormal electrical loops between the thalamus and cortex, such as brief staring spells.

name: Thallium poisoning
formal: Heavy metal poisoning with painful ascending neuropathy, alopecia, gastrointestinal upset and encephalopathy.
simple: A poisoning causing painful nerve damage, hair loss and stomach upset.

name: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, typically in alcohol misuse or malnutrition.
simple: Low vitamin B1 that can cause confusion, eye movement problems, poor balance and nerve damage.
more: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy immediately with IV thiamine before glucose; diagnosis is clinical with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion; MRI shows mammillary body and periaqueductal change. Measure red cell transketolase or whole-blood thiamine.

name: Thioridazine akathisia
formal: Akathisia caused by the antipsychotic thioridazine, with inner restlessness and inability to stay still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness and need to move caused by a particular antipsychotic medicine.

name: Thomsen’s disease
formal: Autosomal dominant myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutations with muscle stiffness after rest that eases with exercise, with muscle hypertrophy.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles stay stiff after rest but loosen with repeated movement.

name: Thoracic arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)
formal: Spinal vascular malformations in the thoracic region causing progressive myelopathy, venous congestion or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal tangles of blood vessels in the mid spine that can cause leg weakness and numbness.

name: Thoracic radiculopathies
formal: Dysfunction of thoracic nerve roots, causing band-like trunk pain and sensory loss in a dermatomal pattern; causes include disc or spondylotic compression, herpes zoster, diabetes and tumour.
simple: A pinched or irritated nerve at chest level that causes belt-like pain or numbness around the ribs or abdomen.
more: MRI of the thoracic spine and sometimes EMG guide diagnosis. Treat the cause (decompression, antivirals, glycaemic control) plus neuropathic pain drugs; diabetic forms often improve over months.

name: Thoracic spine degenerative disease
formal: Wear-related degeneration of thoracic discs and joints, rarely causing myelopathy or radiculopathy with band-like pain.
simple: Age-related wear in the mid back that can sometimes press on the spinal cord or nerves.

name: Thoracic spine disease
formal: Disorders of the thoracic spine such as degenerative disease, tumour or infection causing myelopathy and radicular pain.
simple: Problems in the middle of the spine that can compress the spinal cord or nerve roots.

name: Thought disorder
formal: Disorganised thinking evident as derailed, tangential or incoherent speech, a core feature of schizophrenia and some organic brain states.
simple: Muddled, jumbled thinking that makes speech hard to follow.

name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
formal: Thrombotic microangiopathy from ADAMTS13 deficiency causing haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, renal dysfunction and fluctuating neurological deficits.
simple: A blood clotting disorder causing low platelets and tiny clots that can cause confusion, stroke-like symptoms and kidney problems.

name: Thunderclap headache
formal: Abrupt severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, requiring exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, RCVS, dissection and venous thrombosis.
simple: A sudden extremely severe headache that peaks within a minute and needs urgent investigation.

name: Thymoma
formal: Tumour of the thymus often associated with myasthenia gravis, requiring surgical removal; also linked to red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia.
simple: A growth in the thymus gland in the chest, often linked with a muscle weakness disease.

name: Thymoma, myasthenia gravis
formal: Thymoma associated with myasthenia gravis, producing fatigable weakness due to acetylcholine receptor antibodies; thymectomy is recommended.
simple: A thymus gland tumour that frequently occurs with myasthenia gravis, a condition causing tiring muscle weakness.

name: Thyroid disorders
formal: Over- or underactive thyroid states that affect nerve and muscle: thyrotoxic myopathy and periodic paralysis, hypothyroid myopathy with slow reflexes, neuropathy, carpal tunnel and ataxia.
simple: Problems with the thyroid gland that can cause muscle weakness, cramps, numbness or slowed reflexes.
more: Diagnosed with thyroid function tests and raised CK in hypothyroid myopathy. Correcting the hormone level usually reverses the neuromuscular problems, though recovery can take months.

name: Thyrotoxic myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness and wasting in hyperthyroidism, often with normal CK, and thyrotoxic periodic paralysis in some patients.
simple: Muscle weakness and wasting caused by an overactive thyroid.
more: Treat hyperthyroidism, and give propranolol; strength usually recovers in weeks.

name: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
formal: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis triggered by hyperthyroidism, with episodic proximal weakness, mainly in Asian men.
simple: Episodes of sudden muscle weakness in people with an overactive thyroid, due to low potassium shifts.
more: Check low potassium during attacks with low urinary potassium excretion; thyroid function is abnormal and CACNA1S is usually normal. Treat attacks with cautious oral potassium, avoid rebound hyperkalaemia, give propranolol, and cure the hyperthyroidism.

name: Thyrotoxicosis chorea
formal: Chorea resulting from hyperthyroidism, typically resolving when thyroid function is normalised.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by an overactive thyroid.

name: Tic convulsif
formal: Hemifacial spasm sometimes combined with trigeminal neuralgia, producing painful facial spasms.
simple: Painful twitching of one side of the face combined with facial nerve pain.

name: Tic disorders
formal: Group of neurodevelopmental conditions with sudden repetitive movements or vocalisations, including Tourette syndrome and persistent motor or vocal tic disorders.
simple: Conditions causing sudden repeated movements or sounds that are hard to control.
more: Diagnosis is clinical (DSM-5): onset before 18 years, with motor and vocal tics for more than a year in Tourette. Treat with behavioural therapy (CBIT), alpha-2 agonists or antipsychotics, and botulinum toxin; many improve in adolescence.

name: Tic douloureux
formal: Paroxysmal severe stabbing pain in the trigeminal distribution, usually vascular compression of the nerve root, treated with carbamazepine.
simple: Older name for trigeminal neuralgia: sudden electric-shock facial pain.

name: Tick paralysis
formal: Acute ascending flaccid paralysis caused by a neurotoxin from feeding engorged ticks, producing areflexia and ataxia through blocked neuromuscular or axonal conduction.
simple: Weakness spreading up the body from a tick bite, which usually goes away once the tick is found and removed.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, by finding the tick, often on the scalp. Nerve studies may show low motor amplitudes. Prompt tick removal leads to recovery within hours to days; untreated cases can cause respiratory failure.

name: Tickborne disease
formal: Infections transmitted by ticks with neurological involvement, such as Lyme neuroborreliosis, tick-borne encephalitis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
simple: Infections spread by tick bites that can sometimes affect the brain and nerves.

name: Tics
formal: Brief, stereotyped, suppressible movements or vocalisations preceded by premonitory urge, characteristic of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Sudden repeated movements or sounds that a person feels a build-up urge to make.

name: Tilted optic disc
formal: Congenital anomaly where the optic disc appears oblique, causing a bitemporal visual field defect that mimics chiasmal disease.
simple: A harmless birth variation in the shape of the optic nerve head that can mimic a visual field loss.

name: Tin neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity of organotin compounds causing headache, cerebral oedema, seizures and cognitive changes.
simple: Brain damage from poisoning with tin-containing chemicals.

name: Tocopherol (vitamin E) deficiency
formal: Vitamin E deficiency causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy, from malabsorption or ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (TTPA gene).
simple: Low vitamin E causing poor balance, nerve damage and sometimes vision problems.

name: Todd’s paralysis
formal: Transient focal weakness after a seizure, lasting minutes to hours, and resolving spontaneously.
simple: Temporary weakness of a limb after a seizure that usually clears within hours.

name: Tolosa–Hunt syndrome
formal: Painful ophthalmoplegia from idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus or orbital apex, responsive to steroids.
simple: Painful inflammation behind the eye causing eye movement problems that responds quickly to steroids.

name: Tongue protrusion dystonia
formal: Focal oromandibular dystonia where the tongue pushes involuntarily out of the mouth, often task-specific or tardive.
simple: Involuntary pushing of the tongue out of the mouth.

name: Tongue tremor
formal: Rhythmic tongue movement from essential tremor, parkinsonism or palatal tremor.
simple: Shaking of the tongue.

name: Tonic limb and axial seizures
formal: Seizures with simultaneous tonic stiffening of axial and limb muscles, as in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
simple: Seizures where the trunk and limbs stiffen suddenly.

name: Tonic seizures
formal: Seizures with sustained muscle contraction and stiffening, often in children with diffuse brain disease.
simple: Seizures in which muscles stiffen and the body becomes rigid.

name: Tonic spasms
formal: Brief painful contractions of muscle, as in multiple sclerosis (paroxysmal tonic spasms) or stiff-person syndrome.
simple: Short, painful muscle tightening episodes, often seen in multiple sclerosis.

name: Tonic–clonic seizure
formal: Generalised seizure with tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking and postictal state.
simple: A seizure with stiffening followed by shaking and then drowsiness.

name: Tonic–clonic status
formal: Prolonged or repeated generalised tonic-clonic seizures without recovery between them, a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs.
simple: A seizure emergency with prolonged convulsions that requires urgent drug treatment.

name: Torsion dystonia
formal: Generalised dystonia, typically early onset (DYT1), with sustained twisting postures and torsion of the limbs and trunk.
simple: Twisting, sustained abnormal body postures from muscle contractions, often starting in childhood.

name: Touch epilepsy
formal: Reflex epilepsy in which seizures are provoked by tactile stimuli.
simple: Seizures triggered by being touched.

name: Tourette’s syndrome
formal: Chronic tic disorder with multiple motor and one or more vocal tics for over a year, onset in childhood, often with ADHD or OCD.
simple: A condition with repeated movement and sound tics, starting in childhood.

name: Toxic and metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement or toxins, causing confusion, asterixis, tremor, myoclonus and seizures.
simple: Confusion and brain dysfunction caused by poisons or body chemistry problems.

name: Toxic and nutritional neuropathies
formal: Neuropathies caused by toxins such as alcohol, solvents, metals or drugs and nutritional deficits such as B vitamins, causing distal sensory-motor loss.
simple: Nerve damage from poisons or poor nutrition.

name: Toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies
formal: Optic nerve damage caused by toxins, such as methanol or ethambutol, and deficiencies, leading to central visual loss and colour impairment.
simple: Vision loss from poisoning or poor nutrition that damages the optic nerves.

name: Toxic cooking oil-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from contaminated cooking oil poisoning, historically reported in outbreaks.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by eating poisoned cooking oil.

name: Toxic encephalopathies
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from exogenous toxins, with delirium, seizures and coma.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by poisons.

name: Toxic encephalopathy
formal: Acute or subacute brain dysfunction due to poisoning, causing confusion and reduced consciousness; often reversible when the toxin is removed.
simple: Confusion or drowsiness caused by a poison affecting the brain.

name: Toxic leukoencephalopathy
formal: White matter injury from toxins such as toluene, heroin vapour or chemotherapy, causing subacute dementia, ataxia and spasticity.
simple: Damage to the brain's wiring from poisons or certain drugs.

name: Toxic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus secondary to toxins or drugs such as bismuth, lithium or antibiotics.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by drugs or poisons.

name: Toxic neuropathies
formal: Nerve disease due to toxin exposure including heavy metals, solvents, drugs and alcohol, usually with distal sensory-motor deficits.
simple: Nerve damage caused by chemical poisons or certain drugs.
more: Diagnose from exposure history plus NCS showing axonal, length-dependent neuropathy; check blood and urine levels (lead, arsenic, thallium). Removal of the agent is key, and recovery is slow and often incomplete, especially with arsenic or thallium.

name: Toxic oil syndrome
formal: Epidemic multisystem illness in Spain in 1981 linked to ingestion of adulterated rapeseed oil, with eosinophilic pneumonitis then scleroderma-like change, myalgia and sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: A mass poisoning from contaminated cooking oil that caused lung illness, muscle pain, skin hardening and nerve damage.
more: Contaminant anilides in denatured oil were implicated; eosinophilia was a marker. Treatment is supportive with steroids and immunosuppressants; many survivors had chronic neuropathy and pain.

name: Toxic serotonin syndrome
formal: Excess serotonergic activity causing hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and agitation, usually after serotonergic drug combinations.
simple: A dangerous reaction to excess serotonin from medicines, causing fever, muscle jerks and agitation.

name: Transient global amnesia (TGA)
formal: Sudden temporary anterograde amnesia lasting hours, with preserved alertness and personal identity, typically in middle-aged or older people and without lasting deficits.
simple: Sudden temporary memory loss lasting some hours, after which memory returns.

name: Transmissible encephalopathies
formal: Prion diseases transmitted between individuals, including kuru, iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and variant CJD.
simple: Brain diseases caused by abnormal proteins that can be passed from one person to another.

name: Transverse myelitis
formal: Inflammation of a spinal cord segment, causing weakness, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction, from MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, infection or post-infectious causes.
simple: Inflammation across the spinal cord causing leg weakness, numbness and bladder trouble.

case.story: One week after a viral illness, 2 days of numb legs rising to the chest and inability to pass urine.
case.exam: Legs 3/5, T8 sensory level, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, palpable bladder.
case.tests: MRI: T6–T8 cord swelling with enhancement, no compression; CSF lymphocytes 40.
case.q: What must the first MRI rule out?
case.a: Compressive myelopathy (disc, abscess, tumour, haematoma), which needs surgery.
