Longitudinally extensive lesion, AQP4-IgG
Areflexia, no sensory level, bladder spared early
Hyperacute, anterior cord pattern with dorsal column sparing

aN: tm | acute transverse myelitis | atm | myelitis

det.patho: Transverse myelitis is immune-mediated inflammation across one or more spinal cord segments, damaging ascending and descending tracts and the grey matter. It may follow infection or vaccination, or be the first event of MS, NMOSD or MOGAD; systemic diseases (SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis) and direct infections (HSV, VZV, HIV, syphilis, TB, schistosomiasis) are other causes. When no cause is found it is labelled idiopathic.
det.clinical: Symptoms develop over hours to days and peak within 4 hours to 3 weeks: bilateral but often asymmetric weakness, a sensory level, band-like truncal pain and early bladder and bowel dysfunction. Reflexes may be reduced during spinal shock before becoming brisk. A partial myelitis with asymmetric sensory symptoms and a short lesion is typical of MS, whereas a complete, severe myelitis with a longitudinally extensive lesion (three or more segments) points to NMOSD or MOGAD. Hyperacute onset within minutes suggests infarction rather than inflammation.
det.diagnosis: Image the whole spine urgently to exclude compression, then confirm intrinsic cord inflammation (T2 lesion, often enhancing). CSF usually shows pleocytosis and/or raised IgG index; check oligoclonal bands. Test serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG with cell-based assays, and screen for systemic autoimmunity, infections, B12, copper and HIV/syphilis. Brain MRI estimates future MS risk. Mimics include cord infarction, dural arteriovenous fistula (venous congestion), compressive myelopathy, radiation myelopathy and nutritional myelopathy.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (commonly 1 g per day, given for 3–5 days); plasma exchange is added for severe or steroid-unresponsive cases, especially when motor function is poor. Antimicrobials are given if an infectious cause is suspected. Supportive care covers bladder catheterisation, bowel care, DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, pain and spasticity management and early rehabilitation. Long-term immunotherapy depends on the cause — MS disease-modifying therapy or NMOSD relapse prevention.
det.prognosis: Roughly a third of patients recover well, a third have moderate and a third severe residual disability; rapid onset, complete paraplegia and spinal shock predict poorer recovery.
pearls: Every acute myelopathy is compressive until the MRI says otherwise.
Longitudinally extensive myelitis: check AQP4 and MOG antibodies.
Onset in minutes with back pain and a spared dorsal column suggests cord infarction.

name: Trauma cervical dystonia
formal: Cervical dystonia that follows neck or head injury.
simple: Neck twisting or abnormal head postures that begin after an injury.

name: Traumatic axonal injury (TAI)
formal: Diffuse shearing injury to white matter axons after rotational head trauma, producing coma or persistent disability with microbleeds on MRI.
simple: Widespread stretching damage to brain wiring from a severe head injury.

name: Traumatic brachial plexus lesions
formal: Injury to the brachial plexus from trauma, such as traction or avulsion, causing arm weakness and sensory loss, depending on roots involved.
simple: Nerve damage at the shoulder from injury, causing arm weakness and numbness.

name: Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
formal: Brain injury from external mechanical force, causing a spectrum from concussion to coma, with focal contusions, haematomas and diffuse axonal injury.
simple: Brain damage caused by a blow or violent movement of the head.

name: Traumatic optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve injury following head trauma, causing sudden visual loss, relative afferent pupillary defect, and variable optic atrophy.
simple: Vision loss from damage to the optic nerve after an injury.

name: Traumatic SAH
formal: Subarachnoid haemorrhage resulting from head injury, commonly overlying cortex, associated with contusion.
simple: Bleeding around the brain surface after a head injury.

name: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space following head trauma, often over convexities.
simple: Bleeding around the brain after a head injury.

name: Tremor
formal: Involuntary rhythmic oscillation of a body part, classified into rest, postural, kinetic and intention tremors; includes essential tremor and parkinsonian tremor.
simple: Involuntary rhythmic shaking of a body part.

name: Tremor akinetic–rigid syndromes
formal: Syndromes combining tremor with akinesia and rigidity, such as Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism.
simple: Conditions with shaking along with slowness and stiffness.

name: Tricyclic antidepressants akathisia
formal: Akathisia caused by tricyclic antidepressants, with restlessness and inner urge to move.
simple: Restlessness and need to keep moving caused by a type of antidepressant.

name: Trigeminal neuralgia
formal: Episodic severe unilateral lancinating facial pain in trigeminal territory, usually from vascular root compression; treated with carbamazepine or surgery.
simple: Sudden severe stabbing facial pain, often triggered by touch or chewing.

Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, cold wind

case.story: Stabbing jolts in the right cheek and jaw lasting 2 seconds, dozens per day; she has stopped brushing her teeth on that side.
case.exam: Normal facial sensation and corneal reflex.
case.tests: MRI: superior cerebellar artery contacting the right trigeminal root.
case.q: First-line drug?
case.a: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine); microvascular decompression if refractory.

Younger, bilateral TN or other relapses, demyelinating lesions
Constant burning after zoster, usually V1

det.patho: In classical TN a blood vessel, usually the superior cerebellar artery, compresses the trigeminal root near its entry into the pons, causing focal demyelination and ectopic, ephaptic firing. Secondary TN arises from MS plaques in the pontine root entry zone or from tumours such as epidermoids or meningiomas. It is more common in women and after 50.
det.clinical: Patients describe abrupt, very brief stabs or electric jolts confined to one or more trigeminal divisions (V2 and V3 most often), triggered by innocuous stimuli such as touching the face, talking, eating, shaving or a draught. Refractory periods follow volleys, and spontaneous remissions lasting months occur. Some patients have a concomitant continuous background ache (TN with concomitant persistent pain). Bilateral pain, sensory loss, onset before 40, hearing loss or other cranial nerve signs suggest a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the ICHD-3 description of paroxysmal, triggered pain in a trigeminal distribution. All patients should have MRI with thin-slice brainstem and cisternal sequences to identify neurovascular contact with morphological change (supporting classical TN) and to exclude MS or a tumour. Examine sensation and corneal reflexes carefully. Dental pathology, temporomandibular disorder, post-herpetic neuralgia and SUNCT/SUNA are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Carbamazepine is first-line, with oxcarbazepine as an alternative; check sodium and blood count, and screen for HLA-B*15:02 in patients of Han Chinese, Thai or other Southeast Asian ancestry before carbamazepine because of the risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin or pregabalin can be added or substituted. For drug failure or intolerance, microvascular decompression gives the most durable relief in classical TN; percutaneous procedures (balloon compression, glycerol, radiofrequency) or stereotactic radiosurgery suit older or unfit patients. Severe exacerbations may need IV fosphenytoin or lidocaine in hospital.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to drugs initially, but many need escalation over time; microvascular decompression gives long-term relief in roughly 70–80% at ten years.
pearls: Ask Thai and other Southeast Asian patients' HLA-B*15:02 status before starting carbamazepine.
Facial numbness between attacks is not classical TN — image for a lesion.
Patients may avoid eating and lose weight; check nutrition and hydration.

name: Trigeminal schwannomas
formal: Benign tumours of the trigeminal nerve root or ganglion, causing facial numbness, pain or weakness of chewing muscles.
simple: Non-cancerous tumours of the facial sensation nerve, causing numbness or pain in the face.

name: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy
formal: Disease of the trigeminal nerve causing facial numbness, often with connective tissue disease or idiopathic, sparing motor function.
simple: Numbness of part of the face due to disease of the trigeminal nerve.

name: Trilaminar myopathy
formal: Rare congenital myopathy with trilaminar fibres on oxidative staining, with variable weakness.
simple: A very rare muscle disease named from the three-layered appearance of fibres on biopsy.
more: Biopsy is diagnostic; supportive care.

name: Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive glycolytic enzyme defect causing haemolytic anaemia, progressive neuromuscular disease and early death.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic disorder causing anaemia and progressive nervous system damage.

name: Trochlear (IVth) nerve palsy
formal: Palsy of the fourth cranial nerve causing vertical diplopia, head tilt away from the lesion and difficulty looking down and in; causes include trauma and microvascular disease.
simple: Weakness of an eye muscle causing double vision, often with the head tilted.

name: Tropical ataxic myeloneuropathy
formal: Myeloneuropathy in tropical regions linked to cassava cyanide toxicity and nutritional deficiency, with ataxia, spastic paraparesis and optic atrophy.
simple: A disease in tropical areas causing leg weakness, unsteady walking and nerve damage, linked to diet.

name: Tropical spastic paraparesis (TSP)
formal: Chronic myelopathy associated with HTLV-1 infection, causing progressive spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction.
simple: A slowly progressive stiffness and weakness of the legs caused by a virus (HTLV-1).

name: True primary myoclonic epilepsies
formal: Generalised epilepsies with myoclonic seizures as the main feature, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: Epilepsies in which the main seizure type is sudden muscle jerks.

name: Trunk tremor
formal: Tremor of the trunk, as in essential tremor or orthostatic tremor.
simple: Shaking of the body trunk.

name: TTR-related amyloidosis
formal: Hereditary or wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis with progressive sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: A condition where an abnormal transport protein forms deposits in nerves and heart.
more: Diagnosed by TTR gene testing and biopsy; treat with patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen, tafamidis, or liver transplantation.

name: Tuberculosis
formal: Infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can involve the CNS as meningitis, tuberculoma or spinal disease.
simple: A bacterial infection that mostly affects the lungs but can spread to brain and spine.

name: Tuberculous abscess
formal: Pus-filled collection within brain parenchyma caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain caused by tuberculosis.

name: Tuberculous granuloma
formal: Focal intracerebral mass of inflammatory tissue due to tuberculosis, presenting with seizures or focal deficits and with ring enhancement.
simple: A lump of inflamed tissue in the brain from tuberculosis.

name: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM)
formal: Subacute basal meningitis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis with cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, stroke and low CSF glucose.
simple: A serious infection of the brain coverings from tuberculosis, causing headache, fever and confusion.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากวัณโรค — ปวดศีรษะไข้เป็นสัปดาห์ เส้นประสาทสมองอ่อนแรง โพรงน้ำในสมองโต
feat: Weeks of headache, fever, weight loss, then confusion
Cranial nerve palsies (especially VI and III), basal exudates
Hydrocephalus, vasculitic infarcts in basal ganglia, hyponatraemia
inv: CSF: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose; AFB stain, GeneXpert, culture
MRI with contrast: basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas, infarcts
Chest X-ray, HIV test

case.story: Three weeks of fever and headache; now double vision and drowsiness.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, right sixth nerve palsy, GCS 13.
case.tests: CSF: WBC 220/µL (lymphocytes), protein 2.8 g/L, glucose ratio 0.25; MRI basal enhancement with hydrocephalus.
case.q: Which adjunct improves survival with anti-TB therapy?
case.a: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) — plus manage hydrocephalus.

ddx.pt: Very high opening pressure, cryptococcal antigen positive
Hyperacute, neutrophilic CSF
Known cancer, malignant cells on cytology

det.patho: Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeds the brain or meninges during haematogenous spread, forming small subpial or subependymal foci (Rich foci) that later rupture into the subarachnoid space. A thick gelatinous exudate collects around the base of the brain, entrapping cranial nerves, obstructing CSF flow and inflaming arteries that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. It is the most lethal form of tuberculosis and is common in high-burden countries such as Thailand, especially with HIV.
det.clinical: Onset is subacute over one to several weeks with fever, headache, malaise, weight loss and vomiting, followed by confusion, meningism and declining consciousness. Cranial nerve palsies, most often VI, III and VII, are frequent; vision may fail from optochiasmatic arachnoiditis or papilloedema. Strokes in the basal ganglia, hydrocephalus, seizures, tuberculomas and hyponatraemia are typical complications. Severity is graded by the modified British MRC scale (GCS and focal signs), which predicts outcome.
det.diagnosis: CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis (often a few hundred cells, sometimes neutrophilic early), markedly raised protein, a low glucose ratio and raised opening pressure. Ziehl–Neelsen staining is insensitive; Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra adds speed and rifampicin-resistance data, and culture is slow but the reference. Large-volume CSF samples (6 mL or more) improve yield. Contrast MRI may show basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarcts and tuberculomas. Look for TB elsewhere (chest X-ray, sputum, abdominal ultrasound) and test for HIV; empirical treatment should not wait when suspicion is high.
det.treatment: Standard treatment uses rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, then rifampicin and isoniazid to complete 9–12 months total, with pyridoxine. Adjunctive dexamethasone, tapered over 6–8 weeks, improves survival in HIV-negative patients. In people with HIV, delay antiretroviral therapy for several weeks to reduce the risk of severe paradoxical reactions. Hydrocephalus may need ventricular drainage or shunting; monitor sodium and liver function.
det.prognosis: Death or severe disability occurs in a third or more of patients overall, with worse outcomes in late-stage presentations, HIV coinfection and drug resistance.
pearls: Subacute meningitis with a sixth nerve palsy and hyponatraemia in Thailand: treat for TB early.
A low CSF glucose with lymphocytes narrows the field to TB, fungi, partially treated bacteria, malignancy or listeria.
Paradoxical worsening (new tuberculomas) on treatment does not mean drug failure.
det.thd: TBM เป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากวัณโรค พบบ่อยในประเทศไทยโดยเฉพาะผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV เชื้อทำให้เกิดหนองข้นที่ฐานสมอง กดเส้นประสาทสมอง ทำให้โพรงน้ำในสมองโตและหลอดเลือดอักเสบจนสมองขาดเลือด อาการเป็นสัปดาห์ด้วยไข้ ปวดศีรษะ น้ำหนักลด แล้วซึมลง ตาเหล่จาก CN VI น้ำไขสันหลังมี lymphocyte โปรตีนสูงมาก น้ำตาลต่ำ ส่ง Xpert และเพาะเชื้อ รักษาด้วยยาวัณโรค 4 ตัวรวม 9–12 เดือนร่วมกับ dexamethasone และจัดการ hydrocephalus

name: Tuberculous spondylitis
formal: Pott disease: tuberculous infection of vertebrae, causing back pain, kyphosis, paraplegia and paravertebral abscess.
simple: Tuberculosis infection of the spine causing pain, deformity and possible leg weakness.

name: Tuberous sclerosis
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from TSC1 or TSC2 mutation with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, seizures, angiofibromas and cognitive impairment.
simple: An inherited disorder causing benign growths in the brain, skin and organs, with seizures and learning problems.

name: Tubular aggregate myopathy
formal: Myopathy with proximal weakness, myalgia or cramps where biopsy shows tubular aggregates of sarcoplasmic reticulum; caused by STIM1 or ORAI1 calcium-handling gene variants or sporadic forms.
simple: A muscle disease causing weakness and cramps in which muscle samples show abnormal tube-like clumps.
more: CK may be mildly raised; diagnosis by biopsy and genetics, often dominant inheritance. Treatment is supportive; progression is usually slow.

name: Tumour-related epilepsy
formal: Seizures caused by brain tumour, particularly low-grade glioma.
simple: Seizures caused by a growth in the brain.

name: Type II glycogenosis
formal: Pompe disease from GAA deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation, with infantile cardiomyopathy or adult-onset proximal and respiratory weakness.
simple: An inherited disease where muscle cells cannot break down glycogen, causing weakness and breathing problems.
more: Reduced acid alpha-glucosidase activity and gene testing; enzyme replacement with alglucosidase or avalglucosidase alfa.

name: Type III glycogenosis
formal: Cori-Forbes disease from AGL debranching enzyme deficiency causing hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, myopathy, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: An inherited problem storing sugar in liver and muscle, causing low blood sugar and weakness.
more: Diagnosed by AGL testing and enzyme assays; frequent high-protein feeds and cornstarch.

name: Type IV glycogenosis
formal: Andersen disease from GBE1 mutation producing abnormal polyglucosan, with liver cirrhosis, myopathy, or adult polyglucosan body disease.
simple: An inherited glycogen-storage condition forming abnormal sugar chains, damaging liver, muscle, or nerves.
more: Biopsy shows polyglucosan bodies; GBE1 testing; liver transplantation is considered in progressive liver disease.

name: Type IX glycogenosis
formal: Phosphorylase kinase deficiency with X-linked or autosomal recessive forms (PHKA1, PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2), causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, or exercise intolerance.
simple: An inherited glycogen-processing problem causing an enlarged liver or muscle cramps.
more: Diagnosed by gene testing; dietary management with cornstarch and protein.

name: Type V glycogenosis
formal: McArdle disease, myophosphorylase deficiency (PYGM), with exercise intolerance, cramps, second-wind phenomenon, and myoglobinuria.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles run out of energy during exercise, causing cramps and dark urine.
more: Forearm exercise test, CK, and PYGM sequencing; pre-exercise sucrose and graded aerobic exercise help.

name: Type VII glycogenosis
formal: Tarui disease, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exertional cramps, myoglobinuria, and haemolysis, and carbohydrate-triggered worsening.
simple: An inherited condition where muscle cannot use sugar properly, causing cramps on exercise and sometimes anaemia.
more: Diagnosed by enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exercise and high-carbohydrate meals before activity.

name: Type VIII glycogenosis
formal: Older designation for phosphorylase b kinase deficiency, now classed with type IX, with exercise intolerance or hepatic glycogenosis.
simple: An old name for a rare inherited sugar-storage disease affecting muscle or liver.
more: Diagnosed by genetic testing of PHKA/PHKB genes; treatment is supportive with dietary management.

name: Type X glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency (PGAM2) with exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria.
simple: A rare inherited condition where muscles lack an enzyme needed for energy, causing cramps and dark urine after exercise.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exertion; no specific therapy.

name: Type XI glycogenosis
formal: Lactate dehydrogenase A deficiency (LDHA) with exertional myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, and skin lesions.
simple: A rare condition with muscle breakdown and pain after exercise from lacking a muscle enzyme.
more: Low lactate production on forearm test; gene testing; avoid heavy exercise.

name: Type XII glycogenosis
formal: Aldolase A deficiency (ALDOA), with exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, and haemolytic anaemia.
simple: A rare inherited enzyme deficiency causing muscle pain and breakdown with exercise, and anaemia.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; supportive care and exercise avoidance.

name: Type XIII glycogenosis
formal: Beta-enolase deficiency (ENO3) causing exercise intolerance and myalgia with raised CK.
simple: A very rare inherited muscle enzyme deficiency causing exercise-related pain and fatigue.
more: Gene testing; supportive management.

name: Type XIV glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglucomutase 1 deficiency (PGM1), a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hepatopathy, myopathy, cleft palate, and hypoglycaemia.
simple: A rare inherited condition affecting sugar processing, with muscle, liver, and other problems.
more: Galactose supplementation is effective; diagnosis by transferrin glycosylation and gene testing.

name: Typical absence seizure
formal: Brief generalised nonconvulsive seizure with abrupt impaired awareness and 3 Hz spike-wave on EEG, typical of childhood absence epilepsy.
simple: A brief staring spell with sudden loss of awareness, mainly in children.

name: UDD distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy (tibial muscular dystrophy) from titin gene variants, causing anterior compartment weakness with foot drop after age 35 to 45.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in middle age, causing weakness in the front of the lower legs and difficulty lifting the foot.
more: MRI shows tibialis anterior involvement; confirmed by TTN testing, with severe disease in homozygotes (limb-girdle phenotype). Progression is slow and most remain walking; orthoses help.

name: Ulcerative colitis
formal: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease associated with neurological complications such as venous thrombosis, neuropathy and myelopathy.
simple: A bowel inflammation disease that can sometimes affect nerves and brain vessels.

name: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy (UCMD)
formal: Collagen VI-related congenital muscular dystrophy with proximal weakness, distal joint hyperlaxity, proximal contractures, follicular hyperkeratosis and respiratory failure, from COL6A1-3 variants.
simple: An inherited muscle disease present from birth with weakness, very loose finger joints, tight hips and knees, and breathing problems.
more: Diagnosis by collagen VI immunostaining and gene testing; inheritance may be recessive or de novo dominant. Management is respiratory support, orthopaedic care and nocturnal ventilation.

name: Ulnar neuropathies
formal: Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist, causing numbness of little finger and hand weakness.
simple: Pressure on the nerve at the elbow or wrist causing tingling in the ring and little fingers.
th: เส้นประสาท ulnar ถูกกด (มักที่ข้อศอก) — ชานิ้วก้อยและนิ้วนางครึ่งนิ้ว กล้ามเนื้อมือลีบ Froment sign
feat: Numbness of little finger and ulnar half of ring finger, including the dorsal ulnar hand (elbow lesions)
Weak finger abduction, first dorsal interosseous wasting, Froment and Wartenberg signs
Clawing of ring and little fingers; worse with elbow flexion or leaning
Guyon canal lesions spare dorsal hand sensation
inv: NCS: slowing or conduction block across the elbow; inching study
Ultrasound: nerve enlargement at the cubital tunnel

case.story: Tingling little finger for months, worse when he talks on the phone; now drops coins.
case.exam: Reduced sensation little finger and dorsal ulnar hand, wasting of first dorsal interosseous, Froment sign positive, Tinel at the medial elbow.
case.tests: Ulnar motor conduction block across the elbow segment; normal C8 paraspinal EMG.
case.q: Why is the dorsal ulnar hand sensation useful?
case.a: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch leaves above the wrist — its involvement places the lesion at or above the elbow, not at Guyon canal.

ddx.pt: C8 root: neck pain, medial forearm sensory loss, thenar (median) muscles also weak
Thenar wasting with medial forearm numbness; cervical rib
Split hand with no sensory loss and UMN signs

aN: ulnar neuropathy | ulnar neuropathy at the elbow | une | cubital tunnel syndrome | guyon canal

det.patho: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable where it runs superficially behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel under the aponeurosis of flexor carpi ulnaris. Elbow flexion narrows the tunnel and stretches the nerve, while external pressure from leaning adds compression. Less common sites are Guyon's canal at the wrist (ganglion, cycling, fracture) and the axilla. Leprosy, diabetes and HNPP increase susceptibility.
det.clinical: Elbow lesions cause numbness of the little finger, the ulnar half of the ring finger and the ulnar border of the hand both dorsally and on the palm. Motor involvement causes weak pinch and finger spreading, wasting of the first web space, and clawing of the fourth and fifth digits in advanced cases. Froment's sign reflects adductor pollicis weakness, and Wartenberg's sign is a persistently abducted little finger. Symptoms are worse at night or when the elbow is held flexed. Wrist lesions vary by branch involved and may be purely motor.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies localise the lesion by showing focal slowing or conduction block across the elbow; short-segment inching improves precision. EMG documents axon loss and, by sparing flexor carpi ulnaris or not, can help. Check the dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory response to separate elbow from wrist lesions. Ultrasound shows nerve swelling and can reveal subluxation or a mass. Exclude C8/T1 radiculopathy, lower trunk plexopathy and motor neuron disease, which affect median-innervated hand muscles too.
det.treatment: Mild cases are managed conservatively: avoid leaning on the elbow and prolonged flexion, use a padded elbow or a night splint holding the elbow in extension, and review after several months. Persistent sensory symptoms, progressive weakness or axon loss justify surgical decompression (in situ release or transposition), which have broadly similar outcomes. Space-occupying lesions at Guyon's canal need excision.
det.prognosis: Sensory symptoms usually improve; established wasting recovers incompletely, particularly in older patients with long-standing denervation.
pearls: Dorsal ulnar hand numbness places the lesion proximal to the wrist.
Medial forearm numbness suggests C8/T1 root or lower trunk, not ulnar nerve.
Thenar weakness with ulnar signs: look beyond the ulnar nerve.
det.thd: Ulnar neuropathy มักเกิดที่ข้อศอก (cubital tunnel) จากการงอข้อศอกนานหรือวางศอกกดทับ ทำให้ชานิ้วก้อยและครึ่งนิ้วนาง รวมถึงหลังมือด้าน ulnar กล้ามเนื้อมือลีบ และพบ Froment sign วินิจฉัยด้วย NCS ที่เห็น conduction block บริเวณข้อศอก และใช้ dorsal ulnar cutaneous nerve แยกจากรอยโรคที่ข้อมือ รักษาเบื้องต้นด้วยหลีกเลี่ยงการกดทับและใส่เฝือกกลางคืน ถ้าแย่ลงหรือมี axon loss พิจารณาผ่าตัด

name: Unilateral peripheral vestibulopathy
formal: Acute unilateral vestibular loss from vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, causing vertigo, nystagmus and imbalance.
simple: Inner ear balance nerve damage on one side, causing a spinning sensation.

name: Unilateral visual failure
formal: Monocular or binocular visual loss on one side from optic neuropathy, retinal or visual pathway disease.
simple: Loss of vision in one eye or one side.

name: Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS)
formal: State of preserved wakefulness without awareness, formerly called vegetative state, after severe brain injury.
simple: A condition where a person appears awake, eyes open, but shows no signs of awareness.

name: Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1)
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutation (Baltic myoclonus), with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, seizures and ataxia.
simple: An inherited condition causing muscle jerks, seizures and unsteadiness beginning in adolescence.
more: Diagnosis by CSTB dodecamer repeat expansion testing; autosomal recessive, with generalised spike-wave on EEG. Valproate, levetiracetam, zonisamide and piracetam help; avoid phenytoin, which may worsen the disease; prognosis is better than in Lafora disease.

name: Upper motor neuron lesions
formal: Damage to corticospinal pathways causing spasticity, weakness, hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses.
simple: Damage to brain or spinal cord pathways that causes stiff, weak muscles.

name: Uraemic encephalopathy
formal: Encephalopathy from renal failure with asterixis, myoclonus, seizures and confusion, reversible with dialysis.
simple: Confusion and brain dysfunction caused by kidney failure.

name: Uraemic neuropathy
formal: Distal sensory-motor polyneuropathy in chronic kidney failure, improved by dialysis or transplantation.
simple: Nerve damage in the feet and legs caused by kidney failure.

name: Uraemic restless legs syndrome
formal: Restless legs syndrome occurring in patients with renal failure, often improved with transplantation.
simple: Restless legs with an urge to move that occurs in kidney failure.

name: Urea cycle disorders
formal: Inborn errors of ammonia detoxification causing hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, vomiting, seizures and coma.
simple: Inherited disorders where ammonia builds up in the blood and harms the brain.

name: Uremic neuropathy
formal: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy in advanced chronic kidney disease, with painful feet, restless legs, and cramps.
simple: Nerve damage with numbness and burning in the legs from kidney failure.
more: Dialysis and renal transplantation improve it; neuropathic pain control; intensive dialysis helps.

name: Uveomeningeal syndromes
formal: Group of inflammatory conditions, including uveitis with meningitis such as Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Behcet disease or sarcoidosis.
simple: Conditions involving inflammation of both the eye and the brain's coverings.

name: Vacuolar myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord degeneration with vacuolation of white matter, such as HIV vacuolar myelopathy or B12 deficiency.
simple: Spinal cord damage that causes leg weakness and loss of position sense.

name: Vacuolar myelopathy, HIV infection
formal: Progressive myelopathy in advanced HIV infection with spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and bladder dysfunction.
simple: Spinal cord damage in advanced HIV causing leg weakness and unsteady walking.

name: Valproic acid catatonia
formal: Catatonia occurring with valproate-associated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy.
simple: A state of reduced movement and response linked to a seizure medicine.

name: Vanishing white matter disease
formal: Leukodystrophy from EIF2B mutations with episodic deterioration after fever or trauma, ataxia and spasticity.
simple: An inherited disease of brain white matter with sudden worsening after fever or head injury.

name: Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD)
formal: Prion disease from bovine spongiform encephalopathy exposure, with young onset, psychiatric symptoms, pulvinar sign on MRI and fatal course.
simple: A rare fatal brain disease caused by eating beef contaminated by mad cow disease.

name: Vascular cognitive impairment and dementia
formal: Cognitive decline due to cerebrovascular disease, ranging from mild impairment to dementia, with executive dysfunction and white matter lesions.
simple: Memory and thinking problems caused by poor blood supply to the brain.
th: ความจำและการคิดเสื่อมจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง — ช้า วางแผนไม่ได้ เดินซอย มักมีปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด
tempoNote: Stepwise after strokes or slowly progressive with small vessel disease
feat: Slowed processing and executive dysfunction more than early memory loss
Stepwise course after strokes, or insidious with small vessel disease
Gait disturbance, urinary urgency and pseudobulbar signs
Often mixed with Alzheimer pathology
inv: MRI: white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, microbleeds, strategic infarcts
Cognitive testing emphasising executive function (e.g. MoCA)
Vascular risk factor profile

case.story: Over two years he has become slow, apathetic and unable to manage his bills; walks with short steps.
case.exam: MoCA 19/30 with poor trails and fluency, brisk reflexes, short-stepped gait, normal arm swing.
case.tests: MRI: confluent periventricular white matter hyperintensities and bilateral thalamic lacunes.
case.q: Which cognitive domain is most typical here and why?
case.a: Executive function and processing speed — small vessel disease disconnects frontal–subcortical circuits.

Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to atrophy; improves after CSF tap
Fluctuations, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder

aN: vci | vad | vascular dementia | subcortical ischemic vascular dementia | multi infarct dementia | post stroke dementia

det.patho: Cerebrovascular disease damages cognition through several routes: multiple cortical infarcts, single strategic infarcts (thalamus, angular gyrus, caudate), and — most commonly — small vessel disease with white matter rarefaction and lacunes that disconnect frontal–subcortical circuits. Hypertension, diabetes, smoking and ageing drive arteriolosclerosis; CAA and genetic arteriopathies such as CADASIL are other causes. Mixed vascular and Alzheimer pathology is the norm in older people.
det.clinical: The cognitive profile is dominated by slowed thinking, poor attention, executive dysfunction, apathy and depression, with memory retrieval worse than storage. Course may be stepwise after strokes or gradually progressive with small vessel disease. Associated features include short-stepped gait, falls, urinary urgency, pseudobulbar affect and focal signs. Post-stroke cognitive impairment is common in the first year after stroke.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires cognitive impairment plus imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease judged sufficient to explain it, using frameworks such as VICCCS. MRI shows white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, microbleeds, enlarged perivascular spaces and infarcts. Neuropsychological testing should include processing speed and executive tasks; MoCA is more sensitive than MMSE. Screen for depression, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and NPH, and consider amyloid biomarkers when mixed disease is suspected.
det.treatment: Aggressive vascular risk control — BP, diabetes, lipids, smoking, physical activity — is the core and may slow progression. Treat depression and support function with rehabilitation and caregiver education. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest benefit and are mainly used in mixed or post-stroke cases. Antithrombotics are given for prior stroke, not for white matter disease alone.
det.prognosis: Progression is variable and often steeper than in Alzheimer disease, with higher rates of further stroke and death.
pearls: Slowness and dysexecutive features outweigh amnesia in subcortical VCI.
Most late-life dementia is mixed — vascular plus Alzheimer pathology.
Young onset with migraine aura and anterior temporal white matter lesions = test for CADASIL (NOTCH3).
det.thd: ความบกพร่องทางสติปัญญาจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง เกิดได้จาก infarct หลายจุด infarct ในตำแหน่งสำคัญ (strategic) หรือที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ small vessel disease ซึ่งตัดวงจร frontal-subcortical อาการเด่นคือคิดช้า สมาธิไม่ดี วางแผนไม่ได้ เฉยเมย ร่วมกับเดินก้าวสั้น ปัสสาวะกลั้นไม่อยู่ วินิจฉัยด้วยการทดสอบ cognition เช่น MoCA ร่วมกับ MRI ที่พบ white matter hyperintensities และ lacunes การรักษาหลักคือคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือดอย่างเข้มงวด และใช้ยากลุ่ม cholinesterase inhibitor ได้ในบางรายที่เป็นแบบผสม

name: Vascular dementia
formal: Dementia caused by cerebrovascular disease, with stepwise decline, executive dysfunction and focal signs.
simple: Memory loss and thinking problems caused by blood vessel damage in the brain.

name: Vascular malformations
formal: Abnormal vessel structures of the brain or spinal cord, including AVMs, cavernous malformations, venous angiomas and dural fistulas.
simple: Abnormal blood vessel tangles in the brain or spinal cord that may bleed.

name: Vascular malformations, spinal
formal: Abnormal spinal vessels such as dural arteriovenous fistula or cavernoma, causing progressive myelopathy or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal blood vessels in the spine that can cause leg weakness or bleeding.

name: Vascular myelopathies
formal: Spinal cord disorders from ischaemia, infarction or venous congestion, such as anterior spinal artery infarct and dural fistula.
simple: Spinal cord damage caused by a loss of blood supply.

name: Vascular parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism from small vessel disease affecting the basal ganglia and white matter, with lower-body parkinsonism and poor levodopa response.
simple: Slowness, stiffness and shuffling walking caused by multiple small strokes.
more: MRI shows extensive white matter hyperintensities with lacunes and basal ganglia infarcts; DAT-SPECT is usually normal, unlike Parkinson disease. Treat vascular risk factors, antiplatelets and physiotherapy; levodopa response is modest.

name: Vascular progressive supranuclear palsy
formal: Vascular lesions mimicking progressive supranuclear palsy with vertical gaze palsy, postural instability and falls.
simple: Small strokes that cause balance problems and eye movement problems similar to progressive supranuclear palsy.

name: Vasculitic neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies due to inflammation of vasa nervorum, with mononeuritis multiplex and painful asymmetric neuropathy.
simple: Nerve damage from inflamed blood vessels that supply the nerves.
more: Diagnosis is by nerve and muscle biopsy showing necrotising vasculitis, with raised ESR and ANCA or cryoglobulin testing; EMG shows asymmetric axonal loss. Treat with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab for systemic disease.
th: เส้นประสาทเสียจากหลอดเลือดอักเสบ — ปวดมาก เส้นประสาทเสียทีละเส้น (mononeuritis multiplex)
feat: Painful, stepwise, asymmetric deficits in named nerves (peroneal, ulnar, radial…)
May later look symmetric as lesions overlap
Systemic clues: rash, arthritis, renal disease, weight loss, fever; nonsystemic form has none
inv: ESR/CRP, ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C, ANA, complement
NCS: multifocal axonal loss; guides biopsy site
Nerve (± muscle) biopsy: transmural vessel inflammation

case.story: Over 6 weeks, burning pain then a dropped right foot, followed by weakness of the left hand. Lost 6 kg; night sweats.

aN: vasculitic neuropathy | nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy | nsvn | mononeuritis multiplex vasculitis

det.patho: Inflammation and necrosis of the walls of epineurial arteries cause ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles. Because nerve blood supply is patchy, infarcts produce discrete axonal lesions in individual nerves, often in watershed regions of the mid-arm and mid-thigh. Systemic causes include ANCA-associated vasculitis (especially EGPA and MPA), polyarteritis nodosa, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, cryoglobulinaemia from hepatitis C, and drugs or infections. Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy is confined to the peripheral nerves.
det.clinical: Classic presentation is acute or subacute painful mononeuritis multiplex, with new deficits appearing in different nerves over days to weeks, often peroneal, tibial, ulnar or median. As lesions accumulate, the picture may resemble an asymmetric or even symmetric distal polyneuropathy, so the history of stepwise onset is key. Burning or deep aching pain is prominent. Systemic vasculitis adds constitutional symptoms, skin lesions, arthritis, renal or pulmonary involvement, and eosinophilia with asthma in EGPA.
det.diagnosis: NCS show asymmetric axonal loss, sometimes with pseudo-conduction block in the first days after infarction. Investigations include inflammatory markers, ANCA, ANA, ENA, rheumatoid factor, cryoglobulins, complement, hepatitis B and C, HIV, eosinophil count, urinalysis and renal function. A combined nerve and muscle biopsy (e.g. superficial peroneal nerve with peroneus brevis, or sural nerve), chosen from an affected but not absent nerve, gives the highest yield. Definite diagnosis requires vessel wall inflammation with damage; supportive features are probable. Diabetic and infectious mimics must be considered.
det.treatment: Treat promptly to prevent further nerve infarcts. Induction uses high-dose corticosteroids, combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for systemic vasculitis or severe/progressive nonsystemic disease; maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. Hepatitis-related vasculitis also needs antiviral treatment. Neuropathic pain, physiotherapy and orthoses are essential, and steroid-related bone and infection prophylaxis should be considered.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise with treatment and many improve slowly over months to years, though residual pain and weakness are common. Systemic vasculitis outcome depends on organ involvement; relapses occur.
pearls: Painful stepwise mononeuropathies in different limbs: rule out vasculitis.
Biopsy a nerve that is affected but still conducting.
Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy has normal markers — biopsy is the only route to diagnosis.

name: Vasculitic plexopathies
formal: Plexus lesions from vasculitis such as diabetic or non-diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy, with painful weakness.
simple: Painful nerve damage in the limb nerve networks from blood vessel inflammation.

name: Vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of blood vessel walls, which may be primary or secondary, affecting the CNS or PNS with stroke or neuropathy.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels that can reduce blood flow to organs.

name: Vasculitis associated with connective tissue disease
formal: Necrotising inflammation of small to medium vessels in lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren or scleroderma, causing mononeuritis multiplex and sometimes central nervous system involvement.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels in people with autoimmune connective tissue disease that can injure nerves, causing sudden weakness or numbness.
more: Nerve and muscle biopsy, ANCA and complement help diagnosis. Treated with high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab; early treatment limits permanent nerve loss.

name: Vasospasm
formal: Narrowing of cerebral arteries, usually after subarachnoid haemorrhage, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia.
simple: Temporary narrowing of brain arteries, often after a bleed, which can cause stroke.

name: Versive seizures
formal: Seizures with forced head and eye turning to one side, from frontal eye field or other frontal onset.
simple: Seizures in which the head and eyes turn forcibly to one side.

name: Vertical gaze palsy
formal: Loss of voluntary upward and/or downward gaze from midbrain lesions, as in Parinaud syndrome or PSP.
simple: Inability to look up or down because of damage in the upper brainstem.

name: Vertigo (BPPV)
formal: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: brief positional vertigo from dislodged otoconia in a semicircular canal, treated with canalith repositioning.
simple: Brief spinning dizziness when moving the head, caused by tiny crystals in the inner ear.

name: Vestibular migraine

simple: Dizziness attacks linked to migraine.

name: Vestibular neuritis

simple: Sudden severe spinning dizziness caused by inflammation of the balance nerve in the ear.

aN: vestibular neuronitis | acute vestibular syndrome | labyrinthitis

det.patho: Vestibular neuritis is presumed to be inflammation of the vestibular nerve, most often its superior division, probably from reactivation of latent HSV-1 in the vestibular ganglion. Sudden loss of input from one side creates an imbalance between the two vestibular nuclei, giving vertigo and nystagmus until central compensation occurs. When hearing is also affected the term labyrinthitis is used.
det.clinical: Severe rotatory vertigo begins over minutes to hours and persists for days, with nausea, vomiting and unsteadiness; patients often prefer to lie still. Any head movement worsens symptoms. A viral upper respiratory illness may precede it. Hearing is preserved and there are no other neurological symptoms. Symptoms settle over days to weeks, though motion-provoked dizziness can linger, and some patients go on to persistent postural-perceptual dizziness or BPPV.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis of the acute vestibular syndrome made at the bedside. The HINTS examination in a patient with ongoing vertigo and nystagmus favours a peripheral cause when the head impulse is abnormal toward the affected side, nystagmus is unidirectional (beating away, increased with gaze in that direction and suppressed by fixation) and there is no skew deviation. Any central sign — a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, severe truncal ataxia (unable to stand unaided) or new hearing loss — requires MRI with DWI, remembering that early DWI can miss small posterior circulation strokes. Video head impulse testing and caloric testing confirm the deficit.
det.treatment: Use vestibular suppressants and antiemetics only for the first 1–3 days, since longer use delays compensation. A short course of oral corticosteroids started early may improve caloric recovery, though functional benefit is uncertain. Early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation exercises are the most important interventions for long-term recovery.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover functionally within weeks to months through central compensation; recurrence on the same side is uncommon.
pearls: HINTS is only valid in a patient with continuous vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus at the time of examination.
A normal head impulse in acute vertigo is a dangerous finding — it suggests stroke.
Get patients moving early; bed rest and prolonged vestibular sedatives slow recovery.

name: Vestibular schwannoma
formal: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve sheath, causing unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance; bilateral in NF2.
simple: A non-cancerous growth on the hearing and balance nerve causing hearing loss and unsteadiness.

name: Vestibulocochlear (VIIIth) nerve disorders
formal: Disorders of the eighth cranial nerve causing hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo.
simple: Conditions affecting the nerve for hearing and balance.

name: Viral agents producing poliomyelitis
formal: Neurotropic enteroviruses, chiefly poliovirus and also enterovirus 71 and D68, that infect anterior horn cells and cause acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation.
simple: Viruses that attack the nerve cells controlling muscles and cause sudden floppy weakness of the limbs.
more: Diagnosed by stool or CSF viral studies and CSF pleocytosis. No antiviral cure exists; vaccination prevents polio, and post-polio syndrome can develop decades later.

name: Viral and post-infectious myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following viral infection or post-infectious inflammation, such as opsoclonus-myoclonus.
simple: Muscle jerks that develop after a viral illness.

name: Viral encephalopathies
formal: Brain dysfunction due to viral infection or post-infectious processes causing confusion, seizures and altered consciousness.
simple: Brain illness caused by a virus, causing confusion or seizures.

name: Viral meningitis
formal: Aseptic meningitis, usually enteroviral, with fever, headache, neck stiffness and lymphocytic CSF, self-limited.
simple: Mild infection of the brain coverings by a virus, causing headache and fever.

name: Viral spinal infections
formal: Viral infections of the spinal cord or nerve roots, such as poliovirus, herpes zoster or West Nile, causing myelitis.
simple: Viral infections of the spinal cord causing weakness or numbness.

name: Virus-associated vasculitis
formal: Cerebral vasculitis triggered by viral infection such as VZV, causing stroke or aneurysm.
simple: Inflammation of brain blood vessels caused by a virus, leading to strokes.

name: Vision neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
formal: Juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease) with progressive visual failure, seizures, dementia and ataxia.
simple: An inherited childhood disease with progressive vision loss, seizures and loss of skills.

name: Visual agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects visually despite intact vision, due to lesions in occipitotemporal cortex.
simple: Seeing but not being able to recognise objects, caused by damage in the visual part of the brain.

name: Visual simultanagnosia
formal: Component of Balint syndrome: inability to perceive more than one object at a time, from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
simple: Being able to see only one object at a time, unable to take in a whole scene.

name: Visuospatial agnosia
formal: Inability to appreciate spatial relationships and locate objects, from right parietal lesions.
simple: Trouble judging where things are in space.

name: Vitamin A deficiency
formal: Nutritional deficiency causing night blindness, xerophthalmia and, in neurological settings, raised intracranial pressure in infants and impaired mucosal immunity; seen in malabsorption and malnutrition.
simple: Not getting enough vitamin A, which can lead to night blindness, dry eyes and increased infection risk.
more: Serum retinol confirms it; replacement with vitamin A supplements is effective early, but corneal damage can be permanent.

name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration, megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy and cognitive impairment.
simple: Low vitamin B12 causing numbness, balance problems, memory trouble and anaemia.

name: Vitamin E deficiency
formal: Deficiency of vitamin E causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy.
simple: Low vitamin E causing poor balance and nerve damage.
more: Check serum alpha-tocopherol with the lipid ratio; abetalipoproteinaemia and cholestatic malabsorption must be excluded, while AVED has TTPA mutations. Treat with high-dose oral vitamin E, which can halt progression.

name: VLCAD deficiency
formal: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADVL) with cardiomyopathy in infants, or rhabdomyolysis with exertional myalgia in adolescents.
simple: An inherited fat-burning defect causing muscle pain or heart weakness, especially during fasting or exercise.
more: Acylcarnitine and gene testing; avoid fasting, a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides, and triheptanoin.

name: Vocal tics
formal: Involuntary vocalisations as part of Tourette syndrome, ranging from simple sounds to words.
simple: Repeated sounds or words made involuntarily.

name: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease
formal: Autoimmune panuveitis with meningoencephalitis, poliosis, vitiligo and hearing loss, in pigmented populations.
simple: An immune disease causing eye inflammation, headache, hearing loss and patchy loss of skin or hair colour.

name: Von Economo’s disease
formal: Encephalitis lethargica, epidemic 1916-1927, with sleep disturbance, oculogyric crisis, parkinsonism and psychiatric features.
simple: A rare epidemic brain illness causing excessive sleepiness and later parkinsonism.

name: Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VHL mutation with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
simple: An inherited condition causing tumours in the brain, eyes, kidneys and adrenal glands.

name: Von Hippel–Lindau disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VHL mutation with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
simple: An inherited condition causing tumours in the brain, eyes, kidneys and adrenal glands.

name: Walker-Warburg syndrome
formal: Severe congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, cerebellar malformation and eye anomalies, due to defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMT1, POMT2, FKTN and others).
simple: The most severe inherited muscle and brain malformation syndrome of newborns, with floppiness, brain and eye abnormalities.
more: Very high CK; autosomal recessive with prenatal diagnosis possible. Treatment is supportive and most affected infants die in the first years of life.

name: Wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia
formal: WEBINO: bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia with exotropia, from midbrain lesions affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
simple: Both eyes drift outward and cannot turn inward, from damage in the brainstem.

name: Welander distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy beginning in the hands, especially finger and wrist extensors, linked to a TIA1 variant; mainly reported in Sweden and Finland.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in older adults that starts with weak hands and fingers and slowly spreads.
more: CK is normal or mildly raised and biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles. There is no specific treatment; progression is slow and lifespan is normal.

name: Werdnig–Hoffman disease
formal: Infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (SMN1 deletion) with hypotonia and early respiratory failure.
simple: A severe inherited muscle wasting disease in babies.
more: Diagnosis by homozygous SMN1 deletion with one or two SMN2 copies; EMG shows denervation and fasciculations. Untreated, death occurs by two years; nusinersen, onasemnogene and risdiplam have changed survival, and early treatment is vital.

name: Wernicke syndrome
formal: Acute thiamine deficiency encephalopathy with the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, associated with alcoholism, malnutrition and hyperemesis; MRI shows periventricular lesions and mammillary body change.
simple: A brain emergency from lack of vitamin B1 that causes confusion, eye movement problems and unsteady walking.
more: Treat immediately with high-dose intravenous thiamine before glucose to prevent Korsakoff syndrome. Early treatment can fully reverse features.

name: Wernicke’s aphasia
formal: Fluent aphasia from left posterior superior temporal lesion, with impaired comprehension and paraphasic speech.
simple: Speech that sounds fluent but makes little sense, with poor understanding.

name: Wernicke’s encephalopathy
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, often in alcohol misuse, treated with parenteral thiamine.
simple: A brain emergency from low vitamin B1 causing confusion, abnormal eye movements and unsteady walking.
more: MRI may show mammillary body and periaqueductal T2 hyperintensity; diagnose clinically, and thiamine should be given before glucose. Treat with high-dose IV thiamine, 500 mg three times daily; untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome and death.

aN: wernicke encephalopathy | thiamine deficiency | wernicke korsakoff | we

det.patho: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a cofactor for enzymes of glucose metabolism; body stores last only a few weeks. When thiamine is depleted, energy failure and oxidative injury hit regions of high metabolic demand around the third ventricle, aqueduct and fourth ventricle — the medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, oculomotor and vestibular nuclei and cerebellar vermis. Alcohol use disorder is the classic setting, but hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, cancer, dialysis, starvation and refeeding are increasingly recognised.
det.clinical: The full triad of confusion, eye movement abnormalities and gait ataxia is present in only a minority; many patients show just one or two elements or only altered mental state. Eye findings include nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, conjugate gaze palsy and, rarely, pupillary change. Hypothermia, hypotension and coma occur in severe cases. If untreated, patients develop Korsakoff syndrome, with profound anterograde and retrograde amnesia and confabulation, which may be permanent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; the Caine criteria (two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, and altered mental state or memory impairment) improve sensitivity in people with alcohol use disorder. MRI showing symmetric T2/FLAIR or DWI change in the medial thalami, mammillary bodies and periaqueductal region supports it but a normal scan does not exclude it. Blood thiamine (or transketolase) levels can be drawn but treatment must not wait for the result. Exclude hypoglycaemia, hepatic encephalopathy, intoxication, posterior circulation stroke and Miller Fisher syndrome.
det.treatment: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately — commonly 500 mg IV three times daily for several days, then lower doses — before or together with glucose. Correct magnesium, which is needed for thiamine-dependent enzymes. Give prophylactic parenteral thiamine to at-risk patients (alcohol withdrawal, hyperemesis, refeeding). After the acute phase, continue oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol treatment.
det.prognosis: Eye signs often improve within hours to days and ataxia over weeks, but memory deficits frequently persist; untreated, mortality is substantial.
pearls: Treat on suspicion: thiamine is cheap and safe, missed WE is devastating.
Low magnesium can make thiamine therapy ineffective.
Think of WE after bariatric surgery or hyperemesis, not only in alcohol use.

name: West syndrome
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy in infancy with infantile spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
simple: A serious infant epilepsy with clusters of spasms and developmental regression.
more: EEG shows hypsarrhythmia; MRI and metabolic and genetic work-up should be done urgently (tuberous sclerosis, ARX, CDKL5). First-line treatment is ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin, especially in tuberous sclerosis.

name: Westphal Huntington’s disease (rigid
formal: Rigid variant of juvenile Huntington disease with CAG repeat expansion, bradykinesia and dystonia.
simple: The stiff form of Huntington disease, mostly beginning in childhood.

name: West’s syndrome (infantile spasms)
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy in infancy with infantile spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
simple: A serious infant epilepsy with clusters of spasms and developmental regression.

name: Whipple’s disease
formal: Tropheryma whipplei infection with arthralgia, diarrhoea and CNS involvement including oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: A rare bacterial infection of the gut that can affect the brain, causing memory loss and eye movement problems.

name: White matter disorders
formal: Disorders affecting cerebral white matter, such as leukodystrophies, MS and small vessel disease.
simple: Diseases that damage the brain's wiring.

name: Wilson’s disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation causing copper accumulation, with hepatic disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings, tremor, dystonia and psychiatric symptoms.
simple: An inherited disorder where copper builds up in the liver and brain, causing tremor and mood changes.
more: Diagnosis by low serum caeruloplasmin and high 24-hour urinary copper, with slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings and MRI showing face of the giant panda sign; ATP7B genotyping. Treat with chelators (penicillamine, trientine) or zinc.

case.story: Declining grades, emotional lability and slurred speech over 6 months; mild jaundice last year.
case.exam: Coarse proximal arm tremor when arms are held forwards, dystonic smile, golden-brown corneal ring.
case.tests: Caeruloplasmin 0.08 g/L, urinary copper raised; ATP7B variants.
case.q: Why is this diagnosis urgent?
case.a: It is treatable with chelation/zinc; delay leads to irreversible neurological and hepatic damage.

ddx.pt: Chorea, family history, normal copper studies
No liver disease or KF rings; genetic parkinsonism
Eye-of-the-tiger sign, normal copper

det.patho: Biallelic mutations in ATP7B impair copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile, so copper builds up in the liver and spills into the blood, brain, cornea and kidneys. Free copper drives oxidative injury, especially in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. It is autosomal recessive with a prevalence near 1 in 30,000.
det.clinical: Hepatic presentations (asymptomatic transaminase rise, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure with haemolysis) dominate in childhood, whereas neurological or psychiatric presentations usually start in the teens to 30s. Neurological forms include a coarse proximal 'wing-beating' tremor, dystonia with a fixed open-mouth smile, parkinsonism, ataxia, dysarthria and drooling. Psychiatric changes — mood disorder, impulsivity, falling school performance or psychosis — may precede motor signs. Kayser–Fleischer rings are present in about 95% of neurological cases but are often absent in purely hepatic disease.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical signs with copper studies: low caeruloplasmin (below about 0.1 g/L is strongly suggestive), raised 24-hour urinary copper, and slit-lamp examination for KF rings. The Leipzig score integrates these with liver copper content and ATP7B genotyping. MRI often shows symmetric T2 change in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. Pitfalls: caeruloplasmin can be falsely normal during inflammation and low in heterozygotes, protein loss or malnutrition. Screen all first-degree relatives.
det.treatment: Lifelong decoppering therapy is required: chelators (D-penicillamine or trientine) for symptomatic disease, and zinc salts (which block intestinal copper absorption) for maintenance or presymptomatic cases. Introduce chelators gradually, because neurological worsening can occur early in treatment, especially with penicillamine. Avoid copper-rich foods such as shellfish, nuts, chocolate and liver early on. Monitor urinary copper, blood count and renal function; liver transplantation is curative for fulminant failure or decompensated cirrhosis.
det.prognosis: With early, adherent treatment survival approaches normal and many neurological signs improve over 1–3 years; stopping therapy can be fatal.
pearls: Any unexplained movement disorder or liver disease before age 40 deserves copper studies.
Neurological Wilson disease without KF rings is unusual — look with a slit lamp, not just a penlight.
Early paradoxical worsening on chelation is a known hazard; start low and titrate.
det.thd: Wilson's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากยีน ATP7B ทำให้ขับทองแดงทางน้ำดีไม่ได้ ทองแดงจึงสะสมในตับ สมอง และกระจกตา อาการทางสมองพบในวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น เช่น สั่นแบบกระพือปีก dystonia พูดไม่ชัด และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน มักมี Kayser–Fleischer ring การวินิจฉัยใช้ caeruloplasmin ต่ำ ทองแดงในปัสสาวะ 24 ชั่วโมงสูง ร่วมกับตรวจตาและยีน รักษาตลอดชีวิตด้วย chelator หรือ zinc ถ้ารักษาเร็วผลดีมาก

name: Wilson’s disesae
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation causing copper accumulation, with hepatic disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings, tremor, dystonia and psychiatric symptoms.
simple: An inherited disorder where copper builds up in the liver and brain, causing tremor and mood changes.

name: Woodhouse Sakati syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder with hypogonadism, alopecia, diabetes, intellectual disability and extrapyramidal features.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing hormonal problems, hair loss and movement problems.

name: Writer’s and craft cramps
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia triggered by particular activities such as writing or craft work.
simple: Hand cramps and twisting that appear when doing a particular activity such as writing.

name: Writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia with cramping during writing.
simple: Hand cramping that occurs only while writing.

name: Writing tremor
formal: Task-specific tremor occurring during writing, a variant of essential tremor.
simple: Hand shaking that occurs when writing.

name: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy
formal: X-linked ABCD1 peroxisomal disorder with very long chain fatty acid accumulation, cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency or adrenomyeloneuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease affecting the brain wiring and adrenal glands, mostly in males.

name: X-linked ataxia syndromes
formal: Group of hereditary ataxias with X-linked inheritance, including fragile X tremor ataxia syndrome.
simple: Inherited balance disorders passed through the X chromosome.

name: X-linked CMT disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy from GJB1 (connexin 32) variants, with intermediate conduction velocities, male-predominant distal weakness and milder disease in female carriers.
simple: An inherited nerve disease passed on the X chromosome that causes weak, wasted feet and hands, usually worse in men.
more: Diagnosis by nerve conduction and GJB1 testing; transient central nervous system episodes can occur. Treatment is supportive with orthoses, physiotherapy and surgery for deformity.

name: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag)
formal: Lubag: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism in Filipino men, TAF1 haplotype, with focal dystonia progressing to parkinsonism.
simple: An inherited movement disorder in men of Filipino descent causing dystonia then parkinsonism.

name: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy (XMEA)
formal: X-linked vacuolar myopathy from VMA21 variants causing slowly progressive proximal weakness in boys, with autophagic vacuoles and sparing of cardiac muscle.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in boys causing slowly worsening weakness in the hips and thighs.
more: CK is mild to moderately raised; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features. Treatment is supportive, and many remain ambulant into adulthood.
nN: x linked myopathy with excessive autophagy xmea
aN: xmea | x linked myopathy with excessive autophagy

name: Xp21 dystrophies
formal: Dystrophinopathies (Duchenne and Becker) arising from DMD gene on Xp21, with progressive proximal weakness and cardiomyopathy.
simple: Inherited muscle wasting diseases, mostly boys, from changes in the dystrophin gene.

name: Yellow star thistle poisoning in horses
formal: Equine nigropallidal encephalomalacia from ingestion of Centaurea solstitialis, causing necrosis of globus pallidus and substantia nigra with dystonia, dysphagia and abnormal chewing; a veterinary toxic parkinsonism model.
simple: A poisoning of horses from eating a weed that damages deep brain areas, causing stiff face muscles and trouble eating.
nN: yellow star thistle poisoning in horses

name: Zebra body myopathy
formal: Rare congenital or early-onset myopathy with distinctive zebra-striped subsarcolemmal inclusions on electron microscopy, with proximal weakness and hypotonia; genetics heterogeneous, ACTA1 linked in some.
simple: A rare muscle disease in which muscle samples under the electron microscope show zebra-like stripes, causing weakness.
more: Diagnosis relies on biopsy ultrastructure and gene testing. Care is supportive including respiratory monitoring; course varies from mild to severe.

name: Zinc deficiency
formal: Deficiency that can cause neuropathy, myelopathy or, via copper deficiency, ataxia; excess zinc causes copper deficiency myeloneuropathy.
simple: Low zinc can contribute to nerve and taste problems.

name: Zoster-associated encephalitis
formal: Encephalitis complicating VZV reactivation, with headache, fever, confusion and vasculopathy, mostly in immunosuppressed patients.
simple: Brain infection after shingles virus reactivates, causing confusion and fever.

name: Α-synucleinopathy
formal: Group of neurodegenerative diseases with pathological aggregates of alpha-synuclein, including Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.
simple: A group of brain diseases caused by build-up of an abnormal protein called alpha-synuclein.
more: Diagnosis is clinical with biomarkers such as DaT scan and skin or CSF seed assays. Treatment is symptomatic and disease-modifying therapy remains under study.

name: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune encephalitis caused by IgG antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor, producing psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, decreased consciousness and autonomic instability; associated with ovarian teratoma in young women.
simple: An immune attack on brain receptors, often in young women, that starts with strange behaviour or psychosis and progresses to seizures, abnormal movements and reduced consciousness; it is treatable.
th: สมองอักเสบจากภูมิต้านทานต่อตัวรับ NMDA — เริ่มด้วยพฤติกรรมแปลก ประสาทหลอน แล้วชัก ปากขยับเอง ซึมลง พบร่วมกับเนื้องอกรังไข่
feat: Prodromal fever/headache, then psychosis, agitation, insomnia
Seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesia, catatonia
Reduced consciousness, central hypoventilation, autonomic instability
Ovarian teratoma in young women
inv: CSF NMDAR antibodies (more sensitive than serum); CSF pleocytosis
EEG: extreme delta brush
Pelvic ultrasound/MRI for teratoma

case.story: After a flu-like illness she became paranoid and sleepless and was admitted to psychiatry; then had a seizure and grimacing mouth movements.
case.exam: Fluctuating consciousness, orofacial dyskinesia, labile BP and pulse.
case.tests: CSF WBC 30 (lymphocytes), NMDAR antibody positive; pelvic MRI: ovarian teratoma.
case.q: What are the first treatment steps?
case.a: Tumour removal plus first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange); rituximab/cyclophosphamide if no response.

ddx.pt: Fever, temporal necrosis on MRI, HSV PCR positive
Rigidity and fever after antipsychotic, high CK, no CSF inflammation

aN: anti nmdar encephalitis | nmda encephalitis | nmdar | autoimmune encephalitis nmda

det.patho: IgG antibodies to the GluN1 subunit cross-link NMDA receptors and cause their internalisation, reducing glutamatergic signalling without much neuronal death, which explains the potential for full recovery. Triggers include ovarian teratomas containing neural tissue and prior HSV encephalitis; many cases have no identifiable trigger. Among autoimmune encephalitides it ranks as one of the most frequent, mainly in children and young women.
det.clinical: A viral-like prodrome is followed by psychiatric symptoms — anxiety, insomnia, agitation, bizarre behaviour, psychosis or catatonia — and then by memory loss, speech reduction, seizures and abnormal movements, especially orofacial and limb dyskinesias. Later stages bring decreased consciousness, autonomic instability (tachy- or bradycardia, labile BP, hyperthermia) and central hypoventilation needing ventilation. Children more often present with seizures or movement disorders; men less often have a tumour. Many patients are first admitted to psychiatry.
det.diagnosis: Test for GluN1 IgG in CSF, which is more sensitive and specific than serum testing (serum can be falsely positive or negative). CSF often shows mild lymphocytosis and oligoclonal bands; MRI is normal in most or shows non-specific FLAIR change. EEG commonly shows diffuse slowing, and the extreme delta brush pattern is characteristic in severe cases. Search for a teratoma with pelvic ultrasound and MRI in women, and consider testicular imaging in men. The Graus criteria allow probable diagnosis and early treatment before antibody results.
det.treatment: First-line immunotherapy is high-dose IV methylprednisolone with IVIG (total 2 g/kg, split across 2–5 days) and/or plasma exchange, combined with prompt removal of any tumour. If there is no clear improvement in about two weeks, escalate to rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide; refractory cases may receive other agents within specialist care. Supportive ICU care for dysautonomia, hypoventilation and seizures is often prolonged. Antipsychotics can worsen dyskinesia and mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome — use them cautiously.
det.prognosis: About 80% of patients achieve good functional recovery, though it may take 1–2 years; relapses occur in around 10–15%, less often after tumour removal and second-line therapy.
pearls: A young woman with new psychosis plus seizures, dyskinesia or dysautonomia needs an LP and NMDAR antibodies.
Test CSF, not only serum.
Recovery is slow; long ICU stays are not a reason to stop aggressive treatment.
det.thd: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบจากภูมิต้านทานต่อ GluN1 ของตัวรับ NMDA พบในวัยรุ่นและหญิงสาว อาจสัมพันธ์กับ ovarian teratoma หรือเกิดตามหลัง HSE อาการเริ่มด้วยไข้คล้ายหวัด แล้วมีพฤติกรรมแปลก โรคจิต นอนไม่หลับ ต่อด้วยชัก ปากและแขนขาขยับเอง ซึมลง ความดันชีพจรแปรปรวน วินิจฉัยด้วยแอนติบอดีในน้ำไขสันหลัง EEG อาจเห็น extreme delta brush รักษาด้วยการตัดเนื้องอกร่วมกับ steroid, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวดีแต่ใช้เวลานาน

name: Spinal cord compression
formal: Compression of the spinal cord by extrinsic lesions — metastatic tumour, disc or spondylosis, epidural abscess or haematoma — producing back pain, myelopathic weakness, a sensory level and sphincter dysfunction; a neurosurgical emergency.
simple: Something (often cancer, a slipped disc or an abscess) presses on the spinal cord, causing back pain, leg weakness, numbness from a certain level downwards and bladder trouble; it needs urgent treatment.
th: ไขสันหลังถูกกดทับ — ปวดหลัง ขาอ่อนแรง ชาจากระดับหนึ่งลงไป ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน
feat: Back or neck pain (often preceding weakness), worse lying flat or with cough
UMN weakness below the level, sensory level, sphincter disturbance
Root pain/LMN signs at the level of compression
Red flags: cancer history, fever/IV drug use, anticoagulation
inv: Urgent MRI whole spine
Dexamethasone for malignant compression; cultures for abscess

case.story: Six weeks of mid-back pain, worse at night; now 2 days of leg weakness and hesitancy of urine.
case.exam: Tender T9 spine, legs 4/5, sensory level T10, extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI: T9 vertebral metastasis with epidural extension.
case.q: What are the immediate management steps?
case.a: High-dose dexamethasone and urgent oncological/neurosurgical review for decompression and/or radiotherapy.

ddx.pt: Intrinsic cord inflammation without compression
Areflexia without sensory level
LMN pattern, saddle anaesthesia, areflexia

aN: cord compression | mscc | metastatic spinal cord compression | compressive myelopathy | epidural abscess | cervical spondylotic myelopathy

det.patho: Extrinsic pressure compromises cord tissue directly and through venous congestion and ischaemia, producing oedema and eventually infarction if not relieved. Malignant compression arises mostly from vertebral body metastases (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma, lymphoma) and is most common in the thoracic spine. Other causes include degenerative cervical myelopathy, disc herniation, epidural abscess (diabetes, IV drug use, bacteraemia, spinal procedures), epidural haematoma (anticoagulation) and trauma.
det.clinical: Back or neck pain usually comes first, often worse at night, lying flat or with coughing, and may radiate in a band (radicular pain). Weakness, numbness below a level, gait ataxia and later urinary retention and constipation follow; once a patient is non-ambulant, recovery is much less likely. Cervical spondylotic myelopathy evolves slowly with clumsy hands, Hoffmann sign and spastic gait. Fever and raised inflammatory markers suggest abscess; sudden onset on anticoagulation suggests haematoma.
det.diagnosis: Obtain MRI of the whole spine as an emergency (within 24 hours, sooner if neurological deficit), because multiple levels are often involved. Use CT myelography if MRI is contraindicated. Investigate the cause: blood cultures and inflammatory markers for abscess, coagulation studies for haematoma, and staging or biopsy when malignancy is new. Examine sensory level and perineal sensation, and measure post-void residual volume.
det.treatment: For malignant compression give dexamethasone (commonly 16 mg/day in divided doses with gastric protection) and arrange urgent oncology and spine surgery review; decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy benefits selected patients with good prognosis, while radiotherapy alone suits others. Epidural abscess needs IV antibiotics and usually surgical drainage; haematoma needs reversal of anticoagulation and evacuation. Degenerative myelopathy with progressive deficit is treated by surgical decompression. Pain control, bladder care, VTE prophylaxis and rehabilitation are integral.
det.prognosis: Functional outcome mirrors the neurological state at treatment: most patients walking at diagnosis remain ambulant, whereas few paraplegic patients regain walking.
pearls: New back pain in a patient with cancer deserves early MRI before weakness develops.
Image the whole spine — skip lesions are common in metastatic disease.
Fever plus back pain plus neurological signs = epidural abscess until proven otherwise.
det.thd: ไขสันหลังถูกกดทับเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน สาเหตุสำคัญคือมะเร็งแพร่กระจายไปกระดูกสันหลัง หมอนรองกระดูก กระดูกเสื่อม ฝีหรือเลือดออกในช่อง epidural อาการมักเริ่มด้วยปวดหลังตอนกลางคืนหรือนอนราบ แล้วขาอ่อนแรง ชาจากระดับหนึ่งลงไป ปัสสาวะไม่ออก ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังโดยเร็ว ถ้าเป็นจากมะเร็งให้ dexamethasone และปรึกษาศัลยกรรมกับรังสีรักษาทันที ฝีต้องให้ยาปฏิชีวนะและระบายหนอง ผลการรักษาขึ้นกับว่ายังเดินได้หรือไม่ตอนเริ่มรักษา

name: Migraine with aura
formal: Migraine in which attacks are preceded or accompanied by fully reversible focal neurological symptoms — usually visual, sometimes sensory or speech — that develop gradually and spread over at least 5 minutes and last up to an hour.
simple: Migraine with warning symptoms such as zigzag lights or spreading tingling that build up slowly over minutes before or during the headache, then go away completely.
th: ไมเกรนที่มีอาการนำ — เห็นแสงหยัก ๆ หรือชาลามช้า ๆ 5–60 นาที แล้วตามด้วยปวดศีรษะ
feat: Positive phenomena (scintillations, tingling) that march slowly, then negative after-effects
Successive aura symptoms occur one after another, not all at once
Headache usually follows within 60 minutes
inv: Clinical; image if aura is atypical (sudden, motor, prolonged, first after 50)

case.story: A shimmering zigzag crescent grew from the centre of her vision toward the right over 20 minutes; as it faded, tingling crept from her right fingers to her lips, then a throbbing left headache with nausea began.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and fundi between attacks.
case.tests: None needed; she has had four similar episodes since her teens.
case.q: Which feature of the timing argues most strongly against a TIA?
case.a: The gradual spread of symptoms over minutes, with one symptom following another — ischaemia causes deficits that are maximal at onset.

ddx.pt: Sudden negative symptoms that reach maximum at once
Faster spread (seconds), brief, may have motor jerking
Older patient, spreading episodes from cortical siderosis

aN: classic migraine | migraine aura | visual aura | scintillating scotoma | fortification spectra

det.patho: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depolarisation, a slowly propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation (about 3 mm per minute) followed by suppressed activity; this explains the gradual march of symptoms. Activation of the trigeminovascular system with release of CGRP generates the headache. Migraine with aura carries a small increase in ischaemic stroke risk, amplified by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraceptives.
det.clinical: Visual aura is most common — a scintillating zigzag or scotoma expanding across the visual field over minutes — followed by sensory aura (tingling spreading up the hand to the face) and less often speech disturbance.
