det.patho: Brief focal ischaemia of brain, retina or cord that resolves before infarction develops; the modern definition is tissue-based, so a DWI lesion makes it a minor stroke whatever the duration. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: artery-to-artery embolism from carotid plaque, cardioembolism, small vessel disease and low-flow states distal to a tight stenosis.
det.clinical: Most episodes last minutes and begin suddenly with negative symptoms: weakness, numbness, loss of speech or monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax). Repeated stereotyped events, especially limb-shaking, suggest critical carotid stenosis with haemodynamic failure. Isolated dizziness, syncope, confusion or amnesia are rarely TIA. Crescendo TIAs signal an unstable lesion and need same-day assessment. The stroke risk after TIA is front-loaded, highest within 48 hours.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the history, ideally from a witness. Every patient needs urgent brain MRI with DWI, vessel imaging of the neck (duplex, CTA or MRA), ECG with prolonged rhythm monitoring, glucose, lipids and HbA1c. Scores such as ABCD2 are less useful than imaging and vessel findings for triage. Exclude migraine aura, focal seizures, hypoglycaemia and transient global amnesia.
det.treatment: Start antithrombotic treatment immediately: for minor non-cardioembolic events, short-term dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 21 days) then single agent. Anticoagulate if AF is found. Add a high-intensity statin, BP control, diabetes management and smoking cessation. Symptomatic 50–99% carotid stenosis should be revascularised, preferably within 2 weeks.
det.prognosis: With rapid specialist assessment and treatment the early stroke risk falls by most of its magnitude; without it, roughly one in ten patients have a stroke within 3 months.
pearls: Duration does not define TIA; a DWI lesion upgrades it to minor stroke.
Amaurosis fugax is a carotid TIA — image the neck vessels urgently.
Limb-shaking TIA mimics seizure but reflects severe carotid stenosis.
det.thd: TIA คือสมองหรือจอประสาทตาขาดเลือดชั่วคราว อาการหายเองโดยไม่มีเนื้อสมองตายใน MRI (ถ้าพบรอยโรคใน DWI ถือเป็น minor stroke) อาการมักเป็นแบบ negative เกิดทันทีและหายในไม่กี่นาที เช่น ตามัวข้างเดียว ต้องตรวจ MRI, หลอดเลือดที่คอ และ ECG ด่วน เพราะเสี่ยง stroke สูงที่สุดใน 48 ชั่วโมงแรก รักษาด้วย antiplatelet คู่ระยะสั้น statin คุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง และผ่าตัดหรือใส่ stent หลอดเลือดแดง carotid ที่ตีบมากภายใน 2 สัปดาห์

name: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT)
formal: Thrombosis of the dural venous sinuses and/or cortical veins causing raised venous pressure, headache, papilloedema, seizures, venous infarction or haemorrhage; associated with prothrombotic states, pregnancy, oral contraceptives and local infection.
simple: A clot in the veins that drain blood from the brain, causing headache, swelling, seizures or bleeding; more common in young women and around pregnancy.
th: หลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน — ปวดศีรษะ ชัก หรือมีเลือดออกในสมอง พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อย ระหว่างตั้งครรภ์หรือกินยาคุม
tempoNote: Headache evolving over days in most; may be thunderclap
feat: Progressive headache, often worse lying down, with papilloedema
Focal or generalised seizures
Bilateral or parasagittal deficits; haemorrhagic infarcts not obeying arterial territories
Risk factors: pregnancy/puerperium, oestrogen, thrombophilia, dehydration, ear/sinus infection
inv: CT/MR venography (empty delta sign, absent flow)
MRI with SWI for venous infarcts and cortical vein clot
Thrombophilia work-up after the acute phase

case.story: Five days of worsening headache, then a generalised seizure this morning.
case.exam: Drowsy, bilateral papilloedema, mild left leg weakness.
case.tests: CT: right parasagittal haemorrhagic lesion; CT venography: superior sagittal sinus filling defect.
case.q: Should she be anticoagulated despite the haemorrhage?
case.a: Yes — CVT is treated with anticoagulation even when there is a venous haemorrhagic infarct.

ddx.pt: Raised pressure with normal venography — always exclude CVT first
Thunderclap onset; arterial aneurysm, blood in basal cisterns
Hypertension/eclampsia with posterior vasogenic oedema and patent sinuses
Lesion obeys an arterial territory; no venous filling defect

aN: cvt | cerebral venous thrombosis | cvst | cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | sinus thrombosis | dural sinus thrombosis

det.patho: Clot in the dural sinuses or cortical veins impedes venous outflow, raising venous and intracranial pressure and reducing CSF absorption; local congestion produces vasogenic oedema, venous infarcts and haemorrhage. Most patients have at least one prothrombotic trigger — pregnancy and puerperium, oestrogen-containing contraception, inherited or acquired thrombophilia, cancer, dehydration, infection of the ear or sinuses, or vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia. Young women are most often affected.
det.clinical: Headache is present in about nine in ten, usually building over days, sometimes thunderclap or isolated intracranial hypertension. Other presentations are focal or generalised seizures, focal deficits that may be bilateral, and encephalopathy. Deep venous system thrombosis causes bithalamic lesions with drowsiness or coma. Cavernous sinus thrombosis gives proptosis, chemosis and painful ophthalmoplegia. The picture often fluctuates.
det.diagnosis: MR venography or CT venography shows the absent flow or filling defect; MRI with SWI/T2* displays thrombus in sinuses and cortical veins. Plain CT may show a dense sinus or cord sign but is often normal. D-dimer can be normal, especially with isolated headache or late presentation. Look for the underlying cause, including full blood count (platelets), infection, malignancy and thrombophilia testing timed appropriately.
det.treatment: Anticoagulate promptly with low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin even when haemorrhage is present. Switch to oral anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC, which trials suggest is similar) for 3–12 months, longer for persistent risk factors. Treat seizures, raised pressure and the trigger; stop oestrogen. Endovascular therapy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and decompressive craniectomy can be life-saving for large mass lesions. Vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia requires non-heparin anticoagulation and IVIG.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully or with minor deficits; poor outcome is linked to coma, deep venous involvement, haemorrhage and malignancy.
pearls: Haemorrhage is not a contraindication to heparin in CVT.
Always exclude CVT before labelling raised pressure as IIH.
Bilateral parasagittal haemorrhagic lesions = think superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
det.thd: ลิ่มเลือดอุดหลอดเลือดดำหรือ dural sinus ในสมอง ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูง สมองบวม และอาจมีเลือดออกแบบ venous infarct พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อย ตั้งครรภ์ หลังคลอด หรือกินยาคุม อาการคือปวดศีรษะที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง ชัก อ่อนแรง และ papilloedema วินิจฉัยด้วย MRV หรือ CTV การรักษาคือให้ heparin ทันทีแม้มีเลือดออก แล้วต่อด้วยยากินต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด 3–12 เดือน

name: Cervical artery dissection
formal: Tear in the wall of the carotid or vertebral artery producing an intramural haematoma, local pain and pressure signs, and thromboembolic stroke; a leading cause of stroke in young adults.
simple: A tear inside a neck artery that can cause neck pain or headache and a stroke, often after minor neck strain or trauma.
th: ผนังหลอดเลือดแดงที่คอฉีกขาด — ปวดคอ/ศีรษะข้างเดียว อาจมี Horner และ stroke ในคนอายุน้อย
feat: Unilateral neck, face or occipital pain preceding ischaemic symptoms
Painful partial Horner syndrome (carotid) or posterior circulation stroke (vertebral)
Lower cranial nerve palsies or pulsatile tinnitus may occur
inv: CTA or MRA of the neck; MRI fat-suppressed T1 shows crescent intramural haematoma

case.story: Left-sided neck pain after a chiropractic adjustment, then 2 days later clumsy speech and right hand weakness.
case.exam: Left ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis of the face, mild expressive dysphasia, right hand weakness.
case.tests: MRI: small left MCA infarcts; neck MRI: crescent of intramural blood in the left ICA.
case.q: Explain the Horner syndrome.
case.a: Sympathetic fibres travel on the internal carotid wall; the dissection injures them (third-order neuron), sparing facial sweating fibres that follow the external carotid.

ddx.pt: Atherosclerotic/cardioembolic stroke lacks preceding neck pain and Horner
Recurrent stereotyped aura; no vessel wall haematoma
Recurrent thunderclap headaches; multifocal intracranial narrowing

aN: carotid dissection | vertebral dissection | cervical artery dissection | cad | arterial dissection

det.patho: An intimal tear or rupture of the vasa vasorum creates an intramural haematoma that may narrow the lumen, expand outward as a pseudoaneurysm, or seed emboli — the commonest route to stroke. Triggers range from obvious trauma to trivial neck movements; connective tissue disorders, migraine and recent infection are associated. It accounts for a large share of strokes under 50.
det.clinical: Carotid dissection classically combines ipsilateral head, face or neck pain, a partial Horner syndrome and later hemispheric ischaemia; lower cranial nerve palsies (especially XII) and pulsatile tinnitus may appear. Vertebral dissection presents with posterior neck or occipital pain followed by lateral medullary, cerebellar or other posterior circulation stroke. Pain may precede ischaemia by hours to days, offering a window for prevention. Some cases are bilateral or multivessel.
det.diagnosis: CTA or contrast MRA shows tapering stenosis, occlusion, flame-shaped occlusion, pseudoaneurysm or intimal flap. Fat-saturated T1 MRI of the neck shows the crescent of intramural haematoma, though it may only become bright after a few days. Ultrasound can miss distal and vertebral lesions. Consider fibromuscular dysplasia and inherited connective tissue disease in recurrent or multivessel cases.
det.treatment: Ischaemic stroke from dissection is treated with IV thrombolysis and thrombectomy under the usual criteria. For secondary prevention, antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation performed similarly in trials; most centres use antiplatelets, reserving anticoagulation for selected cases such as recurrent events or occlusion with free-floating thrombus. Treat for 3–6 months then re-image. Endovascular stenting is reserved for recurrent ischaemia despite medical treatment. Avoid chiropractic manipulation and heavy straining during healing.
det.prognosis: Most dissections heal or recanalise within months, and recurrence is uncommon; outcome is set mainly by the initial stroke.
pearls: Neck pain + Horner + stroke in a young adult = carotid dissection.
The Horner is postganglionic, so facial sweating is largely preserved.
Vertebral dissection is a common cause of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome in the young.
det.thd: ผนังหลอดเลือดแดง carotid หรือ vertebral ที่คอฉีกขาดจนเกิดเลือดคั่งในผนัง ทำให้หลอดเลือดตีบหรือเกิดลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปอุดสมอง เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของ stroke ในคนอายุน้อยกว่า 50 ปี อาการคือปวดคอหรือศีรษะข้างเดียว ร่วมกับ Horner syndrome บางส่วน แล้วตามด้วยอาการ stroke วินิจฉัยด้วย CTA/MRA และ MRI คอแบบ fat-saturated T1 รักษาด้วย antiplatelet หรือ anticoagulant 3–6 เดือนแล้วตรวจซ้ำ

name: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
formal: A dose-related, mostly length-dependent sensory (sometimes motor or autonomic) neuropathy caused by neurotoxic anticancer drugs such as platinum agents, taxanes, vinca alkaloids, bortezomib and thalidomide.
simple: Nerve damage from cancer medicines that causes numbness, tingling or pain, usually starting in the fingers and toes.
th: ปลายประสาทอักเสบจากยาเคมีบำบัด — ชา เจ็บแปลบ ปลายมือปลายเท้า ขึ้นกับขนาดยาสะสม
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months of treatment; platinum damage may keep worsening for months after stopping (coasting)
feat: Symmetric stocking-glove numbness, tingling or burning that tracks cumulative dose
Oxaliplatin: cold-triggered acute paraesthesia of hands and mouth, jaw or throat tightness within hours of infusion
Cisplatin: pure sensory neuronopathy with loss of proprioception and ataxia
Vincristine: sensorimotor with foot drop, cramps, constipation, jaw pain; worse with CMT
Bortezomib/taxanes: painful small-fibre symptoms; possible autonomic features
inv: Clinical grading (e.g. CTCAE) at each cycle; quantitative sensory exam
NCS: reduced sensory amplitudes (axonal) — confirms and grades, but is not needed in typical cases
Exclude other causes: glucose/HbA1c, B12, thyroid, paraprotein, tumour infiltration or paraneoplastic disease

case.who: 58-year-old man with colon cancer on FOLFOX
case.story: Each infusion leaves his fingers tingling when he touches cold water; after 8 cycles numbness persists and he drops coins and buttons.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and joint position at toes and fingers, absent ankle jerks, positive Romberg; power normal.
case.tests: NCS: low sural and radial sensory amplitudes with normal motor responses; HbA1c and B12 normal.
case.q: What should the oncology team consider now?
case.a: Dose reduction, delay or stopping oxaliplatin, since persistent functional neuropathy usually outweighs further benefit; duloxetine can be tried for pain. Warn that symptoms may worsen for a few months after stopping.

det.patho: Most agents injure the dorsal root ganglion or distal axon. Platinum drugs accumulate in dorsal root ganglion neurons and damage DNA, giving a neuronopathy; taxanes and vinca alkaloids disturb microtubules and axonal transport; bortezomib affects proteasome function and mitochondria. Oxaliplatin's acute cold-induced symptoms reflect a transient sodium-channel effect on peripheral nerve excitability.
det.clinical: Sensory symptoms dominate and start distally, with risk increasing with cumulative dose, pre-existing neuropathy, diabetes and alcohol. Vincristine adds motor weakness, cranial nerve palsies and autonomic constipation, and can be severe in undiagnosed CMT1A. Cisplatin and oxaliplatin may show 'coasting' — progression for 2–6 months after the last dose. Ototoxicity accompanies cisplatin.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: a typical pattern arising during exposure to a known neurotoxic agent. NCS shows axonal sensory loss and helps when the picture is atypical. Rapid, asymmetric, motor-predominant or proximal deficits suggest something else, such as GBS/CIDP triggered during treatment, tumour infiltration, leptomeningeal disease or paraneoplastic syndromes.
det.treatment: The only proven preventive approach is modifying the dose or schedule. Avoid cold during oxaliplatin infusion. For established painful CIPN, duloxetine has the best evidence; gabapentinoids and tricyclics are used with weaker support. Physiotherapy, balance training, fall prevention and foot care are important.
det.prognosis: Taxane and bortezomib neuropathy often improve over months; platinum neuronopathy may be partly permanent.
pearls: Ask about family foot deformity before vincristine — CMT1A carriers can develop severe weakness.
Platinum neuropathy can worsen after the drug stops; do not mistake coasting for a new disease.
Duloxetine is the only agent with good trial support for painful CIPN.
det.thd: CIPN เป็นปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากยาเคมีบำบัด เช่น platinum, taxane, vincristine และ bortezomib อาการชาหรือเจ็บแปลบเริ่มที่ปลายนิ้วมือนิ้วเท้า และรุนแรงขึ้นตามขนาดยาสะสม oxaliplatin ทำให้ชาเมื่อโดนความเย็นหลังให้ยา การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติเป็นหลัก ควรตัดสาเหตุอื่น การรักษาสำคัญคือปรับขนาดหรือหยุดยา และใช้ duloxetine สำหรับอาการปวด

ddx.pt: Asymmetric, non-length-dependent, often precedes chemotherapy; anti-Hu positive
Long-standing diabetes; no relation to chemotherapy cycles
Low B12 with high MMA/homocysteine; may add myelopathy and anaemia

aN: cipn | chemotherapy neuropathy | oxaliplatin neuropathy | vincristine neuropathy | taxane neuropathy | bortezomib neuropathy

name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) toxicity neuropathy
formal: A sensory neuropathy or ganglionopathy caused by chronic high intake of pyridoxine, usually from supplements, producing distal or widespread numbness and sensory ataxia that improves after withdrawal.
simple: Too much vitamin B6 from pills can damage sensory nerves and cause numbness and unsteady walking.
th: ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสียจากกินวิตามินบี 6 ขนาดสูงนาน ๆ — ชาและเดินเซ หยุดวิตามินแล้วมักดีขึ้น
tempoNote: Weeks to years depending on dose; very large doses cause rapid ganglionopathy
feat: Numbness and tingling in feet and hands, sometimes face or trunk
Loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia and Romberg sign
Strength preserved; reflexes reduced or lost
History of B6-containing supplements, multivitamins, energy drinks or 'neuro' vitamin combinations
Lhermitte-like or burning symptoms in some
inv: Plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate (often markedly raised)
NCS: reduced or absent sensory amplitudes with normal motor studies
Exclude B12 deficiency, paraneoplastic and Sjögren ganglionopathy, diabetes

case.story: For 18 months has taken a vitamin B1-B6-B12 tablet three times daily for hand numbness, plus a separate B6 supplement; now her feet feel wooden and she sways in the shower.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and absent joint-position at toes, Romberg positive, absent ankle jerks, normal power.
case.tests: PLP 380 nmol/L (high); NCS shows low sural and median sensory amplitudes; B12 and HbA1c normal.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Stop all B6-containing products and recheck PLP; most improve over months. Review every supplement label — combination B-vitamin tablets are a common hidden source.

det.patho: Excess pyridoxine is toxic to dorsal root ganglion neurons, which lack a protective blood–nerve barrier. Very high doses (grams per day) cause an acute neuronopathy, while chronic intake of a few hundred milligrams daily, and sometimes much lower amounts over years, causes a length-dependent sensory axonopathy. Individual susceptibility varies.
det.clinical: Symptoms are purely sensory: distal numbness, paraesthesia, unsteady gait and clumsy hands. In severe cases sensory loss affects the face and trunk. Motor power is normal, which is an important clue. Many patients take B6 for carpal tunnel, premenstrual symptoms or 'nerve health', sometimes several products together.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about vitamins, energy drinks and over-the-counter combinations, as patients rarely volunteer them. Raised plasma PLP with a sensory axonal pattern on NCS supports the diagnosis. Rule out other ganglionopathies (Sjögren, anti-Hu, cisplatin) and B12 deficiency before attributing symptoms to B6.
det.treatment: Withdraw all sources of pyridoxine; no antidote exists. Provide balance and gait training, and symptomatic treatment for painful paraesthesia. Repeat PLP to confirm falling levels.
det.prognosis: Most improve over months after withdrawal, sometimes after a short worsening; severe neuronopathy may leave residual ataxia.
pearls: Ironically, B6 taken for neuropathy may be the cause of the neuropathy.
Pure sensory with normal strength: always take a supplement history.
Combination B1-B6-B12 tablets are widely used in Thailand; count the total daily B6.
det.thd: การกินวิตามินบี 6 ขนาดสูงเป็นเวลานานทำลายเซลล์ประสาทรับความรู้สึกใน dorsal root ganglion ทำให้ชาปลายมือปลายเท้าและเดินเซ แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ ตรวจพบระดับ PLP ในเลือดสูงและ NCS เป็น sensory neuropathy การรักษาคือหยุดวิตามินบี 6 ทุกแหล่ง รวมถึงวิตามินบีรวม ส่วนใหญ่อาการดีขึ้นในหลายเดือน

ddx.pt: Immune or paraneoplastic causes; no supplement history; may be asymmetric
Low B12 with myelopathy signs; responds to B12 rather than stopping B6
Diagnosis of exclusion with normal PLP and no toxic exposure

aN: vitamin b6 | pyridoxine toxicity neuropathy | vitamin b6 toxicity | pyridoxine intoxication | pyridoxine induced sensory neuropathy | b6 megadose neuropathy

name: HIV-associated distal sensory polyneuropathy
formal: A length-dependent, predominantly small-fibre axonal sensory neuropathy occurring in people with HIV, caused by the infection itself and historically by neurotoxic nucleoside antiretrovirals.
simple: Nerve damage in people with HIV that causes painful burning or numb feet.
th: ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสียในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV — ปวดแสบชาที่เท้าทั้งสองข้าง พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่มโรคประสาทจาก HIV
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years; antiretroviral toxic forms appeared weeks to months after starting the drug
feat: Symmetric burning, aching or electric pain in the soles and toes
Allodynia; patients avoid shoes or bedsheets touching the feet
Reduced pinprick and temperature distally, reduced or absent ankle jerks
Little or no weakness
Risk factors: older age, height, low nadir CD4, past stavudine/didanosine exposure, diabetes
inv: Clinical diagnosis; NCS may be normal (small fibre) or show low sural amplitudes
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density if NCS normal
Screen for other causes: glucose/HbA1c, B12, syphilis serology, TSH, alcohol, isoniazid without B6

case.who: 46-year-old man living with HIV for 15 years
case.story: Took a stavudine-based regimen early on; now on TDF/3TC/DTG with suppressed virus. Both feet burn at night and feel like walking on hot sand.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick to ankles, vibration slightly reduced at toes, absent ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: HbA1c 5.6%, B12 normal, VDRL non-reactive; NCS normal; skin biopsy shows reduced epidermal nerve fibre density.
case.q: Which neuropathic pain treatment has trial support in HIV neuropathy?
case.a: Evidence is weak overall; topical capsaicin 8% and smoked cannabis showed benefit in trials, while amitriptyline, gabapentin and pregabalin performed no better than placebo in several studies — though they are still often tried.

det.patho: HIV does not infect neurons directly; viral proteins (such as gp120) and activated macrophages in dorsal root ganglia and nerve trigger inflammatory and mitochondrial injury that causes distal axonal dying-back. 'd-drug' nucleoside analogues (stavudine, didanosine, zalcitabine) added mitochondrial DNA polymerase-gamma toxicity. With modern ART incidence has fallen, but prevalence remains significant among long-term survivors.
det.clinical: Pain and paraesthesia in the feet are the main complaints, with mild sensory signs on examination and preserved strength. Hands are affected only in advanced cases. Symptoms may worsen briefly after starting ART. Weakness, asymmetry or rapid progression point to other HIV-related neuropathies such as CIDP, mononeuritis multiplex or CMV polyradiculopathy.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, combining symptoms with distal sensory signs and reduced ankle reflexes in a person with HIV. NCS may show low sural amplitudes; skin biopsy confirms small fibre loss when NCS is normal. Exclude diabetes, B12 deficiency, syphilis, alcohol, isoniazid neuropathy without pyridoxine cover, and other neurotoxic drugs.
det.treatment: Keep the viral load suppressed and avoid neurotoxic antiretrovirals. Treat pain using a stepwise approach with topical agents (high-dose capsaicin patch, lidocaine), and trial of duloxetine, amitriptyline or gabapentinoids, accepting that evidence is limited. Address coexisting diabetes and nutrition, and give pyridoxine with isoniazid.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and persistent; pain may stabilise but nerve loss rarely reverses.
pearls: Always ask about isoniazid without pyridoxine in HIV patients with TB.
Weakness is not part of HIV-DSP — look for another cause.
Normal NCS does not rule out small fibre neuropathy.
det.thd: HIV-DSP เป็นโรคปลายประสาทที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV เกิดจากผลของเชื้อและยาต้านไวรัสรุ่นเก่า เช่น stavudine ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบชาที่ฝ่าเท้าสองข้าง กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก อาจต้องใช้ skin biopsy เมื่อ NCS ปกติ และต้องตัดเบาหวาน ขาด B12 ซิฟิลิส หรือ isoniazid ที่ไม่ได้ให้ B6 การรักษาคือคุมไวรัส หลีกเลี่ยงยาที่เป็นพิษต่อเส้นประสาท และรักษาอาการปวด

ddx.pt: Weakness and areflexia with demyelinating NCS and CSF pleocytosis
Raised HbA1c; can coexist and worsen symptoms
Low B12 with posterior column signs; treatable
